For anyone who wishes to get an impression of the Soviet view of modern Russian history this monumental film is a treasure. The story starts at the turn of the century (1900) in the yellowish sepia colours of old photographs which improves to black and white during the middle of the century and to full colour when the story approaches modern times (i.e. the 1960s).

The story focuses on a boy in a remote Siberian village, who is marked by the arrival and arrest of an anarchist during the czarist era. He later joins the Bolsheviks after the revolution and brings soviet communism to his village. His son, by the local beauty, fights the Germans during the Second World War. When he returns to the village, the oil industry takes off and we are treated to some Soviet economic idealism.

This film is long and slow, but utterly logic and very well made. It can be seen in three parts.

Harman and Isings 'Old Mill Pond' is a true masterpiece of the art of animation. The consummate skill and artistry that characterise this duos work is nowhere more in evidence than in this cartoon. It is a shame that so many people can see only offence in what is, and was always intended to be, a light hearted piece of entertainment that in no way sought to denigrate black people. If anything it is a tribute to the infectious humour and musicality of the black race. I have not been able to view this confection for many years as the 'race commissars' in England have deemed it too offensive to be shown in multi racial Britain. If anyone knows where I can obtain a copy I would dearly love to view this masterpiece again. I think those who routinely look for messages and intent that were never intended in these cartoons, which are, after all, sixty years old, should try to lighten up and remember that the world is a very different place today, but that does not mean that anyone has the right to censor what is viewable from the past.

I used this film in a religion class I was teaching. The golden fish is swimming happily in his bowl in an upper floor apartment. A young boy and his mother are away from home. The boy has been given money to buy milk. On the way home, he stops at carnival to play a game. Next to him stands a man in a black suit looking a little scary. The boy drops the bottle of milk. It breaks. The man in the black suit gives him money to replace the milk. This scene alternates with what is happening at home. A black cat climbs the fire escape and enters the apartment. He(?) discovers the fish bowl and watches it. The fish swims energetically and flips out of the bowl. By now, a bunch of teenagers in my class and I have fallen in love with the fish. The cat takes the fish in his mouth and we all hold our breath. The cat drops the fish into the bowl. The double story line includes the suspicious man in black and the suspicious black cat. Both inspire prejudice. Both are innocent. It was a great discussion starter in my class.

I was lucky enough to see the Cineteca di Bologna's flawless new restoration of an Italian silent print at the Tribeca Film Festival. I haven't seen the talkie version yet, but I think it's safe to assume the silent version is much more satisfying, since by all reports the dubbing is poorly done (Louise Brooks is clearly speaking English, so there's no way her lips could be matched.) I saw "Brother's Shadow" at the Tribeca Film Festival and found myself still thinking about it two days later. The story of a prodigal son (Scott Cohen) returning to his family's custom furniture business after a stint in jail, it offers all the necessary qualities of a solid drama--memorable characters; sharp, observant dialog; sensitive use of the camera by a filmmaker who thinks visually.

But more than that, it presents something that is all too rare at the multiplex these days: the uncompromising vision of a mature sensibility. The talent of director-screenwriter Todd S. Yellin seems to emerge full-blown, but we get the sense he (like his protagonist) has paid his dues. He knows how real people struggle in this world, and he knows how we yearn to see--or at least, to experience vicariously--success. Yet Yellin respects his audience too much to blow happy smoke up our rear ends. In the end, we see that Jake's triumph doesn't lie in commissions, or even in the esteem of his family, but in "the work" he couldn't abandon if he tried.

It's an essential theme in a world (and especially a movie industry) that can't rise above "the bottom line".

A childless couple (Brooke Adams, Jeff Hayenga) go to a doctor (James Karen) to try to conceive. It works but Adams slowly becomes aware that there's something seriously wrong with the baby...

Pretty interesting idea is thoroughly done in by a lousy script--the basic idea is OK but becomes screamingly predictable towards the end. I saw every "twist" coming. The direction is poor--he seems to have no idea how to shoot a basic scene. The production values are--to be nice--lousy. Very shabby. And, the gore scenes are too unpleasant (I almost turned it off when a pregnant woman started stabbing herself in the stomach) with lousy special effects. The film completely derails at the end when it becomes quite clear they had no idea HOW to end this film.

Some good acting makes it somewhat bearable. Adams, Hayenga and Karen are all good at their roles and kept me watching but that was about it. This film barely got released in 1991 and still remains unknown--it's easy to see why. I give it a 4.

Featuring a fascinating performance by Will Smith and a story that tugs at your heartstrings harder than a rock guitarist mid-solo, "Seven Pounds" races past the director's previous collaboration with the actor (The Pursuit of Happiness), a flick which I also loved. Remember Gabriele Muccino's name because some of his movies may skip by unnoticed if the actor attached to the project isn't quite so high-profile.

Too bad I figured out Will Smith's scheme early on, I put two and two together when he calls in his own suicide in the first scene and the scene when Rosario Dawson's character is introduced as having an incurable heart-disease.

However, I still think the writer/director made the right choice putting the bookends (bookends are the first and the last scene) in that way, it's the source of urgency and tension in the movie, finding out gradually how exactly a man can be driven to that ultimate sacrifice, and it was heartbreaking to see the relationship between Smith's and Dawson's character flourish and develop, knowing in the back of the mind always what was in store for these unlucky two.

With such a stellar cast and such an interesting premise, I was expecting a tremendous film; the problem is New York I Love You doesn't add up. It remains the sum of its parts. The film strongly resembles a high school or college project by a teenager convinced that her own intimate loves and melodramatic obsessions are as fascinating to us as to her. Perhaps if she hadn't cast herself it might have worked. She just can't act, whether playing herself or not. Pretentious, over-ambitious, dull, and silly.

Okay, I'll admit the casting in the film is REALLY strange--part of this is due to the plot, but I still had a bit of trouble believing Pierce Brosnan playing this lead (though he really did a pretty good job).

It's based on a true story of an Englishman who went to live with the Canadian Indians in the early 20th century. He claimed to be a mixed blood Indian. He was, in fact, so successful and well thought of that people came from all over to hear his lectures and be taken on his wilderness treks--even though he was not a mixed blood Indian and all his knowledge was from books or faked! The movie centers on this and what occurred when the hoax was uncovered.

The acting and settings were great and I really liked the film (once I suspended disbelief about Brosnan). It didn't get widespread distribution--probably because it was pretty cerebral--not a Bond film nor a romance--just a really odd film about a remarkable man.

If you like films about school bullies, brave children, hilarious toddlers and worm eating, then How to Eat Fried Worms will appeal to you.

The film is about a boy named Billy, who when arriving on his first day at a new school, discovers that some of his classmates have played a prank on him by putting worms into his lunch. The school bully, Joe and his "team" of friends start teasing Billy and calling him "worm boy".

Billy decides to play along by saying that "he eats worms all the time". Joe and his friends don't believe him but Billy assures them and bets Joe that he can eat ten worms in one day otherwise he will come to school with worms in his pants.

The boys take Billy up on his bet, leaving the weak stomached child with a mission to gain respect from his classmates by eating worms cooked, fried, or alive.

The film may sound gross but there are a lot of messages in it. For one, it portrays true friendship and how to accept people for who they are. It also shows you why some bullies resort to bullying other children.

"Dressed To Kill", is one of the best thrillers ever made. Its dealings with sex and violence make this a film for adults. Brian De Palma, once again, proves why no other director can match his use of the camera to tell a story. He directs many scenes without dialog, and he tells much of his story, strictly through the use of his visuals, and Pino Donnagio's brilliant score. Filmed in Panavision, the film MUST be seen in widescreen, as De Palma uses the entire width of the film to tell his story. Cropped, on video, "Dressed To Kill", is barely the same movie. Solid performances from its cast, superb direction, and, perhaps, the finest film score ever written, make "Dressed To Kill" a must see.

The US State Dept. would not like us to see this movie, because they have a beef with the Iranian govt. However, it shows us just how civilized Iran really is, despite the content of the film, which centers on the struggle of women there for equal rights in the simplest of terms: the ability to watch a soccer game at the stadium, which is strictly limited to male audiences alone. The film is hilariously funny, and in and of itself is proof of freedom of speech and expression in Iran. I enjoyed this movie intensely. Five girls try to penetrate the police border at the ticket gates to a soccer match between Iran and Bahrain. The ensuing comedy is too funny to describe, from the bus trip to the stadium, to the interceding of the police and subsequent detention of the girls, to the resulting end. Don't miss this classic film. Its a MUST see. One of the best foreign films I've seen in years.

This film is fantastic. The storyline stays very true to the classic book by Mark Twain. It begins with a charming scene where Hank sings a song called "When You Stub Your Toe on the Moon" with a group of children. The tune evokes Sinatra's "High Hopes," and is both fun and uplifting. The music throughout the movie is exceptional, with my favorite number performed by the King, Hank (Bing Crosby), alongside Sir "Saggy" Sagamore. Overall, it's an excellent family film or even a delightful choice for a date night. It's a movie I can watch again and again. Rhonda Fleming's portrayal of the princess is stunning. I absolutely love this film! If you enjoyed Danny Kaye in "The Court Jester," you'll surely enjoy this movie as well.

George P. Cosmatos' "Rambo: First Blood Part II" is essentially a fantasy of redemption. The reality of the Vietnam War was that the United States did not emerge victorious, leaving behind immense destruction and trauma that are often glossed over in this film. Instead, it perpetuates the myth of noble American soldiers fighting against a corrupt leadership that orchestrated the conflict. Rambo's character exemplifies this perspective: fiercely patriotic, he laments that ordinary Americans fail to recognize and honor the heroism of individual soldiers, yet he harbors deep suspicion toward commanders and politicians. Like other war-promoting movies such as "We Were Soldiers," this film sidesteps the complex, nuanced reasons behind the US involvement in Southeast Asia, ignoring the broader political and moral debates. It also neglects to explore the individual motivations of each soldier present. Instead, Rambo becomes a symbol of collective national suffering, seeking vengeance for a wounded nation. A more honest approach might have been to address how to confront and heal from these painful memories rather than suppress them. As for whether victory is achieved this time—yes, it is.

In attempting to foster audience sympathy for Jake Roedel (Tobey Maguire), the filmmakers cast the North and the Jayhawkers in a negative light. Missouri never seceded from the Union, and the Union Army was not an invading force. The Southerners were fighting for state's rights—the right to own slaves, to elect corrupt legislatures and judges, and to maintain a political spoils system. There is nothing noble in these causes. Missourians could have easily moved eastward to join the Confederate Army.  
It seems to me that the story is not about ambiguity. When Jake leaves the Bushwhackers, it is not because he recognizes the error of his ways, nor because he is driven by a moral commitment to abolition.

Yes, I understand—you're bubbling with anticipation. However, *The Secret Lives of Dentists* won't surprise you: it's competently crafted but largely uninspired, honest yet monotonous. It tells the story of a married couple who are both dentists sharing a practice—already a setup for trouble; without our separate work lives, many of us might simply abandon our partners out of frustration. Campbell Scott, whose mustache and demeanor evoke Ned Flanders from *The Simpsons* rather than the average guy, plays the mild-mannered, over-the-top dad husband. Hope Davis portrays the bored housewife who vents her frustrations through amateur opera singing. One evening, while the husband and their daughters attend one of her performances, he stumbles upon something more revealing: he sees his wife kissing and flirting with the opera's director. An interesting detail—his face remains unseen, maintaining some mystery. Faced with the prospect of filing for separation, divorce, and custody—costly and often lucrative for lawyers—Scott opts to ignore his wife’s infidelity, pretending he’s unaware.  

Already, the more discerning viewers might feel their interest waning: yet another tale of the Pathetic, Sniveling Little Cuckold. But...

Although this film's style isn't as subtle and authentic as a sound version might have been, it remains a highly commendable movie. In fact, during its release, it was regarded as an excellent film and was even nominated for the inaugural Best Picture Oscar (which went to WINGS). While I personally believe WINGS is the superior film, this one stands out as quite good, despite some overacting by the lead, Emil Jannings.

Jannings plays a general from Czarist Russia who is spending his last days earning a few dollars as a Hollywood extra in the 1920s. His fortunes seem to change when he receives a casting call to portray an Imperial Russian general fighting against the Communists during the revolution. This role isn't much of a stretch for him, but it also prompts the old man to reflect on his past and the revolutionary times.

I’ll leave the specifics of what happens next to your imagination, but I can assure you it's a fairly good film—especially towards the conclusion. Oh, and keep an eye out for William Powell, who appears as the Russian director. Despite being made in 1928, his makeup makes him look nearly as aged as he did in many of his later works.

I would rate this film a 7 out of 10, as the villains were compelling in their roles and the mysterious Batwoman added an engaging "whodunit" element. However, the movie could have benefited from more Robin; he only appeared at the start and sporadically afterward. I’ve always felt that the new animated series didn’t do justice to the innovative Robin character, let alone Nightwing, and this film continues that unfortunate trend. Additionally, too much focus is placed on Bruce Wayne and his romantic subplot, which would have been more tolerable if the romance felt more genuine. Nonetheless, it remains an enjoyable movie, especially for Batman enthusiasts, and I would recommend giving it a watch.

The film was truly terrible. The lead actor performed adequately, but the plot and overall story were completely rubbish and inaccurate. It could have been a sequel to almost anything else, as it bore little to no resemblance to Carlito's Way. Fans of the original should steer clear, as this movie offers no mention of Gail—he ends up with someone else—no references to Kleinfeld, and no explanation of how he was caught or ended up in jail. It attempted to mimic the original with flashbacks at the start, but honestly, I was tempted to give it zero stars. Regrettably, I had to rate it higher. This was a poor attempt to cash in on one of the best films of the 90s. Overall, I wasted about £6 and two hours of my life. Despite the action sequences, it was painfully slow, dull, and predictable. Any fans of Carlito's Way should definitely avoid this disaster.

Good grief, I can hardly find the words to express just how disastrous this film is. To be fair, I wasn't expecting much from the start. Let's face it, a PG-13 slasher movie is inherently limited—it's almost destined to lack the most thrilling slasher elements, so the absence of gore shouldn't have come as a surprise. However, what truly floored me was the sheer level of incompetence and clichés permeating every other aspect of the film.  

The protagonist is so utterly useless that you end up rooting for the villain. And here's the surprising part—she never undergoes any change, blatantly breaking the fundamental rule of screenwriting: character development. If you think she’ll have a change of heart and finally start fighting back by the end, you're in for a disappointment.  

Adding to the disappointment, the killer is arguably the most uninteresting—and unquestionably the least frightening—villain to ever appear in the genre. I'm not exaggerating when I say Dora the Explorer's villains are scarier than this one.  

Finally, all potential for tension or even gratuity is completely drained by the film’s overall ineptitude.

Home Room explores the aftermath of a Columbine-like high school shooting, shifting focus from the event itself to its impact on the survivors—highlighting their trauma, guilt, and denial. 

*Spoilers* The shooting is depicted as a given, with no footage of the actual event beyond an almost teenage SWAT team member reacting after shooting the high school shooter. The story centers on three main characters: a detective investigating the crime—where no suspects remain—and two teenage girls who survive the incident, portrayed by a youthful Erika Christensen and Busy Philipps.

These two girls, connected solely through the tragedy, are brought together, and the ensuing drama unfolds. 

At 24, Erika Christensen already demonstrates a dependable, nuanced acting style, familiar to viewers. Meanwhile, Busy Philipps, three years older and relatively unknown to me, impressed me profoundly with her intense dramatic presence and screen charisma—she embodied the role completely.

This film is powerful, resonating deeply through its intimate exploration of the delicate and evolving bond between two scarred young women.

This film kicks off with a wager between Edgar Allan Poe and a journalist: Poe bets that the man cannot spend a whole night in a haunted castle. Naturally, he can, but whether he emerges unscathed remains to be seen. The castle is filled with strange, seemingly out-of-place characters, including the enigmatic Barbara Steele, who exudes icy menace. The movie is quite peculiar in its presentation, alternating between French and English dialogue, perhaps to compensate for lost lines. Its atmosphere is dark and oppressive, with limited visibility beyond the flickering candlelight, creating a pervasive sense of dread and foreboding. The version released by Synapse is uncensored; I initially wondered what might have been cut from a 1964 film until I noticed the topless scene—likely the reason. Overall, the film is quite good, rendered in gloomy black and white, and Barbara Steele's performance is a significant highlight. I give it an 8 out of 10.

Last weekend, I picked up this 'zombie movie' from the bargain bin and decided to watch it with some friends, thinking it would be a low-budget imitation of "Land of the Dead."  

Boy, was I mistaken.  

It appears that they lavished most of their budget on the cover art, which is very misleading for fans of the zombie genre.  

We made it as far as when the zombie women come to life and hop into a car with some yuppie who’s out in the middle of nowhere, discussing business on his cell phone. They actually speak to him before one of the girls kills him. But once they started driving, I couldn’t keep up my suspension of disbelief.  

Some people claim this is a "so bad, it's good" movie, but they’re lying. I didn’t finish watching it, though I read a review claiming that the zombies somehow become police officers by the end, which honestly makes me glad I didn’t see it all the way through.  

This movie is even worse than "Zombiez." DO NOT WATCH!

The only reason I ended up seeing this film in the cinema was because it was a sneak preview; otherwise, I would never have bothered with this dreadful teenage slasher. Honestly, haven't we had enough of these? At least "Scream" and "Scary Movie" knew not to take themselves seriously! The story is painfully weak, and the acting is among the worst I've ever seen. Only Godzilla movies come close to matching this level of badness—those are the only films I could say compete with this one for the worst I've seen in theaters.

The plot is riddled with holes, and the characters are so similar that you can't tell who has been killed and who’s still alive—and frankly, you don't care. The only actress I recognized was Denise, and she was arguably the most talentless performer in this sorry excuse for a movie.

Avoid this film at all costs. I’d give it a 2 out of 10.

We have a typical family. Dad is a famous rapper, we have the rebellious teenage daughter, an adopted white kid, and a cute little one. Then there’s the careless housemaid—who’s had shows with housemaids like that? Do we have a chaotic version of The Brady Bunch? Yes! When it first aired, I thought it was really cool, mainly because I was young. The music, though, was pretty bad—the raps were terrible and overly G-rated. His songs were mostly about family, friends, and typical issues. The dad was like the "Danny from Full House" type—always giving advice but not a neat freak, since they had a housekeeper for that. Remember? The storylines generally involved Lil’ Romeo getting into some sort of trouble—or sometimes preteen drama. Yeah, that kind of stuff isn’t great, but it’s still a decent show for kids. However, Nickelodeon could do better.

When my sister said this movie was going to be good, I was skeptical at first, but I watched it and ended up finding it surprisingly funny. The plot centers around a quirky girl who travels to a small town where no one seems to like her. Her main goal is to attend her aunt’s reading of the will so she can leave, but nothing is that simple. The film is packed with hilarious humor, featuring a witch, a spellbook with recipes, a mentally challenged uncle, and a dog. By the end, you'll truly understand the meaning of the word “freak.” I definitely recommend rushing out to find this classic old movie. I hope you enjoy it! Overall, I’d give it a 9—I promise you’ll laugh, maybe scream, and possibly get a little offended.  

Love, yours truly: Dakota  
You can email me at dakota_loves_it@hotmail.com if you'd like!

I believe this film is truly remarkable, resonating deeply with the core of human emotion. The portrayal of love is profound and intense. I consider it Will's finest performance so far, complemented by excellent direction and skillful editing. The soundtrack was superb, and the creative use of flashbacks enhanced the storytelling. This is the kind of movie everyone should experience, and I hope viewers will find something truly meaningful in it. Overall, it’s an outstanding film. I also believe Hollywood should produce more movies that contain meaningful substance; even action films can tell heartfelt stories. I appreciated Will’s subtle approach to his role—his purpose and dedication are rare qualities. I recommend watching this either alone or with someone you care about deeply. For me, the world seemed to pause, and my entire focus was on the film. The outside chaos faded away temporarily, which was a refreshing feeling in these turbulent times. In a generation often focused on oneself, it was inspiring to see characters who genuinely care about others more than themselves.

Why is Colin Firth appearing in this pointless movie? Has he really run out of better options?  

The film itself is unclear about its core message—grief, exotic locations, ghosts, or simply a showcase for Mr. Darcy? It’s a confusing, jumbled mess.  

There seems to be an unwarranted assumption that Italy is inherently wonderful and that the Italian language has some intrinsic value, but ultimately, the girls just want to return to the U.S.  

There are pointless scenes set on the beach, in churches, and on busy roads, but the overall purpose or reason for caring about any of it remains elusive.  

There’s also an American woman in the film whose role isn’t clear; she mostly seems there to make superficial, inappropriate, and overly sentimental comments to the girl. Was the film trying to address paedophilia?  

Overall, it’s a terrible mess. I rated it a 2 instead of a 1 because it lacks the charm of a truly dreadful film.

Back in 1985, I came across this film (and I hesitate to even call it that) while channel surfing. I was in college at the time, accompanied by a high school friend whose hormones were running wild. From the start, I knew we were in for a letdown. The script was absurd—a bunch of older men hiring young guys to teach them how to pick up women—and the acting, aside from one actor, was poor. The jokes were pathetic. The female nudity sprinkled throughout kept my friend amused for a while, but even he lost interest after half an hour. Keep in mind—this was a teenage boy's experience! This was before the internet made nudity so easily accessible. We kept watching, hoping for something funny or interesting, but it never came. The only amusing thing about it was the studio's original ad campaign, which openly acknowledged the film's poor quality. One poster featured a fake review claiming, "This is the best movie I've seen this afternoon!" Grant Cramer, the lead, showed some talent and went on to build a career in the industry. Apart from that, it was a low-budget, dull T&A flick. Just skip it.

It's easy to overlook, in hindsight, how earlier episodes of The X-Files occasionally explored the alien conspiracy storylines with more nuance, producing episodes like "GenderBender" and "Fearful Symmetry." These episodes depicted aliens not as mere little gray men or mind-control goo but as entities capable of genuine surprises. 

"Fearful Symmetry" opens with an "invisible elephant"—actually a dislocated elephant in space and time, situated just near "The Walk"—and culminates with the kidnapping of a pregnant gorilla. The episode is filled with memorable moments that shine brightly. Its subplot, though somewhat preachy—highlighting the ethics of zoos—still offers intriguing, visually striking, and thought-provoking ideas. It addresses a rarely considered aspect of abduction: why would humans be the sole focus of alien interest?

While it may not be an instant classic, it remains an enjoyable and memorable episode. It’s also something you wouldn’t expect many other shows to attempt, making it uniquely noteworthy in the series.

"Grey Gardens" (1975) is an eccentric documentary by the Maysles brothers that chronicles the strange life of Jackie Bouvier Kennedy Onassis's eccentric aunt and first cousin. They reside in a dilapidated 28-room mansion on East Hampton, Long Island, living in apparent squalor. 'Big Edie' Bouvier Beale, age 78, is witty and dry, while her daughter, 'Little Edie' Beale, age 56—though emotionally around 13—remains a striking woman who once had a promising future. They live in almost complete isolation, surrounded only by their numerous cats and raccoons that inhabit the attic. Their days are spent bickering, listening to the radio, or singing to each other—remarkably, they do not own a television. Their dramatic fall from high society is both astonishing and compelling, drawing viewers into the world of these uniquely peculiar yet undeniably captivating individuals. Considered one of the greatest documentaries ever made, it remains a cult classic to this day.

I'm generally not quick to dismiss a film as not worth watching, but this one truly falls into an exceptional category. The only redeeming qualities are Cornelia Sharpe, who looks quite attractive, and the fact that the movie is remarkably short.

The storyline is incredibly dull and makes little progress throughout its runtime. None of the characters are remotely engaging, leaving viewers with no reason to care about anyone involved. I honestly can't understand why Sean Connery chose to participate in this project; he definitely should have passed on it.

The only possible reason to watch this film is if you're a devoted Sean Connery fan eager to see all of his work—just be sure to save this one for last.

If, by some miracle, you watch this movie despite my review (or any other on this site), I hope you enjoy it more than I did. Thanks for taking the time to read.

It's not amusing—how anyone could connect this to Monty Python is beyond me. Honestly, it's utterly absurd—no laughter, no humor. It's exaggerated, but also unattractive and bizarre, seemingly created just for the sake of weirdness, which makes me think these people might have been under the influence of something at the time. Unfortunately, that didn't translate into comedy.

It might deserve some recognition for effort or intent, I suppose. Interestingly, it seems like there might be a laugh track—if there is, it’s hard to tell. Given the scarcity of genuine laughs, that question remains open.

Perhaps I’m being unfair—maybe this is some kind of performance art or exercise. If so, then all rules are off, and anything goes.

However, the guys dressing up as women with high-pitched voices and exaggerated features—come on! That’s not funny.

In my view, the only heirs to Monty Python’s sharp wit are Stephen Colbert and possibly Jon Stewart.

I rented this film solely because of the director, who’s created some intriguing movies in the past (if you haven't seen Waxwork, you're missing out on a fun ride). Nevertheless, I had my reservations from the start but decided to give it a chance anyway. Unfortunately, it’s a disaster—really bad. If you haven’t seen the film and don’t mind spoilers, keep reading. 

First off, the old adage "You can’t judge a book by its cover" definitely applies here. The DVD cover suggests that Jill is a stunning, long-haired beauty with highlights. The back features an eye-catching shot of Jill in red leather and some other images. The description sounds promising, making you want to rent it because it seems so good. 

But as soon as you start watching, you realize the movie inexplicably takes place in 1977. Jill, who’s supposed to be the star, turns out to be a total dud—not the girl on the cover. The film isn’t as predictable as you might expect, which is actually a downside here. The characters engage in incredibly stupid actions without any clear motivation, making the whole thing cringe-worthy to watch—especially about ten minutes before the ending.

This lesser-known de Sica film truly delivers. It echoes the adage "the meek shall inherit the earth." On the surface, it appears to be a story about class, but beneath that lies a poignant allegory for the homeless populations that flooded Europe after the Great War. These individuals are homeless yet optimistic, living in societies too impoverished and selfish to care for or even acknowledge them—mere footnotes for the Italian nouveau riche. de Sica chooses to tell this story as a fairy tale, reminiscent of Cinderella. Although I haven't read the original book, I can't say whether the deus ex machina originates from the author or de Sica himself. The film opens with "Once upon a time..." to emphasize the universal and timeless nature of its tale, capable of fitting anywhere and everywhere. Sharp caricatures of the aristocracy cut deeply, while the whimsical depiction of the homeless—especially as they begin to realize their wishes—adds a charming touch. An ending reminiscent of a Spielberg film makes this film accessible and enjoyable for all audiences. de Sica's most approachable work, and arguably one of his finest, shifts away from neo-realism. Straddling the line between that and classic filmmaking, he crafts a movie that is both touching and emotionally powerful.

Wes Craven, you must be joking… at our expense. TheRed Eye plot is utterly ludicrous. We watch as a guy claims to have spent eight weeks stalking a girl, then miraculously shows up behind her at the airport—who knows if he even bought a ticket or just followed her in—flirts and charms her effortlessly, somehow lands a seat right next to her in a two-seat row (not stuck in the middle of a five-seat block, is he contacts at check-in?), and then, during a painfully slow buildup, plays the cheesiest flirt. Once airborne, trapped in the tight confines among strangers, he immediately turns threatening—warning Rachel McAdams’s character with clichés like "We got your daddy, do what I say or else." Honestly, didn’t they already have her father lined up for the slaughter long before she boarded? Wouldn’t it have been far simpler to just snatch her off the street and terrorize her somewhere private, skipping all the convoluted dad-in-peril subplot? Maybe pull her nails out or do whatever it takes to get her to make that crucial "call." Or—since this is the movies and things have to be exaggerated—something even more unreal.

As someone who loves horses and appreciates hand-drawn animation, I had high expectations for DreamWorks' new film, *Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron*. Unfortunately, I ended up feeling a bit let down. The animation is stunning, and the story initially appears simple and perfect—a tale about a wild horse in nature. Unlike many animated films, the animals neither sing adorable songs nor speak, which is a welcome change. However, the film is marred by unnecessary narration by Matt Damon, a sentimental soundtrack by Bryan Adams, and enough action sequences to rival a Jerry Bruckheimer blockbuster. If the filmmakers had embraced the film's simplicity, it could have been a true masterpiece. While it's not a classic, it offers decent entertainment for young children. I recommend it for families, as it sincerely aims to be wholesome and is one of the few recent offerings that doesn’t upset or offend kids. It’s certainly visually beautiful, but overall, it could have been much better.

The only time I saw "Shades" was during a sneak preview; it hadn't even premiered yet. I recall there was someone from the director's team present — I can't remember who. It was a Belgian film that we had never heard of, so we approached it with a neutral stance, unsure of what to expect. Mickey Rourke is an exceptional actor, far surpassing the rest. In this film, he plays an actor whose career has long since stalled, assisting in the production of a movie in Belgium titled "Shades."

As soon as the film began, it became immediately apparent how heavily it relied on profanity. I have no problem with the occasional curse word, but this was excessive and almost grating. When Rourke's character uses the F-word naturally in dialogue, it feels genuine. But when cast members, especially non-English speakers, throw around the F- or S-words, it comes across as arrogant and aggressive.

We quickly lost track of how many times those words were uttered. By the end, everyone was just eager to get out of the theater. We were asked to rate the film, but with only a 0 to 10 scale, it was difficult — honestly, we were more inclined towards a -10.

I absolutely adore this film; I can watch it countless times without ever getting bored. The only line I really can't stomach is when Riff refers to herself as a teenage lobotomy—aside from that, everything else is flawless. I've never been a huge fan of PJ Soles, and knowing that she didn’t even know who the Ramones were until filming didn’t help, but I can mostly overlook her sour expression. Most viewers who watch this repeatedly are big Ramones fans, and honestly, that’s the main reason I love it so much. I never tire of DeeDee messing up his pizza delivery lines or Joey repeatedly mispronouncing the teacher’s name—it's hilarious. One of the film’s highlights is watching them sing "Do You Want to Dance" down the high school halls—I love those scenes. The special edition DVD includes a great retrospective, surprisingly without PJ Soles. Maybe she was working on another project at the time *laughs*. Overall, it's a fantastic film, especially if you’re a Ramones enthusiast.

This is the finest sci-fi I've encountered in my 29 years of watching the genre. I also believe that Dark Angel is destined to become a cult classic. The action scenes are fantastic, but Jessica Alba stands out as the most stunning and captivating star on television today.

It's encouraging to see that Vintage Film Buff has accurately classified their superb DVD release as a "musical," which perfectly captures the essence of this film—unmistakably straightforward. Much like its unofficial remake, Murder at the Windmill (1949), the murder scheme serves merely as a backdrop for an extravagant girlie revue led by Kitty Carlisle and Gertrude Michael, supported by a stunning lineup of actresses including Ann Sheridan, Lucy Ball, Beryl Wallace, Gwenllian Gill, Gladys Young, Barbara Fritchie, Wanda Perry, and Dorothy White. Carl Brisson also makes an appearance, lending his powerful voice to "Cocktails for Two," arguably the film's most beloved song, which is featured four times. Yet, Gertrude Michael truly steals the spotlight, delivering a memorable performance of "Sweet Marijuana" and convincingly portraying the hero's rejected lover. Regarding the rest of the cast, Jack Oakie and Victor McLaglen could have been omitted altogether. The sole highlight of Oakie’s part is his feeble running gag with cult star Toby Wing. To illustrate just how overly indulgent and strained the comedy becomes, the inept Inspector McLaglen spectacularly fails to find the killer, despite...

I just finished watching this film. It wasn't utterly terrible, but I can't say I was truly impressed. I'm still unsure why anyone would choose to make a movie like this. It was somewhat entertaining, but it felt as if the creators had conflicting visions—Monday, the writer was the boss; Tuesday, the director; Wednesday, the coffee guy—and so on. It almost seems like they intended to make a couple of different movies but only had the resources to produce one.  

Someone else mentioned that the acting was impressive, but I have to disagree. Although, if the actors managed to keep a straight face during filming, perhaps they’re better than I give them credit for.  

The back of the DVD suggests the film would be a mystery—more along the lines of a historical Law and Order or National Treasure. It begins that way, but suddenly veers into territory reminiscent of a cheesy Twilight Zone episode or... what was that other show that wasn’t quite as good? A poor episode of The Outer Limits.

Slither is a horror comedy that struggles to deliver enough of either element to truly qualify as one or the other. While it features a standout scene and several witty lines, it falls short on delivering genuine scares and maintaining consistent humor throughout. Additionally, the screenplay neglects to focus adequately on the main characters—particularly the hero and heroine—and veers off course at various points.

A significant flaw lies in how the film introduces and then abandons its protagonist (Fillion), instead shifting focus to Grant Grant (Michael Rooker) as he transforms into the monster. This entire segment feels sluggish; Michael Rooker's character isn't particularly compelling on his own, and observing his descent into the creature might be intriguing if the film were a character study titled "Grant—Portrait of a Man Turning Into a Monster." However, as a horror-comedy alien invasion movie, it feels out of place. Ultimately, the film's issues stem from the screenplay—it's not compelling to watch how the monster acts or spreads. The core appeal of a horror-comedy is to place the heroes in peril with shotguns at the ready, and this aspect is underdeveloped here.

Gus Van Sant has directed some truly outstanding films, and I am genuinely a fan. 

However, I feel that the sharp intellectual edge of Tom Robbins' novel "Even Cowgirls Get the Blues" doesn't fully translate onto the big screen. While both Tom Robbins and Gus Van Sant are exceptional visionaries and highly talented individuals, this particular adaptation fell short. 

It's not that the characters weren't well fleshed out or that the story lacked vitality. Rather, it's that reading the book allows our imaginations to soar, transporting us to different times and places, where we sometimes envision the best or the worst, heightening the emotional roller-coaster that Robbins artfully constructs. Films, on the other hand, often limit this expansive imagining, which can diminish the emotional impact and overall experience. I believe this is what happened with this adaptation. 

My recommendation: read the book!

What an utterly dreadful piece of rubbish! Who are all these people endlessly praising it? Yes, it’s “artsy” and “foreign,” but that’s simply not enough. The storyline is dull and disjointed, resembling a reality show, but poorly produced.  

The characters are inherently uninteresting; they lack the complexity needed to evoke any empathy. If they’re based on real individuals, I sincerely feel sorry for them.  

The violence, which is quite intense at times, comes across as showy and unnecessary, as if the producer is trying to imitate Quentin Tarantino. Personally, I’m not a fan of his work either.  

And yes, if I had neighbors like these, I’d definitely move!

This is a straightforward B-level science fiction film, and the director made no secret of that. The story revolves around a dragon brought back to life by a scientific team. Everything about it feels familiar, with scenes and tropes you've seen many times before. The script is weak, lacking in well-developed characters; in fact, it is filled with stereotypical personalities and situations. The director simply embraces the formulaic nature of the film, without trying to deceive or surprise the audience. This approach gives the movie a mild charm, though it’s unlikely to leave a lasting impression. It’s best enjoyed as background entertainment—something to watch while cooking, cleaning, or working out—offering mindless fun. It certainly has its place in the realm of entertainment, but it’s not the kind of movie you’d gather friends to watch unless everyone is drunk and indifferent. The overall rating of 3.2 seems fair. I don’t think it’s as terrible as many suggest, but I am surprised that some reviewers found it to be spectacular. That confuses me, as there’s no real effort to make this film memorable.

I was living in Rawlins when this movie was filmed, and I was fortunate enough to be involved in the production. I worked both as an extra and with Eddie Surkin on special effects. It was exciting to see behind-the-scenes operations, from the barbed wire coming to life to the electric chair and even the warden’s office floor. Meeting the cast, from Viggo to Tiny, was a highlight as well. Interestingly, the gate cut into the prison wall for the film is still called "Disney Gate" by locals. If anyone ever visits Rawlins, most of the movie sets remain intact and are accessible via a self-guided tour. Working with R. Harlan was an incredible experience, and I wish I had another chance to be part of it.

My favorite scene in this movie, the one that perfectly highlights the absurdity, foolishness, and senselessness of the entire story, occurs at the climax. Doctor Ted Nelson and his single, unmarried friend, the Sheriff, finally corner the Melting Man on a staircase landing inside an electrical generating station. Remember, Nelson has been searching for the Melting Man almost throughout the entire film, and by this point, the creature has already killed and devoured several victims, including Nelson's boss. Nelson is fully aware that the Melting Man is dangerously insane and ravenous for human flesh and blood.

The Sheriff has his gun aimed at the creature, which, and I commend the film and Rick Baker for this, is the most grotesque and horrifying creature humanity has ever seen. He then asks a crucial question to Doctor Ted Nelson: "WHAT DO WE DO NOW?!?!" 

The camera shifts to Nelson, and it’s painfully clear he has no idea what action to take next. It seems that Nelson was so focused on tracking down the Melting Man that he never considered bringing any restraints or plan for handling the creature.

Perhaps. How Francis Veber, one of the finest comedy directors in the world—at least within France—managed to produce such a completely unwatchable film surpasses the understanding of ordinary minds. It's not merely that the characters are unlikable or that the movie lacks even the simplest wit; watching it is genuinely physically uncomfortable, a relentless display of poor writing, acting, and filmmaking that makes it hard to believe this is the work of seasoned, talented professionals. The extensive time spent in the editing room and the prolonged shelf life before its brief theatrical release speak volumes about its quality. What could they have been thinking?

Having been captivated by the stunning visuals of "Hero," I eagerly anticipated this film, which was promoted as being similar but even better—and starring one of my favorite actresses, Ziyi Zhang. Unfortunately, I was let down on both fronts. I purchased the DVD without seeing it first, and it turned out to be a mistake; it wasn't an improvement.

I understand that these fantasy martial arts films—featuring characters flying through the air—are purely imaginative. However, the storyline was stretched so far beyond plausibility that it left me shaking my head in disappointed disbelief. A blind woman defeating hundreds of enemies? That’s pushing the limits too far. Additionally, the main male character, Jin (Takeshi Kaneshiro), was so grating—his dialogue, goofy expression, and silly laugh— that he detracted significantly from the film.

Despite the vibrant colors and spectacular action sequences, I found the story lacked the substance needed to make it a film worth owning. This movie simply doesn’t hold a candle to "Hero" in my eyes.

This film was absolutely terrible, plain and simple. It was so poorly made that I felt compelled to create an IMDb account just to warn others about its pitfalls.

As someone well-versed in campy horror movies, having seen titles like "Redneck Zombies," "House of the Psychotic Women," "Slumber Party Massacre II," and many more, I know my trash. And this film genuinely sucks.

Most of the movie is just characters frantically running from one side of the screen to the other. When they’re not doing that, they’re spouting random lines that lack any real emotion or purpose. When the acting occasionally reaches a tolerable level, the direction unravels completely. The film is riddled with abrupt, low-angle shots—so many that it seemed like Leif Jonker was using a tiny tripod. He repeatedly employed what I call the "Leif Maneuver," which is amateurish zooming out from an object of interest. It’s as if the filmmakers couldn’t be bothered to shoot a sunrise, so they filmed a sunset and reversed it. With such lazy direction, it’s almost impressive that the final bloody scene exists at all. The only explanation is that the last five minutes were probably shot before the first eighty-five.

This film missed the opportunity to delve into the animals' humanity, leaving me with a sense of emptiness. [Spoiler alert] I wasn't convinced that Dr. D truly had a compelling reason to decline the lucrative buyout in favor of helping his furry friends. Unlike Babe—the original—that defied typical big-budget formulas by highlighting the nobility of the animals over their human counterparts, the creatures in this movie are reduced to mere comic caricatures, practically deserving of being ground up (especially if their nonsensical chatter could be understood). Without Eddie Murphy’s wild antics, the film would likely fall flat.

THHE2 provides plenty of entertainment through humor and cringe-worthy moments, likely prompting reactions like "oh sh*t!" and "get your face away from the damn hole, you idiot." However, I’m unsure if it’s really worth seeing. I was consistently frustrated by the poorly written military characters who seem clueless about combat. 

While the film features more violence, gore, and a higher body count than the first, I’m still contemplating whether that compensates for the overall absurdity— which isn’t the fun, campy kind like in Dead Alive or Feast. Honestly, my time might have been better spent watching Aja’s remake for the fifth time.

So, if you’re looking for laughs or some gruesome moments, go for it. Just don’t expect to walk away truly satisfied.

Rating: 21 by The Film Snob. (For details on our rating system, visit our blog What-To-See-Next.)  

Here's a film so excruciatingly dull that the only relief is clawing at your own face to escape the on-screen monotony.  

You won't be wringing your hands, rolling your eyes, or sighing into your popcorn. No, for a movie of this degree of mediocrity, only face-clawing will suffice.  

When you start clawing — and rest assured, you must — begin at the lower part of your face. Keep your upper face intact, especially your tear ducts, because the truly tear-jerking third act may force you to your knees—unless you’ve managed to claw your way out of the theater beforehand.  

In an era celebrating Joe Six-Pack and Hockey Moms as the new icons of leadership and foreign diplomacy, perhaps a movie as tedious as this will be appreciated as something anyone could produce. Watching it, however, is a far more perilous endeavor.  

And so our story begins...  

Sidney Young, a London publisher of a third-rate celebrity and entertainment magazine, is on the verge of seeing his publication...

In the days before the Toxic Avenger, the low-camp pioneers at Troma Films attempted to venture into more respectable territory by producing straightforward slasher films. I like to think that watching the results here was what prompted them to abandon any remaining pretensions and embrace self-aware parody instead.

Splatter University is yet another film designed for the die-hard fans of discomfort. As it drifts through two separate casts and countless pointless subplots, it becomes genuinely difficult to watch. Let me try to give a brief overview.

The story kicks off with news that a violent psychopath has escaped from a nearby hospital, leading the action to shift to a Catholic university—let’s call it St. Splatter for the sake of the title. The students seem apathetic and moody, bickering petty disputes and embodying a generation of slackers before their time. Meanwhile, the new professor, Julie Parker, displays complete ineptitude at her duties. The students grapple with relationships, infidelity, unwanted pregnancies, lecherous priests, and dodging academic responsibilities; Julie contends with a creepy boyfriend, the rigid administration at St. Splatter, counseling unwed mothers, and the blank, emotionless expressions of her pupils. None of it adds up to anything meaningful.

Written by a woman and directed by another, this film hints at a feminist perspective—so buckle up, ladies, as we're about to journey through a world filled with ruthless men and well-meaning women. 

In this soap opera, Trish encounters a man at the employment agency who behaves, looks, and dresses like a pimp—and he offers her a job with the ulterior motive of seducing her later. In his office, he even touches her chin in a manner reminiscent of a villainous character from a Bond film, just before he might align with the typical trope of villainy. Later, this same man stalks Trish in a women's dressing room, harrasses her, and nearly assaults her. Oh, these villainous men—every one of them depicted as entirely evil. 

In today's world, it seems women can't even seek employment without fearing harassment, right? Well, we're here to stand against that! The film features a divorced women’s club, led by a character reminiscent of Janet Leigh, who claims on behalf of all women involved that "men are all s**t," expressing frustration and disillusionment with the male gender.

Frailty—8/10—Despite its rather awkward title and the curious "Bill Paxton Directs" headline, this film delivers a solid, old-fashioned biblical horror thriller full of intense, gripping moments. While it might ultimately stand as the Southern Gothic, inbred cousin to Kubrick's "The Shining," that's part of its charm—an intriguing and entertaining comparison. The movie features a shocking plot twist and an intentionally ambiguous moral message, adding to its depth. Years from now, viewers will likely stumble upon this film late at night on cable, and find themselves genuinely frightened. It's a shame Bill Paxton felt compelled to star in his own directorial effort—yet, despite that, it's still an incredibly enjoyable and chilling watch.

The Sopranos stands as perhaps the most critically acclaimed TV series of all time, so naturally, my expectations were sky-high, yet the show exceeded even those. While I have a deep appreciation for the mafia and crime genres in film and enjoy engaging with stories set within these worlds, The Sopranos offers so much more. With over 86 hours of content, it crafts a narrative that is not only one of the most exhilarating and unpredictable mafia and action tales but also a powerful family drama, a startling character study, a side-splitting comedy, an insightful psychological exploration of good and evil, and an artistically rich blend of dreams and hallucinations—all woven seamlessly together. David Chase's masterwork manages to achieve this remarkable feat and more, establishing HBO as the platform closest to cinematic perfection on television and setting the stage for many other series that continue to astonish audiences.

The series embodies realism where it counts, but Chase’s strategic departures from strict realism—such as the surreal dream sequences—add further depth and complexity. Alongside a talented writing team including Matthew Weiner and Terrence Winter, who would go on to create Mad Men, Chase crafts a layered and multifaceted masterpiece that elevates television storytelling to new heights.

A riotously funny play that humorously explores sex, family, and Beverly Hills social classes, milking more laughs from the zip code than it has since Granny and Jed Clampett. The story revolves around two chauffeurs who bet on which one can seduce his employer—two attractive, single (or soon-to-be single) women, played by Bisset and Woronov—first. If Manuel wins, his friend will settle his debt to a violent Asian street gang; if he loses, he must serve as his friend’s submissive partner! 

The production features plenty of raunchy dialogue and some rather sick physical humor, but much of the comedy is subtly layered. Bartel stands out as an irresistibly sensual family member who ends up taking his sexy teenage niece on a year-long "missionary trip" to Africa. 

Overall, a hilarious and entertaining experience.

Despite multiple remakes, this film remains a classic, especially for first-time viewers. Witty dialogue and a brilliantly inventive final scene showcase its true genius, deserving greater acclaim than critics have provided. Highly recommended—it's one of the funniest films of recent years.

Without any particular bias toward any genre of filmmaking and a genuine appreciation for documentaries, I can honestly say I was frustrated with myself for enduring the entire running time of "20 Dates." I won't bother with the plot—others have likely covered that—but I will mention that Berkowitz's over-the-top, Woody Allen-esque narration was incredibly irritating. It felt like he either needed to cut back on the coffee or take some tranquilizers. It’s also possible Berkowitz himself recognized that this film was a mistake, as some parts reveal his struggles to fund the project. Forgive me for couching criticism as praise, but I have to acknowledge Berkowitz's ability to persuade someone to finance this truly dreadful film. I understand the intentions and boundaries he aimed for, but even by his own standards, he fails on nearly every level. Ultimately, I doubt many of these women felt comfortable going out with a jittery aspiring filmmaker, which makes me question the authenticity of the portrayal. Hey Myles, I initially loved your film... when I first saw it as

As a kid, I absolutely loved both Bill & Ted movies. The other night, I saw that Bogus Journey was on, and since it had been at least five years since I last watched it, I decided to tune in. I ended up loving it all over again! Even after all these years, the film remains incredibly funny. While 'Excellent Adventure' might be the favorite, this one still rocks just as much. Admittedly, some of the performances are a bit cheesy, but in a totally cool way. Plus, it features the coolest depiction of Death ever in a movie! In conclusion: totally a non-bogus movie, dude! Way excellent! STATION!!!

CRY FREEDOM serves as an excellent introduction for those seeking a concise overview of apartheid's brutality in just a few hours. Renowned director Richard Attenborough (GANDHI) is well-versed in this genre, and the involvement of the real-life Mr. and Mrs. Woods—who are the primary white characters in both the book and the film—adds a layer of authenticity to CRY FREEDOM. The current version of the film runs slightly over two and a half hours, incorporating an additional 23 minutes of footage that expanded it into a two-part television miniseries following the film’s original theatrical release. This extended length helps to mitigate some of the film’s minor shortcomings, such as uneven character development and broad stereotypes. However, one potential flaw—focusing more on the whites’ plight than on that of the African characters—may actually serve as a strength, emphasizing the historical and political context. Seen primarily as an educational tool about the injustices of apartheid, rather than purely for artistic achievement, CRY FREEDOM narrates a story deeply familiar to black Africans, though it may be essential for younger generations to see it portrayed on screen to grasp its full impact. Ultimately, the film and the book aim to engage white audiences, encouraging understanding and reflection.

This film resembles real life in that very little occurs within its roughly two-hour span, and it lacks a clear plan or compelling plot. The cast often appears invisible—an effect attributed to the "experimental" lighting noted by many reviewers. 

It's quite dull, unsurprising that Altman is at the helm—he’s a director with a mixed track record. While some may cherish "Gosford Park," others might recall the flops like "Pret A Porter," "Kansas City," or "Dr. T. and the Women." Given that the story is based on a John Grisham novel and features a talented cast, the film’s flaws become even more noticeable as you find yourself drifting into sleep. Ultimately, this is a prime example of a poor film—not "so bad it's good," but simply bad.

I have now watched "Miracles Still Happen" at least four times and I never grow tired of this incredible film. From the very beginning, it captivates the viewer’s attention. As the story unfolds and the plane crashes, the tension escalates as we watch a young girl struggle to survive alone and terrified in the Amazon. Being the sole survivor of the crash, which also claims her mother’s life, adds an even greater layer of drama, illustrating the harrowing challenges she faces during her ten days in the wilderness. The reality that such an event actually occurred is astonishing, and the idea that anyone could survive it is almost beyond belief. The film vividly depicts the fierce wildlife, snakes, reptiles, vast forests, and countless insects that surround her. As the story advances, we witness her confront numerous dangers while she's determined to follow the river, hoping it will lead her to civilization. She recalls her father’s advice—that a stream always leads to a larger river, and ultimately, to a bigger body of water—believing this will guide her to safety.

I'm not certain if it's available worldwide, but if anyone involved in selecting titles for videotapes and video store distribution happens to read this—please, I beg you, purchase it! (In case I wasn't clear: GET THIS MOVIE INTO VIDEOSTORES!)  

It's impossible to explain—must be seen!

About a year ago, I was watching television when a story aired about a zombie film being shot in my neighborhood. Since then, I’ve kept a close eye on this movie called "Fido" as it wrapped up filming and started making the rounds at festivals. Two weeks ago, it finally opened at my local theater. Just yesterday, I read in a newspaper that "Fido" isn’t drawing much of an audience during its limited release, except at our local theater. Remarkably, it’s even outpacing every other film at The Paramount, including "300." That makes sense, considering many residents want to see their city on the big screen or catch a glimpse of themselves in zombie makeup. For those locals who haven’t seen "Fido" yet and are thinking about it, I can assure you there are plenty of recognizable scenes—from the schoolhouse to the city park to the restricted zone—that you’ll identify with. In fact, the Okanagan Valley looks stunning in the film. Yes, you read that right—beautiful scenery in a zombie movie! And I must say, "Fido" itself is a very good film. Despite some flaws, it’s better than most of the twenty other movies currently showing in my area.

I saw this at a test screening, and all I can say is: What...the...hell? The movie unfolds about as effortlessly as Mickey Mouse attempting to read the script for "Scarface." It's surreal beyond any semblance of logic; and even if you manage to turn off your brain, the film is so strange that it stops just short of being amusing.  

The storyline centers on crocodile hunter Steve Irwin trying to rescue a crocodile that secretly harbors a CIA probe. The CIA then pursues Irwin to retrieve their device, but he mistakes them for poachers and sets out to stop them.  

That's pretty much the entire plot; the rest is filled with exaggerated stereotypes of Australian culture ("Didja see dat?" and "Crikey!") and bizarrely coordinated action scenes. At one point, Irwin climbs onto a speeding RV and engages in a knife fight with a CIA agent atop it. Yes, you read that right—Steve Irwin in a knife fight on top of an RV. Let this be your warning: this film is ridiculously bad.

In my view, this celebrity skit show is quite enjoyable. I particularly liked Greg Kinnear as the host. There are several reasons why I feel that way. Although Hal Sparks was an decent host, I occasionally wish Greg Kinnear hadn’t left the show. It seems these days that few hosts remain with a TV series for its entire duration. Nevertheless, I appreciated seeing different hosts and others comedy impersonate celebrities. Personally, I found it genuinely funny. Before I finish, I have to admit that I do miss this show. In conclusion, I wholeheartedly recommend it to all fans of sketch comedy—you’re bound to enjoy it.

My enduring admiration for Italian actress Lucianna Paluzzi, who vividly sparked my adolescence through her performance in the 1965 film "Thunderball," has led me to explore some quite unconventional avenues. One such example is the British film from 1959, "Carlton-Browne of the F.O.," which features Lucianna in one of her early roles. She portrays a princess, although the film primarily highlights the talents of Terry-Thomas and Peter Sellers, both of whom were quickly ascending stars at the time. This charming and often hilarious movie introduces us to the fictional island nation of Gaillardia, reminiscent of Madeira, which had been a British colony until 1916 and subsequently faded into obscurity. However, forty-three years later, it attracts global attention and becomes embroiled in international espionage upon the discovery of valuable cobalt deposits. The British government dispatches the inept Carlton-Browne from the Foreign Office to oversee the situation. Terry-Thomas delivers a subtle performance, and Sellers is amusing as Prime Minister Amphibulos of Gaillardia. Notably, this was Seller’s second 1959 film involving a tiny nation challenging global powers—the first being "The Mouse That Roared." Ian Bannen nearly steals the scene as Gaillardia’s charming king.

What’s Great About It: It features inventive and genuinely unsettling effects that will creep out even the most experienced horror aficionados. The film sidesteps the common trope of relying on cliché soundtrack jump scares. Even if you think you've seen it all, there are moments here that will make your jaw drop.

What Could Have Been Improved: At times, the acting felt flat and unconvincing. The visuals occasionally had a “shot-on-video” vibe, though overall the film successfully created its intended atmosphere. The camera work is often cluttered with unnecessary close-ups of trivial actions. While the effects are effectively creepy, some were used too frequently, diminishing their impact. The ending feels rushed, leaving critical moments underdeveloped. Many details are left for viewers to interpret, not intentionally, but because they simply missed them.  

Nevertheless, it’s a solid indie horror flick that stands out noticeably above the average. Definitely worth a rental.

Bloodsuckers shows some promise as a somewhat decent film, with its premise of military personnel hunting vampires in space holding a certain cheesy charm. The idea of a universe populated by various vampire breeds, each possessing unique traits—many of which the characters have yet to discover—is also quite intriguing. However, the notion that most of the galaxy’s life forms outside of Earth are vampires raises questions about how that could realistically work, considering the nature of vampires. If nearly everyone is a vampire, it’s unclear who they would be feeding on, leaving that aspect confusing. Overall, the film feels like a low-budget cross between Firefly/Serenity and vampire movies, sprinkled with a bit of Aliens. The action sequences are rather standard and derivative—especially of Serenity—but adequately executed, with enough gore, including some humorously over-the-top blood spurts, to satisfy fans of the genre. The film also features a significant amount of character-driven drama, much of which comes across as tedious, dominated by conflicts among characters who often seem like imploring, immature figures.

I've fallen asleep during movies before, but never twice in the same film, so it actually took me three attempts to watch it all the way through. The dialogue was terrible; the women spoke in awkward, unnatural mannerisms, while the men were nothing more than exaggerated stereotypes. Additionally, two of the supposed Japanese women looked Chinese, bore Chinese names, and spoke with distinct Chinese accents. I'm still puzzled about why the Emmenthal men were so intimately involved with each other. Considering all this, I'm torn between giving the movie a one-star or a two-star rating—it's a tough call.

This is clearly illegal. Pedophiles take advantage of content like this. How did they manage to produce such a film? The entire movie can be summed up in one word: sickening. Where do people find the audacity to create and watch these kinds of films? While watching, I didn’t expect that they would depict a young girl, perhaps around 12, actually sleeping with an adult woman. Sorry if that’s a spoiler, but I wish I hadn’t seen it. Where has everyone’s sense of morality gone? Could the filmmakers themselves be pedophiles? Our society is increasingly plagued by predators who target children, and yet filmmakers continue to produce movies that seemingly encourage such dangerous behavior. I also saw a comment asking if there was a version showing nudity—about a child—what’s wrong with this picture?

I'm a big fan of the comic book series, but this film completely failed to meet my expectations. I was hoping for something akin to Heavy Metal 2000—slow-paced, with gritty dialogue and plenty of blood—but this movie was even worse than I could have imagined. 

The storyline closely mirrors the comic, but that’s about where the similarities end. The characters lack the energy and spirit that made the original series compelling. The film only adapts a small segment of the comic, and surprisingly, that part drags even more than the later, more exciting sections. Instead of highlighting the engaging overall plot, the movie fixates on trivial events that do little to captivate the audience.

With the right team behind it, this project could have been fantastic. Unfortunately, that wasn’t the case. Now, it’s yet another terrible movie that few will watch, and even fewer will appreciate. My copy will likely sit untouched for years until I finally decide to toss it out.

If you're into gangster films, this is the first one you should consider purchasing or at least renting. Al Pacino delivers a phenomenal performance, and the story is a timeless classic! I give it a perfect 10/10! Why isn't this movie on the TOP 250 list??

Although the 3-D animation—serving as the show's highlight—performed its role well, most of the other elements fell flat. It seemed as though the filmmakers believed, "Since it's a 3-D movie, we can cut corners on the plot and character development." And having a children's movie is no excuse; audiences are just as eager to connect with three-dimensional characters like Shrek and Nemo’s dad as they are to enjoy the visual effects. The only character with any depth was the two-dimensional Scooter, who occasionally twists the plot with his relentless hunger for everything around him. 

The real punchline? Buzz Aldrin's cameo at the very end. After spending an hour and a half watching a monotonous cartoon version of the legendary astronaut, his appearance only dampened the mood by calling the main characters "contaminants" and declaring that the scenario depicted was impossible. 

Did they just want to casually reveal to kids that the Easter Bunny and Santa Claus aren’t real?

Ariauna Albright is a talented actress, yet her involvement in this poorly written production remains a mystery. What should have been entertaining ultimately devolved into dullness. One of Ariauna's strengths is her ability to act convincingly while also appearing genuinely attractive, unlike her partner Lilith Stabs, who looks appealing but clearly invested her funds in spa treatments or beauty salons rather than acting lessons. This project was crying out for some visual allure and, with a more imaginative script, could have achieved that naturally. Nevertheless, Ariauna did her best within the circumstances and manages to somewhat preserve her reputation. The Tempe company should understand that dressing two attractive women in revealing fetish cop uniforms naturally sets expectations for some fetish elements and eye candy. Enough said.

It's peculiar to observe a film where certain scenes feel notably underwhelming—especially when compared to others within its legacy—while its subplots or supporting stories deliver surprisingly provocative and compelling moments. Sudden Impact exemplifies this disparity; Clint Eastwood, serving as star, producer, and director, demonstrates his best moments alongside those less impressive, particularly when handling a crime, mystery, or detective narrative rooted in his iconic Dirty Harry persona. We hear the famous "Make my day" line, and unlike the first film, where his "Do I feel lucky?" speech was playful and cool initially, and tough as nails the second time at the end, here the tone is reversed. Eastwood finds himself tangled once again in department conflicts—typical of his "fight crime his way" approach—such as a diner robbery (perhaps an inspiration for Pulp Fiction?) and a high-speed chase involving a senior citizen bus. He's told to "take a vacation," but that's the last thing he has in mind. The main plot itself feels unconvincing beyond the anticipation of the story and dialogue, which only adds to the frustration. Yet, eventually, his storyline intertwines with the subplots that Eastwood masterfully navigates.

The Sunshine Boys is a comedic gem from 1975, adapted from Neil Simon's play, focusing on a retired vaudeville duo—played by Walter Matthau and George Burns—who had a bitter falling out and are reluctantly asked to reunite for a television special. The catch is, neither of them wants to see or work with the other. Richard Benjamin portrays Matthau’s nephew, a theatrical agent tasked with orchestrating this unlikely reunion. This charming and heartfelt comedy serves as a loving tribute to the once-popular vaudeville tradition, largely thanks to Neil Simon’s sharp screenplay and exceptional performances by Matthau, Burns, and Benjamin. Burns earned the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for his role, but it’s Matthau who truly steals the show with his impeccable and side-splitting portrayal of Willy Clark. Although nominated for Best Actor, Matthau was up against Jack Nicholson’s iconic performance in One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest; nonetheless, in another year, his performance would have been deserving of the award. Matthau commands every scene he’s in, delivering a perfectly timed, authentic performance—especially memorable is the audition scene, showcasing his comedic genius.

This is a review of The Wizard, not to be confused with The Wiz or Mr. Wizard. The Wizard is a late-eighties film about a profoundly silent boy's talent for playing video games and walking throughout the entire opening credits. The Wiz is an unnecessary remake of The Wizard of Oz, and Mr. Wizard is that guy who attached 100 straws together for a kid to sip Tang through.  

Now that we've cleared that up, let me say this: there’s really no reason to watch this movie. It’s essentially a 100-minute Nintendo commercial intended to promote the Powerglove, The Legend of Zelda, and Super Mario Brothers 3. I use the word "designed" very loosely here because it feels like this film was hastily written over a weekend by a team of people who had never played Nintendo, and directed by someone with less style sense than my grandmother. Perhaps if the writer and director had actually played some games together, they’d realize they were about to produce complete garbage and might instead consider learning how to install car stereos at vocational school.

This is perhaps one of the dullest slashers I've ever seen—if you can even call it that. I wouldn’t bother watching it, even if it turned out to be some sort of adult film, since it bears a striking resemblance to one. Watching a small group of middle-aged people wandering through the woods is truly excruciating. These types of movies are usually made for teenagers, so I wonder who the intended audience really was for this tedious snooze-fest. The only reason I even picked up this film was because of its cover art, which caught my eye and motivated me to check it out. It happened to be part of a Suspense Classics 50 Movie Pack, and after watching the other films in that collection, it’s clear this one doesn’t belong among them. If you're craving a decent slasher set in the woods, I’d recommend watching *Just Before Dawn* or *The Final Terror.*

I found Cinderella 2 and Jungle Book 2 quite disappointing, but this one perhaps surpasses both in disappointment. Firstly, I disliked the animation; it felt like a low-budget Saturday-morning cartoon, and in some scenes, it was even worse. I enjoyed a few characters, particularly Thunderbolt and Patch, but others like Cruella were unimpressive. In the original, Cruella was a true villainess, but she lost her edge in this sequel. Her lines were forgettable, and her animation looked somewhat unattractive. Additionally, her artist companion Lars was more of a joke, and Roger seemed to have abruptly quit smoking. The voice performances were generally strong, especially Barry Bostwick as Thunderbolt, though Jodi Benson’s accent was a distraction for me. There were some nice moments, but overall, the story felt overly stretched, resembling a drawn-out TV episode. Overall, it was a significantly disappointing follow-up to the beloved Disney classics of the 60s, like Cinderella and Jungle Book. Sorry, but I can only rate it a 3 out of 10—it just wasn’t my thing. Bethany Cox

For me, this story begins with some amusing jokes about Frank's fantasies—whether he's traveling with a staircase or sitting in business meetings. The issue is that after an hour of watching, these same fantasies and humorous scenarios recur repeatedly, making it highly predictable. It feels more like a TV show, where you can easily tune out and return without missing anything. 

I enjoy Felix Herngren as Frank, but that alone isn't enough. Even in a comedy, there needs to be more variety and a meaningful message for the audience.

"Ruby in Paradise" is a captivating coming-of-age tale about a young woman, Ruby Lee Gissing, who leaves behind her restrictive upbringing to find her true self. While the title role is beautifully portrayed by Ashley Judd—likely her first film appearance and one to be proud of—the story does not focus on becoming "somebody" fame, akin to the next Madonna, whether as the Virgin Mary or a flashy, attention-seeking singer. 

Rather, the film highlights the importance of trusting one's instincts and engaging in introspection to evolve into the mature, ideal version of oneself. Please note: this is not an action-packed movie! It features occasional voice-over narration by Judd as her character journals her thoughts—perhaps alienating some male viewers. However, patience reveals a quietly stunning film where happiness is found in simple acts like carrying water and chopping wood.

Todd Field, who played Nick Nightingale in "Eyes Wide Shut," co-stars as Ruby Lee's noble love interest, helping her mend her once-distorted views on relationships learned during her youth. Yet, even his character isn't the ultimate answer for Ruby Lee—there's no external hero imposed upon her journey.
