This marks at least the third remake of this film, so if you experience a sense of deja vu while watching, don't be surprised. The filmmakers merely changed the setting and presented the story from a different angle, but the differences are negligible. Unfortunately, the movie doesn't improve because the original plot is fundamentally flawed and never quite works. As with the earlier versions, the acting remains mediocre. 

The story features a unique ending that might catch first-time viewers off guard, but it feels out of place within the narrative. If the film had concluded ten minutes earlier, it would have been more satisfying and worthwhile. Here's the spoiler: ultimately, crime seems to pay since the criminal isn't caught. I dislike this message that the movie leaves us with.

At least it's not filled with pointless violence or superficial filler. However, it also lacks depth and a cohesive, smooth narrative. The story showed promise, but it seems the director lost sight of its core. It feels disjointed, drifting aimlessly into strange directions without resolving anything. Additionally, it doesn't seem the director has much experience with golf country clubs, as some portrayals are quite absurd. Overall, it's not very engaging.

Me? No, I'm serious. That's actually what it says on the DVD case.

Brief plot summary: A gorgeous woman stands around smiling, and inexplicably, this causes all the men to turn against each other.

"Find Ariel... Where's Ariel... Can't find Ariel..." She's right behind you, you knucklehead.

Most of what's worth commenting on about this terrible little space opera has already been said.

A group of cheesy actors, mostly convicts, come in after the initial batch of actors is quickly eliminated. Then they meet the same fate. Each scene seems to be broadcast nearly fifteen minutes in advance. Maybe they drew straws to decide which actors would get the most screen time and larger paychecks. The alien virus, hologram, VR witch, or glitch appears to be completely powerless and does nothing. Why doesn't she just stay inside the computer instead of performing her so-called "teleporting vampire" act? (Honestly, it might have been more interesting if she had actually been a vampire or did more than just stand around staring at people—something she never does. Ironically, her presence is enough to make all the men kill each other. Go figure.)

This isn't really a space movie.

"Strange Case" may not stand as John Cleese's most successful TV venture, feeling more like an early draft hurried into production without adequate revisions. The series is sprinkled with some foolish concepts alongside a few witty moments, but overall, the story fails to make a significant impact. 

On the bright side, Arthur Lowe delivers a delightful performance as Dr. Watson, complete with bionic enhancements. "Good Lord," indeed.

I absolutely loved the original *Scary Movie*. Parody is my favorite type of humor, often considered the sharpest and most clever form. The Wayans brothers seemed to understand this perfectly in the first film, but they seemingly lost their way when creating the sequel. I believe the Wayans family is composed of comedic geniuses; however, even geniuses can slip up sometimes.

The film started off with promise. I particularly enjoyed the parody of *The Exorcist*, especially the "come on out, ma" scene—that’s classic Wayans humor. Aside from that moment, I can recall only two other parts that made me laugh: first, when Tori Spelling is seduced by a spirit in the middle of the night, then becomes overly clingy and starts talking about marriage, even as the spirit protests, "It was just a booty call!!" That scene was pretty funny. The second was the parody of *Save the Last Dance*, where Cindy accidentally assaults a girl while practicing her new dance moves. Still, even these brief moments of humor couldn't compare to the uproarious laughs of the original *Scary Movie*.

Unfortunately, the rest of this sequel is disappointing—full of cheap, gross-out gags and recycled jokes from the first film that relied on subtle humor.

What’s wrong with you people? If you weren’t blown away by the adrenaline-pumping car chases and Jessica Simpson’s stunning looks, then something must be seriously off. Of course, the film isn’t a cinematic masterpiece—and I don’t think it was meant to be. It’s fun and funny, and even though I didn’t watch the show when I was younger, I recently caught an episode and felt the movie captures that same vibe. The theater seats were practically vibrating, and the action scenes were exciting without being boring or overly drawn out like some moments in *2 Fast 2 Furious*. Jessica Simpson is absolutely gorgeous, and I only wish she had been more involved in the action. Overall, I had a fantastic time watching it—I might even see it again soon and definitely plan to buy it on DVD. People, just enjoy it for what it is!

This film was completely terrible, with a capital "C." The opening scene showed some potential, but that promise quickly fizzled once the plot direction became clear. 

The wooden statue, Morty, who looked somewhat unsettling in the original film, now appears utterly ridiculous. It was painfully obvious that a guy in a cheap plastic costume was behind it. By the way, does anyone else think "Morty" is one of the least scary names on the planet? It ranks right up there with "Jimmy" or "Fred" when it comes to horror appeal. Why not just call the statue Henry-Kissinger—"Run! It's Dr. Kissinger!"—which would be just as terrifying as "Morty." 

Then there's a scene where the "hero" smashes his father's tombstone with—guess what? A sledgehammer? Or maybe a two-by-four? Nope. He frantically beats it with a twig—a freakin' twig. And to make things worse, after the characters leave, the tombstone inexplicably starts bleeding. Oh, brother! 

There's also a Native American character living with the main character's grandparents, but he seems to do nothing but maintain Morty. He keeps telling creepy Morty legends, warnings to scoffers, and even repairs Morty's arm when it gets damaged—

Brokedown Palace tells the story of two best friends, Alice and Darlene, who embark on a spontaneous trip to Thailand only to be imprisoned after drugs are planted in their luggage. While the film had the potential to be a poignant and impactful drama reminiscent of "Return to Paradise," it ultimately shifts its focus away from their dire circumstances and instead centers on the dynamics of their friendship. 

Claire Danes and Kate Beckinsale deliver outstanding performances, with the film emphasizing the intricate interplay between suspicion, jealousy, and the testing of loyalty—highlighting the sacrifices made in the name of friendship. The movie opts not to explore the political backdrop or the grim realities of prison life in depth, instead concentrating on the personal and emotional aspects of their relationship.

However, there are some plot inconsistencies and moments that strain believability. The portrayal of their fear and despair doesn’t quite capture the true intensity of their predicament, and the depiction of life beyond the prison walls feels limited. Bill Pullman appears as a character meant to embody sleaze, but the overall portrayal remains somewhat superficial.

I find it hard to believe that the talented Alan Ball had any involvement in this mess. Having watched the first two episodes, I can confidently say this show isn't going on my must-watch list. There are just too many issues working against it.  

None of the cast members stand out as particularly skilled. Anna Paquin, playing the lead Sookie, is honestly terrible. I remember her being much better in other roles I've seen, so perhaps it's the writing that's to blame. She’s not exactly easy on the eyes either—at times, she looks downright unattractive. The actor portraying Bill fares slightly better, mostly because his character is meant to be somewhat stoic and detached. The rest of the cast tries their best, but with clichéd characters and difficult accents to pull off, it's a tall order. Tara, in particular, is tough to watch; Rutina Wesley’s accent is painfully bad—almost nails-on-chalkboard terrible. Nelsan Ellis isn't much better; it’s often hard to understand what he's saying. Both their performances, along with...

I adore this film—Jouvet, Arletty, Blier, Carné... nearly everything has already been said about it, but there’s one detail I’d like to highlight: no footage of the actual Hôtel du Nord, which still stands (or did at least—I've heard it's slated for demolition), was used in the film. The entire scene was reconstructed on a set, primarily because they couldn’t shut down traffic on the St. Martin canal for several weeks to shoot on location.

'Presque Rien' is a tender story about two young boys discovering love during a summer by the seaside. I prefer not to spoil the plot, as it's not the core of what makes this film special—although I can assure you, it's intriguing and original. The true highlight of this movie is its cinematography. The visuals are breathtaking, so much so that they warrant the highest praise, leaving viewers enchanted by their beauty.

Regarding the storyline, it unfolds in a non-linear, somewhat complex manner. There’s no straightforward chronology, and not all questions posed by the film are answered. This layered approach adds to the film’s allure, making it even more compelling. I recommend 'Presque Rien' to anyone who values the artistic craft of filmmaking—they will surely find it rewarding.

Films such as Chocolat, Beau Travail, and others have elevated French director Claire Denis to the ranks of the world's most distinctive and accomplished filmmakers. Her 2004 film, The Intruder (L'Intrus), further enriches her impressive body of work. This cinematic poem exudes an atmosphere of persistent loneliness and grief, offering a window into the mind of a man who is physically and mentally declining, traveling across the globe in search of redemption and serenity—yet finding these elusive. Loosely inspired by Jean-Luc Nancy's memoir about undergoing a heart transplant, The Intruder is an intensely opaque piece that remains challenging to articulate clearly, even after multiple viewings, often described best through subjective, impressionistic impressions.

Louis Trebor (Michael Subor), a man in his seventies likely battling a heart condition, resembles the professor from Ingmar Bergman's Wild Strawberries in his effort to reconcile with past mistakes while still alive. Though physically vigorous and wealthy, he appears emotionally exhausted, with a visage marked by quiet acceptance. Our understanding of him is limited to this single perspective, adding to the film's enigmatic quality.

I've seen this film twice and intend to watch it again. It immerses you in the director's perspective on his romantic relationships and the political climate in Israel. It also moved me to tears, recalling both the beautiful moments and the tragic murder depicted in the story. Absolutely worth the watch.

This isn't your typical vampire tale—no Bram Stoker or Anne Rice here. It's a uniquely original vampire story. These vampires are genetic mutants unaffected by sunlight, and they are utterly evil.  

The movie isn't perfect; many of the actors come across as amateurs. However, the two leads—who portray Van Helsing and the vampyre girl—deliver solid performances. The film is intensely violent, which might be unsettling for some viewers. Additionally, it’s packed with scientific detail that could be confusing or tedious for many.  

I was drawn in by the clever storyline and the couple of strong performances. It’s hard to say how successful this film might be with a bigger budget and wider distribution, but it certainly shows potential.

It appears to be a biography of Claude Monet, but in truth, it is a sharply focused narrative about the relationships among three teenage girls on a French synchronized swimming team. The story features no parents or teachers, no school setting, and boys are represented by a single peripheral figure, the handsome François, who enters periodically with clear intent but always departs puzzled.

Pauline Aquart is the youngest of the trio, merely aspiring to join the team she admires so much. She has an unconventional appearance, still in the throes of her adolescence growth spurt, with long, angular limbs, oversized feet, and a lacking in curves. She has a prominent jawline and wears notably full, pursed lips. Over time, her looks grow on you, and from certain angles, she can even seem captivating.

Adele Haenel is the more mature of the three — more developed physically and striking in her swimsuit, confidently strolling around, teasing the boys, and flicking her long blond hair. Yet, she is not as straightforward as she appears. Or is she? I found her character elusive. The French are known for their paradoxes and their inconsistency. No wonder François is always sniffing.

Those who criticize this film are probably harboring bitterness from some deeply unrequited love. It’s an excellent movie for anyone who appreciates Johnny Mathis’s music or tunes from that golden era—think Bobby Darin’s “Beyond the Sea” or Stan Getz’s “The Girl From Ipanema,” among others.  

I evaluate films by how many times I need to watch them before I feel satisfied... and Chances Are kept drawing me back for multiple viewings.  

I also pay close attention to the chemistry among the cast, and I thought they worked beautifully together.  

Open your heart and allow the comedic magic of cinema to carry you away.  

— Alan

It's obvious they only spent five dollars on this production. It's a complete waste of your time—ugh. There's nothing remotely decent about this film. I honestly don't know why I kept watching. The actress isn't attractive, and the acting is terrible. You could do something much more worthwhile with your time, like watching TV or playing lousy video games. I feel completely robbed—robbed of my time. Usually, I don't bother reviewing movies, but I felt compelled to warn others before they watch this mess. I checked IMDb and read the comments, hoping for some redeeming qualities, but unfortunately, there were none. No action, no attractive characters, no budget, and awful acting—it screams "bad movie." The entire film is set in one room.

The film defies easy categorization—perhaps it’s an avant-garde spy thriller? Mother Night stands out as a highly regarded Vonnegut novel and is notably one of his works most adaptable into a feature film. The adaptation remains remarkably faithful to the original text. Its indie production approach likely proves more effective than relying on a major Hollywood studio. In today’s industry climate, a thoughtful novel like Mother Night probably wouldn't receive green light from the big studio system. While that’s often disappointing, in this instance, it works in favor of the film. With sharp direction and a strong cast, it’s a compelling watch. Nick Nolte continues to land increasingly diverse roles as he ages, maintaining that relatable “everyman” quality. Sheryl Lee is stunning and delivers her usual excellent performance. I’ve always felt she deserved more substantial opportunities in the industry. Her debut as a dead girl in Twin Peaks, with limited screen time, wasn’t exactly the most glamorous start, even if the show became a minor cultural phenomenon. Anyway, this film is thoroughly enjoyable, and you don’t need to have read the book to appreciate it.

After examining the numerous comments on this film, it becomes evident that there are two types of science fiction movie enthusiasts. The first group consists of those who are highly educated, well-read, and intellectually sharp. They are familiar with the genre's history and, more importantly, understand the heights it can achieve through the work of talented authors. For many years, science fiction was marginalized within the broader literary landscape, often dismissed as mere stories about ray guns and extraterrestrials aimed at adolescent audiences. Today’s informed fans recognize this history and are acquainted with legendary writers such as Asimov, Heinlein, Bradbury, and Ellison, who elevated science fiction beyond its humble beginnings. Their contributions fostered thought-provoking, sophisticated stories that challenged conventions and explored the essence of human existence. This knowledgeable audience tends to scrutinize Hollywood's adaptations carefully. Their critique is not born out of cynicism but from a discerning appreciation for storytelling; they approach each new release with a wary eye, rightly so, given Hollywood’s uneven track record. For these fans, the narrative holds paramount importance. They are not easily deceived by dazzling visual effects or relentless action sequences. When the emperor has...

This film was truly eye-opening. I've watched it multiple times—initially at age four, and I still remember it clearly, then again at twelve. The core message the director aims to convey is for everyone to awaken and avoid the mistake of neglecting God in our daily lives or, worse, intentionally disrespecting Him. It's a powerful movie that resonates with both believers and non-believers alike!

A film lacking moral conscience, where a drifter agrees to murder a man for a mobster in exchange for money, only to be betrayed by his employers. Meanwhile, he falls in love with the slain man's wife, unaware of his role as the killer, and moves in with her. When she eventually discovers the truth, he "accidentally" kills her. Embodying a rugged, WALKING TALL-style hero, he then seeks revenge on the mobsters who double-crossed him. However, the core issue lies in his moral descent: by accepting the hired murder, he abandons all sympathy, virtue, and heroism. His character becomes unworthy of any moral regard, making it difficult for audiences to care about him. The wife, portrayed by the attractive Kari Wuhrer—known for her role as the sheriff in EIGHT LEGGED FREAKS—initially a refined woman running a homeless mission, also loses some sympathy by quickly falling into bed with the homeless drifter, despite her weakened state after her husband's death. When she uncovers his true identity, her response—locking him inside her house (assuming all houses are secured with locks)—further diminishes her credibility and moral standing.

Twenty years ago, five-year-old Michael Hawthorne witnessed his father brutally murder his mother with an axe on an empty road before taking his own life. Now, in the present day, Michael (Gordon Currie) invites his girlfriend Peg (Stacy Grant) and his closest friends—Chris (Myc Agnew), Jennifer (Emmanuelle Vaugier), Lisa Ann (Kelly Benson), Ned (Brendon Beiser), Mitch Maldive (Phillip Rhys), and Trish (Rachel Hayward)—to spend Halloween at his grandparents' farmhouse in the countryside. He encourages his friends to wear costumes that embody their deepest fears. Alongside his Indian friend Crow (Byron Chief Moon), they plan to perform an ancient Indian ritual using a carved wooden dummy named Morty (Jon Fedele), intended to banish their fears forever. Michael's greatest fear is becoming a serial killer like his father, but when the ritual goes awry, Morty transforms into his father, slaughtering his friends.

"The Fear: Resurrection" is a disappointing and pointless slasher film that attempts to explore the idea of confronting and eradicating one's deepest fears before they take hold. Unfortunately, it is bogged down by a confusing screenplay filled with clichés. Performances vary wildly—from exaggerated portrayals like that of Betsy Palmer to some notably weak acting—ultimately failing to deliver a compelling or cohesive horror experience.

There have been difficult moments in my life when I felt lost and despondent. Watching Rancid Aluminium was one of those times.

The signs were evident from the start—no premiere (even the stars declined to attend) and a complete absence of reviews in magazines. The only reason I endured the film was in the hope of catching some sleep.

Nothing about the film was clarified; the narration was nonsensical. I momentarily cheered when it seemed the protagonist had been shot, only to be disappointed when it was revealed he hadn't, ruining my brief moment of hope. I genuinely wish all those involved in creating this film faced severe consequences for this travesty.

There were minor, unintended moments of humor. For instance, the scene where the main character, inexplicably, relieves himself manually in a toilet stall while instructing the person in the next cubicle to put their fingers in their ears.

My words cannot fully convey the anger I feel, so I will leave it at this.

Rancid Aluminium: a film for sadists, wastrels, and regressives seeking self-torture.

I watched this film approximately five years ago, and its memory continues to haunt me to this day. I was fully aware of its notorious reputation before viewing, so I only have myself to blame. However, like many others, I didn't believe all the negative reviews. As a fan of Sandler, it seemed impossible that one of his films could be truly that bad. I thought critics and haters were overreacting. I couldn't have been more mistaken.

What we have here is a comedy that contains not a single moment of genuine humor. Achieving that in itself is quite an accomplishment. You would expect that, in a 90-minute comedy, the filmmakers might have accidentally created something remotely amusing. Instead, it's simply terrible. It's not "so bad it's good"; it's just plain bad. There's no laughter provoked by its flaws—only despair. You wait in vain for a joke to even elicit a chuckle, but they never arrive.

Have you seen the movie "The Ring," where viewers watch a cursed tape and die seven days later? If this film were on that tape, people would likely die instantly, driven to despair by its sheer awfulness.

Most American war films produced during World War II were entertaining to watch but often lacked realism, as they were primarily created for propaganda purposes to boost morale on the home front. I don’t mean to criticize these films, as many remain quite enjoyable. However, their tendency to sideline authenticity prevents them from achieving true greatness. A notable example is John Garfield’s film *Air Force*, where a single B-17 nearly destroys half of the Japanese air force—a highly exaggerated scenario. In contrast, *Pride of the Marines* stands out as a refreshing departure, earning praise for its relatively accurate portrayal of a true story. When I first watched it, I thought it couldn’t be real because the events seemed too unbelievable. But after doing some research, I discovered that it was indeed based on the remarkable true story of two men who performed extraordinary acts to earn the Medal of Honor—a case where real life proved even more incredible than fiction.

discovered this film after reading the book that inspired it. While not a strictly biographical piece, it is "loosely based" on actual events. Nonetheless, I found it to be a gripping and unsettling dive into themes of evil and madness, with Michel Serrault delivering an unforgettable portrayal of Dr. Petiot.

The film is rich with memorable imagery; notably, Petiot moving through the night like a vampire, cloaked in black with his cape billowing behind him, has become almost iconic. The movie also employs elements of expressionism—Petiot's hunched silhouette ascending the stairs from the cellar where his victims' remains are prepared for cremation evokes scenes from 'Nosferatu'.

However, what captivated me most was the sound design. The soundtrack is filled with ominous tones, beginning with the dark, foreboding music of the opening credits, accompanied by wordless cries. Petiot’s clinic, set within a building housing various small shops, hums with background noises: the constant sound of knives being sharpened, a peddler playing uncanny tunes on a saw, and animal sounds—an unseen goat kept by the concierge, and distant cats wailing. Later in the film, these auditory elements continue to heighten the eerie atmosphere.

This film lacks any artistic merit worthy of recognition, and it certainly doesn't warrant an audience. Ironically, one of its few accolades is for cinematography, but to be honest, the camera work is more unsettling than impressive. Each shot feels as though you're being denied a complete view, as if the edges are being "cropped" out deliberately. The storyline is utterly disappointing. Frankly, I couldn't even bring myself to watch the entire movie. The most excruciating scene was when soldiers were partying in their barracks, and one of them encouraged another to drink liquor—scenes like these, along with many others, evoked nothing but Steven Seagal's style. 

My advice: steer clear of this trash.

Creating such a film requires a complete disregard for Nietzsche's writings and personality, a superficial understanding of psychoanalytical methods, and a lack of knowledge about Vienna's history. Pick a famous genius you haven't studied, portray him as insane, add eccentric doctors attempting to cure him, include a couple of attractive women, cast an actor with a massive mustache in the lead role, have all characters speak with exaggerated regional accents, depict absurd dreams, insert another distinguished figure like Freud who has no real connection to the first, sprinkle in a few words from his works, and exaggerate every element—especially the music. And there you have it. Audience, please steer clear.

As the nephew of the director, I’ve spent years trying to get my hands on a copy of this film, and I can confidently say it ranks among the worst movies of all time. I even asked my uncle, and he no longer has a copy himself. I'm planning to surprise him with a copy soon.  

Currently, the film holds an average rating of 1.9 out of 10. Based on that, it probably ranks in the mid-30s on IMDb’s "bottom 100," but with only 206 votes, it hasn’t officially made the list yet.  

It’s unfortunate that the film doesn’t even earn a spot among the bottom 100 titles.  

This year, I’m giving copies of the movie to family members as holiday gifts. Is this the best or worst present I’ve ever given?

Initially hesitant to join the "Lost" fandom, I accidentally watched an episode at the start of season one—the one with the polar bear—and it captured my full attention from that moment on. Not the polar bear, just the show. So please bear (pun intended) with me as I attempt to share an endless stream of somewhat chaotic but heartfelt praise.  
"Lost" takes a straightforward concept—a passenger flight crashing on a deserted island—and gradually reveals profound complexity by delving deeply into each character’s story. It explores their motivations, identities, and origins with unflinching honesty. It quickly becomes evident that the island itself serves as a unifying element in their lives—whether they’re fleeing from something (like Sawyer and Kate) or seeking spiritual connection (like Locke and Claire). Yet, "Lost" also turns its gaze inward, examining the island’s enigmatic terrors... all intricately linked in ways that keep viewers guessing.  
While TV actors aren't typically celebrated for subtlety or exceptional acting, most of the "Lost" cast are genuinely outstanding performers, bringing their characters to life with remarkable depth and authenticity.

I watched this film late on a Saturday night or early Sunday morning with my brother after a few drinks. It’s one of the most hilariously terrible movies I’ve ever seen. From the 'luxury' ocean liner that’s actually a ‘roll on, roll off’ ferry — complete with cast iron fixtures — to doors with stickers labeled 'staff' that somehow appear in different scenes, this film just rocks! The continuity is so bad you can’t help but notice it; it hits you right in the face with its flaws. In the final scene, the hero jumps off a life raft with the ferry in the background. Cut to his son and his new girlfriend — the ship’s PR director who apparently knows kung fu and used to work in the police, but was fired for doing things her way (true story) — speeding away from the explosion. Then, somehow, the father is there, hugging them. How? Who cares — it’s magic. There’s not a single redeeming feature. The casino’s the size of a large bedroom with just one table. And when the villains are chasing them, you’ve already guessed where they hide.

A series of murders plagues a remote desert town in Texas. Who's behind the carnage? The film introduces a few faint mysteries and touches on racial tensions—though the latter feels somewhat out of place. Overall, it's tailored primarily for slasher aficionados, who will enjoy the expected gore and nudity, staples of the genre. 

Dana Kimmell, known for her role in FRIDAY THE 13TH PART 3, stars as a bratty teen acting as a semi-detective. 

*1.5 out of 4 stars*

MPAA: Rated R for violence, graphic gore, nudity, and some language.

Although it's rated R, I honestly doubt you'll find much enjoyment in this film unless you're a teenager.  
 
Why? Because it lacks a coherent plot, character development, and any genuinely funny moments.  
  
The only notable aspect is the abundance of nudity—countless scenes featuring almost naked women (quite attractive, I might add) for your visual pleasure.  
  
I can't understand why this movie bears the American Pie title, as it seems to be a poor mix of an erotic film and a comedy, failing to succeed as either.  
  
My recommendation is to watch it only if you're interested in seeing nudity but feel too shy to rent or purchase an explicit film.  
  
I rated it 1 out of 10 for the two fleeting smiles I managed to crack during the movie, and another 2 out of 10 for the attractive women featured.

Once again, a cult reveals its true nature. This isn't a spoiler, since the genuine ending unfolds only after you delve into the background of those behind this excessively lengthy, pseudo-scientific infomercial—Ramtha's School of Enlightenment. Whenever a religion or philosophy feels the need to hide behind a false veneer of deception, I choose to walk away. Thank goodness I watched a borrowed copy of this film based on a friend's recommendation; spending valuable resources on this New Age mind-numbing nonsense would have been a tragedy. I can only hope that those involved truly believe they can walk on water enough to follow that belief to its logical conclusion—either walk, drown, or keep quiet. As a piece of entertainment, it barely deserves a score of 1, especially for introducing what might be the most unlikable character in film history—the photographer's roommate... truly unsettling. If you must see this film, borrow it from one of those who recommended it—perhaps to better understand the depths of their conviction.

This early Adam Sandler movie can be likened to his stand-up routines from 1989, reflecting his comedic style during that period. His character’s frequent inner monologues about possessing hidden comedic talent and frustration with his humor seem more drawn from Sandler himself than from the screenplay. Unlike his later blockbuster hits like Big Daddy or even the cheesy Billy Madison, this film falls flat. At the time, Sandler hadn’t yet mastered the art of expressing his humor consistently, which is also evident in his character’s struggles. Most of the “jokes” revolve around Sandler talking to himself, lamenting his overlooked comedic ability, obsessing over his looks, and feeling inadequate with women. The movie is uncomfortable to watch because it doesn’t treat itself like a proper film—Sandler directly addresses the camera and audience, often mentioning the low budget or questionable content. Ultimately, it feels awkward and embarrassing, leaving me eager to forget I ever saw it, fearing that revealing it might tarnish Sandler’s reputation. Skip this one altogether.

Anyone who truly had the ability to sit through this movie and come away thinking it was a good film clearly doesn't appreciate quality cinema. Watching this film was an insult; the direction resembled a high school film project, and the cinematography was equally amateurish. The Blair Witch Project had better cinematography—and I despise that movie with a passion. The storyline had the potential to be intense and compelling, yet it completely fell flat from the first ten minutes onward. Someone mentioned that the film was about a child's imagination—okay, that's fine. But even so, the script could have been executed much better. For instance, the scene in the store with the Indian idol—did the kid look at the tiny figure and suddenly imagine an Indian spirit called Wendigo? They mention it to the store clerk, who casually responds that she's the only employee there, hinting at a creepy ghost story. But then she just haggles over the idol's price, and we completely forget about the kid seeing this spirit. It all felt disjointed and poorly developed.

To everyone who thinks 1. this was a boring telecast and 2. Halle Berry and Denzel Washington didn't deserve their Oscars—shut the hell up! This was one of the most historic Academy Awards shows because it marked the moment a Black actress—Halle Berry—won the Best Actress Oscar. For too many years, our Black sisters have been overlooked by the Academy. Honestly, I had stopped watching the awards because of the lack of diversity among winners and nominees. It often felt like a group of white folks congratulating each other. The Academy had plenty of opportunities to honor talented Black actresses like Alfre Woodard, Whoopi Goldberg, Diana Ross, and Mary J. Blige, but they didn't. 

Halle Berry absolutely earned her Oscar—there was no contest. The Academy was under immense pressure to award her because deserving Black actresses have long been ignored, despite their brilliance. Most voters are white, and it's time that Black talent is recognized. Sure, Nicole Kidman sang beautifully in *Moulin Rouge*, but it was past due for Black artists to be acknowledged at these awards. As for Denzel Washington, the Academy really owed him big after that unfair treatment.

If you enjoyed Deep Cover, you'll likely appreciate this film as well. Many of the poetic monologues Fishburne delivers in Deep Cover are drawn from the lyrical screenplay of "Once In the Life," a movie adaptation of a play penned by Fishburne himself. If you're a fan of Larry like I am, you'll find this film to be a true showcase of his fiery talent—completely centered on Larry, intense, and fully developed. Naturally, it features gunplay and illicit drug use—it's a gangster film, after all—but the script is beautifully written, and the story is heartfelt, even edging into a touch of romance.  

This movie is phenomenal—dark, haunting, sexy, and exhilarating. If you ever sneaked out at night or hung around in a clubhouse, you'll fully grasp the impact of the tight, claustrophobic sets, symbolically reflecting the feeling of being trapped in that lifestyle. Rich with clever foreshadowing and intricate relationships, the film is tightly crafted, with every emotion echoed in the set design and cinematography. Truly impressive work!

May 1938. Hitler in Italy. Preparations for a momentous meeting with Mussolini. Emotions run high, tensions simmer, and the desire for self-assertion manifests in various forms. An empty town, a housewife, and a journalist—these elements intertwine to depict the meeting of two contrasting worlds. It is a refuge for a mother burdened by a sorrowful life—a brief glimpse into a classical victim’s existence. The narrative explores themes of solitude and silence, revealing life's hidden corners and the struggle to reconcile inner longing with outward resistance. A great character emerges—a book gifted on a spring afternoon, symbolizing hope and introspection. This film is a poetic work, distinguished by its capacity to portray the subtle nuances of everyday loneliness. It is a plea for an ineffable connection with reality and the inner world. Through images of Il Duce, the awkwardness of Antonietta, and the patient vulnerability of Gabriele, the director masterfully conveys a nuanced script. The exceptional performances of these two actors elevate the film to a sublime level—a delicate anticipation of subtlety and grace. A remarkable movie about hypocrisy, arbitrary judgment, the essence of life, and the oppressive nature of tyranny. Loren and Mastroianni deliver a brilliant, intelligent acting tour de force. A definitive masterpiece.

Due to the numerous negative reviews, I nearly skipped watching this film. However, I was pleasantly surprised to find it quite an enjoyable horror movie. The acting was generally unimpressive—except for the excellent Alice Krige—but some lines, like "Just consider yourself lunch," were quite amusing. Overall, it's a above-average Stephen King adaptation, earning a 7 out of 10.

Somewhere out there must exist a list of the all-time worst gay films ever made—movies filled with excessive, drawn-out shots of the stars sitting pensively in silence or painfully long close-ups of cats eating spaghetti. This particular film, a visual disorientation of a story about two boys who live, love, swim, and get lost in grottos, is a prime example. One of them has a depressed mother, while the other has no mother at all. They talk, walk, swim, have sex, get drunk, break up, and one ends up in the hospital for eight days before being discharged. The film is riddled with rapid cuts, fast-forward moments, rewind sequences, and lengthy, contemplative shots of one of the boys staring into space or simply sitting idly. It's likely a gimmick—perhaps a misguided filmmaking technique—or maybe the film is so poorly made that they drag it out with long, purposeless shots because, without them, the story would only last about 14 minutes. Don't get me wrong; this is just about the 30th gay film I...

If there was any mistake Akira Kurosawa made in creating *Dodes'ka-den*, it was partnering with the so-called "Four Knights"—Kobayashi, Ichikawa, and Konishita. They aimed for a blockbuster to launch their collaboration, but Kurosawa, arguably the leader of the group, presented an abstract, humanist art film set in a severely impoverished slum, featuring characters facing profound tragedies. Perhaps he should have produced it more independently or aligned with a different studio. This misstep, along with other financial and creative difficulties, contributed to his suicide attempt in 1971. Nonetheless, as an artist, Kurosawa remained true to his signature themes: celebrating the resilience of the human spirit amid hardship. While the unusual setting of the film should not be overlooked, it is by no means a flaw on his part.

*Dodes'ka-den* offers compelling material, though it diverges from Kurosawa’s typical style by focusing more on character than plot. There are elements...

As a Pokémon enthusiast, I thoroughly enjoyed this film. It features new legendary Pokémon, as is customary with each installment, and enriches the relationships among the characters. However, I wouldn’t expect non-Pokémon fans—most adults included—to find it equally appealing. Some of the dialogue was a bit cheesy, but that's often unavoidable when dubbing into English. The animation was stunning overall, though a few scenes fell short visually. The villain may come across as somewhat cheesy, but I appreciate how the series explores a variety of villain types, and this one definitely isn’t representative of them all. To those who didn’t enjoy it, I respect your opinion, but Pokémon fans are sure to love it.

What unfolds when a crowd of undocumented immigrants, extremists, and secular Eastern European communists rally south of the border? Naturally, Gary Busey steps in to handle the situation. Once again, Bulletproof exemplifies some of the less thoughtful remnants of Reagan-era culture, featuring a talented supporting cast led by L. Q. Jones and Thalmus Rasulala.

This is undoubtedly Lars von Trier's masterpiece—my favorite of his films. I rank it above "Breaking the Waves" and even the latest "Dancer in the Dark." I am captivated by the stunning visuals; the framing is uniquely inventive, and the performances are exceptional. A must-watch.

I believe the criticisms labeling the show as cheesy are somewhat overstated. When viewers tune into a TV show, their primary goal is usually to be entertained, unless they are critics or story analysts. Most of us watch for relaxation and enjoyment. FULL HOUSE is an excellent choice for unwinding after a long day at work or school. It brings laughter and offers more than just humor.

Certainly, the Tanner family exemplifies an idealized, perhaps fictional, family. If such a family did exist in reality, it would serve as a wonderful role model. However, this is a television show, not real life, and portraying a hypothetical family is perfectly acceptable. The fact that the show enjoyed such a lengthy run indicates that audiences appreciated it, regardless of subsequent comments.

Another noteworthy aspect is that viewers of all ages can enjoy the show and often take away a message, no matter how simple or childish it may seem. Those moments with Jesse and the others often leave a lasting impression, adding to the show's charm.

Having endured watching this film at least ten times each Christmas for the past two years because of my children, I feel sufficiently qualified to critique this adaptation of Dr. Seuss's beloved story—and honestly, it's not very good. First, attempting to follow in the footsteps of Chuck Jones's iconic animated TV special is a daunting task for anyone, but this version is so heavy-handed and bloated that it becomes almost numbingly dull. I will admit there are a few clever moments, but overall, the film feels more like a calculated attempt to cash in on the franchise, even as it claims to criticize the commercialization of Christmas. Jim Carrey's performance is typically exaggerated, but it clashes completely with the character of the Grinch. Boris Karloff’s portrayal depicted a slow-burning, sly, and methodical Grinch; Carrey’s wild antics lack any sense of that calculated nature. This fundamental misstep is just the tip of the iceberg. Talented actors like Jeffrey Tambor and Christine Baranski are completely underused here. Why, Universal, why? I understand that actors like Anthony Hopkins are willing to take on almost any role, much like Michael Caine, but this particular role should have been passed over.

Not only was this the most expensive Canadian film ever shot in BC, but it was also arguably the worst, never making it to general release. The director isn't even Canadian—he's British—and that clearly shows. The film portrays Canadians as a bunch of over-sexed, drug-obsessed fools, completely lacking the spirit of what it means to be Canadian—something supposedly justifying its funding. Naturally, the British characters come across as normal, while the rest are a parade of sitcom stereotypes—can you say "Norm"? The cinematography varies from picturesque postcard scenes to dim, indoor silhouettes. The actors often appear restless, fidgeting throughout. Are they just as bored as the audience, or is this the director’s idea of cinema? Steer clear of this mess and instead watch films by Bruce McDonald, a true Canadian filmmaker with fresh, original stories to tell. His movies won't have you wanting to walk out after ten minutes.

This film ranks among the worst I've ever seen. I attended the premiere at SXSW and left completely disappointed. The director demonstrated a surprising lack of knowledge about John Lennon, even admitting as much during the event. While intended to be a drama, the movie was riddled with cheesy moments that elicited laughs from the audience—never a good sign. The only bright spots were Dominic Monaghan and Jason Leonard, who played Livien's roommates and bandmates; their humor provided some relief amid the overly earnest tone of the rest of the film. The awkward and gratuitous inclusion of Beatles lyrics was particularly laughable. On a positive note, the soundtrack was excellent and arguably the film’s highlight. Unless you're a hardcore Dominic Monaghan fanatic, I wouldn’t recommend wasting your time on this one.

"Fear of a Black Hat" is an expertly made film that had me laughing almost nonstop from beginning to end. If you have the opportunity, I wholeheartedly suggest watching this movie—it's hands down the funniest film I've ever seen. Don't miss out—go grab your copy!

Why should you delve into the captivating nature documentary "Earth"? How much time do you have to truly appreciate its wonders? I won't stretch my review endlessly, but I must emphasize why this film is an absolute "must watch." "Earth" takes viewers on a breathtaking journey along the migration routes of three remarkable animal families: a female polar bear and her cubs, with a compelling subplot of the father bear bravely hunting for food on his solitary path; a mother whale and her calf embarking on an epic migration in search of prey; and an elephant mother guiding her young (who may be larger than they seem) across the African landscape. Directors Alastair Fothergill and Mark Linfield have crafted a "out of this world" achievement, masterfully capturing not only mesmerizing scenes but also the incredible survival skills of numerous species beyond the three featured families. The cinematography team—Richard Brooks Burton, Mike Holding, Adam Ravetch, and Andrew Shillabeer—demonstrated extraordinary talent behind the camera, capturing awe-inspiring natural landscapes and instinctive animal behaviors. Their skill in slow-motion shots of prey, in particular, elevates the film to a whole new level of cinematic excellence.

The romantic element of the film, which serves as its central theme, is well-crafted and effectively conveyed. However, the context surrounding the love story is overly poetic, visually stylized, and unrealistic. Additionally, the main character's psychology is peculiar and difficult to understand, culminating in a conclusion that feels similarly perplexing. If the film piqued your interest, I recommend giving it a watch, but manage your expectations accordingly.

I'm not surprised that even cowgirls get the blues if this film is any indication. I had higher expectations from Uma Thurman, which is why I endured this experience in the first place. Unfortunately, it’s a terrible movie with only the music as a redeeming feature. It's a pity that we can't rate it zero out of ten in these reviews—this film truly deserves it.

This film is quite lengthy at 2 hours and 20 minutes, but it covers a significant portion of Pearl Buck’s renowned novel. In other words, there's a lot of ground to cover. At times, it has a soap-opera feel, but it also features visually striking moments, culminating in an impressive locust swarm scene that was truly remarkable to watch. Considering the film's age—around 70 years old—the special effects team did an outstanding job. 

Paul Muni and Luise Rainer, both esteemed actors of their era, deliver compelling performances that do not disappoint. However, the film's credibility is somewhat compromised by the casting choices: all the Asian characters are played by Caucasian actors, and some, like Walter Connolly, don't quite look convincing. I would love to see a remake featuring an all-Asian cast—not for political correctness, but to enhance the authenticity and believability of the story.

Thomas Clay has been associating with the wrong crowd. That’s the problem with young people nowadays—they seem to lack respect.

Honestly, this film should be avoided at all costs. The majority of the action is slow, dull, and meanders toward a drug-fueled ending as if the director himself has nowhere better to go. We are introduced to the protagonist, an outsider who struggles to fit in both at school and at home, feeling awkward—just like many teenagers do. Robert drifts with a rough crowd, skips school, and starts using drugs, eventually spiraling into violence and sexual assault.

The real issue with this film is Clay's complete misunderstanding of the relationship between violent imagery and violent behavior. He appears to believe that a generation of disturbed youth is sparked by war scenes on TV. Meanwhile, he has created some of the most grotesque simulated violence on screen. Is he serious?

If Clay hasn’t seen YouTube, perhaps he’s naive or unaware of what can be done with brutal scenes like the climactic one.

Emily Watson’s portrayal of Natalia is unquestionably the most tender and romantic protagonist I have ever seen on screen. She stands as the undeniable queen of this film—yet, could she be transformed into the king? The intricate interplay of the chess matches and the families' relentless quest for dominance, influence, and victory is truly mesmerizing. Just as the film’s chess masters strategize, the director orchestrates multiple layers of complexity, weaving them into overarching or subtle motifs. The setting—the early 20th-century Italian lakeside district—is rendered with stunning authenticity, from period costumes to evocative imagery. Every inch of the scene is meticulously crafted, with no space left unfilled.  

There are so many remarkable moments throughout that I couldn’t possibly list them all. I recommend setting aside enough time to watch this film twice, perhaps a week apart, as one viewing cannot fully grasp the layered poetry within its 64 squares—each one multi-dimensional and richly textured.  

Although I haven't read Nabokov’s original novel, I’d compare this film to another poetry-infused game of romance—Barry Levinson’s *The Natural*. Like the film, it abandons the darker, tragic ending of Malamud’s novel in favor of a more romantic, impressionistic vision, celebrating triumph and hope.

This movie is truly pointless! Rachel Griffiths must have been desperate for cash. It feels like the film was shot on a shoestring budget, given the complete lack of proper lighting. I swear, if I ever meet Pete Postlethwaite again, I might as well end it all. I’d love to know—was there even a plot or a script? My greatest regret is wasting my time on this garbage.

Can you say "All shock, no plot"? This film was filled with unexplored avenues. There was almost no backstory about the room beyond the deaths associated with it. *Why* was it inherently evil? What caused its malevolence? Why was there an "hour" countdown? Additionally, there were several hints at mysteries left unaddressed—for instance, we saw a camera in the air vent that was mentioned, yet when the character climbed into the vent, the camera was nowhere to be found.  

Furthermore, all the ghosts appeared "digital," and objects "winked out" before hitting the ground, accompanied by static noises. When you consider all these elements together, Room 1408 resembles a high-tech haunted house—yet, there was no further exploration or explanation for this.  

And let’s not forget—electronics don't function in 1408... well, except for the TV. The cell phone has no signal, but the wireless internet works perfectly. How many inconsistencies can one film cram in? Honestly, this movie was just a series of "shock after shock," much like countless others before it—mirrors reflecting strange images, things just out of sight, shifting paintings, bleeding walls, the classic "it was all just a dream" twist, only to deny it later. If the room...

I watched this movie with my girlfriend after randomly coming across it while flipping through channels.  

We both were hoping for a sweet, feel-good Christmas family film, but we were deeply disappointed.  

The actor portraying the soldier seems to have zero emotion; his face remains expressionless whether he's chopping down Christmas trees, witnessing his love interest being kissed by her boyfriend, or reacting happily to her surprise. He's a terrible actor, and we couldn't help but laugh at his performance throughout.  

Then there's the cute blonde girl, who apparently has the odd talent of counting dots and is also unfaithful to her boyfriend—what a catch! Her life's ambition seems to be living with her parents and counting more dots.  

Essentially, the story is about an emotionally detached guy falling for a girl who counts dots and cheats on her boyfriend. It's as predictable as it gets and a complete waste of time. Watching it offers nothing but some awkward laughs because everything is so cheesy.  

I did enjoy when her dad mentioned that he only eats French fries and nothing else.

I might be one of the few who truly stuck with this film. I also saw it when it first came out, and I agree with the previous comment that Up The Academy was truly ahead of its time. The humor in the movie is pure MAD Magazine style. I don’t understand why MAD would endorse this film. It was also one of the few movies from the early '80s to feature a killer soundtrack, showcasing the punk and new wave bands emerging from L.A. at the time. I own the soundtrack and listen to it constantly even now. Honestly, there are definitely worse movies out there. I don't think Porky's is as funny as Up The Academy; however, it has some genuine laughs, mostly revolving around stereotypes or sex jokes. But hey, nobody expected this to be The Maltese Falcon.

I'm not a dedicated John Cleese collector (though I did find "Fawlty Towers" to be brilliant), but I am a fan. When I noticed this sitting neglected on a shelf at my local Blockbuster, I decided to give it a shot. What I discovered was a delightful surprise—one of the funniest 50-minute viewing experiences I've ever had. The writing features classic British "goon show" humor. In fact, as an audio sketch, it could easily fit on a "Firesign Theater" album. However, the sharpness of the execution and impeccable timing elevate "Strange Case" into a performance that can turn viewers into lifelong British comedy enthusiasts.  

British comedy has a unique talent for blending broad satirical parody with keenly observed character quirks and precise timing, and the creators use both masterfully here. Cleese's portrayal of "Holmes" bears a resemblance to the antics of Arkin's and Sellers' "Inspector Clouseau," but Cleese’s exceptional talent for physical comedy ensures he holds his own. The real standout, however, is Arthur Lowe, who plays "Watson" as a friendly but utterly clueless fool—delivering his lines with such impeccable timing that he becomes the most memorable part of the performance.

Do you remember the early days of Pay-Per-View? I do, and I can almost recall the number you had to call to rent a movie on your TV. As a kid, we often wanted to rent Playboy, but that meant actually calling PPV and asking for it. Summoning the courage to do that led to four hours of softcore, no-angle content—you know the drill. I bring this up because this movie was also on PPV. I remember nearly every scene from the trailer. Lately, I've been on a quest to find all the great movies I enjoyed as a kid, and this one is among them. It's one of those films that’s hard to turn off once it starts. It features an all-star cast attempting the perfect bank heist, but everything keeps going wrong. Along with many spoof bank capers, this one stands out, offering enough action and humor to keep things lively. Dare to check it out!

Honestly, this approach isn’t beneficial for the Australian film industry. Making movies that lack any meaningful values doesn’t advance our reputation. If you're just a stoner with too much free time, perhaps. I believe our filmmakers should focus on showcasing the incredible talent we have to the world, and this isn’t the way to do it. Let’s be honest—this film comes off as cheap and tacky.

First off, I never considered myself an Uwe Boll critic since I hadn't even seen any of his films. However, after watching the so-called movie "Seed"—which is supposedly about a serial killer by that name—I find myself on the verge of joining the haters. The film makes absolutely no sense; the plot is a complete joke. While Boll clearly aims to shock and grab attention, 90% of this movie is just plain dull. Here's a summary of what you'll encounter: 

1. A hooded killer watches footage of animals being tortured on TV. This is real footage from pelt farms, and the film awkwardly opens with a nonsensical attempt to make a "statement about humanity," even including a PETA address. Since the film lacks any meaningful message and indulges in the worst kind of torture porn exploitation, there's already plenty to dislike from the start.

2. The killer is electrocuted, with a cliche scene that reveals what happens later in the film—it's so blatant that even the slowest viewers will get it.

3. Police watch disturbing videos of animals, babies, and women suffering from starvation, adding to the film’s aimless and grotesque content.

John Carpenter's Halloween stands as a true horror classic. It chronicles the timeless tale of the escaped mental patient Michael Myers, who returns to his hometown on Halloween night to haunt and kill a group of babysitters.  

This film is both the first and arguably the finest entry in the Halloween series. Carpenter demonstrates remarkable restraint, carefully pacing the story with a slow build and developing sympathetic characters—an uncommon approach in horror films.  

What makes it even more remarkable is the absence of excessive blood and gore, yet it remains one of the most terrifying Halloween movies to date. Quite an achievement!  

Halloween also marked the film debut of Jamie Lee Curtis and represented a pivotal moment in the late great Donald Pleasance's career. A genuine masterpiece.

While watching this movie on video last night, I couldn't help but feel a series of tingles that hinted this film was destined to last. I have a strong sense that I’ll find myself revisiting it countless times over the years. 

It possesses all the enduring qualities one expects from a great story or film. Although certain cultural references are somewhat obscure to me as a Western viewer, at its heart, this is a timeless and universal tale.

Disowned by Richard C. Sarafian, this disaster debuted in Japanese cinemas before making its way to the United States, where it was quickly relegated to home video. It wasn't seen again until the Turner networks, desperate to fill their late-night slots between 3 a.m. and 6 a.m., unearthed this tape from the bottom of their storage bins. The Smithee alias is traditionally reserved for films so badly mishandled by studios that the director renounces his involvement, but in this case, Sarafian can't entirely blame the studio. The cast, mostly recent graduates of "Overacting 101," deliver one absurdly cheesy line after another. The storyline is complicated and confusing, the special effects unimpressive, and the parts that aren’t outright laughable are simply dull. The script or source material must have been promising—why else would Palance, Matheson, Boyle, or Heston agree to star in such a fiasco? Yet, something went terribly awry in translation from page to screen. Bottom line: Avoid. It’s not even bad enough to be entertaining as a so-bad-it’s-good flick.

In the traditional sense of the four humors—though not specifically tied to humor or entertainment—Altman's "H.E.A.L.T.H." explores each of these elements in surprisingly humorous and engaging ways. The Phlegm is embodied by Lauren Bacall's reserved, cautious Esther Brill, whose primary concern seems to be preserving her youthful appearance and hiding her age rather than her health. Paul Dooley portrays the Choleric Dr. Gil Gainey, who flails about like a fish—perhaps more a seal—frantically barking and urging crowds to embrace his aquatic chaos. Glenda Jackson's melancholy Isabella Garnell channels a Shakespearean Hamlet—troubled, self-righteous, and delivering a soliloquy or two. Henry Gibson's Bile character, Bobby Hammer, proclaims that "the breast that feeds the baby rules the world." Meanwhile, Harry Wolff and Gloria Burbank, played by James Garner and Carol Burnett, are relatively sane figures seeking some equilibrium amid the chaos of the other humors—a sort of global H.E.A.L.T.H. organization that, paradoxically, has little to do with actual health.

I was in France around March 5th and have always enjoyed attending film festivals. Although I knew about Cinémas d'Amérique Latine de Toulouse, I had never visited it before. I finally decided to go and ended up watching "Cero y Van 4."  

The film is visually stunning. While it didn't resonate with me as strongly as it did with Mexican viewers—mainly because it was French subtitled—it still left a deep impression.  

This movie is a satirical take on urban violence, focusing on kidnapping and crime on the streets of Mexico. It offers a raw and unfiltered portrayal of the city—a true metropolis. Similar themes are explored in "Secuestro Express," featuring the remarkable Mia Maestro. While that film also satirizes kidnapping, it does so with a more serious tone and perhaps has some thematic links to "Cero y Van 4." Both films could be seen as stories of redemption, raising questions about how much is too much.  

"Man on Fire" was equally powerful—intensely gripping—though not a satire, but a stark depiction of Mexico's streets. Similarly, "The Brave One" shocks and hits you hard, delivering a visceral experience.  

In terms of storytelling, "The Usual Suspects" comes to mind, with its intricate plot twists and turns that keep you guessing.

Firstly, there is no hint of flirting in this film—none involving Anthony or anyone else. These characters don't flirt; they simply do. Your initial challenge is to endure over fifteen minutes of intense violence and sexual perversion. While I personally enjoy a bit of violence and perversion, without any meaningful context, it comes across as utterly repellent. After surviving the torture and chaos, we are introduced to Donna, and the film shifts into something entirely different—not better, just different: a road movie lacking any real emotional core. The attempts at comedy are weak, largely due to cameos played broadly by actresses like Judy Tenuta and Mink Stole, along with a few sex workers and drag performers. They all deserve more than this. The cinematography is deliberately disorienting; if you suffer from motion sickness or any kind of illness, this film is definitely not for you. Honestly, I’m not sure who this movie is really meant for—perhaps gay and bisexual S&M enthusiasts who enjoy poorly written, badly shot independent films about themselves.

What an extraordinary autumn for Sean Ellis.

You gather a group of friends at your place, all buzzing with anticipation for Sean Ellis's latest project. Your knowledge of the storyline is vague—no spoilers to spoil the surprise—just sky-high expectations.

It's late at night, the perfect setting for this kind of film.

Fifteen minutes in, you tell yourself it will soon pick up; by twenty-five, you're contemplating whether to just call it a night and save your full attention for another viewing, when you can truly appreciate the subtle details you’re sure are there. After half an hour, you realize that half of your excited audience has already nodded off, and you decide to end it.

A few days later, with all other options exhausted, you revisit the film during daylight, hoping a different mood will keep you engaged. Ten minutes in, you're fast-forwarding through the overly long, unnecessary scene transitions and images. Normally, you'd have given up by now, but there's something about the legacy—like cashback—that keeps you going. Still, even that legacy has its limits.

This is probably one of the worst films I have ever watched. I couldn't care less about the critics' opinions; it genuinely misses the mark. I believe the issue stems from Kundera's novel. It's not that his work can't be adapted to the screen; rather, like 99% of his writing, it's pretentious and excessively drawn out. He appears to be self-obsessed, with his characters often engaging in navel-gazing, and his novels generally exude misogyny. I've read many of his works, including his Socialist Realist poetry—which was truly dreadful—and I simply don't understand what all the hype is about. The traits, such as self-absorption, make his novels painfully irritating to read. In film form, all the qualities I dislike about Kundera are amplified. Perhaps I missed something, but I doubt it. On a different note, I can't believe this is a Criterion Collection DVD—there's no way this movie is THAT essential.

Reunion shows come in various forms. One type involves bringing back aging actors to reprise characters they haven't portrayed in twenty or thirty years. These tend to vary in quality. For instance, "Return to Mayberry" was somewhat entertaining despite some silly moments; in contrast, "Return to Green Acres" was disastrous—Eddie Albert reportedly used a word for the script I won't repeat, and both the show and the movie were poor. "Rescue from Gilligan's Island" addressed a necessary gap in the storyline of the castaways, though even from a "Gilligan's Island" perspective, it was still rather silly. Generally, these scripts are weak; sometimes they contain a level of silliness that seems overly knowing—and in comedy, it’s almost always detrimental when characters are aware they’re funny. New characters added to the mix often feel out of place. Overall, most of these reunion shows are quite underwhelming. 

A second type of "reunion" program features the cast setting aside their past characters to sit together, share stories, reminisce, and occasionally include flashbacks from the original shows. Then there are movies based on the series, which tend to be disappointing, and films inspired by the show's history itself. For example, "The Brady Bunch" has...

I rated Timecop a perfect 10, but this one gets a 1. The story is incredibly dull and bears little resemblance to the original Timecop. Much of the original plot was cut, replaced by foolish new elements. The story is set in 2060 (if I recall correctly), yet for some reason, time travel has become even more perilous :confused:. As for the action scenes, most are disappointing—only the first stands out—there are hardly any, and they’re all quite brief. At one point, the protagonist seems to jump through time about five times in just a few minutes… actually, wait—make that two times. In short: don’t bother watching this movie; it’s not worth your time.

This feels like one of those films we assume we'll enjoy, but I didn't. It seemed to be overextending itself in a desire to appear 'artsy,' relying heavily on flashy visuals without much substance. While it features some stunning scenes that are pleasant to watch individually, putting them all together makes it a chore to sit through. I rented it based on the rave reviews on the box and my love for Shakespeare, but I was ultimately disappointed. I found it somewhat pretentious and, at times, dull.

After Harry Reems' teenage girlfriend is assaulted by Zebbedy Colt (The Night-Walker), Reems falls into despair and seeks comfort through encounters with some lesbians. Meanwhile, Colt, who wields a cane and dresses like a magician, continues to assault more women. Eventually, Reems decides to pursue him and put an end to his spree. The film features scenes of shooting and some disturbing content but otherwise resembles a typical 70s adult film and is poorly executed. The scenes depicting rape and abuse are surprisingly muted, and the attempt to capitalize on "Death Wish" comes off as comical. R. Bolla ("Cannibal Holocaust") appears as a police officer. While Colt, usually exaggerated, loses his composure in a few scenes, overall he's too restrained for my taste. This roughie could have been much more intense.

Ugh! My brain feels shattered! And honestly, after enduring this film, I can’t say I’m surprised. I have no idea how I managed to stay tuned without hitting the fast-forward button—only the gods know.  

Maybe it’s just me! Maybe I don’t understand the premise, or perhaps I’m not meant to appreciate its supposed mystical vibe. But in my honest opinion, the film’s mystical atmosphere is about as convincing as a trip to McDonald’s.  

Moreover, the characters were utterly dreadful; there’s more depth in a Tom & Jerry cartoon. Ugh! Why do I put myself through this? Why do I watch such junk? It’s enough to make anyone consider running away to a monastery or joining the Foreign Legion! Yikes! This was an absolutely terrible film in nearly every way.  

But—despite everything—there’s a tiny part of me that thinks it’s not all bad.

This is truly an excellent film that I’ve enjoyed watching multiple times. Michael Caine delivers another fantastic performance, as always. Although Caine has developed a reputation for accepting roles in movies of varying quality, he’s particularly compelling in his portrayal of Sidney. From the very beginning, the screenplay is so well-crafted. Who would have guessed that Ira Levin, known for his chilling works like The Boys from Brazil and Rosemary’s Baby, could also write something so sharp and witty? Let’s be honest—starring Michael Caine, Christopher Reeve, Dyan Cannon, and Henry Jones—it's hard to go wrong with such a stellar cast, especially under Sidney Lumet’s direction.

I hesitate to say too much because revealing any details would truly be a crime. Just watch the film and enjoy it to the fullest.

Oh my goodness! Few horror movies have bored or made me laugh as much as this one. It kicks off with a lively and intriguing premise but quickly devolves into nothing more than a slasher film, sprinkled with some supernatural and sexual elements. Alice Krige, usually outstanding, is squandered here, and the plot twists are utterly absurd. Only watch if you're truly desperate. Rating: 3/10.

I watched this film during Joe Bob Briggs's Monstervision on TNT. Even he couldn't make it watchable. The only reason I stuck with it until the end was because I teach video production and wanted to ensure my students never produce something this terrible... but it took all my strength to endure it. It’s like witnessing your great-grandmother flirting with a 15-year-old—utterly excruciating.

Honestly, if you took the actual film, dipped it in paint thinner, and watched it, you’d find that more entertaining. No joke.

If you come across this movie in the bargain bin at S-Mart, steer clear as if it were a venomous snake.

Typically, I wouldn't choose to watch a Farrelly Brothers film—I can't even remember ever doing so. The same goes for Jimmy Fallon movies; I haven't seen many. The only exception might be "Taxi," which I watched and subsequently felt I owed an apology for. However, this movie featured Drew Barrymore, and I think she's absolutely adorable. There's something about her that makes me smile the entire time she's on screen—she just has that effect on me. In fact, I even watched "50 First Dates" partly just to see her, even if it meant sitting through Adam Sandler's performance. How sad is that? This wasn't exactly a top-tier baseball movie, nor was that its aim. Instead, it told a heartfelt love story about a lonely soul who clung to the one thing that never let him down—until he found something truly worth risking everything for. The ending was predictable, but the journey there was filled with enough moments to make it truly worthwhile.

It's a bit embarrassing that I just watched this film for the first time, 13 years after it came out. The story resonates with any father or brother—one brother's a bit 'wild,' while the other is the classic older sibling. Craig Sheffer's portrayal as the older brother feels a little detached emotionally, but Brad Pitt delivers an outstanding performance, and James Spader is perfectly cast as the father. The fishing scenes shot in Montana are absolutely stunning—I never realized fly fishing could be so captivating. The film stays true to the book, with only minor tweaks to suit the cinematic format. Unlike many adaptations, it actually lives up to the source material. It's an ideal choice for a peaceful evening—quiet yet emotionally powerful.

This film features the funniest jokes of all the Cheech & Chong movies. It was the first one I ever watched with these guys, and I thought it was really great. My dad actually recommended I get it, which was pretty awesome. Even my grandma bought it for me, knowing exactly what it was—what a family! Overall, this movie is quite good and makes a great rental when you're craving a classic comedy. However, I should mention that it's not side-splittingly hilarious; it has its funny moments but doesn't reach the level of humor in Something About Mary. Still, I think you'll enjoy it and get a good laugh—unless you're someone who opposes all drug-related humor or something.

A complete waste of my time. The director should feel embarrassed. I can't understand why anyone would think making such pointless movies is worthwhile. When she died at the end, I couldn't help but laugh. I had to switch channels several times during the film because I felt embarrassed by the poor acting. I sincerely hope the actor who played Heath never works again. Additionally, I hope the director never makes another film and that his paycheck for this mess is revoked.Rating: 0.2 out of 10

This film fails to capture interest, with only scattered glimpses of nudity attempting to jolt viewers into engagement—though ultimately, they fall flat. The highlight is Lena Olin, who delivers a compelling and skillful portrayal of her character. In contrast, Daniel Day-Lewis struggles with clarity, often muddling his lines. Director Kaufman seems uncertain about how to approach the storytelling, as the abrupt shifts between personal domestic conflicts and political upheavals feel jarringly mismatched. Character motivations shift inexplicably, leaving the narrative feeling disjointed and poorly cohesive.

I approached "Still Crazy" without much expectation, assuming it to be just another rock'n'roll film—perhaps a nostalgic nod to the baby boomers. While it does contain elements of that, it offers so much more. Director Brian Gibson, known for his successful biopic of Tina Turner, brings a distinctive style to the project. Interestingly, this turned out to be his final film.

The cast is brilliantly cast. Bill Nighy excels as the band's lead singer, capturing the essence of the character perfectly. Actor-turned-director Bruce Robinson makes a notable appearance as the band's aging guitarist, delivering a remarkable performance despite his long absence from the big screen since the late 1970s. If you're in the mood for a heartfelt, humorous film with some fantastic songs, this is definitely worth watching.

Rating: 7.4 out of 10

For my 8th birthday, I received the book version of Kazaam. People often say that book adaptations are always better than the movies, but in this case, they were wrong. At least with the movie, it’s over quickly.  

The acting is terrible, which I expected from a film starring Shaquille O’Neal as a magical, rapping genie who emerges from an old ghetto blaster—probably because there was a good reason he was trapped inside it. The kid portraying Max is whiny and a terrible actor. He gets bullied by neighborhood kids, which I don’t blame them for, since he’s kind of a little douchebag.  

The plot is just plain dumb and overly cliché—a boy whose father is always working and never around finds a new friend who improves his life and, in the end, helps him reconnect with his dad.  

Even at 8 years old, I thought this was a stupid story. It's a surprise that anyone involved in making this film continued their careers afterward, because it’s embarrassing and should never have been made. I could go on about how much this movie sucks, but I’ll leave it at that.

This film was terrible! It must have been competing with some real duds to earn a Golden Globe nomination. They distorted the story of the first renowned female Renaissance painter beyond recognition. My issue isn't with them taking creative liberties—if the story had been compelling, that would be understandable. But what really baffles me is how the true story—arguably a much better basis for a film—was ignored in favor of this dull, uninspired script. Perhaps they thought the real tale lacked enough nudity to attract viewers. The movie awkwardly wraps up with a quick summary of the artist’s life—honestly, we could have spared ourselves a couple of hours if they had simply kept it brief throughout.

In reality, it's essentially the same movie, and they couldn’t even get the timeline of events right. Perhaps that was intentional, born of laziness or apathy. Either way, this film is a complete letdown and doesn’t even deserve to be called a movie. I watched it as a so-called second feature on the disc that also includes the original The Boogeyman. It was so bad that I felt my head might explode. I strongly advise you to steer clear of this disaster if you happen to stumble upon it—you’d be wise to run in the opposite direction. It should come with a warning label like: "Caution—may cause a significant drop in your IQ if you’re nearby." For me, there’s no doubt: this film is a solid 0 out of 10.

In my opinion, this is a rather quirky film filled with plenty of humor. I wouldn't classify it as particularly frightening, but rather entertaining—especially if you're a fan of horror movies. The Scarecrow reminded me somewhat of "Children of the Corn," though not entirely. When comparing the two, I found this one much more enjoyable to watch. =)

Alright, alright, don’t get all uptight. I was just joking.

In any case, “Bustin’ Out” is actually a much better and more accurate title.

Our satirical critique of racism and crime dramas comes through loud and clear from our X-rated animator buddy Ralphie Boy. And he’s really on top of his game here.

When it comes to crime, it reflects the truth: they build their empire, defend it fiercely, then boredom and tougher competitors threaten to tear it down. Check it out yourself to see what unfolds.

As for racism? Who knows? With Scatman (RIP) and the love walrus (also RIP) being Black and serving as the main perspectives, I took it as primarily an attack on racism. Plus, Richard Pryor’s approval speaks volumes. And it was a pleasant surprise to see young Phil Mike Thomas, pre-“Miami Vice.”

This is an animated “Blacksploitation” film—and that’s a good thing. Done skillfully, it leaves a strong impression. It’ll make some viewers uncomfortable, especially during the lynching scene, but unfortunately, that’s rooted in reality.

Still, Ralphie really should have given that title a second thought.

Last night, I finally watched "Starlight" on TV, and all I can say is... wow! It's tough to know where to start—perhaps with the hilariously cheesy special effects, like the laser beams emanating from Willie's eyes, or the dreadful acting, the sluggish dialogue, the mismatched stock footage, or the overall sense of earnest pretentiousness that permeates the entire film. It’s truly a unique experience, and I think we should all be grateful for that. I’d even go so far as to nominate Jonathon Kay as the modern-day successor to Ed Wood!

What can I say? I ignored the reviews and decided to see it for myself. Turns out, the reviews were spot-on. It was a total waste of money, especially given its budget.
