Fortunately, I watched Kill Bill afterward, which was a much better choice.  

If you're looking for a genuinely scary movie, I recommend Crossroads!  

In the end, I honestly prefer "Girl in Gold Boots" over this disappointing film.

I completely agree with jamrom4. This was the worst movie I have ever seen—absolutely terrible. I was warned not to watch it, but I was foolish enough to go ahead anyway. About ten minutes in, I couldn't stand it anymore and wanted to turn it off, but I forced myself to sit through the entire film just to see if it would get better. Sadly, it didn’t. The movie was disgusting—nothing of substance happened, and the ending was overly preachy. A film this bad doesn’t deserve to exist. I urge everyone to save themselves from the nightmare that is "Fatty Drives the Bus." If only I had listened to the warnings, I could have spared myself this ordeal. Those who rated it highly probably had a hand in making it—and honestly, they should all be erased from the planet.

This is by far my favorite movie ever. I've watched it at least ten times, and I still find myself crying every single time. My family often pleads with me not to watch it so I won't get emotional. I deeply admire that it’s based on a true story written by Antwone himself; I love the story just as much as I love the film. The acting is exceptional, and every actor was perfectly cast. Denzel Washington is one of my favorite actors, but this film remains his best work in my opinion. 

I once cared for a little boy who was also born in jail—a truly precious child, the sweetest I’ve ever met. Fortunately, he was adopted by an incredible family after nearly two years of fighting for him. I watched this movie while his adoption was still uncertain, and I’m overjoyed that he is now safe, loved, and cared for. It also warms my heart to see Antwone happy and reunited with his family. 

I would love to learn more about him and how life has been since he met his family. I simply cannot express how much I love this story and everything about it!

I’ve never been a fan of Farrah Fawcett... until now. She delivered an truly remarkable performance in this film. The emotional toll she must have endured through countless re-takes is almost unimaginable. Watching this movie was profoundly difficult—the subject matter is deeply disturbing, and it’s almost unbearable to sit by helplessly as a woman endures prolonged abuse. I felt the impact waned somewhat when her friends returned to the house, and I found the ending somewhat unconvincing. The director clearly favored using height in his shots and frequently employed mirror reflections, but I believe he could have improved the pacing in the latter half. While I’m sure this would be a powerful theatrical experience, for me, the film, despite its strengths, ultimately fell short.

Save yourself the trouble and don’t bother renting this trash. I’m honestly baffled at how it even got produced. (Not sure why there’s a requirement for at least 10 lines—I've already summarized how terrible this movie is, but here we go...) The acting was garbage, as if they all skipped their lessons. The storyline was flimsy, and the ending? Completely underwhelming. To their credit, the cinematography was the only aspect that didn’t completely suck — maybe the sound quality was passable too. The only silver lining is that if they managed to make this movie and even turn a profit, it gives hope for any screenwriter with a genuine idea. So, stay encouraged! The same goes for actors: if these folks got paid for this, then there’s hope for you too!

POTENTIAL SPOILERS:

Wow, this film was really disappointing. A Catholic/superstitious/suspense thriller that rehashes familiar tropes from earlier movies.

The familiar themes include the doubting priest, issues of sex and the priesthood, politics intertwined with religion, church hypocrisy, and conspiracies involving ecclesiastical power. It also delves into a supposed new age of darkness, with scenes of dark magic and voodoo battles between good and evil.

Overall, it felt quite foolish and poorly developed, with a weak plot that served as an excuse for the clichés. The story primarily hinges on two concepts: Absolution, specifically the Sacrament of Anointing the Sick—last rites that offer forgiveness before death—and Excommunication, the act of expelling someone from the church. Essentially, an excommunicated person cannot receive absolution. This introduces the character of the Sin Eater, but I won't spoil further. Combine all these elements, and you get "The Order."

The scene involving a priest's sexual encounter, intercut with images of the Virgin Mary, struck me as disrespectful to Catholics. It concludes with Heath Ledger's character declaring (roughly paraphrased), "I am the redeemer and damner of sins, I live on without love," before walking into darkness.

Haha! So this is the film that the "Next Action Stars" were about to dive into. Glad I didn't get involved or come out as a winner...

Isn't it amusing how just ten seconds into a movie can often be enough to judge it? Seriously! Just check out those titles! I caught this movie—or rather a segment of it—one evening during my military service. The audience with me was a mixed bag of average guys who occasionally watch shows like Las Vegas, mainly for the eye candy. So, the bar wasn’t exactly set high. The most popular film among us was Girl Next Door—and that was barely for the storytelling, if you catch my drift. This movie's total lack of originality, weak acting, poor scripting, and everything else that makes a film worthwhile made it an easy choice to switch over to Las Vegas—or was it CSI? I can't quite remember—without any complaints from the group. And that’s saying something!

For goodness’ sake, avoid this movie! If it happens to be on TV, just change the channel.

I'm concerned that most of those who rate this film a perfect 10 are predominantly Christian. I am not. If you're seeking a film with a Christian theme, I would recommend this one. However, if you're looking for a well-rounded, general movie, you might want to look elsewhere.

I found the characters frustrating due to their illogical actions. The core premise suggests that teaching morality without acknowledging Jesus as its foundation is inherently flawed. There's a scene where the protagonist tells a boy that stealing is wrong, and then claims that Jesus was the one who taught us this. I find this offensive—are we to believe that the commandment "Thou shalt not steal" originated with Jesus? Did he write the Ten Commandments? Was theft acceptable before that? I rented this film through Netflix and should have anticipated its nature from the reviews. Oh well.

This film is not only highly entertaining, featuring stellar comedic performances, but also offers a compelling political commentary. Created toward the end of the Soviet Union, it satirizes the Soviet mentality from start to finish. Set during the early days of the Soviet regime, the story questions the underlying logic of the revolution—both culturally and practically. By the late 1980s and early 1990s, the rigid constraints of Soviet society had begun to loosen, yet the underlying ideology and mindset persisted, providing rich material for sharp deconstruction. Fortunately, all these profound philosophical insights are delivered within a humorous and engaging framework!

I absolutely loved this film! As a devoted Tom Hanks fan, I've always admired his diverse body of work. His performances in intense roles like Cast Away, The Green Mile, Saving Private Ryan, Forrest Gump, Apollo 13, and Philadelphia are truly remarkable. At the same time, his comedic talents shine in films like A League of Their Own, Turner & Hooch, Catch Me If You Can, The Ladykillers, Big, and of course, Toy Story. In this movie, Hanks isn't alone in capturing our attention; Tyler Hoechlin, an emerging star with great potential in Hollywood, co-stars as Hanks' son and delivers an outstanding performance. He's definitely someone to keep an eye on for the future—I believe he'll accomplish great things. Paul Newman, as always, provides a brilliant on-screen presence; he remains a true legend. We shouldn't forget the talented supporting cast who, though they had smaller roles, contributed significantly to the film's success. Jennifer Jason Leigh, whose powerful performances in Bastard Out of Carolina and Single White Female I will never forget, brings grace and depth as Hanks’ wife in the story, adding a special touch to the film.

The film is simply a blast—perhaps even more so for those of us who were young and fans of "The Ramones" when it first came out. I've watched it countless times, solo and with friends, and it still feels fresh and hilarious. Without sounding too serious, the idea of being a devoted fan of a band is timeless, just like the boredom high school students feel with the dull routine of certain classes.  

The movie is packed with memorable lines and scenes—like the references to how our "permanent records" from high school can supposedly haunt us forever. (Let me say, I’ve been out of high school for many years, and thankfully, that record hasn’t followed me!) Then there’s the classic "getting some static" line—"I'm getting some static," followed by Principal Togar's retort, "Not as much as you're going to get." The scene with the school board member so frail he's constantly attended by nurses is another gem, as is the Nazi-like hall monitors' obsession with body searches.  

Principal Togar's declaration, "I give you the final solution," as he burns the Ramones records—recalling the era when vinyl was the norm—and Joey Ramone's remark about how much everything has changed since they were kicked out of high school, are unforgettable moments. Togar's subsequent question leaves you eager to see what comes next.

I really enjoyed this show—it seems to be the first and possibly only series of its kind in the UK, aired on Channel 4. The character development was spot-on, reminiscent of The Simpsons in how it captured the various facets of small-town life. 

Notably, there was no laugh track, which was unusual for an American comedy at the time outside of Larry Sanders. This choice actually enhanced the show's authenticity, making the quirky police characters feel genuinely like that rather than just playing for the cameras. 

Overall, it was a charming, offbeat series that struck the right chord with me. I do wonder if it missed connecting with certain audiences. Had it been broadcast at a more viewer-friendly hour in the UK, I believe it could have become a cult favorite. 

To wrap up, my usual question—where the hell can I find a way to watch this again? Any suggestions?

It may be hard to believe, but this film was condemned as immoral by more pulpits than any other movie made before the strict enforcement of the Hayes Code. In fact, priests openly told their congregations that viewing this film was equivalent to committing a mortal sin. 

I'm not exaggerating. They had several reasons for their condemnation:

First: Jane's fondness for sex. In one scene, she and Tarzan wake up in their treetop shelter. She stretches sensuously and, with a teasing look, remarks, "Tarzan, you've been a bad boy!" This implies not only that they've been intimate, but that their encounters are somewhat kinky. Under the later Hays Code, depicting women taking pleasure in sex was strictly forbidden.

Second: Jane prefers an innocent yet clever and resourceful savage—Tarzan—to a civilized, respectable man with a typical nine-to-five job, like Holt. When Holt first impresses her with a fancy dress from London, she hesitates. Later, when Holt attempts to kill Tarzan and both believe Tarzan is dead, her doubt grows. But once she discovers her true love is alive and well, her interest in the comforts of civilization quickly fades. After all, Tarzan's...

"THE BRAIN THAT WOULDN'T DIE" was deemed so offensive in 1959 that several edits and a three-year delay were necessary before its release in 1962. Today, it's hard to fathom how anyone could have taken it seriously even back then; the film is both shockingly lurid and unabashedly lewd, yet it also comes across as remarkably absurd in a boastful, over-the-top manner.

The plot centers on a scientist obsessed with limb transplants—when his girlfriend dies in a car accident, he hastily transports her head to his clandestine lab. Using a jumble of telephone cords, a handful of clamps, and what resembles a shallow baking pan, he seemingly revives her head. But her reaction? Not exactly one of gratitude. Instead, she's downright annoyed, especially when she learns that the doctor intends to graft her head onto a different body.

As it turns out, the doctor is quite selective about his new body: he prefers one designed for speed. His pursuits lead him to roam the city streets, bothering disoriented women, frequenting strip clubs, entering beauty contests, and chasing after glamorous models—all in his bizarre quest.

This film captures that enchanting moment in life when innocence of childhood gives way to the confusing chaos of growing up. It’s a cherished transition, and the story revolves around this pivotal phase.  

Danni, portrayed wonderfully by Reese Witherspoon, finds herself right at that crossroads when the story begins. She adores Elvis, spinning his records and dreaming of love with hope and wonder. Her sister Maureen, soon to leave for college, easily charms boys, is stunning, and appears to have everything together—though she’s not as confident as she seems. Maureen dates a local troublemaker whose father also has his eye on her; she longs for a kind-hearted boy to sweep her off her feet. Meanwhile, Danni, like most young teens, wishes she could be anyone else but herself—believing she isn’t good enough. She envies Maureen’s beauty but fails to see her own worth.  

The innocence starts to fade when Danni encounters Court Foster for the first time. Court’s father has recently passed away, and he has moved back to their old farm with his mother and two younger brothers to work the land.

Emma remains my favorite Jane Austen novel. Despite her shortcomings, Emma's good intentions make her relatable and endearing, allowing readers to forgive her flaws and develop affection for her. Her relationship with Mr. Knightley is particularly charming—warm, familiar, respectful, yet playful—creating that comforting, romantic thrill. Mr. Knightley embodies the ideal gentleman, and Emma, at just 21, exemplifies a rare independence, intelligence, and confidence for her time—traits that suggest she would have grown and matured beyond her initial imperfections. Who wouldn't wish to be Emma? Who wouldn't enjoy a playful scolding from Mr. Knightley? Unfortunately, this adaptation of Emma misses the essence that makes her so lovable. I couldn't even bring myself to finish watching it because I found it so unpleasant. The warmth and generosity that define Emma—the patience she shows her father and the close bond she shares with Mrs. Weston, reflecting her willingness to prioritize her friend's happiness—were absent. Instead of the genuine kindness that makes Emma so compelling, the portrayal of Mr. Woodhouse came across as odd rather than quaint, stripping away that charming quirkiness.

I genuinely tried to enjoy this show; I really did. I even purchased the pilot episode, initially on VHS and later on DVD. Nonetheless, I found it difficult to connect with the story because its two main characters—David (Bruce Willis) and Maddie (Cybill Shepherd)—seemed overly obsessed with themselves. While I did recognize some clever dialogue that contributed significantly to the show's success, I couldn't quite get into it.  

Essentially, the series resembled the classic screwball comedies of the '30s and '40s, featuring a battle of the sexes. Frequent arguments, accusations, shouting, and yelling characterized their interactions. Although many viewers seem to enjoy that kind of bickering, it’s not my cup of tea, which is why I never jumped on the Moonlighting bandwagon.  

The only character who truly entertained me was Allyce Beasley's lovable, hapless assistant, Agnes. It's unfortunate she had so little screen time. Shepherd was visually appealing, and I suppose women might say the same for Willis, but the incessant arguing eventually put me off.

This movie has scared me ever since I first saw it.  

My mom watched it when it aired on TV back in 1992. I vividly remember being awakened in the middle of the night by her tearful yelps as my dad helped her upstairs.  

She was saying something like, "Don’t let her get me," or something along those lines. When I asked what had upset her so much, she explained that she’d been watching The Woman in Black.  

Naturally, I had to see it too, and even though I was only eleven, she let me. It terrified me to death. Since then, I’ve become completely immune to horror films!

This isn't so much a film as it is a high-budget children's TV show. As far as I can tell, the antagonist is a massive swarm of chocolate-covered espresso beans. This idea seems to be confirmed by the subtitles, which label it as 'Insomnia.' When I first heard that a civilization had been wiped out by insomnia, I thought, "Wow! A nihilistic martial arts film!" but unfortunately, that’s not the case. You have to wonder about the film’s experimental nature when the villain is literally strangled by an old man’s long, white eyebrows. *Zu Warriors* makes just as much sense whether the subtitles are on or off, which isn't a good sign. I would describe the special effects as somewhere between Ray Harryhausen’s work and *Xena: Warrior Princess*—rudimentary at best.

I've always been a devoted fan of Woody Allen and continue to appreciate much of his past work. However, only a blind admirer could overlook how dull, superficial, pretentious, and most troublingly, how poorly this film was acted. It feels like empty mental masturbation, built on shaky, inconsistent foundations. The concept of artificially recreating a supposed "Allen-esque actor"—casting Will Farrell to mimic Allen’s mannerisms and speech as if he were 30 years younger—was a disastrous idea. The result was unmistakably absurd. And then there are the dialogues—what was meant to be philosophical introspection instead came across as unintentionally comedic, a mockery of deep thought that only highlighted its lack of substance. It's truly unfortunate.

This rarely seen film is a slow-paced and relaxed example of a giallo. It moves away from many of the genre's typical clichés, embracing a more freeform storytelling style. The plot centers on a woman in search of her missing lover—a psychiatrist who has unexpectedly disappeared without explanation. Her investigation brings her to a secluded villa inhabited by a quirky group of individuals. True to giallo tradition, violence and murder are never far behind.

The cast is quite impressive. It includes Aldofo Celi (Thunderball), Alida Valli (Suspiria), Horst Frank (Cat o' Nine Tails), and a very young Sybil Danning, who would become an 80s scream queen. The lead performance is by Rosemary Dexter, whom I wasn’t previously familiar with, but she delivers a solid performance anchoring the film.

A standout feature of Eye in the Labyrinth is its music. Uncharacteristic for a giallo, it features a jazz-rock fusion soundtrack. Composed by Roberto Nicolosi, the score recalls Miles Davis’s work on In A Silent Way. It is an exceptional soundtrack that imparts a distinctive mood to the film, setting it apart from typical gialli. The fusion groove enhances the slow, relaxed atmosphere and complements the bright, seaside scenery that dominates much of the film.

Usually, a filmmaker's debut is something you can afford to overlook—it's often marked by the inexperience of everyone involved, and this film is no different. However, what makes it even more problematic is that, even by 1982 standards, it’s so poorly executed that it becomes unintentionally hilarious. Shot entirely around Chicago on a shoestring budget, the acting across the board is stiff, wooden, and cartoonish—reminiscent of a high school play or amateur community theater. Background noise from traffic frequently drowns out the dialogue, which itself is painfully bad—delivered in a forced, declarative manner that feels more hurried and artificial than natural. Scenes are awkwardly staged and jarringly edited, and although the story spans several years, neither the children nor the adults show any aging, adding to the overall flaws. 

I believe it’s possible to create a Christian film that appeals to a broad, secular audience, but too often, the creators focus so heavily on their message—or, in this case, their personal ties to the story—that they neglect essential production quality. Unfortunately, this film exemplifies that tendency.

The Unborn is an impressive low-budget horror film that taps into the fears surrounding pregnancy. Brooke Adams delivers a compelling performance, as always, supported by the reliable James Karen. The supporting cast is fairly typical for a film of this caliber. Notably, the score by Gary Numan adds a compelling layer to the movie. Henry Dominic's screenplay demonstrates a surprising level of intelligence for a horror of this nature, though it occasionally hints at misogynistic undertones. Rodman Fender's direction is functional but falls short of exceptional, and there are some moments involving cheap, unnecessary jump scares. If you're a fan of Brooke Adams—whose acting career deserves greater recognition—this film is worth a watch; she remains excellent throughout.

Roald Dahl's The BFG is a beloved classic, but this animated version fails to capture its enchantment. Staying quite true to Dahl's original narrative, the shortcomings cannot be blamed on John Hambey’s script. Instead, the film suffers from dull, monotonous animation, sluggish pacing, and lackluster voice performances. One would naturally expect this story to become a lively, colorful, and joyful movie—yet it instead becomes an extremely dull experience, making it tedious to watch. For children unfamiliar with the story, reading the book first is highly recommended; otherwise, this film may discourage them from discovering what is truly a timeless children's classic.  

In the tale, young orphan Sophie (voiced by Amanda Root) resides in a less-than-warm orphanage overseen by the harsh Mrs. Clonkers. One night, she gazes out the window and spots a towering figure quietly moving along the village street. The giant notices her gaze, reaches through the window, and swiftly lifts Sophie from her bed, placing her into its massive pocket before rushing away into the darkness. Sophie soon learns that she has been abducted by a giant from

What a tragedy...

You neglected to brush your teeth. Let's turn this into a 30-minute episode with lively kids making noise, followed by the dad giving a heartfelt lecture because that's just what he does.

Meanwhile, Uncle Joey will be cracking strange noises and goofy faces, and Uncle Jesse will step in sporting his black leather jacket and jeans, looking sharp for a few moments while everyone reminisces about how Mom would have handled things if she were here.

It's a series of comical little escapades about seemingly nothing, wrapped around an overly long storyline.

Full House won't just put you to sleep; it'll make you feel a decade older in no time.

This film is one of the most renowned works of French sexual liberation cinema from the seventies, featuring Gerard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere in highly satirical roles. It also belongs to the category of dark psychological dramas from the same era, alongside films like "Serié Noire," "Buffet Froid," and "Beau Pere," all directed by Blier. 

Nevertheless, I would like to correct a previous comment regarding the movie: the English title is quite different from the original French one. While both protagonists are "going places," the French title could be literally translated as "the waltz dancers," which serves as a metaphor for the movement of testicles...

It's a sight to behold, but the first thing you'd do upon discovering Atlantis is to explore it! This was a golden chance to take viewers somewhere truly extraordinary. Instead, Disney fell back on their usual formulaic storytelling.

This was the worst film I've ever watched, yet oddly, it was also the most entertaining. Sci-Fi original movies are known for their low quality, and that’s part of the charm! The line, "I like my dinosaur meat well done!" might just be the greatest quote ever! The storyline sounds like something conjured up in a drug-fueled dream. I can picture the writers waking up after a wild night of getting high and playing Dance Dance Revolution, then brainstorming this: space marines landing on an alien planet teeming with dinosaurs and medieval-style houses, all to protect a scientific team studying the planet. Genius! It ticked every box on the Sci-Fi original movie checklist: guns, dinosaurs, medieval elements, space travel, and terrible acting. 

So, go ahead and watch this movie, but save your money—don’t buy it.

There are no likable characters—the protagonist seems to embody the worst qualities of Woody Allen, Paul Provensa, and Reiser—and the overly forced scenes, like the inevitable collision with the kid on rollerblades, were simply painfully unconvincing.

It was simple yet incredibly touching. I believe the film subtly depicted the often harsh reality of gender segregation in society, conveying its bitterness with delicate finesse. There was a subtle humor intertwined with the somber tone. The fact that most of the actors were not professionals added a sense of authenticity and immediacy to the story. The movie also had a documentary-like quality that enhanced its realism. The most memorable scenes were those where the girls, forbidden from watching, eagerly listened to the soldier—who was supposed to be monitoring them—broadcasting the game. For Iranians, the familiar cheers and street celebrations after a victory evoke a deep sense of national pride. Even if you're not Iranian, you'll find yourself captivated by it all.

As Christmas has transformed over the years, whether one emphasizes its religious or secular aspects, it remains a season when people are encouraged to show greater kindness and generosity to one another. Yet, this spirit seems to have bypassed Ebenezer Scrooge, a miserly merchant and moneylender in 19th-century London.  

As his nephew reminds him, he doesn’t truly observe Christmas because he deems it all a humbug. The compassion and humanity that once might have been part of him have long been extinguished. Scrooge is a hardened individual, much like his 20th-century counterpart, Mr. Potter of Bedford Falls, New York.  

However, Charles Dickens’s story reminds us that it is never too late for redemption. Through the visitation of a lonely ghost and three spirits, Scrooge learns how to change.  

A Christmas Carol is a timeless holiday classic, but it also functions as a sharp social critique of 19th-century Great Britain, much like Oliver Twist. Its characters belong to the middle and lower classes. The Cratchits, while a step above the impoverished street children of Oliver Twist, still struggle to maintain their modest position in society.

This film is exquisitely crafted with impeccable attention to detail. Every element—from the set design and lighting to the soundscape and storyline—is flawless. The screenplay invites viewers into a layered game where participants undertake a straightforward mission. 

Paxton delivers his finest performance here; his mannerisms and vocal inflections are precise and compelling. Every frame is carefully composed, enhancing the overall experience. As the narrative unfolds beyond the first hour, unexpected twists keep emerging, adding depth and excitement. While it may not be the definitive film of the year, it is a thoroughly refined gem. This movie challenges the viewer's intellect and is not suited for those seeking simplicity.

Growing up, my babysitter was a fan of the show, so I watched many of the older episodes. I wasn’t particularly a Scooby-Doo fan, so I’m not sure why I left the TV on when this show first premiered. To my surprise, I found myself enjoying it. For me, Shaggy and Scooby were the most interesting characters—*dodges tomatoes from fans of the others*—so I appreciated that the focus was mainly on them. However, this might upset fans of the original series. I enjoyed the voice acting, especially Dr. Phinius Phibes; I liked listening to him even before I realized he was Jeff Bennett. Jim Meskimen as Robi also stood out, sounding like he truly enjoys his role as an actor. I also got a kick out of the techies, with their slightly autistic personalities and their love for playing Dungeons and Dragons or acting out scenes from Star Wars—though, of course, those names aren’t used in the show.

"The Crush" is an enjoyable romantic chick flick for women in their 40s, spanning roughly the first two-thirds, as it attempts to emulate a British "Sex and the City." I especially appreciated the unexpected development of the young, handsome trophy husband, whose character remains somewhat underdeveloped—though, to be fair, we don’t see much of him physically either, and Kenny Doughty is someone I’d like to see more of. The film notably places greater emphasis on the theme of a young man paired with an older woman than on similar dynamics in either version of "Sabrina" (neither of which I favor) or in the high-profile Douglas/Zeta-Jones or Dion/Svengali marriages. 

Supporting Andie MacDowell as a multicultural expat are familiar faces from British dramas and comedies, such as the sharp-tongued Anna Chancellor. The plot twists near the end come across as contrived and overly convenient. It wasn't until the credits rolled that I realized the underlying issue might stem from the fact that, like "Sex and the City," the film was written and directed by a man—first-time filmmaker Scott John McKay. I suspect he had a deeper story in mind about three gay men, perhaps about their journeys of coming out.

I initially watched this film on MST3K, and while I couldn't stop laughing at the jokes, I wouldn't say the movie was terrible. Admittedly, it was somewhat difficult to follow and clearly low-budget, but its Hitchcock-inspired storyline genuinely held my interest. When I saw the non-MST3K version, I was genuinely entertained. This film definitely deserves a Hollywood remake.

Redline is a cheap imitation of Fast & Furious, lacking all of its charm and excitement. It doesn't need an intricate plot filled with twists and turns, but it desperately needs some substance! Instead, it offers almost nothing—similar to a porn film where the story and dialogue are compressed into a minute at the start and the same at the end. But this is even worse, as you get nothing in return for your time. The film is excruciatingly dull, featuring absurdly unrealistic race sequences and a complete waste of stunning, costly cars—so much so that their presence almost becomes a negative. Sure, the female lead is attractive, but who is truly craving more on-screen female presence? It feels as though the director tossed a hat full of dialogue and plot ideas into the air, then randomly selected snippets with an eight-ball each time a scene changed. Any serious racing enthusiast or someone familiar with the sport would find no enjoyment in the race scenes presented here.

Kirstie Alley, slightly slimmer but not significantly so, appears alongside a man who resembles MacGyver, complete with bleached blond hair. The film's plot centers on an older woman in her fifties struggling to get her screenplay produced due to age discrimination, prompting her to send her younger nephew to pretend he's the writer. The story is unoriginal and poorly executed, featuring lackluster acting, silly dialogue, and a ludicrous storyline. There's an additional subplot involving a writer who admires or has a crush on Kirstie's character, though its relevance remains unclear. The actor playing Kirstie's brother delivers a stiff, miscast performance, making their scenes uncomfortable to watch. Overall, this film offers little worth recommending. Just steer clear of it.

This is arguably the worst movie I have ever watched. Once again, I fell into the trap of purchasing it because the synopsis on the back sounded intriguing and the cover looked appealing. After buying this and the film "Malevolence," which I also reviewed here, I've definitely learned my lesson. I enjoy horror films set in the woods, deserts, or farms—settings I find particularly compelling. This movie claims to be set in the woods of Texas but was likely filmed in the director's backyard. The production quality was among the worst I've ever seen. The acting was absolutely dreadful. The storyline bore no resemblance to what the back cover promised. I even tried to sell it to F.Y.E. and some local used DVD stores, but neither was interested. That’s how terrible this miserable excuse for a movie was. I've seen some bad films before, like Troll 2, but this one truly takes the cake. I didn't think there could be a worse movie than Troll 2, but I was sorely mistaken. Do not buy this film unless someone gives it to you for free—though even then, I’d advise against it.

This visually refined and intellectually engaging piece unfolds as 'a story within a story.' The central figure is scriptwriter Bart Klever, who tirelessly wrestles with his new manuscript—simultaneously the screenplay of the film we are viewing. Within the film, Bart embodies a screenwriter crafting the script for his own story, blurring the lines between creation and reality. His struggle with the text becomes a central thematic thread, intertwined with the setting of his modest flat, where he both works and cares for his young daughter. The intimate surroundings provide fertile ground for illusions involving spatial manipulation, lighting, colors, and a couple of cats. The seemingly straightforward room is further complicated by the fluid and unstable dimensions of the ongoing text, which is continually altered by the filmmaker’s interventions—shown on a computer monitor—creating a dynamic contrast with the mutable environment. The shifting perspective constantly challenges viewers to question what is 'truth' and what is 'illusion,' to determine which of these layered worlds takes precedence, and whether any fixed point of reference exists within this narrative universe.

The film appears cheap and unattractive, failing to amuse the young audience except for a single, somewhat funny toilet joke. Christopher Lloyd is well past his prime and comes across as quite tedious in this part, partly due to the weak attempts at humor by the writers. Elizabeth Hurley's performance is embarrassingly amateurish in what should be a comedic role. Meanwhile, Jeff Daniels and Darryl Hannah manage to steer clear of complete embarrassment. Overall, there’s little reason to make this movie, especially since it inevitably invites comparison to Robin Williams's often brilliant improvisations in Mork & Mindy.

It was everything this isn’t: lively, energetic, and featuring actors who weren’t afraid to go over the top. It also boasted a solid script. Conversely, this one left me puzzled. If Farrah isn’t genuinely committed to a career, why does she have a manager—and why is he wasting his efforts? If Kate and Barney are truly "artists," why do they sign up for the Mother of All Jiggly Shows (similar to the "Brady Bunch" movie where Robert Reed wants to do Shakespeare but ends up in a cheesy TV special)? They weren’t big industry stars, but they weren’t exactly starving either. Plus, while the timeline about the poster release before Farrah landed her show was accurate, scenes showing Silverman rejecting pitches for "Funniest Home Videos" and "American Idol," and Spelling promising his daughter Tori that he would create a show for her someday, clearly did not happen. 

What troubled me most was how Spelling’s role was misrepresented. He's depicted as the showrunner and creator, which isn’t true. And his so-called "idea" for CA is downright laughable. 

How could Spelling and Goldberg be allowed to enforce Farrah's oral contract while the others had formal signings? And why didn’t Farrah or Bernstein come forward to clarify these issues?

This film, produced in 1999, boasts quite solid production values. The cast features attractive, reasonably talented actors. There are no over-the-top antics with minor characters firing endless rounds without hitting anything, nor are there chaotic car chases with expensive vehicles being wrecked in senseless crashes. 

The interior sets are convincingly modern in design, and the equipment appears up to date. However, there's a high-tech computer room furnished with what seem like remnants from a 1950s electronics lab, which feels out of place. The fake corpse makeup, resembling dried pancake batter rather than traditional prosthetics, amuses me. It's intended to depict bodies that have calcified—though how a virus could cause such a transformation is left ambiguously to the viewer's imagination.

Speaking of the virus, I wish I could say this isn’t the worst premise for a sci-fi horror film I’ve encountered, but I can't. The idea of a computer virus transmitted through a television or computer monitor that turns into a deadly biological threat? Sorry, that's a stretch. It reminds me of...

This film is exceptional for three main reasons. Firstly, its aesthetic appeal is stunning; I was captivated by its bold color palette, complemented by extraordinary costumes and picturesque sets. The cinematography appears costly—though it likely wasn't—adding to the grandeur of the visual experience. I have a fondness for stories about misfits or loners banding together to form a family, and this film handles that theme with freshness, avoiding clichés. The cast vividly brings to life flawed yet highly charming characters. Alan Larkin delivers a standout performance—his presence, along with the van and the road trip motif, immediately brought to mind my favorite film from last year, Little Miss Sunshine. I also discovered Fabrizio Bentivoglio, an intriguing actor, though I found Til Schweiger's performance occasionally a bit irritating. The opening scene and the sequences where the characters fumble their tricks are particularly humorous. Throughout the film, humor and emotion intertwine seamlessly. I especially appreciated the ending. And ultimately, the story revolves around the magician theme—where a skilled magician guides the audience's gaze to create convincing illusions, and indeed, illusions are made to happen.

The title says it all. I watched this film with my dad when it was released, and having served in Korea, he held a great admiration for the man. The main disappointment is that the movie focuses only on a brief period of his life—remarkably, his entire life could have formed an epic biopic, and imagining the production costs is staggering. 

Some posters hint at the man’s flaws, but these are petty shots. The film’s core themes—"Duty, Honor, Country"—are not just hollow words spoken by a high-ranking officer; they represent a profound expression of his unwavering dedication to his nation.

Ironically, Peck’s liberal perspective gave him a deeper understanding of the man. He does an excellent job portraying the fearless general, balanced with the compassionate side of his character.

This clever film explores love across different eras. It follows Keaton as he searches for a romantic partner in the Stone Age, ancient Rome, and the 1920s. In each period, he remains the endearing, hapless Buster and competes with Wallace Beery for his beloved. Among the three settings, I found the Roman segment to be the most enjoyable, despite also being the perhaps the most cheesy. I particularly liked the scenes featuring the lion, played by a man in costume, as well as the quirky snow-filled chariot race. Most of all, I appreciated Keaton’s incredible acrobatics throughout. While all three eras provide classic entertainment, the film, though not his very best, is still a standout and thoroughly enjoyable. Definitely give it a watch!

When I first watched this movie, I honestly expected everyone to mock it. To my surprise, even kids over the age of seven seemed to enjoy it. I personally found the movie enjoyable—mainly because my little sister, who’s only 10, and I spent the entire time making fun of it.  

Sorry, Jordan, but the acting was downright terrible. You know a film is doomed when the lead can't act. Plus, it lacked a strong script or compelling plot to make up for it. I also found the character of Pamela to be painfully lame—borderline pathetic.  

That said, there were a few decent performances from actors like the stunning Spencer, Hollywood, and Ronnie. However, it wasn't enough to save the movie.  

There are two things about this film that I just can't get past:  

1.) The fact that Spencer would fall for her. Seriously, ew. I looked up their ages—while in reality he’s only about four years older—but in "Go Figure," the age difference seemed much greater. Jordan is a very pretty girl, but in GF, she seemed like...

I might be giving this more praise than it truly warrants, mainly because it's Halloween. I recently visited Knott's Scary Farm and was in the mood to watch a cheesy Halloween flick. Plus, it only cost me a dollar. Usually, I’d fast-forward through movies like this to reach “the good parts,” but for some reason, I didn’t do that this time. I’m still not sure why. From the very first shots, it was clear this wasn’t a “real” movie—probably not even a B-movie. It falls more into the category of DeCoteau’s “horror” films like The Brotherhood, shot on video with a film-look effect, costing about 50 cents. Honestly, I half expected one of his burly college boys to stagger out in his underwear, rubbing himself. There were no cutaway shots—probably too costly to film multiple angles—and the lighting was flat overall. Yet, it’s hard to put my finger on what made it intriguing. There’s something oddly refreshing about watching a director with zero budget manage to create a halfway decent movie. That he managed to do anything worth watching is commendable. The film has its merits—acting isn’t too bad, and the cinematography is fairly good, though perhaps too brightly lit to truly be frightening.

Sidney Franklin's "The Good Earth" has attained classic status due to its enduring story and exceptional performances, notably by Luis Rainer, who received an Oscar for her portrayal of O-Lan. Rainer's performance is so authentic and complete that she is nearly unrecognizable; with minimal dialogue in a lengthy film, she masterfully communicates through subtle facial expressions and body language. Her convincing portrayal of a Chinese woman is so authentic that viewers unfamiliar with her work might easily mistake her for Chinese.  

The film remains relevant today as it delves into the timeless rags-to-riches narrative and universal themes associated with it. After years of famine and hardship, Lung and his wife O-Lan attain financial success, only to discover a life filled with possessions but devoid of true meaning. It is only when they return to the earth after battling a swarm of locusts—whose special effects are still remarkably impressive and visually stunning—that they find genuine fulfillment. This story, told from the perspective of a Chinese family—a rare approach for 1937—makes the film a true classic. Ultimately, it underscores that money has little value without the support of friends and family, a message the film conveys powerfully.

All the discussions claiming this is a bad movie are unjustified. In fact, it's the best film I've ever watched. The story is exceptional, and the actors are among the finest I've seen. I have no criticisms for any of their performances. This movie stands out as the best, and it will remain that way forever.

Busy Phillips delivered an outstanding performance, showcasing both her comedic and dramatic talents. Erika Christensen was impressive, but Busy truly stole the spotlight. It was a great follow-up after *The Smokers*, a film starring Busy that didn't quite live up to expectations. If Busy doesn't receive any nominations for this movie, it would be a real tragedy. Forget *Mona Lisa Smile*—check out *Home Room*.

Although I generally dislike Hollywood, I love cinema, so I feel compelled to see these subpar movies in theaters. I was particularly hopeful that Vanilla Sky would be worthwhile. I wished that they would either stay true to the original "Open Your Eyes" or craft their own unique version. Unfortunately, it was a bit of both, and it was disappointing.

The movie started off well—I’m a big Radiohead fan and wished there was more of their music. However, by the end, we’re subjected to "Good Vibrations" by The Beach Boys. The contrast was jarring, spanning from some decent club tracks to that overused classic. They had a few good songs in the club scene, maybe a couple more here and there, but why did they have to blast GV during the climax? It was more irritating than meaningful, especially since it had no connection to the plot. At least choose songs with some relevance—Kid A was primary, after all. Whatever.

He also did a decent job with the club scene—it looked cool. Otherwise, the film seemed filled with arrogance, as if expecting audiences to understand its complexity. Those who could grasp it would read the subtitles, and the rest...

When the United States entered World War I, the government compelled Hollywood to produce propaganda films. Among them, *The Little American* stands out as perhaps the best, featuring a memorable performance by Mary Pickford.

In the film, Pickford portrays a young woman caught between two suitors: Jack Holt, a German, and Raymond Hatton, a Frenchman. Her choice is postponed due to the war, as both men enlist in the military. 

A pivotal scene occurs when the ship she is traveling on is torpedoed by German forces—evoking the sinking of the Lusitania—because it is secretly carrying munitions. Pickford delivers a powerful moment as she stands on the lifeboat, shouting at the German commander. Later in the story, she encounters Holt and Hatton again while being held as a prisoner of war in a château.

Director Cecil B. DeMille crafts a particularly memorable scene in the film as Pickford and Holt walk through a village ravaged by bombs. They pass a church destroyed to its foundation, with only a lone wall remaining. Against this wall hangs a large crucifix. As they watch, the wall collapses, yet the figure of Jesus remains suspended in midair—creating a haunting, surreal image in an otherwise straightforward and unpretentious film.

Last night, I watched this film on DVD and decided to read the reviews this morning. It appears that "I, Robot" has divided the critic community on IMDb, sparking some harsh words and name-calling along the way. 

I'm somewhat surprised by this reaction, as the film isn't particularly great—or even good—yet it's far from terrible. What the film truly is, however, is disheartening. It's disheartening to see how eager American audiences are to embrace bland, clichéd rehashes and celebrate them as groundbreaking cinema. The film feels like a tried-and-true retread—from its storyline, which mixes elements of Asimov with modern blockbuster action, to Will Smith’s character, a witty yet cynical hero with a tough exterior, to the overused special effects borrowed from movies like The Matrix.

Unfortunately, "I, Robot" might just be the quintessential action flick for today's viewers: a shallow plot, overly snappy dialogue, and relentless adrenaline. Smith’s performance is mediocre, a fact we've come to expect—perhaps Hollywood's latest attempt to craft a black version of Bruce Willis. The narrative is riddled with plot holes of varying sizes, but I don't think...

In Bridgeport, the disturbed high school teacher Richard Fenton (Johnathon Schaech) becomes fixated on his student Donna Keppel (Brittany Snow). She witnesses him murder her family in an attempt to keep her close, leading to Richard's arrest and a life sentence in prison. Three years later, Donna, still haunted by her trauma, begins to recover but remains under psychological care and on medication. On prom night, she attends a party at the Pacific Grad Hotel with her boyfriend Bobby (Scott Porter) and two other couples. Meanwhile, the escaped convict Richard has infiltrated the same hotel floor, stalking Donna, stabbing her friends, and attacking hotel staff who stand in his way. 

The forgettable slasher film "Prom Night" is packed with clichés and lacks any real originality. Its flimsy plot is both shallow and foolish, with a poorly portrayed performance by Schaech as the deranged killer. The screenplay is completely predictable, making it obvious what will happen in the upcoming scenes. I give it a score of three. 

Title (Brazil): "A Morte Convida Para Dançar" ("The Death Invites to Dance")

This has to be the worst piece of junk I've encountered in quite some time.

Heath Ledger as a heartthrob? He looked downright deformed. I wish I had known earlier that he and Naomi Watts are a couple in real life, because I spent two painfully long hours wondering what she saw in him.

Orlando Bloom as a heartthrob? With that scruffy beard and deer-in-the-headlights expression, I just couldn't agree.

Rachel Griffiths remained her usual fabulous self, but Geoffrey Rush seemed eager to get off the set as quickly as possible.

Am I supposed to sympathize with bank robbers and murderers? This is a far cry from *Butch Cassidy*, which was genuinely entertaining. This film was tired, filled with clichés, and utterly dull. We only stuck around because we hoped it would improve, but it never did.

The last 10 to 15 minutes unintentionally turned hilarious. Heath and his gang are holed up in a frontier hotel, causing women and children to suffer because of their presence. That's tragic, not funny. But what made us burst out laughing was when they exited the hotel in full armor, because all we could think of was the Black.

I couldn't connect with this film. It lacked engagement on intellectual, emotional, and aesthetic levels. The dialogue was dense and uninspiring, making it difficult to relate to or care about any of the characters. Consequently, I find it hard to find anything positive to say about it.  

I've heard that a proper understanding of the film requires some familiarity with more obscure aspects of Catholic theology. As an atheist, I admit I am likely unfamiliar with many intricate details of Catholic doctrine. However, I've seen numerous films addressing religious themes that resonated with me because their core messages are universal aspects of the human experience, without depending on specialized knowledge or belief systems.

"The Bourne Ultimatum" launches recklessly into a high-octane chase, then erupts into relentless action as Jason Bourne (Matt Damon, utterly compelling) hunts down the architects of the CIA black ops program that transformed him into a lethal weapon—all in a desperate quest to uncover his true identity. Adding a chilling edge is David Strathairn as the enigmatic "man behind the curtain," whose icy presence contrasts sharply with the returning cast members, including Joan Allen (excellent) and Julia Stiles (less prominent).  

Like its predecessor, I hoped Paul Greengrass's signature shaky handheld camera work would settle during the quieter moments. Nonetheless, this style excellently conveys the tense, claustrophobic atmosphere of close-quarters combat and dynamic rooftop chases, punctuated by car pile-ups and frantic foot pursuits. A key allure of the Bourne series lies in its globe-trotting exploits and the seemingly supernatural manipulation of technology and communication, creating a gritty, hyper-real universe filled with technological magic. It’s baffling how characters always appear precisely where they need to be, as if guided by unseen forces, enhancing the films’ sense of an insidious, high-tech landscape that defies the laws of physics and current capabilities.

This cartoon was unusual, but its story contained more depth and emotion than most animated films. It follows a girl at a camp who struggles with low self-esteem and has few friends, aside from a brother and sister who are just as miserable as she is. She hits her lowest point, and when an opportunity presents itself, she ends up making a literal pact with a devil-like demon. I found the film to be quite authentic and relatable; just when everything seems hopeless, the girl recognizes what she's done, feels genuine remorse, and begins to change. She even helps the dark, mystical creature learn the human emotion of love. The twins also grow through their efforts to assist the little bears, gaining a sense of self-worth in the process. The film delivers a very positive message for children. Although some elements are a bit strange, it remains an enjoyable movie. The soundtrack by Stephen Bishop (known for the songs in *Tootsie*) further enhanced the experience.

This is the perfect kind of movie to enjoy with a glass of wine, the fire crackling, and your feet up. It’s easy to follow and doesn't demand much mental effort, making it a great pick after a long day. While it’s quite unrealistic—so if you're looking for something serious, you might want to skip it—it's incredibly funny. The idea that a businessman would agree to live in a slum for a while, and actually end up enjoying it, is just hilarious. I definitely recommend giving it a watch.

While Ealing comedies are undeniably excellent, this film particularly stands out as one of the finest.  

The story revolves around a small section of Pimlico in London that is unexpectedly revealed to be part of Burgundy rather than the UK. The plot follows the residents as they fight to preserve a treasure uncovered after a bomb explosion and to thwart black market traders who quickly realize that, outside UK law and rationing, they can operate unrestrained. When the government decides to close the border, turning their street into a captive zone, the residents resist the system.  

They are compelled to ration water and food as they stand up for what is just. Ironically, their situation worsens, highlighting the moral core of the story. As they lose all their supplies, they feel defeated and call for surrender—only to be surprised when the entirety of London responds by flooding them with food, enabling them to carry on their resistance.  

Throughout, the film maintains a perfect tone, supported by outstanding performances.

I remember when I was five, and my parents thought we were watching a regular cartoon movie—until the bras and bullets started flying. I have to say, this film is bound to upset everyone because it unapologetically critiques discrimination and societal issues. Yet, beneath its provocative exterior, it's incredibly funny and thought-provoking. I highly recommend it to fans of cult classics. Also, check out Fritz the Cat and The Nine Lives of Fritz the Cat—both by Ralph Bakshi. They tell the story of a cat facing tough times with family, the streets, and work. As I got older, I rented all these movies. Due to its offensive title at the time, Coonskin was also released as Street Fighter. Ralph Bakshi also directed Cool World, starring a very young Brad Pitt. Heavy Traffic is another cartoon that explores the street life of a young man.

Drones, ethnic drumming, poorly synthesized sounds, and children singing—this is the most patronizing "world music" imaginable. It's a tourist film, and a truly poor one at that. What truly undermines it are the disjointed sequences: scenes of India, Egypt, South America, Africa, and more, presented without any transition or visual context to explain the sudden shifts. There's no narrative or visual cue linking these places; instead, we get endless footage of locals with "baskets on their heads," as another reviewer aptly described, walking aimlessly as if that held some profound meaning. If the filmmakers wanted to create a genuine Third World music video, they could have simply traveled a few hundred miles south of Koya’s best spots to film in Mexico—offering a more authentic backdrop for "life in transformation."

Instead, they opted for a jumbled tourist itinerary spanning half the globe, accompanied by mind-numbing, over-filtered shots. The only redeeming aspect is that this film doesn't quite compare to the even more vapid Naqoyqatsi.

Let me begin by saying that I generally appreciate Renny Harlin's directing style, and the cinematography in this film deserves praise for some of its striking shots. Compared to Harlin's "A Nightmare on Elm Street 4" and "Die Hard 2," which I genuinely enjoyed, this movie feels incomplete. The missing piece, unfortunately, is a solid script. The dialogue typical of this genre is often subpar, but this film takes the cake for sheer idiocy. The number of cringe-worthy lines is overwhelming, and I’d rather not dwell on any specific examples. Moreover, the way these lines are delivered is downright embarrassing, resembling something more akin to a poorly scripted adult film than an action adventure. It’s almost as if Harlin believed that slowing down the dialogue could somehow fix the writing—clearly, that was a false hope.

The real tragedy is that talented actors are wasted in poorly written roles with even worse dialogue. I’m not a big fan of Stallone, but here he outshines Lithgow, Turner, and especially Rooker, who is the weakest link. Lithgow, renowned for delivering some of the best villains in films like "Ricochet," is disappointingly underutilized in this project.

Here are the lessons I took away from "The List":

A decent cinematographer, an attractive actress who can actually act, and Malcolm McDowell couldn't save this movie from being a failure.

Blockbusters won't refund your ticket if you regret seeing it.

Even when Malcolm McDowell reads the script and grimaces with an "Ugh! Really?!" he still gives it his effort.

Chuck Carrington clearly needs acting lessons.

Hire a writer.

Jesus hates me too—he punished me by making me shell out $5.50 for this film.

When making a movie, you don't need a proper ending—just leave everything unresolved, unexplained, and dull enough that the audience drifts off before it concludes. Pure genius.

Any random landlord can supposedly cure death just by drawing a cross on a window—so make friends with one.

Your maid might sing you back to life.

Chuck Carrington still needs acting lessons.

Your roommate will scorn you and mock you if you bring home this movie.

And apologies? They won't be accepted.

Campy '70s horror flicks...you gotta love them. Compared to today's dull slasher movies, these K-tel gems actually deliver something frightening without relying on tired clichés.

This B-movie is about the making of a B-movie...that goes catastrophically wrong. Faith Domergue (from This Island Earth) portrays a washed-up B-movie starlet directing a film about a family's gruesome murders in their own home. Her boyfriend and director, who resembles Gordon Jump with an attitude, is filming on location under a tight schedule. The handsome co-star discovers a Tibetan chant book, which they incorporate into the script to add "authenticity." Sadly, that "authenticity" is something they would have been better off without.

John Carradine, having long since stopped searching for the 17th gland (from The Unearthly), ekes out a modest life as the estate's caretaker. His daily routine is overshadowed by frequent run-ins with the director.

The horror gradually intensifies—starting with a dead cat, then Carradine visiting a grave, culminating in seven murders. (At least the film's title is truthful.) It’s unfortunate that the creature didn't grasp the true meaning of horror.

Does anyone know what type of pickup truck John T drove? It appears to be a mid to late 1970s Ford. This film is a favorite of mine and my wife’s—it was the first movie we both vividly remember watching together after getting married. The pickup interests me because it resembles the first truck I ever drove, and I recently found another one like it. I’d love to restore my current pickup to look like the one in the movie. The music was fantastic, and the acting was excellent. Does anyone know the name of the actress who played John’s aunt and where she’s from? Additionally, was a stunt double used for John’s tower scene where he almost fell? Also, what year was the Mustang that Debra W. drove in the show? It looked like a 1960s model. Thanks again!

This Three Stooges film ranks equally with my other favorite, "Disorder in the Court." It’s a hilarious riot that any fan of the Stooges will thoroughly enjoy.

The boys are janitors at a recording studio when they overhear the lovely Christine McIntyre perform a wonderful rendition of "Voices of Spring." She’s about to be offered a record deal but is hesitant to reveal her true aspirations to her father and prove herself as a genuine singer. After she and the others leave, the Stooges decide to have some fun—playing her record and dressing Curly up as Christine. The talent scout who could launch Christine’s career sees Curly and mistakenly believes he is the singer, inviting him to perform at her party. Meanwhile, there's a man at the party they've upset, and when they sabotage his solo in front of everyone, he’s determined to get revenge.

This is a fantastic Stooges flick—definitely not to be missed!  
10/10

In The College Girl Murders, chaos ensues as a mad scientist develops an almost undetectable toxic gas. Just as he prepares to benefit from his invention, he is abruptly murdered by a hooded monk wielding a whip. When a female student is also killed in a church with the same deadly gas, Scotland Yard is enlisted to solve the case. Yet, the murders persist, and the question remains: who is this elusive killer capable of slipping in and out of the college at will?  

What Works:

- The Killer. There's something undeniably captivating about a murderer who lurks in the shadows dressed in a striking red outfit reminiscent of the KKK, complete with matching gloves. His white whip, used with chilling effectiveness, sharply contrasts with his vivid costume. While the notion of a villain clad in blazing red and a pointed hood prowling a girls' school borders on the unbelievable, his sinister appearance is truly memorable.  

- Groovy 60s Music. I’m eager to find the soundtrack of The College Girl Murders. Its jazzy, trendy 60s vibe is absolutely captivating and adds a distinctive flair to the film.  

- Bizarre Touches. Beyond the killer's striking costume, the film is filled with quirky details that enhance its unique charm.

First and foremost, I was particularly struck by the central concept of locating the "intruders"—others within the delicate Self—on various levels, primarily subconscious but occasionally more allegorical. In fact, these intruders are a constant presence throughout the film: in the Swiss-French border where the protagonist leads a secluded life; within his recurring daydreams and nightmares; and inside his weakened body following a heart transplant. As the story progresses, he himself becomes an intruder, returning to an ancient French colony in hopes of atoning for past mistakes.

The overall tone leans toward bitterness rather than pathos, infused with regrets and guilt, with a pervasive sense of failure taking center stage. It offers a rather bleak portrayal of old age—appearing self-reliant on the surface but internally hollow and profoundly lonely. The director’s visual composition aims more to evoke fleeting sensations of anxiety and desire than to communicate explicit messages. Many of these images are mesmerizing, tinged with humor, forming an absurdist tableau that only a somnambulist could truly visualize.

Warning: Major spoilers ahead. I've only seen one other film by Takashi Miike, and that was the intensely disturbing and brutal "Audition," which critically explores Japanese notions of femininity. In "Visitor Q"—which I believe signifies "Visitor Question"—Miike delves into the family dynamic in a grotesquely unsettling manner. His surreal portrayal of a dysfunctional family nearly feels Lynchian in its confusion and cinematic style, yet it ultimately lacks the depth and intrigue of Lynch's work. From the very first scene, we are introduced to a bizarre sequence: the father (Kenichi Endo, who delivers a surprisingly good performance) paying for sex with his displaced daughter, Fujiko. Soon after, the father is attacked at home by a mysterious visitor (Kazushi Watanabe), wielding a sizable rock, and inexplicably, both end up back at the family house. The mother (Shungiku Uchida) is subjected to violence and manipulation by her son (Jun Muto), who himself is bullied and beaten by classmates. When the visitor enters the scene, he takes on a somewhat ominous role, becoming part of the family's chaos. Over time, with the visitor's influence, the family members attempt to improve their relationships through increasingly bizarre and disturbing methods, including milk-related acts, murder, and retention.

I am perpetually struck by the profound horror and outrage inspired by the atrocities committed throughout history in the name of religion. The manipulations of the Catholic Church in Twentieth Century Ireland, in particular, stand out as among the most egregious—especially given that both historical lessons and modern awareness should have curbed such insidious actions.

A Love Divided chronicles the true story of a family deeply wounded by ignorance, intolerance, and prejudice—all justified by an irrational Church doctrine. The film opens with a idyllic depiction of life in a small Irish village, where Sheila and Sean Cloney enjoy a joyful marriage with their two young children. Sean is Catholic, while Sheila is Protestant; however, she has no objection to their children being raised Catholic. The community appears harmonious, free of hostility between Catholics and Protestants. This tranquility is shattered when Sheila wishes for their older child to attend a Protestant school. The local priest intervenes, labeling her desire as a sin, and in doing so, ignites a chain of events that lead to Sean, Sheila, and the entire Catholic community being embroiled in conflict.

This film exemplifies how technically proficient directors—specializing in music videos and commercials—often attempt their first full-length feature. On the positive side, the visuals, cinematography, lighting, CGI, and sound design are meticulously crafted, exuding a markedly upscale aesthetic. Even the actors display noticeable promise—so much so that talented performances can't compensate for the glaring absence of a coherent plot.

In this instance, the story is virtually nonexistent, lacking any substantial narrative substance.

Approximately half of the dialogue revolves around phrases like "What the hell was that?", "What was that?", and "What the hell was that?". None of these exchanges offer either characters or viewers any real insight or explanation. Elsewhere in the script, it often seems as though there was no proper screenplay—actors appear to have improvised their lines, uncertain of the plot's direction or even its existence.

The sole performer whose delivery stands out is Skye Bennet, whose role as an autistic girl perhaps spared her from the awkward, poorly written lines that plague the others.

Are you a fan of unraveling mysteries? Do you enjoy intricate storytelling? If so, this film is perfect for you. Directed by Francis Leclerc, son of the legendary French Canadian singer Félix Leclerc, this brilliant and intelligent movie features striking visuals and sharp editing, qualities that define Leclerc's style. Roy Dupuis delivers a passionate performance in the lead role, adding to the film's intensity.

The story follows Alexandre Tourneur, a veterinarian in his forties, who wakes up from a coma after being mysteriously unplugged. As he struggles to recall who hit him—an incident that occurred while he was tending to a wounded deer on the road—he begins to exhibit strange behavior, as if something else has taken control of him.

While not a horror film, it’s a deeply mysterious and well-acted piece. I have my own theory about the ending—believing that the Indian was responsible for the accident—but the conclusion remains open to interpretation.

Highly recommended—9.5 out of 10.

This film is a bright spot in a gloomy season, shining with a simple yet powerful theme of genuine friendliness. Morgan Freeman portrays a character quite similar to himself—a seasoned actor nearing seventy. He visits a modest, somewhat shabby grocery store to gather material for a potential role as a store manager. Before long, he endears himself to both staff and customers, especially a spirited yet slightly irritable young woman (Paz Vega) who runs the "10 items or less" checkout lane.  

"10 Items Or Less" isn’t here to deliver sweeping messages or grandiose statements. It simply chronicles Freeman and Vega’s growing friendship, as the older man offers heartfelt advice to her. Their connection develops when Freeman offers to give her a ride home after the usual ride-share fails to show, and he’s unable to call for help because he’s forgotten his phone number. On a drizzly Sunday afternoon in New York City, I was feeling a bit down, and this movie happily lifted my spirits.

Ladies and gentlemen, please do not be deceived by the label "A Stanley Kubrick Film." This is a poor movie that, unfortunately, has been mistakenly celebrated as one of the most terrifying horror films ever created. True horror films should evoke such intense fear that viewers shiver at the mere thought of them during the night. In The Shining, there is no genuine horror; instead, what we encounter is a naive and misguided attempt to evoke chills. Anyone familiar with effective horror knows how different it is from reality. The only redeeming aspects of the film are the breathtaking views of the icy valley and the hotel set, which looks quite good. Regarding the cast, Jack Nicholson comes across as a lost, sluggish soul, unsure of his role or purpose. As for the bald, darker-skinned actor, he spends most of his screen time tending to a child actor, leaving little impression. There's no need to blame the bad weather for the film's shortcomings; it’s simply a product of its making. Unfortunately, Stanley Kubrick is no longer alive to make any revisions.

I can't believe this movie was actually made in 1984. The acting is truly laughable, and the plot ranks among the most ridiculous I’ve ever seen. Who in their right mind would have fat Texas sheriff Joe Don Baker escort an Italian he illegally arrested in Mexico back to Italy? And the title—it's so vague that it hardly gives any hint about the story. Honestly, it's about as generic a title for an action/cop film as you could imagine.

Thankfully, I only watched this on MST3K with Mike and the bots as my shields. They kept making comments about the female lead's resemblance to Elaine from Seinfeld (“None of them are spongeworthy”) and continuously ribbing Baker’s weight. While it might not be worse than “Mitchell,” Baker’s reputation definitely precedes him here: when his name appears at the start of the film, Tom quips, “I wish I was illiterate so I wouldn’t have to see that.”

The film boasts a thoughtfully crafted genre story that encapsulates all the classic elements of a Columbo mystery. It showcases Lt. Columbo’s characteristic approach to suspect interrogation and relationship-building, the intricate unraveling of the case from his perspective, and the charming interplay between the cat-and-mouse dynamic—particularly enjoyable in this installment—and is complemented by some well-placed humor primarily centered around Columbo himself. While the storyline relies on familiar tropes, notably involving Columbo investigating a detective and murder novelist—a plot device revisited multiple times—it's executed with style and wit. 

James Frawley’s skillful direction elevates the film, imparting it with distinctive flair and memorable sequences that stand out. Following this project, Frawley went on to helm five more Columbo films in the 1970s and 1980s, cementing his influence on the series’ visual and narrative style.

Though slower-paced than some other entries and not particularly lengthy, the film’s deliberate tempo complements its tone and storytelling approach—an aspect that often challenges other Columbo movies but succeeds here, largely thanks to the strong performances by the cast. Unlike many entries in the series that feature prominent stars or legendary early film icons, this installment’s casting and acting contribute significantly to its effectiveness.

Admittedly, I have a soft spot for Al Pacino. He was a talented actor until Scent of a Woman, where he seemed to overindulge to the point of diminishing his own talents. I had hoped this film, which I had hardly heard of growing up, would turn out to be a hidden treasure—a clever, insightful, city-based political thriller ahead of its time. Unfortunately, it falls short.

City Hall is a film that entangles its story in an overwhelming web of characters, names, and so-called "realistic" urban issues. For a while, you might think its scope is so expansive and provocative that discovering the true story would be mind-blowing. Yet, in reality, these subplots and tangents merely lead to familiar urban tropes: corruption of power, duplicitous politicians, mafia ties to law enforcement, and so on. While this setup could create tense, unpredictable moments—where any character might be compromised or harmed—it ultimately doesn't deliver.

Regrettably, the events are predictable, and the film relies heavily on several "confession" monologues. Collectively, they aim to serve as a modern parable, illustrating the moral complexities inherent in the gritty world of politics. However, the result feels more like a series of familiar cliches than a compelling or enlightening story.

Let's start with the iconic theme song performed by Christopher Cross. The track is "If You Get Caught Between the Moon and New York City." Even after all these years, it's a timeless tune that never loses its charm—a perfect ode to New York City itself. Moving on, the film features the legendary Dudley Moore CBE as a spoiled, drunken millionaire engaged to Jill Eikenberry's character, who later gained fame on LA Law. He is impeccably served by his charismatic British butler, Sir John Gielgud OM, who received an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his role. Arthur, the protagonist, falls in love with Liza Minnelli’s character, who is fantastic in this film—aside from her acclaimed Oscar-winning role in Cabaret. Interestingly, she doesn't sing here; she portrays a diner waitress. I also particularly enjoyed Geraldine Fitzgerald as the Bach family matriarch who determines the family's future fortunes. She was fabulous and truly deserved an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress. Barney Martin, best known as Jerry's dad on Seinfeld, also delivers a memorable performance as Liza's father. The film is well-written, brilliantly acted, and expertly delivered.

This film features Robert Duvall delivering his worst performance, sounding remarkably like William Buckley throughout. His overly theatrical and melodramatic acting detracts from any sense of drama. Whether intentional or not, it feels like scene-stealing, and it's the only memorable aspect—though not for the right reasons—in what is otherwise a forgettable movie. This film should be shown in every amateur acting class as a prime example of what to avoid. Fortunately, Duvall went on to achieve greater success and eventually abandoned attempting to adopt a cultured accent. While he's a competent character actor, this isn't his finest hour. Klaus, on the other hand, offers a much better, more subtle, and notable performance.

This film is a captivating portrayal of Grey Owl's life in 1930s Canada. I found it equally moving and engaging as 'Rudy' and 'Awakenings.' The story begins in Grey Owl's later years, charting his most turbulent and impactful period. 

The plot centers on a Canadian Indian trapper who champions the conservation of beavers, highlighting the dangers of over-trapping. He also forewarns about the shrinking natural lands and the reckless exploitation of Earth's resources—an audacious idea for the 1930s, yet it resonated surprisingly well with audiences. As a result, he becomes a prominent speaker, inspiring many to listen. 

Pierce Brosnan's casting might seem unconventional at first, but it is quite fitting upon viewing. Anyone skeptical should watch the film to appreciate his performance, which is truly excellent, as is Annie Galipeau’s. Galipeau's portrayal is both strong and authentic, providing a refreshing contrast to the often contrived pairings seen in recent James Bond movies. 

I highly recommend this film to anyone who enjoys compelling drama, stunning scenery, or environmental issues. It is also suitable for family viewing; however, children under 10 (depending on maturity) might find it challenging to follow the story.

I'm not quite sure who recommended this to me, but they mentioned it as one of their favorite films. It’s definitely an odd watch—like rubbernecking at a highway accident.  

Someone once said that truth is often stranger than fiction, and this story certainly proves that. I’m perplexed as to how a dramatized version of this documentary is slated for release later this year. How could they possibly improve upon the real events?  

The story involves Jackie Kennedy’s aunt and cousin, who withdraw from New York social circles and retreat to the Hamptons. Over time, they become recluses, best described as “crazy cat ladies.” They would have remained hidden if not for the city condemning their property due to its deplorable condition, leading to Jackie’s rescue. This film was made after that rescue, and watching it, I couldn’t help but wonder, “How bad was it before?”  

It offers a glimpse into high society’s darker side, and it’s utterly captivating.

I was highly anticipating this project during its production, but it turned out to be the biggest disappointment. It was a far cry from the whimsical world of Dr. Seuss, instead feeling vulgar and distasteful—I don't believe Dr. Seuss would have approved. "How the Grinch Stole Christmas" was much better, even with some clever adult jokes that my children haven't yet understood. In contrast, "The Cat in the Hat" seemed to scream vulgarity, catching far more than I was comfortable with. Having grown up with Dr. Seuss, it was disheartening to see this beloved classic so badly misrepresented on the big screen. I'm hopeful that "Horton Hears a Who" will do justice to Dr. Seuss's legacy—fingers crossed.

Oh my goodness! This movie completely insults everyone's intelligence. Honestly, who believes three kids can take on and defeat 30 or 40 ninjas? And don't even get me started on the hilariously pointless humor sprinkled throughout. This film is absolutely terrible.
