It feels more like an omen than entertainment—only suitable as a quick distraction or for some unintended laughs.

A theatrical company cast becomes frightened when a strange murderer known as 'The Fiend' begins targeting them for death. Two reporters and their awkward photographer set out to uncover the story of 'The Fiend' but soon find themselves in danger as well. Just when you think our trio of heroes has unraveled the mystery, another twist emerges, leaving you questioning who the real killer is, according to the DVD sleeve's synopsis.

Taking inspiration from "The Hunchback of Notre Dame," Hollywood producer Sam Katzman’s minimal use of studio sets likely adds a unique charm to "A Face in the Fog," especially in the final scenes depicting 1930s traffic. The direction leaves room for improvement; for instance, the camera angle during the fight scene is unhelpful. The film's budget seems modest, but considering the circumstances, most of the cast, blending silent and talkie performers, deliver commendable performances.

**** A Face in the Fog (2/1/36) Robert F. Hill ~ Lloyd Hughes, June Collyer, Al St. John

"Paris is a moveable feast," as Ernest Hemingway famously declared.

Countless artists have captured Paris’s essence—immortalizing it through paintings, novels, songs, poems, memorable quotes, and films. Renowned director Max Ophüls once described Paris as a city that seduces with its shimmering, rain-slicked boulevards lit by streetlamps, mornings spent in Montmartre with cognac in hand, warm coffee paired with soft brioche, and the allure of nightlife filled with gigolos and prostitutes. He famously remarked, "Everyone in the world has two fatherlands: his own and Paris."

The city is forever linked to love and romance. This is beautifully explored in "Paris, Je T'Aime," a collection of short films—subtitled "Petite romances"—created by eighteen talented directors from around the globe. Each vignette offers a glimpse into one of Paris’s twenty arrondissements and introduces us to Parisians of diverse ages, genders, backgrounds, and cultures—all navigating love in its many forms and phases. Some of these "petite romances" depict spontaneous encounters—strangers meeting by chance that swiftly blossom into friendship or romance—such as Podalydès and Florence Muller’s brief yet meaningful exchange on a Montmartre street in the opening segment, or Cyril’s own encounter...

I've been eager to see this for a long time; James Merendino is a fantastic director. Since SLC Punk is one of my favorite films, I was excited to watch this as a follow-up. The first ten minutes were promising, but thereafter, the story started to lose momentum. The acting and direction were excellent; everything in the film seemed to come together well—except for the screenplay. At times, my only motivation to stay engaged was the presence of Claire Forlani, arguably the most beautiful woman in the world. While the film was enjoyable, I was expecting it to be even better. 

P.S. Keep an eye out for memorable cameos by Chi McBride and Chris McDonald.

This is undoubtedly the funniest movie I have ever watched. From the very beginning, when four delinquents are sent off by their fathers to Wienberg Military Academy, a humorous tone is established that persists throughout the entire film, never letting up for a moment.

Describing this film is challenging because its comedic elements are so precise and brilliantly conceived that at first glance, it might seem like nothing more than a silly 80s teen comedy centered on teenage lust. However, it is so much more than that! Crafted by the creative team behind MAD Magazine, *Up the Academy* delivers a unique style and formula that I have yet to see duplicated by any other Hollywood comedy in recent years. The film is filled with juvenile, cheesy humor—so much so that it’s easy to think the writers might have been teenagers themselves. If you enjoy embracing childlike silliness, this movie is a must-see. A true classic. *****

I must confess that my initial motivation for purchasing this film was my admiration for Gackt and an even greater devotion to Hyde. I anticipated an engaging movie filled with visually appealing scenes that would surely delight the feminine gaze, paired with a story that might lean toward the slightly cheesy side. The synopsis itself seemed quite outlandish. However, having just finished watching it, I feel compelled to share its remarkable quality with everyone! Both Hyde and Gackt delivered truly moving performances, and I’m still emotionally drained from the tears that persisted through the film’s final half. The story pulls you in completely, and by its conclusion, you genuinely sympathize with the characters. The vampiric element—something I love but know can easily be mishandled or overused—was woven in subtly enough to feel natural and exotic within the setting, rather than as an unnecessary plot device. I initially rated it a 9 out of 10, but then I started pondering why I wasn’t giving it that perfect score… and I realized there was something missing.

This film is truly exceptional. If you get the chance to see it, don't hesitate—go watch it right away. Although it bears little resemblance to its 1932 original, Pacino masterfully portrays Tony Montana, convincingly navigating around the differences.  

Pacino has a unique talent for delivering any line in any manner and making it sound fantastic. If you appreciated the use of language in Pulp Fiction (assuming you've seen it), then you'll want to check out Scarface for another perspective on how an actor can deliver such dialogue—it's quite impressive.  

Even though the movie is packed with action and the storyline moves quickly through time—sometimes sacrificing real-time accuracy—it's still straightforward to follow. Just keep your eyes sharp so you don’t miss anything. Personally, I find that watching this film makes three hours feel like nothing at all; it's that compelling.  

This movie is so well-acted and expertly directed that it instantly transports you, making you forget that it was made in a different era.

I happened upon this (Act-I) purely by chance over a decade ago. Interestingly, it wasn't even what the tape’s cover indicated. I was fascinated, yet also overwhelmed and somewhat shocked. Over time, I nearly forgot about it, but nearly ten years later, it randomly came back to mind. I decided to purchase both acts, and I was astonished to find they surpassed my initial impressions.  

My only critique is that while the Tank Police continuously proclaim their ongoing battle against crime—justifying their use of tanks and heavy weaponry—it seems they have little real trouble dealing with criminals. This struggle is rarely depicted or might simply be a fabrication; they appear to handle things quite casually most of the time. If their warlike rhetoric was truly propaganda, it’s not convincingly demonstrated.  

I doubt the original Japanese version could have been as compelling as its American adaptation. However, some nuances of the story were likely lost in translation, though that can be understood and forgiven.

Chris Rock stars in this fresh take on Warren Beatty's Heaven Can Wait, which itself was a remake of the 1941 film Here Comes Mr. Jordan. The comedy centers on a man who dies prematurely, before fulfilling his dreams, and explores his misadventures in his new, albeit temporary, body. In the original Beatty version, the character was a backup quarterback for the Los Angeles Rams. In Rock's modernized, edgier adaptation, the protagonist is a struggling young stand-up comedian with limited talent.

It's hilarious to watch the quick-witted Rock portray a hopeless comedian—much like seeing Tom Hanks play an inept actor. The story follows Lance Barton, who dreams of performing at the legendary Apollo Theater on a serious night rather than as an amateur. However, every attempt at his act results in loud boos—earning him the nickname "Booie." His jokes fall flat, and his delivery is painfully awkward. In many ways, Lance embodies everything that Chris Rock is not.

Lance also works as a bike messenger, pedaling through the city on his way to try out more material when, suddenly—BAM!—he's struck by a truck. Perhaps he was taken from his body just a fraction of a second earlier.

For Christmas, I received the first Bill and Ted movie, and I couldn't pass up getting the second when I saw it in a store. I think this one was just as funny as the first, but the story was much stranger. It was amusing how they each had their own personal hell and how they had to face Death. The funniest part was how they played him in silly games like Clue. The only thing I would change is having Station and Death in the band, but other than that, it was fantastic.

Someone must have been joking when they created this film.

First and foremost, there's no way this movie was made in 1993; the fashion and music clearly scream the 1980s. I suspect it’s been sitting on a shelf for years until some eccentric distributor finally picked it up and released it to an unexpecting audience.

The plot, if you can call it that, is about a strange loner who encounters a bearded man. This man claims that if the loner meditates while singing his favorite song, he can transform into anyone he wishes. I feel compelled to mention that the loner’s favorite song is "London Bridge Is Falling Down." Why is this his favorite? Because he's an idiot. Just a minute into the film, and it already hits an astonishing level of absurdity—only to become even more ridiculous as it progresses.

The loner appears to be a nostril picker—at least, that’s my assumption, given the two scenes showing him picking his nose. This detail finally clarifies the title. He then decides to transform into a girl to get close to something or someone.

A remarkable film by Powell and Pressburger, whose work I now feel compelled to delve into further. The movie explores the elusive line between perception and reality, highlighting just how hard it can be to tell them apart. Visually stunning and excellently performed, although David Niven doesn’t quite appear to be 27, as his character suggests. It was a delight to spot a very young Richard Attenborough. This film sparked both immediate and lingering reflection for me during and after watching.

If you're interested in learning the fundamentals of quantum mechanics, spend your $9 on a used textbook instead of this film. I'm a bit concerned that my money might be going toward sending Kool-Aid to Guyana.  

It seems the directors didn't quite succeed in conveying a clear message, but perhaps they aimed to suggest several ideas: 1) Science can explain everything we do, implying our lives are deterministic; 2) Science can't fully explain our actions, leaving room for free will; 3) Science is genuinely awesome, man; 4) We are like gods; 5) The world only exists in our minds; 6) Sarah Norman is a challenging character to follow; and 7) here, try this tiny paper square in your mouth and experience some pretty far-out effects.

This is the type of movie I fear the most. Arrogant and irresponsible, it offers a superficial and clichéd portrayal of the Colombian conflict that is both dumb and insulting to all Colombians. The performances are abysmal, from Grisales—whose nude scene is embarrassingly bad—to Bejarano, Fanny Mickey (who looks like she stepped out of a Tim Burton nightmare), and Díaz, who tries hard to give life to a character so flat, clichéd, and poorly written that all he has to work with is a mustache. The gratuitous ending is a gore-filled spectacle so cheesy it would even make Ed Wood cringe. The film fails on every level—cinematography, art direction, costumes, makeup, editing—and most notably, in direction. Jorge Alí Triana has never been a great filmmaker, but at least his earlier works had some dignity. I can say nothing positive about this money-wasting venture, except to hope that Colombian filmmakers learn a lesson in honesty, integrity, and responsibility from this blatantly mean-spirited fiasco.

Let me tell you how I first discovered this film. It was winter in Alaska around 1990. A friend from Australia was staying with my girlfriend and me in a tiny apartment—more like a shoebox. Winters there can be brutally cold, so most people tend to stay indoors, drink heavily, and watch whatever happens to be on TV. One day, I found this movie outside a thrift store, lying in a snowbank, and instantly knew it was a hidden gem. It’s arguably the best worst movie ever made. Over the next two weeks, we watched it nonstop, drinking like fish. We loved it so much that we even turned the TV on its side or upside down for a more immersive experience. This film is a true treasure—the laughs are endless, and the memories will last forever. If you see it available for rent in a video store, do yourself a favor and steal it. You won’t regret a single moment!

I initially thought The Sentinel would be a mediocre film. However, when I finally watched it, I was pleasantly surprised. While it's not a masterpiece, it's quite entertaining, and the action scenes are particularly well-executed. The movie reminded me of TV series like 24 or Alias, with a similar vibe, and also brought to mind Wolfgang Petersen's thriller In the Line of Fire. If you're expecting one of the most original or greatest thrillers in cinematic history, you may be disappointed. But if you go in with modest expectations, you'll enjoy The Sentinel.  
**Rating: 7**

If you're looking to watch "THE Gamers" by Dead Gentlemen Productions, you'll be disappointed—this isn't that film. It's simply not amusing and ultimately a waste of your time.

Many of the positive reviews seem to be written by fake accounts or intentionally disguised third parties. It appears the filmmakers are trying to artificially generate interest and credibility.

This film doesn't succeed as a mockumentary; comparisons to "Spinal Tap" or Christopher Guest are entirely unjustified. Instead, it's mean-spirited and fails to evoke genuine humor, especially for those familiar with the subject. If anything, it’s so harshly satirical that anyone being poked fun at would have to harbor some self-hatred to find it funny.

The problem isn't its attempt at bold satire of taboo topics but rather its persistent, pathetic dullness that makes the entire experience feel utterly banal.

This ranks among my all-time favorite films. The sharp, pun-filled dialogue is brilliantly crafted, the cast delivers outstanding performances, and the storyline is remarkably unique.  
  
Don't just take my word for it—watch the movie and experience it firsthand.

There is an abundance of star talent in THE HOUSE OF SPIRITS enough to form another galaxy, yet the final outcome remains highly debatable. The film’s messages are undeniably noble, and I suspect many viewers would concur—proclaiming that liberal democracy is good, while murderous fascist regimes are bad; that open-mindedness is virtuous and racism is condemnable. Unfortunately, these themes are hammered home with such bluntness and lack of subtlety that they become almost tiresome.

Ultimately, we find ourselves watching virtuous characters—flawed yet noble—face off against despicable villains with no redeeming qualities. The tension feels as genuine as a poorly choreographed professional wrestling match.

Jeremy Irons portrays the patriarch, a man riddled with contradictions. Meryl Streep stars as his talented wife, and Glenn Close plays her sister-in-law. When the story focuses on these characters, it tends to flow smoothly and remains quite engaging. Regrettably, THE HOUSE OF SPIRITS is plagued by numerous subplots and a revolving door of characters who appear and disappear like targets in a shooting gallery. We never get the chance to truly know or care about them, leading to a sense of boredom.

If only director and screenwriter Bille August, adapting Isabel Allende’s novel, had...

This was the first regular filmed Columbo movie episode, but surprisingly it aired as the second, following Steven Spielberg's "Columbo: Murder by the Book." Despite its placement, it ranks among the better installments!

Bernard L. Kowalski was an exceptional creative director, and it's no wonder he was later entrusted with directing three more Columbo movies. The film features some truly inventive and innovative shot sequences, and overall it exudes style, passion, and meticulous attention to detail. Every shot serves a purpose, contributing to why this film stands out as both better and more visually appealing than the average TV movie. Undoubtedly, it's one of the best-directed Columbo episodes.

This entry is quite unique for several reasons. The murder is essentially an accident, committed impulsively, leaving the killer no time to plan the "perfect murder" or to clean up traces or dispose of the body. The perpetrator is portrayed not just as a criminal but more as someone who inadvertently helps to facilitate the situation.

Sandra Bernhard is truly a one-of-a-kind personality and undoubtedly one of the funniest women alive. She launched her career as a stand-up comedian in the 1970s, but her breakthrough came in 1983 when she starred alongside Jerry Lewis and Robert De Niro in Martin Scorsese's often-overlooked gem, "The King of Comedy." Although her film career didn't reach the same heights, she did appear in a few quirky yet memorable films like "Dallas Doll" (1994) and "Dinner Rush" (2000), showcasing her talent for creating memorable characters for herself. 

Her most acclaimed work is undoubtedly "Without You I'm Nothing," a film adaptation of her wildly successful off-Broadway show that catapulted her to stardom—and earned her a close friendship with Madonna for several years. Through ten meticulously crafted and staged scenes, Bernhard transforms from Nina Simone to Diana Ross, shares stories from her childhood, discusses icons like Andy Warhol and San Francisco, and performs songs made famous by Burt Bacharach, Prince, and Sylvester. Directed by John Boskovich, the film captures Sandra in a compelling 90-minute performance that is both sultry and uniquely humorous. For fans of Bernhard, this film is essential viewing; it stands as a tribute not only to her distinctive, eccentric beauty but also to her exceptionally unconventional talent.

I picked this up for fifty cents at the flea market and was pretty excited. I enjoyed it for about fifteen minutes, but then it became repetitive and dull. It's interesting to see Mick and the band in their prime, though I wish there wasn't so much overdubbing of dialogue so I could actually hear what they're saying and playing. The skits are politically outdated, incredibly naive, and quite simplistic—like a poorly written Monty Python on acid. I found myself more captivated by the late '60s England backdrops than by the silly skits themselves. This movie serves as a good reminder that times really do change, and what once seemed important quickly turns into something silly. The soundtrack is great, but it's been played to death by this DVD.

I recently acquired the restored version of a film I hold dear from my childhood, and it certainly offers a delightful way to spend a curious afternoon. Watching the complete version of *Bedknobs and Broomsticks* makes much more sense, especially with the inclusion of the deleted scenes—particularly those featuring McDowall—which help connect the storylines more seamlessly. 

However, I found the remastering process somewhat unsettling. Apparently, the original soundtrack of certain scenes had been lost or damaged, leading a creative mind at Disney to dub new dialogue over the footage. While this approach might have been effective, the execution leaves much to be desired, especially since several original cast members weren't available to re-record their lines—some for understandable reasons—and the results feel rather amateurish. The lip-syncing can be awkward at times, and David Tomlinson’s voice has been replaced by someone who sounds entirely different—there’s even a faint German accent in his dubbed voice.

That said, it’s wonderful to hear the full versions of the songs (though 'Step in the Right Direction' still seems to be missing), and the film's magical moments continue to shine through. I defy anyone not to giggle at the sight of young Paul gazing so innocently at Angela Lansbury and her companions, cooing with adorable admiration.

I am definitely not part of the target audience for this film. I’m a man approaching fifty who has only recently begun exploring the world of independent cinema. This discovery happened quite unexpectedly when I tuned into a late-night TV broadcast of *Clerks*. The first two things I noticed about the film were that it was 1) technically rough around the edges, and 2) brilliantly written. After reading an interview with the director in the local newspaper, where he mentioned that *Clerks* was one of his influences, I became intrigued. When he also cited *The Station Agent*—a film I had watched on DVD just a week earlier—I knew I had to see it. Both films share a similar spirit, despite their vastly different stories. They both feature noticeable technical flaws that are ultimately overshadowed by exceptional writing. *Clerks* depicts a day in the life of a man with almost nothing going on and who’s afraid to confront tough questions about himself and his circumstances. In contrast, *Less Like Me* revolves around a man who appears to keep himself perpetually busy, seemingly forcing himself into constant activity.

I went into this film expecting a drama about a man with a supernatural gift who was turned into a monster by society. I thought it would be something different, but it turned out to be a pleasant surprise. My friend and I both found the movie quite romantic—thanks in part to the handsome lead—and it had enough plot twists, action, and even humor to keep us engaged. The moment when they didn't learn each other's names until the third act had the entire theater laughing. Overall, it wasn't what I anticipated, but it was a great surprise. I definitely plan to buy it when it’s released on DVD.

Reportedly kept on the back burner for years, this television reunion of two of sitcom history’s most beloved characters got off to a terrible start—and only worsened from there. Mary Richards (Mary Tyler Moore) and her best friend Rhoda Morgenstern (Valerie Harper) reunite in New York after a long separation to catch up on their lives. An intriguing idea, right? Sadly, nothing significant or even remotely interesting has happened to either of them during the intervening years, making the premise feel uninspired. Instead, the script relies on tired clichés—particularly old-fashioned plot devices about older women in the workplace—failing to capture the quirky charm and sophistication that made the original series a hit. The supporting cast quickly fades into forgetfulness, humor is entirely absent, and the chemistry that once sparked between Moore and Harper is noticeably missing. Moore allegedly delayed the project for years, waiting for the “perfect script,” and if this is what she considered ideal, one can only wonder about the opportunities she declined. It’s not the characters’ age that sinks this effort—inevitably, time would have its way—but the lack of originality and spirit that truly undermine it.

I believe this is potentially the funniest film I have ever watched. Robert Harling's screenplay is nearly flawless—just take a look at the "quotes" section; then again, it’s probably best to just rent the DVD, as the delivery truly elevates the lines to new heights.

Sally Field delivers a comedic, exaggerated performance unlike anything else she's done, while Kevin Kline is effortlessly comedic. Robert Downey Jr. is his usual brilliant self, and in a brief but memorable role, Kathy Najimy is hilariously distressed as the overwhelmed costume designer. Although I wasn't particularly a fan of Elisabeth Shue before, she shines here as the only genuine character amidst a cast of caricatures on the set of "The Sun Also Sets"—and the tremor beneath you might just be Hemingway turning in his grave, or perhaps laughing out loud. 

Five stars. Absolutely hilarious.

Monty Berman and Dennis Spooner followed their work on 'The Baron' with this fantasy series about three superhuman spies, predating 'The Six Million Dollar Man'. It was a favorite of mine in my youth, and I still enjoy watching it today. Stuart Damon and William Gaunt displayed an unmistakable on-screen chemistry as Craig Stirling and Richard Barrett, while the stunning Alexandra Bastedo skillfully portrayed Sharron Macready. The late Anthony Nicholls delivered a wonderfully gruff performance as Tremayne. The strongest episodes were written by Tony Williamson, Terry Nation, and Brian Clemens, with Spooner's own 'The Interrogation' standing out as comparable to 'The Prisoner'. It's a disappointment that the series never received a second season; the concept still had so much potential. I often wonder if Craig and Richard might have competed for Sharron's affections, or what Tremayne’s reaction would have been had he discovered the Champions’ true powers. Did the Champions possess any abilities beyond those we saw? Sadly, we’ll never know.

This film certainly qualifies as a quirky love story. While it may not be groundbreaking, Nicole Kidman carries the entire movie on her shoulders, with the rest of the cast easily forgettable. However, Ben Chaplin provides a charming portrayal of Hertfordshire life, featuring scenic shots of St Albans and Hemel Hempstead that capture the area's true character. What initially appears to be a typical episode of the beloved British TV series "Heartbeat" quickly transforms into a gritty, gangster-inspired action thriller. Although nothing particularly memorable happens in this modest film, it serves as decent weekend entertainment. It's worth a watch, especially if you relate to John, the lonely thirty-something hero—there might be something in his character that resonates with you.

I believe everyone eventually deserves a chance to make a comeback. That’s precisely the goal for Jack Dundee (Robin Williams), a resident of Taft, in "The Best of Times." True to form, the man who went all out with a radio in "Good Morning, Vietnam" is now attempting to relive a football game that cost his high school a coveted championship. However, his former teammate Reno Hightower (Kurt Russell) isn’t about to let him do it without a fight.  

While the film may not be a masterpiece for either actor, Williams and Russell actually form a pretty solid comedy duo. Plus, some of the characters’ names are sure to make you laugh (perhaps quite a bit). Give it a watch.
Avoid this film at all costs. Without question, it's the worst movie I've ever watched. Unlike most films that offer some redeeming quality, this one has none. Absolutely terrible!

In a summer dominated by such dreadful releases as Snakes on a Plane and The Da Vinci Code, that's quite a strong claim. Yet I stand by it. Superman Returns, much like King Kong six months earlier, is excessively long, overly indulgent, and saturated with CGI. Honestly, it's getting to be too much to handle.  

Richard Donner's vision for the original Superman movies was to keep things grounded and authentic. I believe his approach to special effects and optical work was the most fitting. In contrast, Brian Singer bombards us with so much CGI that it pulls you out of the narrative and constantly signals that you're watching a costly blockbuster. The film seems to think that pouring $250 million—an irresponsible figure—into flashy visual effects is the key to impressing audiences. But we've seen it all before; we've been everywhere CGI can take us. There's little genuine atmosphere or emotional engagement. Considering that about 95% of the movie is composed of these effects, well, you can draw your own conclusions.  

I've read numerous reviews from critics obsessed with claiming the film has 'soul' or depth...

I was just thirteen when I first discovered this series, and now, over thirty years later, I’m watching it again on DVD. The images from the opening credits have stayed with me all these years. They’ve shaped my perspective on the world and its people. My parents watched it with me long enough to share in my experience, and we always discussed the program afterward. It sparked my passion for studying history, leading me to earn the highest marks in our school’s public exams.

Sir Laurence Olivier’s voice and delivery are truly timeless and impeccable. I get the sense that those who lived through the era would see this as their definitive account of World War II. I can't imagine ever tiring of watching it. Perhaps a similar series about the Cold War could be created now, though it’s hard to envision anyone replacing Sir Laurence. 

Definitely buy it!

Mario Lewis of the Competitive Enterprise Institute has authored a comprehensive 120-page, detailed rebuttal of this deceptive film, which he aptly titles A CONVENIENT LIE. His thorough analysis, titled "A SKEPTIC'S GUIDE TO AN INCONVENIENT TRUTH," is available on their website at www.cei.org. A condensed 10-page version can be accessed at www.cei.org/pdf/5539.pdf. After reviewing these in-depth demolitions, it becomes clear that the so-called "global warming" threat is as exaggerated and as baseless as the Y2K scare of 1999—an incident endorsed by Gore himself—and equally spurious as the pseudo-scientific film THE DAY AFTER TOMORROW, which was based on a book by alleged UFO abductee Whitley Strieber. Just as James "The Amazing" Randi challenges psychics, Philip Klass debunks UFO claims, and Gerald Posner dissects JFK conspiracy theories, Mario Lewis systematically disassembles Al Gore's film and the entire "global warming" narrative.

Scott Henderson (played by Alan Curtis) is falsely accused of murdering his unfaithful wife. On the night she was killed, he was out with a mysterious woman who refused to reveal her name. Following the accusation, police investigate all the places he visited with her, but witnesses only recall seeing him alone. He is ultimately sentenced to death, prompting his secretary (Ella Raines) to take it upon herself to uncover the real killer because of her love for him.

This film was produced as a B-movie by Universal—highlighted by a cast consisting mainly of character actors and one fading star, Franchot Tone. Despite its modest budget and largely unknown cast, it emerges as one of the finest film noirs of the 1940s. The direction by Curt Siodmak is stunning, and the screenplay—adapted from William Irish’s excellent novel (a pseudonym for Cornell Woolrich)—is sharp and well-paced. The film’s visual style is striking, and it features a memorable scene where Raines and Elisha Cook Jr. share a jam session imbued with intense sexual chemistry, surprisingly uncut by censors.

A few flaws prevent this from being flawless; notably, Tone’s performance falls flat, detracting from the overall impact.

Anyone who praised this film must not watch enough movies. A dull character whines about his dysfunctional family while snapping photos of them; the film is packed with fools and features explicit "teabagging" scenes. That pretty much says it all. Don't bother wasting your time—hoping it improves is futile; it simply doesn't.

I was genuinely excited to watch this film, hoping that Australia had finally produced a decent movie. Unfortunately, I was mistaken. 

This film was perhaps the most disappointing attempt at a slasher flick I’ve ever seen. I feel sorry for Molly Ringwald, who traveled all the way to Australia to star in such a terrible production. 

The acting was subpar, especially that Australian actor trying to do an American accent. The plot was equally lacking in quality. 

When I first heard about the movie’s release, I found the title rather cheesy—it reminded me of the film "Stab" from Scream 2. However, I was willing to overlook that if the movie turned out to be good. 

WARNING: MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD! 

One of the worst aspects was the ending. I anticipated a shocking reveal about the killer’s identity, but it was revealed that the killer wasn’t even human. That twist transformed what could have been a grounded slasher into a dreadful horror flick.

Avoid this film if you value your time—you’ll likely end up disappointed.

Among the three remakes of this story, I enjoy them all. I own all three on VHS and also have a DVD copy of this particular version. Each script offers just enough variation to keep all three fresh, entertaining, and worth re-watching. Has any other film been remade three times with such all-star casts in each version? The leading actors in this film are outstanding, but the supporting cast is equally superb. I especially appreciate William Tracy as Pepi; he was such a scene-stealer that I’ve actively searched for other films featuring him. Although he appeared in many movies, most are hard to find. Like others have mentioned, I highly recommend purchasing this one.

If this film had a $20 million budget, I genuinely wonder where all the money went. A monkey could have created better CGI effects than what was squandered over three hours on this abysmal piece of garbage. Admittedly, the machines and Martians might have looked impressive on an original PlayStation 1 game or early mid-90s PC games, had such games ever existed. What confuses me most is how the funds were used. Pendragon Films could have produced an excellent movie using traditional models, computer-controlled cameras inspired by George Lucas’s techniques from 1975 to 1983, and actors who actually care—well, or at least don't seem to be ruining their parts—for roughly the same $20 million. This might very well be the worst film ever made. I’d rather endure a 24-hour marathon of *Ishtar* than watch this again. I hated it completely! I apologize for rambling, but I truly believe this is the worst film ever, because unlike other notoriously bad movies like *Plan 9 from Outer Space*, *The Killer Tomatoes*, or *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians*, which have earned a sort of cult status, this film is so terrible that it occupies a special, tragic space in cinematic history.

Rated NR (would be Rated R for pervasive strong language and crude sexual humor). Quebec Rating: 16+ (should be 13+). Canadian Home Video Rating: 18A.

Eddie Murphy's *Delirious* marks his debut stand-up comedy special, released in 1983. At the time, he starred in *48 Hrs.* and *Trading Places*, and was a cast member on *Saturday Night Live*. Murphy has released two stand-up comedy specials: *Delirious* and *Raw*. Personally, I favor *Raw* for its more humorous subject matter, but *Delirious* is also very entertaining, featuring Eddie reminiscing about his childhood and parodying celebrities like Mr. T and singers such as Michael Jackson. Anyone who enjoys stand-up comedy films should definitely watch Eddie Murphy's *Delirious*.

I started watching a documentary about Puerto Rico, but I ended up watching one about Nuyoricans instead. When I visit Puerto Rico, I rarely see the 50% living in poverty; when I do encounter struggling individuals, they are usually recent immigrants like Haitians, Dominicans, or Cubans. There's no such thing as Spanglish—either you speak Spanish, or you don't. And from what I've heard, many don't. Pedro Albizu Campos is not Martin Luther King Jr. to me; MLK was a truly great man. Campos is seen as a hero only by those who support independence, which is merely 1%. The rest see him as crazy as Osama Bin Laden. Puerto Ricans advocating for independence are, in my opinion, misguided. To those dreaming of an independent Puerto Rico, just look at Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Bahamas, and the countries across Central and South America, and Mexico—it's not exactly a success story. This documentary isn't really about Puerto Rico; it's about Nuyoricans and their struggles. 

And to the person who complained that the show didn't feature enough African content—this was meant to be about Puerto Rico, not Africa. Denzel Washington will be creating a documentary about Africa soon.

I really enjoy watching early color films—so those 1940s costumes weren't all just shades of grey?  

Margaret Rutherford truly commands this film. Her "eccentric" attire is quite charming, and yes, she sports an incredible hourglass figure. However, I think she was allowed to indulge a bit too much in her character. Likely, she developed this persona over numerous performances, and no one advised her, "If it makes people laugh, just leave it alone." She tends to overdo her eccentric antics when she should be convincingly grounded. The joke about Madame Arcati is that mediums were typically depicted as delicate women draped in soft fabrics. Arcati, on the other hand, acts like a retired headmistress—full of energy ("We'll really put our backs into it!"). The contrast between her casual, everyday demeanor and her bizarre beliefs isn’t really emphasized enough.  

Regarding the accents, even though most actors are British (except Cummings), the Americans felt compelled to toss in words like "Brit," "stiff," "lip," and "upper" for effect. Honestly, enough already! The three leads are constantly losing their tempers and tossing around risqué comments ("Did he make love to you?" "Yes, but very discreetly—he was in the cavalry!").

A remarkable show and an unfulfilled classic, The League of Gentlemen stands as one of the most outstanding modern comedies of recent times.

With its dark, bizarre humor that surpasses the tired, predictable format of its less original but more widely recognized successor, Little Britain, The League of Gentlemen was truly a standout during a relatively quiet period in British comedy.

Before its debut, nothing quite like The League of Gentlemen had existed. Initially seeming like a straightforward sketch show, it quickly reveals itself as a rich, sinister, yet incredibly funny universe inhabited by a multitude of inventive characters. What truly differentiates the show from its peers is its storytelling approach. Instead of delivering a series of recycled sketches that blend into one another, each episode explores the journeys and storylines of individual characters or groups. No two visits are the same, and each encounter offers a new surprise.

Over three series and a Christmas special, the fictional town of Royston Vasey becomes teeming with a grotesque yet hilarious community. And that is...

As other reviewers have pointed out, the film falters significantly in its final half-hour. Prior to that, it suffers from predictability and features a remarkably empty performance by Kate Capshaw, who clearly never fully embodied her character and diminishes every scene she's in. Connery performs adequately, as does Fishbourne, but most scenes are artificially manipulated for dramatic effect rather than genuine storytelling, imparting an overall sense of unreality. The ending is particularly perplexing. It seems the filmmakers, aware that they had a disorganized mess on their hands, simply added a loud, overly dramatic score—complete with orchestral crescendos—to compensate, making every jump scare or dramatic moment almost laughable. If you're looking for an example of truly poor filmmaking, this is one to check out; otherwise, it's best to give it a pass.

Ettore Scola stands as one of Italy's most significant filmmakers. One summer evening, my parents and I watched "C'eravamo tanto amati" together; we enjoyed it, though not as deeply as we loved "A Special Day." I believe Scola is often underrated, possibly overlooked because his recent films haven't lived up to expectations. Last night, my mom and I settled on the sofa to revisit this cinematic gem. The writing, direction, cinematography, score, and production design were simple yet precise. What captivated me most was the incredible chemistry between Loren and Mastroianni. Both are outstanding actors, portraying Antonietta and Gabriele. Antonietta is a housewife married to a fervent Fascist; she has six children, though her husband yearns for another to win a family prize. Gabriele is a staunch Anti-Fascist. They share a poignant day—one that marks the 1938 visit of Hitler to Rome alongside Mussolini. I won't reveal more of the story—just encourage you to seek out this film!

"Like the initial touch of pleasure intertwined with guilt, like a spontaneous youthful flirtation filled with fascination and fear, like a climax of conflicting emotions," remarked one film enthusiast after watching LOVE AT THE TOP, the misinterpreted title of Michel Deville's stylish film LE MOUTON ENRAGE.  

Vincent Canby of the New York Times, however, noted shortly after the film's 1974 debut: "LOVE AT THE TOP, which opened yesterday at the 68th Street Playhouse, is a 1973 French comedy that vaguely echoes several English comedies from the 1950s about ambitious young men on the rise." He also pointed out a key distinction—that LOVE AT THE TOP is not focused on the English class hierarchy...(January 27, 1975).  

Ultimately, leaving individual judgments to viewers, time has proven its worth. Over three decades later, it’s evident that films like LE MOUTON ENRAGE are rare—where decadence seems innocent, youthful liaisons appear enthusiastic, and emotions are so deliberately manipulative.  

For fans of Romy Schneider, it seems unnecessary to emphasize that this film...

A rather dull made-for-TV movie that premiered on the TBS cable network. Antonio and Janine spend their time chasing a malicious computer virus—and that's about all there is to it. For trivia enthusiasts, it's worth noting that this film debuted the same weekend the real-life "Melissa" virus first appeared in email inboxes worldwide.

Some movies are so bad that they become entertaining—unfortunately, this isn't one of them. Based on a true story, the film bears no resemblance to reality, much like Pinocchio's dubious hopes of turning into a real boy. Theacting was abysmal, the direction lacked finesse, and the pacing was alarmingly hurried—almost as if the director simply wanted to finish quickly and go home. 

As for Melissa Joan Hart, I've never seen her as a particularly talented actress, and most of her films tend to be low-budget affairs. In this one, she overacts, speaking so rapidly that it feels as though she's trying to fake intensity rather than genuinely portray a character. Her performance gives the impression she's speaking to a crew behind the camera rather than engaging with the audience, which ultimately weakens the entire film. Any potential it had is thoroughly undermined.

The only slightly redeeming moment was when she got caught at the end—yet even that scene failed to deliver any real satisfaction.

This film is an absolute disaster—a prime example of what a truly terrible movie looks like. It’s unlikely to entertain anyone, not even fans of B-movies. I strongly advise you not to waste your valuable time on this piece of trash. The acting is atrocious, the direction is subpar, and the script is painfully bad—so bad, in fact, that it defies description. It shows a complete lack of understanding of what entertainment truly is. I bought the DVD for three dollars, and I swear I could pay someone to take it off my hands. Burning it might actually be more satisfying than watching it. I enjoy B-movies—killer toys, bizarre lagoon monsters—but this doesn’t even come close. Those movies that are so bad they become funny? Not here. This one is just downright pathetic.

I happened upon this film around 1990 on videotape, completely unaware of what I was about to experience. Many horror enthusiasts might overlook it, mistaking it for a standard prison movie, and those who did watch it may have been disappointed because it didn't fit their expectations. These factors likely contribute to its low ratings, but I recommend ignoring that and giving it a chance if you're a fan of the genre. 

The film excels across all aspects, from its compelling script and immersive atmosphere to strong performances and authentic prison setting. 

An absolute gem—it's a film I still keep on videotape to this day. Definitely worth a watch.

"Pick Up" never received the recognition it deserved. It operates on multiple levels, featuring a complex yet understandable storyline. The cast delivers some of their best performances, with Ann-Margret, Roy Scheider, and John Glover expertly cast, each delivering rich, nuanced portrayals. Vanity impresses with her unexpected acting talent, hinting she could have pursued a serious career in the field, while Kelly Preston's character leaves a lasting impression that lingers in your mind for days. Fans of action alongside intricate, gritty storytelling will find this film highly satisfying.

Initially, I wasn't sure whether I was watching a documentary, propaganda film, or a dramatic reenactment. Given its production era, it seemed to be a blend of all three. Admittedly, the storyline was somewhat predictable, but there was an underlying sense that the film would offer some compelling scenes as it progressed. We were treated to what appeared to be authentic training routines and equipment, adding a layer of credibility.  

The film truly came together for me in the final moments. The scenes achieved a realism—at least in my perception—that I haven't often encountered in cinema. It was easy to place oneself in the midst of the action and to contemplate what the young soldiers might have been thinking. This sense of authenticity was complemented by the challenge of depicting convincing Japanese soldiers, especially considering the scarcity of actual Japanese actors at the time.  

Overall, the movie serves as a valuable snapshot of the American mindset in 1943 during the conflict with Japan. Additionally, it offers an interesting critique of Japan, highlighting the aid the United States had previously provided to Japan in earlier years.

I usually refrain from criticizing films, preferring to focus on their positive aspects rather than the negatives. However, in this case, there are scarcely any redeeming qualities. It raises the question: if you're going to produce something so poor, what's the point? A significant portion of the film consists of lingering shots of Anne's face as she takes deep breaths, accompanied by violin music in the background. The rest of the movie is marred by weak, wooden acting. Rupert Penry Jones appears completely expressionless, and Jennifer Higham portrays Anne's younger sister with modern mannerisms that feel out of place. Anne is depicted as meek and self-effacing, which initially seems acceptable, but she remains unchanged throughout the film, making it difficult to understand why Captain Wentworth would fall in love with her. Overall, the production fails to evoke any sense of the period, plagued by numerous errors—such as characters rushing out of a concert, kissing in the street, and wandering around hatless (why was this scene included at all? The original book's scene was one of the most romantic in literature). In summary, this is a terrible film—highly disappointing.

Al Pacino's powerful delivery of the speech over the young boy's coffin deserves full praise; it would make Shakespeare's Mark Antony envious!

Was it Paul Schrader or Ken Lipper who deserve recognition for the exceptional dialogue? Their words are sharp, insightful, and truly worth your time if you appreciate well-crafted scripts. The story unfolds quite effectively up until the voice-over epilogue.

Beyond that, there's little else noteworthy about this film; even John Cusack has delivered more compelling performances than this. Interestingly, the film is predominantly male-centric—the women are reduced to mere accessories.

If you're a kid—rated 7—if you consider yourself an adult—rated 6—this semi-sequel to The Lion King offers a fresh perspective by focusing on side characters Timon and Pumbaa. It retells the original story through their eyes, including how they first met. True to Disney's tradition, the film is part of a long lineage of sequels and TV series that spotlight minor characters from their biggest hits. While skepticism is understandable, kids and fans of the series will likely enjoy it; the film features plenty of jokes, songs, and engaging moments that elevate it above many other sequels. Its charm stems from beloved central characters, a brisk pace, clever in-jokes referencing the original film, and some humorous references for older viewers. The animation maintains Disney’s high standards, though it’s slightly less flamboyant than the original. The story emphasizes a relaxed, carefree vibe—Hakuna Matata.

Timon and Pumbaa are shown watching scenes from the first film, often pausing mid-clip to joke about what’s happening, almost like a real audience. We learn that Timon is somewhat of an outcast, feeling...

The summer has been overflowing with blockbuster hits and film comebacks—some truly memorable, others disappointingly falling short—and finding a film I could simply relax with and enjoy was a challenge.  

To save you from scrolling through the page (and since there are no spoilers here), here's a quick summary: It’s more mature than *Ella Enchanted*, featuring some questionable violent scenes, moments of death, and a few bloodstained snippets—definitely not suitable for small children. Yet, it avoids excessive cliches or overstepping its bounds. Think of it as a slightly more serious, more magical version of *The Princess Bride*, and you'll be close.  

-------------------------------------------------------------  

I may not be a hardcore movie buff going to the theaters every week—maybe once or twice a month, if I’m feeling up to it. However, I am a passionate Sci-Fi/Fantasy fan. I tend to grow weary of recycled storylines and films that prioritize flashy effects over substance, doing so faster than you can count to ten. This film, however, stands out as a rare gem among the clutter.  

By August, I was so exhausted by the fractured expectations set by blockbuster hits that I decided to skip *The Bourne* sequel altogether.

Michael Stearns portrays Mike, a man whose sexual frustration is coupled with a peculiar moral outlook on sexuality. He has no issue watching nude dancers but becomes enraged when women engage in sexual acts with men. He holds the belief that once women participate in sex, they lose their innocence and beauty. Consequently, he wanders the Hollywood Hills, secretly observing couples making love from afar, eventually shooting the men dead with a high-powered rifle equipped with a scope.

The apparent primary aim of this film seems to be to showcase repeated sexual activity. The plot itself feels like an afterthought, which is likely to appeal to heterosexual male viewers, as the film features extended scenes of nudity—particularly highlighting the attractiveness of the female characters—and sexual acts designed to induce titillation. Viewing these scenes through a scope heightens the sense of creepiness and emphasizes voyeuristic tendencies, with Mike observing couples for long periods before finally shooting the men. This disturbing behavior is further accentuated by intrusive, atmospheric music that underscores the film's tone.

In summary, this film lacks a coherent storyline and consists of 80 minutes of eccentric characters drinking or delivering poor jokes. The soundtrack is subpar, the humor falls flat, and the female characters are portrayed as either overly promiscuous or awkward geeks. It seems as though the script was penned by a 14-year-old who believes that drinking is cool, women exist solely to please men, and anyone who challenges that idea is a nerd. Moreover, the movie bears little resemblance to the original American Pie films, except for a few character names and the minor appearance of Mr. Levenstein. The only redeeming aspect is the attractive cast of girls. Overall, I suggest skipping this movie and disregarding its 5.4 rating, as it is clearly overrated and hardly deserving of more than a 2.

Trailers for this film may hint at scenes of violence or unconventional sexuality, but these glimpses are brief and selected to captivate viewers. They merely reflect the core message of the movie:

It depicts individuals who are repeatedly humiliated and oppressed in their workplaces and personal lives, often using power they may hold elsewhere to systematically suppress others. At the bottom of this hierarchy are predominantly women.

While a film like *Hundstage* presents this reality with brutal honesty, enduring such bleak lives is an even greater challenge. 

Stylistically, the film resembles *Short Cuts*, composed of documentary-style vignettes featuring ordinary people—neighbors, colleagues—who behave naturally. There’s no glamour, and most tragically, there’s no hope. The documentary approach amplifies its disturbing impact, making it clear that such individuals are out there, many in number, despite society’s tendency to focus on superficial appearances. Somewhere, the adult industry operates, domestic violence often goes unreported, and shattered dreams are commonplace. I am familiar with such people.

If you seek a film that...

Bogmeister and others have thoroughly analyzed this episode. Shore Leave marks TOS's initial foray into lighthearted science fiction, a genre they would later master with the beloved Trouble with Tribbles. It offered both the Enterprise crew and viewers a refreshing break from the universe's more threatening challenges, such as those depicted in The Corbomite Maneuver.

Seeking a relaxing destination, the Enterprise encounters a seemingly perfect M Class planet and dispatches an exploratory team to investigate. Before long, a series of bizarre events unfold—some seemingly dangerous—creating a complex tapestry of human emotion set against a backdrop of surreal mystery (McCoy ventures into the looking glass), psychological thriller (Kirk is haunted by an unrelenting childhood bully), and romantic comedy (no further comment).

As the least serialized series within the Trek franchise, TOS is often overlooked for its numerous episodes in the first season that revolve around intense, potentially disastrous drama. Unlike later series, the TOS production team was unafraid to venture into uncharted territory, boldly exploring themes and stories that had never before been attempted on television.

Did HeidiJean actually watch this movie? A true Christmas film? Not even close. It’s dull, boring, and completely devoid of imagination and heart. I kept wondering who thought Carly Pope was suitable for the lead role—she has no discernible personality and delivers a completely underwhelming performance. Baransky, as usual, was the highlight and the only thing remotely interesting in the entire film. Perhaps her involvement was the only reason the project received the green light. Maybe I’m expecting too much from a Lifetime movie aired just two weeks before Christmas, but I sat through it thinking that with a different director and a recast JJ with an actress capable of evoking some sympathy, it could have been a charming little film.

The film opens with a voice-over introducing the setting and characters, and that's when my appreciation for the movie began to wane. Despite the countless creative options available to filmmakers, relying on a voice-over to convey all this information feels like an easy and cheap shortcut. I believe voice-overs often undermine the essence of cinematic storytelling.

I find it frustrating to hear a narrator specify our location, the current date, or the inner thoughts and feelings of the characters. In my view, a director should find visual ways to communicate characters' emotions and thoughts directly to the audience.

However, after this somewhat disappointing beginning, the film transitions into a compelling and well-crafted narrative that holds the viewer's attention for a considerable duration. It offers a realistic portrayal of a middle-class family and each member's individual experiences. The director demonstrates a talent for capturing authentic life situations—for instance, a father needing to make personal calls from the bathroom might seem unusual at first, but life often presents us with such relatable moments.

I never imagined a movie could be this terrible. The marketing seemed so promising, yet with a cast of twenty, you’d expect at least one decent performance. My wife gave up and went to bed after just twenty minutes—she made the right choice.

The film is remarkably comprehensive, captivating viewers throughout with flashbacks to childhood and the development of a bizarre relationship with an eccentric father, seamlessly intertwined with the chilling tales of serial murders. This blending creates an engaging narrative, highlighting the story's intrinsic entertainment value. The plot itself holds immense potential, and director Bill Paxton skillfully maximizes it, delivering a compelling cinematic experience.

From start to finish, the suspense steadily builds, keeping audiences eager to discover what unfolds next. The inventive storytelling is truly exceptional, presenting a beautifully crafted piece from beginning to end. It stands out as a rare gem, devoid of dull moments, with the action progressing smoothly, swiftly, and coherently from scene to scene.

The film also offers a stark reflection on the depths of human depravity—that individuals can commit heinous acts against loved ones and justify such evil acts in the name of 'God,' especially when they become disillusioned.

I understand the jokes; it's just that they aren't funny. The show itself is terrible. I get the humor, but that's part of what's so bad about it. The only interesting character was that one homeless man in a single episode, but when I include that episode with the rest, the entire show is awful. It’s simply not funny—NOT funny at all! I don't want people to say, "Only smart people get it," because if they are so intelligent, why do they judge others they don’t even know and claim they lack the smarts or insight to understand? That’s like saying, "The sky is red," but never actually looking outside. Anyway, this is hands down the worst show I’ve ever seen. The jokes are dreadful—while you might understand them, they’re still a mess. Her controversy comes off as very lame, with fart jokes and other bodily fluid humor that are really stupid, often accompanied by poor acting. I don’t understand what these so-called "smart" viewers see in this show, but judging others without knowing anything about us clearly isn’t the mark of intelligence.

There are countless new styles of sitcoms emerging, but the most effective remains the classic format with an audience and an indoor set. That '70s Show exemplifies this approach perfectly. When it first aired, few had heard of Kurtwood Smith or Debra Jo Rupp, and the adolescent actors, Topher Grace and Ashton Kutcher, impressed us all—though both are departing this year to explore other opportunities. I wish Topher would stay, as the show centered around his character, Eric, and his close-knit group of friends. Ashton has already become a modern-day John Travolta. Remember when John was in love with Diana Hyland from Eight Is Enough? Think of Ashton with Demi Moore. The cast was mostly unfamiliar to us, which was a good thing, since celebrity cast members can sometimes detract from the show. I miss Mo Gaffney, who played Don's girlfriend Joanne. I also miss Lisa Robin Kelly as the original Laurie—the replacement just couldn't match her, and I regret that. I appreciated Tommy Chong's portrayal of the laid-back but beloved father figure to Steven Hyde. Additionally, I enjoyed watching Tanya Roberts beyond her role in Charlie’s Angels.

I would rate it a 2 out of 10.

I was profoundly disappointed.

The plot was underdeveloped; for example, the events were too brief and lacked depth, which made the moral of the story unclear. Brenda Song delivered a solid performance, but Shin Koyamada appeared to struggle with his role. While I understand the attempt to incorporate Western elements into the show, certain aspects, such as the Chinese cultural components—particularly the depiction of the villain—felt out of place. The villain's appearance resembled a robot rather than something rooted in Chinese tradition. The most glaring flaw was the inclusion of inaccurate and distorted facts throughout the show.

Some might argue that since it is a children's show, high standards are unnecessary. However, other Disney productions like Mulan have demonstrated that better storytelling and presentation are indeed possible.

Ultimately, I believe Disney movies should dedicate more effort to thorough research and careful planning. A show relying solely on martial arts sequences does not suffice to create a compelling and authentic story.

Anyone who finds this film dull is simply a hopeless ignoramus who should stick to fast-paced car chases and romantic comedies. This film is captivating and keeps the viewer engaged from start to finish. Why? Because it features sharp, intelligent dialogue among genuine characters facing a critical moment, detailing their struggles to endure. I emphasize—intelligent dialogue! That is a hallmark of nearly all of Rohmer's works, and perhaps why some people dislike them. They prefer nonstop action. That’s perfectly fine; let those who crave adrenaline-fueled fare enjoy themselves. Meanwhile, those of us with refined taste will continue to seek out movies like this.  

Rohmer has often been labeled as "talky." To me, that’s actually a compliment, not a criticism. Shakespeare was quite talkative too. Is there a play with more words than "Hamlet"? Whenever a piece of art centers on ideas and conflicting values, naturally, it involves discussions of those themes. That’s exactly what this film explores—conflicts between aristocratic privilege and egalitarian ideals; the unwavering loyalty to old friends tested in extreme circumstances.

While I don’t mean to be overly critical, Brad Sykes is responsible for at least two of the dullest and most clichéd films I’ve ever watched—this one being among them, along with Camp Blood. The acting is terrible, the quality of the print is poor, and everything about this movie exudes the message, “You could do better yourself.” Perhaps it’s a challenge to everyone to flood YouTube with our own zombie-themed creations? I picked this up for just £1, but remember, there’s no price tag on wasting 71 minutes of your life. It’s best to steer clear of this dud, even at a rock-bottom price.

Have you ever been told to live each moment as if it were your final? Regardless of whether today is truly your last, I urge you not to squander any of it watching this. Nichole Hiltz delivers some appealing eye candy — though unfortunately, it remains hidden — while David DeLuise demonstrates why he should stick to television or dog food ads. With a superficial, unrealistic storyline and terrible dialogue, there’s no true “Art” in the “Art of Revenge.”

I had the opportunity to attend a special preview of this film today. As someone who isn't particularly fond of Dane Cook or Steve Carell, I went in without high expectations. Surprisingly, I found myself quite enjoying it.

"Dan in Real Life" tells the story of a widowed man with three daughters who spends a weekend visiting his family. During a visit to a bookstore, he meets the woman of his dreams, only to discover that she is his brother’s girlfriend.

The movie is well-crafted, with excellent soundtrack, cinematography, and performances—especially from Steve Carell. My main critique is that the film lacks depth in character development, particularly concerning Dane Cook’s character. We don’t get a thorough look at the dynamics between Dane and Steve's characters, which could have added more insight into Dan’s internal struggle over falling for his brother’s girlfriend. Despite this, "Dan in Real Life" is a charming, heartfelt film—offering a pleasant change from the many horror and action movies dominating the year.

One notable aspect of this film is Lola Glaudini's appearance—admittedly, her physique stands out. It's a shame she didn't appear nude, which might have at least added some interest to the film. There is a scene showcasing another actress's breasts, but it doesn't compare to Lola's. Armand Assante also looks noticeably aged and unwell. Overall, "Consequence" falls into the typical B-movie category. The story had potential, with some promising ideas, but the execution was lacking. The cinematography is subpar—unattractive and uninspired. The directing fails to bring energy or creativity, resulting in a dull thriller riddled with predictable twists and featuring actors past their prime. Lola Glaudini delivers a campy, provocative performance, but even her effort can't salvage the film from being outright poor—it's not even amusingly bad, just inept and disappointing.

I read the comment from Chris_m_grant from the United States.

He wrote: "A fantastic documentary about 1924. The early 20th-century geography of today's Iraq was powerful."

I would like to thank Chris and everyone interested in the Bakhtiari Nomads of Iran, the Zagros Mountains, and their landscapes who watched the film *Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life*. The traditions depicted in the movie have persisted for centuries and will continue as long as life endures. I am also from this region of Iran—a Bakhtiari myself.

Chris, I apologize for the inconvenience, but the Bakhtiari region of Zardkuh is in Iran, not Iraq as you mentioned in your comment. Iran and Iraq are two distinct countries. Comparing an Iranian to an Iraqi is almost like comparing an American to a Mexican. Thank you.

Best regards,  
Ziba

Could someone advise Shaq to stick to his strengths in basketball? This movie was barely entertaining, even in a silly way. Shaq plays a genie living in a boom box—hardly an original concept compared to a lamp. He's meant to help a young boy, played by the equally irritating Francais Capra. The storyline was flimsy, reminiscent of Waterworld, and the acting was terrible. I suspect anyone who enjoys this film might be too embarrassed to admit it.

May and her husband traveled to visit their children and grandchildren. The gathering felt strained, as if the grandchildren and "kids" didn't quite know each other as one might expect. The warmth that should have filled the room was absent. After dinner, May's husband suddenly claimed he wasn't feeling well, blaming it on his daughter's cooking, and with irritability, insisted they should go home. That night, he passed away.  

Now a widow, May finds herself adrift. Her marriage was neither passionate nor particularly engaging, but it provided her with a sense of purpose—someone who needed her. Though her own needs had gone unfulfilled for years, she felt she had something meaningful to do each day.  

She falls into a deep depression, lacking motivation. Hoping for comfort, she moves in with her daughter, Paula. Soon after her arrival, Paula confronts her, expressing that she has never felt her mother truly gave of herself. Angry and hurt, Paula criticizes her mother's lack of nurturing. May is taken aback, caught off guard, yet she also seems too weary or disconnected to respond with effort. “I'm your mother, and I love you,” she offers—yet the words feel empty, leaving both of them to wonder what "love" really means.

I wasn't particularly impressed with the first "Cube" film. While the concept was interesting, the bothersome acting and unengaging characters prevented me from truly enjoying it. I didn't see much point in watching its sequel, but when I heard about a third installment that would serve as a prequel to the original, I was curious, hoping it might address some of the earlier issues and introduce a compelling cast. Unfortunately, I was disappointed.  

"Cube Zero" begins decently enough, introducing us to two characters responsible for overseeing the endless maze filled with deadly traps that torments the inmates. The filmmakers do a decent job of creating a sense of mystery through the depiction of the characters' daily routines. This raises several questions about why people are imprisoned there and the true nature of those controlling the operation—all of which are left open to interpretation. The acting was somewhat lacking, but overall, the first half of the movie moved along at a reasonable pace.  

As the story progresses, one of the two "watchers" begins to...

I missed the opening scenes of this film, which might explain why I didn't enjoy it. However, having studied the fall of the Roman Republic for years, I'm familiar with the story. Ironically, that may also be the reason I found this movie unappealing.  

The film is riddled with more historical inaccuracies than actual extras. It seems so deliberately inaccurate that perhaps no effort was even made to portray history correctly, which could be somewhat forgivable. Strangely, there are moments where they go to great lengths to appear historically precise, only to complicate matters—like mentioning Antonius' marriage to Octavia and then dismissing it two scenes later. Why introduce it at all if it doesn't serve the plot and Octavia isn't even shown? Similarly, Antonius is sometimes called by his real name, Marcus Antonius, and other times by the odd English version, Mark Antony.  

Beyond the inaccuracies, the film could have been enjoyable if not for the leading lady. She exudes no dignity; she's hysterical, overly dramatic, and utterly out of control. Instead

Hello. I’m Paul Raddick, also known as Panic Attack from WTAF, Channel 29 in Philadelphia. Allow me to share my thoughts on a terrible film that briefly boosted Adam Sandler’s early career before fading into obscurity.

"Going Overboard" tells the story of an aspiring comedian—played by Sandler—who lands a job on a cruise ship and, supposedly, fails. I initially thought it was a disaster, but there’s more to the story. Sandler's character encounters women who are fans of *History of the World Part I* and *Rebound*. These women were supposed to be interested, but ironically, they are later revealed to be victims of Sawtooth, the cruelest cannibal the world has ever seen. Unfortunately, Sandler's performance in "Going Overboard" was a stinker, though he found greater success with films like *Big Daddy*, *Billy Madison*, and Jen Leone's favorite, *50 First Dates*. And let’s not forget—Drew Barrymore was a stunning presence. Meanwhile, *Spanglish* is sizzling, but "Going Overboard" doesn’t hold a candle. That’s all for now.

This movie chronicles an extraordinary journey of a single family, immersing you in every moment of their remarkable odyssey. Stunningly acted and visually captivating, it feels intensely authentic. The final line, filled with a bittersweet hope, remains one of the most memorable and stirring moments you'll ever experience.

Hey everyone, I wouldn't recommend wasting your time on this movie. Unfortunately, it falls short in many areas with a weak storyline and lackluster performances. Honestly, I’d rather endure anything else than watch it again.

This has always been my favorite film of all time. The special effects for its time are truly remarkable and received well-deserved awards. I can recall the dialogue as clearly as if I just heard it yesterday. It’s a classic, timeless adventure. The score by Miklós Rózsa, one of cinema’s greatest composers, perfectly complements the story. Sabu plays the Thief, and Conrad Veidt is the formidable villain. I keep a copy nearby, ready for another trip down memory lane. Whoa there! Rex Ingram is eager to break free from his genie's bottle!

Elvira, Mistress of the Dark (1988)

Directed by: James Signorelli

Starring: Cassandra Peterson, W. Morgan Sheppard, Daniel Greene, Edie McClurg

Synopsis: Elvira (Cassandra Peterson) leaves her television show behind and journeys to the small Christian town of Fallwell, Massachusetts to claim her late aunt's inheritance. Hoping to fund a Vegas show, she instead inherits a spooky old mansion, a loyal poodle, and a mysterious magic cookbook. During her stay, Elvira endeavors to earn money, energize the local teenagers, win the affection of a charming suitor (Daniel Greene), dodge the threat of being burned at the stake, and prevent her sinister uncle (W. Morgan Sheppard) from using the magic cookbook to bring about the end of the world.

My thoughts: I adore Cassandra Peterson and her alter ego, Elvira. She’s a confident, stunning, and hilarious woman, and as Elvira, she’s all that plus delightfully dark and charmingly naive—plus, she’s got an incredible pair of assets. In this film, her magnetic personality is truly on display.

I particularly enjoyed the film’s humorous fish-out-of-water vibe, especially with Elvira’s signature low-cut black dress and her bold, gothic persona in a quaint, conservative town.

This sequel is an ugly, poorly scripted, and amateurishly paced disappointment that follows Joe Dante's 1981 classic "The Howling." As one of the few truly great werewolf films ever made, "The Howling" deserved better than a series of obnoxious and unbearable sequels like this one. Fortunately, "Stirba" is only connected by name, with no shared characters or storylines from Dante’s film. The plot centers on a bloodthirsty cult of Transylvanian werewolves—mainly female—led by Stirba. Portrayed by Sybil Danning, Stirba instantly transforms from a curvaceous older woman into a striking blond with an astonishing bust, becoming all hairy and feral when aroused. Her main adversary is played by a seemingly exhausted Christopher Lee, whose character, Stefan Crosscoe, is an occult investigator traveling to Stirba’s territory with an American couple seeking to find their missing friend. If you're simply after gruesome gore and gratuitous nudity, this film delivers—every kill is depicted in gruesome detail, including exploding eyeballs and the disturbing image of a dwarf being pierced.

Assessing this film, or any comparable work from the early sound era, using conventional film critique proves challenging. At times, there is an almost palpable desperation as many silent film stars attempt to find their footing in talkies, understandably fearing obsolescence—some, like Rin-Tin-Tin, faltered while others, such as John Barrymore, displayed remarkable ease. The film resembles a vaudeville of disconnected segments, and certain moments stand out, notably Barrymore's soliloquy from Richard II, which is certainly worth preserving. Overall, only those with a background in stage performance seemed to carry themselves with genuine confidence. Nonetheless, the film is reasonably entertaining and is especially recommended for "film buffs" keen on exploring the transition from silent to sound cinema.

I had initially planned to watch this movie in theaters, but it was sold out. Instead, I ended up seeing Solaris, which, unfortunately, turned out to be the worst film released in 2002.  

Victor Rosa (John Leguizamo), a tough and street-smart 'street pharmacist,' panics after witnessing a kid get shot. He decides to go straight and invests all his money with Jack (Peter Sarsgaard). Things seem to be going smoothly until Jack suddenly disappears with his girlfriend Trish (Denise Richards). This revelation occurs very late in the film—if it hadn't been spoiled in the trailer, it might have been a compelling twist. However, since it was, it loses its impact.  

Honestly, there's not a single interesting element in this movie; everything is spoiled in the previews. If you've watched even one trailer, you've essentially seen the entire film, so you might as well just think about the missing parts yourself. Save your money—download the preview from the website and skip the $3.99 ticket. There are no surprises or twists to be found here, aside from how atrociously bad the soundtrack is.  

I genuinely hope that whoever was responsible for creating the soundtrack was...

"The Cobweb" exemplifies many films that showcase powerful, occasionally memorable performances and highlight moments of brilliance, yet are ultimately bogged down by a convoluted storyline and a lack of engaging content for viewers. The film features Richard Widmark as a psychiatrist at a mental institution whose life spirals into chaos due to familial issues and an absurd, overblown conflict that, in reality, seems insignificant.

The storyline is utterly absurd. The institution clearly needs new curtains for its library windows. An elderly patient wants her own drapes, while several other patients insist on making their own. This frivolous and unintentionally eccentric dispute escalates to the point where lives are threatened and families begin to disintegrate. It resembles a disagreement more appropriate to young children than adults.

The implausibility of the plot and its questionable believability are so pronounced that one might wonder if only a genuine lunatic could accept it. Don't misunderstand—there's nothing wrong with the acting. The supporting cast, following Widmark, is composed of other talented performers, but even their efforts can't rescue the flimsy storyline.

There was a genie played by Shaquille O'Neal, named Kazaam, and honestly, it was a disaster. His rhymes were cringe-worthy, and his lines fell flat. There was a dumb kid crying over his foolish dad. The acting was terrible, casting was off, and the special effects looked cheap. What's next? This movie truly sucks. It probably didn't even earn twenty bucks at the box office. The genie lives in a boombox instead of a lamp, and the whole thing hurts—like a cramp or a soggy food stamp.  

Yeah, you get the picture—a silly, rhyming genie who can't act in a ridiculously bad movie with awful effects. Plus, it's confusing as hell. I won’t dwell on it too much. Let's just say it falls into the "so bad, it's funny" category. Watch it once with your friends for a good laugh, but don’t expect anything amazing.

The Dentist opens on the morning of Dr. Alan Feinstone's wedding anniversary with his wife Brooke. At first glance, the Feinstones appear to enjoy an enviable life—residing in a beautiful Los Angeles home, with Alan enjoying a successful, responsible career. However, beneath the surface, things are far from perfect. Alan uncovers Brooke's affair with Matt, the pool cleaner, and to make matters worse, learns that Matt is also involved with Paula Roberts, a neighbor. Adding to his turmoil, Alan is in deep debt to the IRS, who are closing in on him. This revelation pushes Alan toward the brink of madness as he spirals into paranoia, convinced that everything around him is decayed and corrupt—just like the teeth he treats. Determined to "fix" what he perceives as broken, Alan begins to lose control. At work, his frustrations boil over as he lashes out, injuring a young patient named Jody, assaulting another patient named April Reign after hallucinating she's his wife, and deliberately performing unnecessary and painful procedures on others. Alan's descent into chaos continues to escalate.

How The Grinch Stole Christmas captured my heart instantly and became my favorite film from the very first viewing. Even after eight screenings, it continues to resonate with me just as powerfully as it did initially.
