Screenwriters Jeffery Price and Peter S. Seaman, renowned for their work on Who Framed Roger Rabbit, do a remarkable job translating the beloved story onto the screen. Ron Howard's direction breathes life into the narrative, while Jim Carrey's lively and spirited portrayal of The Grinch truly steals the show.  

Some critics argue that the film departs from the true spirit and principles of the original story. Having read the original, I respectfully disagree. The movie conveys the same heartfelt message about Christmas and its real meaning, and it even deepens the story by exploring how and why The Grinch became who he is.  

*MILD SPOILERS* (They probably won’t spoil the movie for you... but if you haven't seen it yet and prefer to avoid any story details until then...)

I would like to commend the series as a commendable effort. The storyline, while in need of some improvements, was quite strong, particularly in Season 1. However, Season 2 shifted towards a more bizarre direction, losing the original charm that made DA special. The plot in Season 1 was more engaging, offering a lighter glimpse into life at Jam Pony alongside a focused and serious storyline involving Manticore and the X-series. I have been eagerly anticipating new seasons, and my enthusiasm remains. I hope the FOX team and DA production crew understand that many fans still await a comeback for DA. Even after two years since its cancellation, DA has the potential to succeed if properly developed. I believe a visionary like James Cameron could take on this challenge and bring DA back to its former glory.

Collusion Course surpasses the usual "villainous white male corporate capitalist" film in its bleakness. Watching it is more uncomfortable than enduring a toothache. Jay Leno demonstrates unexpected acting talent in his underrated debut, The Silverbears, delivering a performance true to the character's requirements. In stark contrast, this film is so poorly made that Leno’s character—a smug bore—is less irritating than Morita’s, who plays an equally pompous fool.

A chemist invents a revolutionary fabric that never dirties or wears out, threatening the very foundations of numerous industries. In this charming Ealing Studios comedy, Guinness shines as the earnest yet determined scientist. Greenwood, with her captivating voice, portrays the romantic interest, while Parker depicts her overwhelmed father. Thesiger provides comic relief as a patriarch of the textile industry. As it entertains, the film also explores provocative themes surrounding science, economics, and politics. Skillfully directed by Mackendrick, who would later helm classics like "The Ladykillers" and the exquisite "Sweet Smell of Success" in the 1950s, it combines humor with thought-provoking storytelling.

How low can one go in the quest to reclaim former glory? ST:HF is here to show you just how far you can fall.

If you're expecting a true Star Trek experience, think again—this is not for you. The writing is a confusing jumble, the actors' characterizations are weak, and most disappointingly, the design work is downright terrible.

Looking for strong captains? Don't bother here. Admire the Federation's values? Forget it—Starfleet is ridiculed, with ensigns sporting spikes in their hair. 

The captain appears mentally vacant, stumbling through scenes, while within moments of the opening credits, Ensign Spikey is already trying to set up a romantic rendezvous with an engineer. Things only get worse from there. Uniforms? Nonexistent—too small or too large, collars down to the chest, a mishmash of TNG Seasons One and Two uniforms with Season Three and DS9 attire. The discipline and traditions that defined the originals are completely absent, evident even in the smallest details. 

The only redeeming aspect is the graphics, which seem to improve slightly with each season—no, I take that back.

If Todd Sheets had come forward and admitted that this film was deliberately crafted as a parody of the zombie genre, I would raise my rating to an eight. Imagine a movie where every scene, line, and even every acting choice is intentionally designed to parody. I could probably produce a more coherent script by scribbling the alphabet, shuffling the letters, and still end up with a better story. Two scenes stand out vividly in my mind—spoiler alert! The first is when Mike's dad and another father casually walk down a staircase crowded with zombies. It's a small staircase, and despite brushing against the flailing undead, they suffer no harm. At the top, the ex-marine turns around, mutters, "God you're a horny bastard," and shoots just one zombie. The second is set in a military complex: a girl stabs a zombie with a machete and is immediately encircled. The camera circles around her for about forty seconds as zombies stand just an arm’s length away. Then, almost nonchalantly, she slips out of the crowd to rejoin the humans. Spoiler over! These moments definitely need to be...

Robert Wuhl is currently instructing a film class at New York University in Manhattan. In his lectures, he explores historical fallacies and reveals truths that have largely been forgotten. I wish there were more episodes of this show, as it is highly entertaining. Wuhl effectively uses examples and visual aids to illustrate his points. For instance, he explained that the famous Midnight Ride of Paul Revere was actually not led by Revere himself; Henry Wadsworth Longfellow chose Revere's name because it sounded more poetic. 

Having followed Robert Wuhl’s career for years—from his stand-up comedy days to his role in HBO’s "Arli$$"—I can attest that he is a talented actor and comedian. However, I believe he is an exceptional educator. I strongly recommend watching at least one episode of this program; it’s a worthwhile use of your time.

A disappointing film.

The story introduces us to Chrissy, a young and somewhat moody character who appears aimless and passive. She contributes little to advancing the plot, which led to the narrative shifting focus to her relatives. It's unfortunate because Chrissy seemed like a potentially intriguing character.

The plot was predictable and occasionally felt overly formulaic. This raises the question: when will filmmakers like the Campions, Jacksons, and Tamahori shift from merely entertaining for two hours to delivering powerful, cinematically compelling stories that inspire as well as entertain?

From a technical standpoint, the film was poorly executed.

A mysterious entity—or perhaps an unseen force—is leaving deadly puncture wounds on the victims' throats, draining their blood and causing their deaths. Detective Karl Brettschneider (Melvyn Douglas, prior to his shift from B-movie horror to more prominent roles) finds himself baffled by the identity of the culprit behind these infamous crimes. The entire village is gripped by panic, and Karl relies heavily on his trusted medical expert, Dr. Otto von Niemann (Lionel Atwill, delivering another compelling mad scientist performance), to help uncover the mystery behind these tragic deaths. Concerned for the safety of his beloved Ruth (the enchanting Fay Wray, making her third collaboration with Atwill after "Doctor X" and "The Mystery of the Wax Museum"), Karl fears she might be in danger, as she works as Niemann's assistant.

Dwight Frye delivers a standout performance as the eccentric village fool, a man obsessed with bats and perpetually exhibiting a deranged demeanor—an obvious suspect amid the mounting paranoia. Adding a touch of humor, Maude Eburne portrays a charmingly naive patient of Niemann’s, convinced she suffers from various ailments she reads about in books near his laboratory. Her suggestibility often results in Niemann humoring her by dismissing her concerns, which are usually exaggerated tales of fictional illnesses she believes afflict her.

I haven't seen the first film, and if it's anything like this one, I have no desire to do so. 

Having just watched it a few hours ago, I can hardly recall a single detail. 

From what I remember, the main plot involves a group of irritating people staying in a house with that creepy old woman from Friday the 13th, while being stalked by a man made out of a plank of wood. 

Some characters meet their demise, the movie wraps up, and I’m considering suing whoever sold me this film for wasting my time. 

I might even pay you £1 to take this film off my hands—oh, wait, I already gave it away to a “friend.”

Even then, they can live without ever seeing it. Honestly, this film—if it can truly be called that—holds any genuine interest only for bondage enthusiasts. Fans of Bettie Page will learn absolutely nothing new; in fact, they won't experience any sense of familiarity, love, or nostalgia. 

Disregard the terrible screenplay, the stiff, amateurish acting, the complete lack of direction, subpar lighting, and all the other bargain-basement production flaws. It’s the kind of "kids throw together a movie" filmmaking at its worst. Perhaps one can be grateful that they at least knew how to operate a camera. Still, none of these issues are what truly make this film fundamentally *wrong*. 

The real problem lies in the casting of the young woman playing Bettie Page—an actress with a curvy figure whose only resemblance to the Queen of Curves is her dark hair and signature bangs. She fails to bring anything to the role beyond a willingness to be restrained and gagged. While this might have helped her in her career prior to and following this disastrous effort, it certainly doesn’t save the film from its many flaws.

I recently watched this film after renting it, initially expecting it to be just another story about a girl trying to prove herself. However, Diane's decision to join boxing was driven by her own choice, which made the film stand out. I really enjoyed it and rated it 8 out of 10—it's that good. Plus, having Michelle Rodriguez in the cast is always a plus, even though she's only been in six movies so far.

This exemplifies a growing issue in modern filmmaking. Why is the background noise and soundtrack so much louder than the dialogue? What sense does that make? Unfortunately, this film isn't unique. Most movies seem to do this nowadays. For two years, I wondered if my TV was at fault, but after upgrading to a new one, the problem persisted—background noise, as if from a city block away, drowns out the dialogue.

The distraction was even greater in this film because, at least in the English version, the woman constantly mumbles. I kept hoping Jean Reno would say, "Excuse me, could you speak up or maybe remove the marbles from your mouth." If you watch it on DVD and have some basic French, I recommend watching the French version with subtitles.

I give it a 4-star rating because Reno was outstanding in Léon. Though many rave about the scenery, having lived in the Rockies for a few years, I found it less impressive—so, "meh."

The film begins slowly, depicting the mundane life of Wallace Napalm, who works at a photo-service drop-off station. His wife is confined to their home with an ankle bracelet after serving time for arson. Wallace is also a dedicated volunteer firefighter, taking his role very seriously.

As we observe Wallace's uneventful routine, an unexpected and startling event occurs: a traveling carnival arrives in town. Among its performers is Wilder Napalm, Wallace's brother. Wilder is a clown with a remarkable talent.

Both brothers share a unique gift—they are pyrokineticists, or "pyrots," able to ignite fires with their minds. Wallace keeps his abilities hidden, while Wilder is open about his powers with friends and acquaintances.

Spoiler alert: Their rivalry traces back to a childhood accident where they unintentionally caused the death of a homeless man. Wallace tends to suppress his fire-starting abilities, whereas Wilder is eager to go public on national television.

Adding to the turmoil, Wilder has feelings for Wallace's wife, a woman they both dated years earlier. This romantic tension fuels their eventual confrontation, culminating in a literal firefight between the brothers.

The film is engaging, though...

First, let me clarify that I am not from the South, but I am American. I don't particularly love country music, though I can tolerate it. I would never wear a cowboy hat, but I do wear hats. I don't live in a trailer, but I do eat tuna salad and own a home. What relevance does this have to my comment? Quite a bit, especially if you're one of those who claim only "country" folks love this movie. The film is loosely inspired by the theme of loving and losing. James Bridges directs a genuine American love story that feels as authentic as possible. In a time when Jerry Springer and the "let it all out" mentality dominate, this film feels more real than ever.  

Bud is "coming of age" and begins to carve out his own path with some guidance from his aunt and uncle, leading him to move to the big city with them. There, Bud finds himself immersed in the local honky-tonk scene—the only escape available to a blue-collar worker. He quickly hooks up with Sissy, who comes from a similar background, and they share a whirlwind romance marked by intense highs and painful lows.  

(*This

Satan's Little Helper stands out as one of the more impressive B horror films I've encountered. When I say "better," I’m referring to the story—it's innovative, introducing a fresh twist that breaks away from predictable horror tropes. Nonetheless, it raises some absurd questions that you'll find yourself pondering throughout the film.

My interest was piqued when I was browsing the horror section at HMV. Tired of the overhyped Hollywood horror blockbusters that all seemed to blend together, I was craving something different. The cover art for Satan's Little Helper instantly grabbed my attention; the unsettling image was enough to draw me in. I was aware it was a straight-to-DVD release, but I decided to give it a shot—especially since I had just watched "Boogey Man" the night before, so things couldn’t possibly get any worse. After watching it, I felt somewhat satisfied. I particularly enjoyed the plot—watching the killer pretend to be the little boy’s friend just to carry out his killings was genuinely creepy. In a disturbingly twisted way, the killer actually believed that he and the boy would become partners—a sinister duo.

Branagh is among the rare few who grasp the distinction between a movie and a theatrical production. His adaptation of Hamlet stands out as perhaps the most faithful translation of Shakespeare to the screen, yet it remains highly energetic, bordering on an action thriller. The moment when Hamlet encounters his father's ghost is unforgettable and lingers in your memory.

Xizao is a rare gem among films—simple and unobtrusive yet deeply moving and joyful. Its straightforward narrative introduces the compelling conflict between tradition and modernity right from the opening scenes. This central theme is what gives the film its core strength, but it would have fallen short without its remarkable characters and the powerful performances that bring them to life.

At the heart of the story is Master Liu, an aging patriarch representing China's bygone era. He manages an old bathhouse nestled in a traditional neighborhood. Every shot inside the bathhouse exudes a sense of nostalgia and tranquility, evoking envy in anyone burdened by life's stresses. Even skeptics cannot deny the charm and authenticity of this setting.

Master Liu’s mentally challenged son, Er Ming, stands as another profound figure in the film, alongside his brother—a symbol of modern life. The interactions among these three, along with the various visitors to the bathhouse, are portrayed with astonishing depth and tenderness. Some scenes evoke such intense emotion that they surpass nearly anything seen in cinema.

Given its critique of the regime, the film faced censorship and was granted limited exposure. It may be coincidental, but the limited coverage underscores the film’s daring message and powerful storytelling.

This is the worst movie I’ve ever seen, but to be fair, it’s somewhat watchable and surprisingly funny. I don’t think the filmmakers aimed for Hollywood blockbuster quality. It’s a silly film about a serial killer who gets covered in toxic waste during winter, resulting in a chemical reaction that turns him into a killer snowman—enough to make you laugh on its own. While it’s incredibly dumb, it’s also amusing. The murder scenes are downright hilarious. I wouldn’t recommend buying it (though I did — the cover looked promising!), but if you happen to catch it on TV one night and are in the mood for a laugh, give it a try.

Haha! Not a bad way to kick things off. I initially thought this was an original piece, but then I realized it was actually a clone of the 1976 remake of KING KONG. I didn't see KING KONG until I was 15, but I watched this film when I was just 9. Its funky disco soundtrack is so catchy, it’ll stay in your head for days! Plus, the theme song by the Yetians adds to its charm. The creature effects are some of the worst I’ve ever seen, yet ironically, this movie remains a beloved cult classic of B-movies. Some memorable quotes include: “Take a tranquilizer and go to bed,” and “Put the Yeti in your tank and you have Yeti power.” I remember watching this on MOVIE MACABRE, hosted by Elvira. There’s a scene that’s like KING KONG in reverse—where, instead of climbing up the building with the girl, the creature climbs down and catches her as she falls! Around the same time, there was another Kong imitator, MIGHTY PEKING MAN (1977) from Hong Kong, featuring lots of traveling matte shots and motorized puppets. This film is so absurd, it’s guaranteed to make you laugh. As I said, it’s just another...

Firstly, I must express my dismay at the widespread inability of the average viewer to appreciate imagination. What makes this show truly exceptional is the vivid hyper-reality it constructs. You don’t need to question why Ned can revive the dead or why his powers last only a minute. It’s a return to the wonder and whimsy of childhood fairy tales, reminiscent of *A Wrinkle in Time*. 

I find it refreshingly original because it stands in stark contrast to the countless ordinary television programs that reveal everything openly, leaving no space for wonder or imagination. 

It’s also a pleasure to experience a touch of escapism through television. 

My favorite aspect of the show is this hyper-reality—the nostalgic 1950s-inspired setting, the innocent yet unique characters, and the scenery that isn’t meant to be perceived as purely real. 

This series cleverly veils the dark truths of mortality, unlike other shows that confront it head-on. While many programs are entertaining, few have managed to overshadow this one in restoring curiosity, imagination, and a sense of wonder to television. 

*Pushing Daisies* quickly became one of my top favorites.

I saw this movie years ago and was genuinely impressed—though I was only 12 at the time. Recently, I rewatched it and wish I could get that time back. Unfortunately, it's quite bad. I do like Lee Majors, Chris Makepeace (check out My Bodyguard (1980) for a great performance of his), and Burgess Meredith, but this role did little to advance their careers.  

In the film, Lee Majors plays Franklyn Hart, a former race car driver who plans to drive his stored race car across the country to California. The catch? The government has banned all private transportation. The premise wasn’t terrible—nothing groundbreaking, but okay—but the execution was a complete failure.

This film serves as a prime example of how even some of the funniest jokes can fall flat. I had high expectations after seeing the trailer, which was incredibly hilarious, but the movie itself was disappointingly lackluster. 

What's odd is that many of the jokes, such as the humorous takes on the smoking ban and the "Jo Bole..." skits, are genuinely witty. I'm unsure who to fault for the movie's failure—perhaps the cast, especially the less-than-talented actors and actresses, or the director himself, or maybe the casting choices. 

If you're incredibly bored—truly, I mean it—then you might consider watching this film. Otherwise, I recommend collecting all the trailers and teasers; they’re far funnier than the actual movie. 

P.S. The only redeeming aspects are Mahesh Manjrekar and the amusing Chappu Bhai.

This film is genuinely unpleasant. Although Rick Baker's special effects are notably impressive—albeit stomach-churning—it offers little else worth praise. Similar to many 70s movies, it leaves you with the unsettling sensation of needing a long shower to wash away the grime. The characters are uniformly unlikable, and the storyline is confusing and nonsensical.

***SPOILERS*** Like a sinister version of the Tinkers-to-Evers-to-Chance double play, "Omen IV" introduces the malevolent offspring of the deceased Antichrist Damien Thorn. This new evil, taking the guise of Delia York, also known as Asia Vielle, begins to terrorize everyone around her—her parents, classmates, neighbors, and ultimately the entire world. She is entrusted to a supposedly deserving couple, Karen and Gene York, and Fay Grant and Michael Woods, by the Catholic Church’s St. Francis orphanage.  

Young Delia wastes no time displaying her dark nature—she bites her mother during a house party. Later, she nearly gets hit by a runaway truck but is saved by a fierce doberman named Ryder. At school, she swiftly deals with a bully by forcing him to embarrass himself in front of his peers. When his father threatens to sue the York family, Delia responds with deadly precision, causing the man to have a fatal traffic accident. It’s clear: messing with her is a dangerous game.  

Meanwhile, Gene York begins to see himself as a rising figure in the town, believing his election to Congress—advocating for clean air and green spaces—will elevate him to greatness.

This story lacked any original ideas whatsoever. Its themes seemed borrowed from various sources, including The Ninth Gate, In the Mouth of Madness (another John Carpenter film), and The Ring. The film even shamelessly reused the same glowing circle from The Ring as its title symbol. Cody Carpenter’s soundtrack was virtually identical to Suspiria’s. Hopefully, no one will dismiss these observations as mere "homage." I noticed the theater was showing Argento’s Deep Red—using that as an excuse for imitation? That’s a weak justification. This film was truly bottom-of-the-barrel. Adding gore and "disturbing" imagery does not make a good horror movie. Carpenter once understood that; now, he seems to have lost his way. Perhaps he should retreat into obscurity or find a time machine.

I experienced this film at a Sundance Film Festival screening and was truly in awe of its profound impact. It deeply explores the psychological toll on courageous soldiers who enlist with the hope of protecting and serving their country honorably, trusting that their government will care for them in return. The documentary vividly illustrates the mental transformations that occur during boot camp, where soldiers are conditioned into "killers for their country," and examines the aftermath once they return home. It also delves into the profound effects that taking lives has on the human mind. Respectful and heartfelt, the film honors our soldiers without criticism; instead, it condemns a system that fails to adequately address their physical and psychological needs after service. 

Powerful, moving, emotionally charged, and thought-provoking, this film serves as a call to action—urging us to support our troops beyond symbolic gestures like stickers and parades. It challenges us to truly listen to their experiences and advocate for changes that prioritize their health and well-being.

Director Vincenzo Natali employed a stylish approach to this film, utilizing intriguing camera angles and impactful close-ups. It was particularly refreshing to see Jeremy Northam and Lucy Liu in leading roles, allowing them to showcase a broader range of their acting talents. The movie also featured one of the most inventive "escape" scenes seen in recent years. The combined efforts of the director and cast resulted in a compelling thriller.

While the plot was somewhat intricate, the story unfolded clearly as layers of corporate greed and deception were gradually uncovered. 

Reflecting on Orwell's 1949 warning in his novel "1984" about a future ruled by a totalitarian state manipulating minds and eroding human freedoms, it was fascinating that this thought-provoking futuristic film portrayed not the State, but the corporate world as the dominant force that controls and diminishes human workers.

I truly believe I should advocate for this film and encourage every horror and cult movie enthusiast to see it…

I did!

It’s fantastic: deeply atmospheric, eerie, and genuinely frightening…

It’s incredible how they managed to create such a remarkable film on such a minimal (read: “none”) budget…

Here's the synopsis from the official website: "One morning, an old man ventures into the woods searching for his runaway cat. Instead, he discovers a child without parents and a murder with no body..."

While IMDb doesn’t feature a trailer, I’ll leave a link to the movie’s official site where you can find one. It’s quite unsettling, so be sure to check it out…

www.softfordigging.com

Initially, I didn't mind the Geico commercials during their first fifty or so airings; I even found them a bit witty and amusing. However, seriously! Is this really the best idea these people could come up with? This show is terrible! It feels dull and resembles an episode of "The Office" with the characters dressed as cavemen. I know many of you might dislike this comparison, but "The Office" just doesn't do it for me. Sure, I understand the setup: a hapless guy trying to stay out of trouble, a terrible boss who hates him, a pseudo-intellectual with a barely functioning mind, and a clueless one seeking acceptance. But so what? I've worked with people like these, and I found them just as irritating in real life as I do on TV. Why would I want to spend another fraction of my week watching more of these types? Please, ask your parents if they dropped you on your head—if, after pondering it, you still believe this is entertainment, then I have to question your judgment.

I immediately realized that this movie was not actually based on Dodie Smith's novel. Nonetheless, I enjoyed the idea that Pongo and Perdita's son now had his own litter of puppies. The most adorable Dalmatian was, without doubt, little Snowball, who remained perfectly spotless until the very end of the film.

Honestly, I was unsure what to make of Cruella de Vil's sudden change to a kind demeanor. I had often considered the possibility that she might become friendly, but her rapid reversion to her original self, declaring once again that she was Cruella, made me almost genuinely worried about Chloe's Dalmatians.

The scene where the puppies watched Lady and the Tramp while Chloe and Kevin had dinner turned out to be better than I expected. I also enjoyed the parrot pretending to be a dog, and it was remarkable how many tricks the dogs had learned for this movie.

Of course, I was glad that the Dalmatians were rescued once again in the end, but I couldn't help but wonder what their future would hold.

Before I begin my commentary, I must say that this film is truly underrated.

Sharon Stone delivers a fantastic performance as Catherine Tramell, and Morrissey is excellent as Dr. Glass. He plays an analyst brought in to assess her after a sports star's death, only to find himself caught in a seductive game that Tramell uses to manipulate him.

The acting overall was solid, except for Thewlis. 

Stone excels in this role—she's charismatic, mischievous, and irresistible, maintaining her youthful appearance from the first film. She really impressed me, much like in Casino. Morrissey also portrayed vulnerability convincingly, adding depth to his character. Unfortunately, Thewlis was disappointing; his performance was over-the-top and diminished his role, which was a letdown.

All in all, the movie isn't quite as good as the first, but watching Stone is always a pleasure. Just ignore Thewlis.

Firstly, it seems the prominent actors were primarily motivated by the paycheck. The surgical scenes were utterly laughable, and anyone with even a basic understanding of medicine would find them completely absurd. Anesthesiologists don't leave the room during a heart transplant, nor do surgeries take place in tiny, instrument-free spaces lacking heart-lung machines and sterile protocols—it's just unrealistic. The film's repeated medical inaccuracies made it hard to focus on the storyline. There was no blood, no medical personnel, and then the hero doctor swoops in to take over—clearly not a movie for discerning adults. Additionally, the budget must have been limited; the street scenes were okay, but I have to wonder who the technical adviser was. It felt like the film was directed by someone utterly clueless. Save your money—wait for the DVD release and definitely avoid renting this one.

Halloween tells the story of a boy misunderstood during his childhood. He channels his frustrations by attacking his older sister, whom he ultimately kills at the start of the film. This act marks only the beginning of the terror wrought by Michael Myers.  

Donald Pleasance portrays the doctor who has been investigating Myers for years. He senses that something inherently evil sets Myers apart—a darkness that cannot be contained or stopped.  

After escaping from a mental institution, Myers pursues his younger sister. Killing her might finally put an end to the chaos caused by this troubled boy. However, Myers struggles to complete his mission as others interfere, forcing him to eliminate witnesses while still searching for the girl he truly seeks.  

Many horror films feature teenagers being slaughtered by a masked or grotesque killer, but Halloween was the trailblazer. If you think about it, many of the most memorable horror movies—those featuring Freddy Krueger or Jason—center on killers stalking nearly naked victims. But none of those would have existed without Halloween.

For anyone who has experienced and fallen in love with the stage musical A CHORUS LINE, the film adaptation feels like a poor imitation. It not only cuts several songs but also introduces unnecessary plot twists, adds new dance numbers, and features choreography that falls flat. Let's face it—Richard Attenborough simply doesn't have a knack for filming dancers convincingly.

On stage, Michael Bennett's A CHORUS LINE was purely his creation: his concept, his choreography, his direction—his heartfelt gift to Broadway and the world. It was a raw, two-hour burst of intense realism that genuinely drew you into the lives of these "boys" and "girls." The movie, in contrast, lacks such empathy and depth; the actors seem more like auditioning for the film than genuinely auditioning for their roles. Every move and line of dialogue feels overly calculated, overly rehearsed. Michael Douglas, portraying Zach, appears too controlled, making it hard to believe he's the passionately fiery choreographer he's supposed to be. Even during his temper tantrums, his performance never quite feels authentic because each gesture and spoken word seems so deliberately rehearsed. As for his dancing—Kevin Kline was once considered for the role of Zach on Broadway. Bennett admired his audition, but Kline couldn't dance well enough, and ultimately, he was passed over.

I own this movie, though not by choice. The other day, I was feeling really bored, and the box caught my attention. I decided to pop it into the old VCR and ended up spending an hour and a half questioning life—"Why, God, why?" The storyline wasn't entirely terrible; as a gamer, I could appreciate certain aspects. If you're into cheesy, super-geeky romantic scenes, you might find this film enjoyable. I always saw myself as a Vulcan—like Mr. Spock—unable to love. Honestly, there aren't many good things to say about this movie; it's genuinely awful. But if you're into badly made films, this one might be just for you! The real story behind it, though, is much more interesting. 😉

If I had to describe this film in one word, it would be:

LAME

I fell in love with this silent action drama. Only Kurt Russell could have performed this role so perfectly. Raised from childhood amidst constant war and combat, Todd (Kurt Russell) is abandoned on a distant planet after becoming obsolete due to genetically engineered soldiers. 

The stage is set, and another timeless action icon is born—SOLDIER. This isn’t Rambo, Schwarzenegger, Bruce Willis, Mel Gibson, or Jason Statham; it’s Kurt Russell’s show, and he completely owns it—original, daring, and profoundly human. I still wish they had made sequels.

Rating: 10/10

—LD
