I didn’t have high expectations for this film, having picked it up as part of a five-movie pack—all of which were pretty dire in their own ways for under five pounds, so what did I expect? And as it turned out, I was right; they were all terrible. This movie has a few (and I mean a few is being generous) interesting moments—the occasional camcorder perspective adds a little flair, and the drummer is quite convincingly obnoxious, which makes sense. Beyond that, there’s not much else to highlight. The main issue is that it’s just painfully dull. In what I can only assume was an attempt to build tension, nothing much happens—and when it does, it’s incredibly boring. I had my thumb hovering over the fast-forward button for most of the film, but I decided to give it a try first. Also, is the lead singer really that handsome? They keep mentioning how stunning he is, but honestly, he reminded me a bit of a meerkat. I haven’t even gotten to the killer yet—I won’t bother, as it’s not worth explaining. Anyway, as far as I’m concerned…

I watched this film primarily because of Al Adamson. He's widely regarded as one of the worst directors ever—on par with Ed Wood Jr. and Ray Dennis Steckler—belonging to the hall of infamy for cinematic disasters. I was a bit let down, though, because while the movie was genuinely bad, it didn’t quite reach the levels of utter disaster that some of Adamson’s earlier, more schlocky films did. As a result, it wasn’t particularly entertaining for us fans of so-bad-it’s-good movies.

I was also cautious about watching this film, especially given the title "Naughty Stewardesses," which suggests it might be a porn film—something I wouldn’t typically review on IMDb. At times, it seemed to be exactly that, especially during the first ten minutes. However, it’s clear that the script went through numerous revisions, as much of the film contains no nudity or sexual content, and towards the end, a sudden, violent plot twist emerges out of nowhere—definitely not sexy, and quite confusing as a result.

Unfortunately, none of the segments are even decent. For instance, as a supposed porn film, it surprisingly shows very little nudity, and it’s baffling why they cast a 71-year-old actor in such a role.

This independent film was one of the best I have ever seen at the Tall Grass Film Festival. I loved it, as there were many wonderful aspects to it. Additionally, the cast and crew I had the pleasure of meeting were absolutely outstanding. Avi did a fantastic job in his role, and Ricky Ullman was remarkably convincing—surprising, considering he's known for Disney roles. I was amazed by his ability to transition seamlessly from cheesy teen comedies to such mature characters. The talent involved in this film was truly impressive. The cinematography was exceptional, making this a must-watch for anyone interested in independent cinema. I believe Mr. Gruver would have been very proud to have such a submission featured in his festival, especially since his parents loved the movie so much that they watched it again after it won the audience favorite award. This film was dark, funny, sad, and deeply emotional—simply fabulous. I am genuinely excited about this film and honestly hope it continues to receive the recognition it deserves.

A delightful adventure for both grown-ups and kids alike, this film operates on multiple levels: from laugh-out-loud car crashes and slapstick face cakes to clever, subtle humor aimed at adults.  

Glenn Close delivers a masterful performance as Cruella ("call me Ella") De Ville, exuding her wicked charm at its finest.  

Having spent three years at Dr. Pavlov's Behaviour Modification Clinic, she's finally overcome her obsession with fur—yes, even the puppy-skin coats she once craved so fiercely. She’s even had all her furs stored away in the dungeon of her towering, eccentric castle.  

Yet, no Dalmatian movie would be complete without Cruella's scheming and cunning plans. You can be sure her plans will shift her behavior once again. This time, she’s on the hunt for one more puppy—bringing her total to 102 Dalmatians—adding another layer to her wicked plot.  

Ioan Gruffudd charms effortlessly as the compassionate hero running the "Second Chance" dog shelter. Though he appeared in "Titanic" and was cast as Pip in last year’s TV adaptation of "Great Expectations," I didn't recognize him at first; in "Titanic," he played Fifth Officer Lowe, and I missed "Great Expectations," so I wasn't surprised by my oversight.  

Gerard Depardieu

In an era when Hollywood profits from highlighting our vulnerabilities—our struggles, despair, crime, addiction, and conflict—this film emerges as a powerful reminder of the "Indomitable Spirit." If you're feeling overwhelmed or defeated, watching this movie can lift your spirits and help you soar once again. We all face hardships, and sometimes we need a gentle reminder that perseverance and bravery can carry us through. That’s exactly what this film provided for me, and I hope it will do the same for you.

I still have grainy, late-night VHS copies of this show from way back when—no cable, just cheap tapes recorded during late-night commercials—when I’d stay up to whatever odd hour they aired it just to tape it.  
The series wasn’t really about Freddy Krueger; only the first couple of episodes featured him as a sort of Rod Serling-style announcer. Each episode was a standalone nightmare, delving into classic horror themes like traumatic childhood, romance gone wrong, cannibalism, money, death, and—surprisingly—more dating.  
From the episode where a teenage boy accidentally tells the girl "I will love you forever" and ends up literally stuck to her (they grow together for a moment), to the one where a young stewardess visits a strange man’s cabin only to find a trophy room filled with other stewardesses—and I vaguely recall an episode comparing blind dates to hockey, complete with injuries and penalties—dating was arguably the creepiest element of the series.  
One episode featured Jeffrey Combs (Re-Animator, etc.) as a driven pizza merchant with a...

A deliriously romantic comedy featuring intricate subplots that seamlessly weave together, complemented by actors who exchange lines with impeccable comic timing—an awe-inspiring skill to witness. When Cher's timid fiancé urges her to help reconcile with his estranged, temperamental younger brother, no one can foresee the cascade of events that ensue. Rich with operatic symbolism, Catholic church confessions, love bites, and falling snow, "Moonstruck" is a timeless and polished masterpiece. It takes approximately fifteen minutes for the film's rhythm to settle—initial scenes, such as the grandfather with his dogs at the cemetery and Cosmo's exchange with the elderly man at the gate, are somewhat uneven—but the ensemble cast skillfully interlaces the plot’s various threads. The film’s quirky tone and whimsical spirit are truly contagious. ***1/2 out of ****

John Boorman's "Deliverance" tells the story of four suburban residents from Atlanta who embark on a daring canoe trip down the swift currents of the Cahulawassee River. The river is on the brink of being submerged due to dam construction, which will flood the last remaining wild areas.  

The four characters each represent different facets of manhood: a vigorous sports enthusiast who has never felt the need for insurance because he perceives no real risk (played by Burt Reynolds); a fervent family man and guitar player (Ronny Cox); an overweight bachelor from the insurance industry (Ned Beatty); and a quiet, reflective married man with a son, who enjoys smoking his pipe (Jon Voight).  

What unfolds is a harrowing journey as these men confront the brutal forces of nature, exploring themes of morality and the fragile veneer of civilization when faced with the primal laws of the wilderness.  

Expertly filmed, this intense adult adventure features several truly suspenseful and memorable scenes.

Just a quick note to clarify my earlier comment. "Fear of a Black Hat" doesn't feature the criminal whose image was stolen by the band—that's from "CB4." It's easy to mix up the two, as they are quite similar, but "Fear of a Black Hat" is substantially the better film... definitely.

How can you take her gritty, glamorously violent bounty hunter story seriously with *that* accent? It's utterly absurd. Moreover, the director's visual style is nauseating and gimmicky, and the plot is a shallow, boring, and confusing rehash of gangster movies. The acting fails to convince, and the film introduces new characters throughout, told through fragmented, mostly out-of-sequence flashbacks—seemingly designed just to keep viewers confused. The film even presents scenes that never actually happen, only to later reveal, "that didn't really happen, this did"—for example, the apparent killing of the (fictitious) 'First Ladies.' Why are we shown the initial, incorrect sequence of events then? 

With poor casting choices, a convoluted and messy plot, and a headache-inducing directorial style, this film is a disaster. I’d give it a 1 out of 5.

I first encountered this film decades ago on a black-and-white television in a small Samoan village and found it absolutely hilarious. Now, after watching it again years later, I realize I no longer find it funny—nothing about it makes me laugh anymore. Yet, despite that, I still appreciate its cleverness and lighthearted charm. The comedy is sharp and breezy, moving swiftly without stumbling, and I enjoyed it thoroughly.

Set in 1945, the story follows Fred MacMurray as a 4F who desperately wants to join the military. While working in the scrapyard he manages, he rubs a magic lamp and a genie appears, ready to grant him a few wishes. The initial setup is fairly standard, but the subsequent fantasies are surprisingly spirited. MacMurray wishes to serve in the army, and suddenly, he’s marching alongside Washington’s troops into a lively USO show, where June Haver and Joan Leslie wear frilly lace or something similar, topped with lavender wigs. Washington then sends MacMurray on a mission to spy on the enemy—the German-speaking Hessians, not the British—who are gathered in a Bierstube, singing a humorous drinking song praising their homeland, the Vaterland.

This film is quite entertaining—if you're into B-grade movies, that is. It’s a quintessential 80s college slasher flick, notable for a single song that repeats throughout the soundtrack. While it's a terrible movie overall, it's worth renting for some laughs, especially to see old men suddenly emerge from closets wielding knives. Honestly, I find it pretty amusing.

This film is truly uplifting for anyone who has faced challenging times, whether financially or emotionally. You'll definitely find yourself laughing—it's the best remedy! :) After losing her husband and being left in a difficult financial spot, Grace must find a new way to earn money, albeit through somewhat questionable means, which only heightens the humor. Even my boyfriend enjoyed it, so don’t assume it’s just a chick flick.

Two houses, a single street, a lone phone booth, a car, a girl next door, a boy next door, and a zombie—these ingredients alone should make for a fantastic horror film. Add some blue lighting, ambient music, and you're all set. But not in the hands of Dutch director van Rouveroy!

I enjoy hosting "bad movie nights" from time to time. The idea is simple: gather some drinks, invite film fans, and revel in the worst movies cinema has to offer. For such an occasion, this piece of cinematic trash is perfect. Guaranteed laughs!

Strangely enough, van Rouveroy continues to defend her film as a major achievement. To witness this firsthand, you just need to listen to the DVD’s commentary track. Once again: prepare for disbelief and guaranteed laughs!

I tend to avoid TV movies because their identity is obvious within seconds of the opening shot. However, this one caught my eye due to its unique title and the somber, meticulously crafted atmosphere that unfolds from the very beginning. Although the persistent rain reinforced my suspicion that the story might be out of place—in spite of its supposed California setting—the film was primarily filmed amid the stormy landscapes of Vancouver, B.C. The bleak, oppressive outdoor scenes perfectly enhance Olmos's outstanding performance.

Caution: Spoilers ahead...

I've watched this film three times, and each viewing has only deepened my appreciation for it. Every time I see it, I'm reminded of its exceptional quality. This HBO made-for-TV movie is executed with the same level of excellence as many of their productions—so much so that, if it had been released in theaters, it likely would have garnered Oscar nominations for its outstanding performances. 

As most readers might already know from other reviews, the story centers on the notorious serial killer Andrei Chikatilo, who murdered 56 people over eight years in the former Soviet Union. Of these victims, three remain missing and unaccounted for, leading to his conviction for 52 murders out of 53 confirmed cases. However, the narrative primarily shifts focus to the diligent forensic analyst Victor Burakov, portrayed brilliantly by Stephen Rea. Burakov becomes increasingly tormented and obsessed with catching the killer, despite facing numerous hurdles imposed by political interference. His character's journey is crucial to the story. 

Near the end, there is a poignant scene that highlights the toll such investigations can take. It mentions how, in the United States, investigators are often removed from serial killer cases after 18 months—whether they want to continue or not—due to the mental strain and frustration involved.

Starring one of my favorite actors, James Spader, I hoped this film would at least be somewhat enjoyable. Unfortunately, it failed to deliver. After just thirty minutes, I found myself watching the rest with the remote in hand, ready to fast-forward through the dull moments. The plot is painfully predictable—so cliché and formulaic that you can anticipate every scene and even memorize the dialogues. It’s one of those movies that leave you wondering, “How on earth did this get greenlit?” On a slightly positive note, there are a few mildly entertaining special effects. However, overall, if you’ve seen five sci-fi movies or are over nine years old, I recommend you save your time and skip this one.

Alan Alda portrays the real-life "Sports Illustrated" writer George Plimpton, who once received an invitation to join the Detroit Lions as an honorary player. The film presents a somewhat weak and unengaging story, intriguingly mixed with elements of fantasy. Director Alex March approaches this material with a unique style, filming it in a semi-documentary manner complemented by macho commentary, while also infusing the story with a touch of Capraesque whimsy. However, by emphasizing visual flair, he inadvertently muddles the coherence of the main storyline. Alda's self-satisfied, lackluster performance adds to the film's shortcomings, although the supporting cast features actual professional athletes and the captivating Lauren Hutton as Alda's girlfriend—an appealing fantasy in itself. *1/2 out of ****

Short Synopsis

The film begins with soldiers being dismissed from their unit. One attempts to pursue another through an unusual scheme, which the latter repeatedly rejects. Later, both find themselves trapped inside an office building, planning to crack a safe during the Christmas holidays. What starts as hostility gradually shifts into playful banter, ultimately escalating into a desperate fight for survival—especially after they deplete all their drinking water, heightening the tension. Displaying exposed, muscular, and well-oiled physiques, they forge a hole in the wall and finally escape only to discover they have been betrayed by women. One is captured, while the other remains free and chooses not to betray his comrade. In a final encounter, they share a cigarette, bid farewell—adieu, l'ami—and part ways.

I found it difficult not to interpret the two leads, played by the iconic Alain Delon and Charles Bronson, as closet homosexuals. Their obvious attraction to each other, coupled with their contemptuous treatment of women throughout, hints at underlying themes. The story appears to carry a strong symbolic undertone, reminiscent of Deliverance, and is imbued with a raw, primal energy.

A couple of nights ago, I watched this film, not expecting much, and unsurprisingly, it didn't turn out to be all that exciting. The premise—about a team of vampire hunters (called V-San, short for vampire sanitation) traveling in their spaceship, periodically exterminating space vamps and rescuing hostages—has potential. If the execution had been better, it might have been quite a standout. Sadly, after a decent opening, the quality quickly declined, leaving behind something that, while still somewhat watchable, was painfully bad. I wasn't expecting much from these kinds of movies that often air on the Sci-Fi Channel, and at least this wasn't one of their creature features featuring an abominable CGI monster shuffling around. Nonetheless, it was still pretty poor, primarily due to weak writing and acting, with the soundtrack contributing significantly to its badness. When the film stuck to generic sci-fi sounds and weird noises, it fared okay, but too often, cheesy soft rock songs interrupted, turning scenes into laughingstocks. I might have tolerated the cheesy acting and writing more if...

Throughout my life, I haven't watched many online movies, but if I had to choose, I would pick Spatula Madness. It's a clever nod to classic films like Star Troopers, utilizing camera work and steel nerves. Jason Steele has mastered transforming ordinary images into artwork, then assembling them with frame-by-frame animation to create a world inhabited by spatulas. The story kicks off in the middle—how's that for a director's treat? Then it shifts, starting from the middle again and so on. When I first saw it, I expected a rough, pixelated look, but Jason, like me, appreciates visual detail and went all out. I wouldn't recommend it for children or most viewers, but I encourage you to look it up online. It's a short film found on FilmCow, and its style is reminiscent of South Park, but less violent. I give it a 10 for style, a 6 for humor, and a 6 for storytelling—overall, a perfect 10/10. Great work!  

Jason Steele, I can't wait to see your next movie.

Hello! This movie is... well... uh... okay. Just kidding! IT'S AWESOME! It's not a blockbuster smash hit, and that's okay. It's a huge hit in my world—and my sisters' too. We’re die-hard rockers. GO RAMONES!!!! This is a fantastic movie... for ME!

Before we get started, I should mention I have a fear of dentists. Watching this movie gives me the creeps and makes me cringe—yet, oddly, that's part of what I love about it. The film tends to be quite slow at times, so I deduct three stars for that.  

*Spoiler Alert*  

The story centers on Dr. Alan Feinstone, who discovers his wife has been unfaithful. As the film progresses, he begins experiencing hallucinations and turns increasingly violent, torturing his patients, killing colleagues, and eventually murdering his wife and her lover.  

*End Spoiler*  

This movie is extremely graphic and bloody. If you're into horror and gore, I would recommend it.  

Overall, I give it 7 out of 10 stars. Dr. Alan Feinstone is certainly not your average dentist!

An independent feature can now serve both as a piece of cinematic artistry and as a professional video résumé. Enter *Broken*, a boldly promoted twenty-minute short packed with style and enthusiasm. But does it stand on its own as a compelling film, or is it primarily a showcase for talent? That’s the question at the heart of the matter.

*Broken* follows the story of Bonnie Clayton, who is kidnapped after awakening from a recurring nightmare one night, by "a sadistic stranger and his colorful entourage" (as described on the video box). During her captivity, it becomes clear that her captors possess knowledge about her that she herself was unaware of. As they interrogate her, a black-clad soldier crashes into their hideout in a desperate attempt to save her, sparking chaos and violence.

Thankfully, director Alex Ferrari demonstrates confidence and skill—if not always subtlety—in his craft. The film boasts impressive visual flair, especially impressive given its modest budget and the inexperience of its team. However, its shortcomings lie in its writing, which feels weak and somewhat derivative—recalling *Long Kiss Goodnight* blended with *The Matrix*, all cobbled together shortly after reading *Fight Club*.

Deliverance is a captivating thriller that delivers as much excitement as any top-tier suspense film, while simultaneously delivering a stomach-churning sense of terror. Although not categorized as a horror movie, it possesses a frightening intensity comparable to that of classic horror classics. The mere idea of an ordinary, red-blooded man enjoying an adventurous weekend far from civilization, only to be captured and violently assaulted by a couple of ruthless hillbillies, represents the nightmare scenario for the vast majority of people worldwide. While it might have been easy for Deliverance to veer into exploitative territory, director John Boorman consciously steered clear of that trap, crafting a film that deeply probes, questions, and challenges the very essence of masculinity. Unlike many films that leave viewers longing to step into the hero’s shoes—to perform brave acts, save the day, or win the girl—Deliverance leaves audiences praying that they never have to endure what these four men face. 

Four city dwellers—Ed (Jon Voight), Lewis (Burt Reynolds), Drew (Ronny Cox), and Bobby (Ned Beatty)—venture into the wilderness for a few days...

I am surprised that reviewers enjoyed this movie. The plot is confusing and poorly constructed. The characters come across as dull and unconvincing. Michael Bowen spends most of the film spying on others and making misjudgments, yet none of the characters exhibit any redeeming qualities or interest. This film is neither edgy nor inventive, nor does it offer any irony or clever ideas. It lacks any straightforwardness and feels painfully tedious. Its lack of a theatrical release is no surprise, and its airing on "This Network" diminishes that channel’s credibility. I strongly suggest tuning into a rerun of the Garden Smart show on PBS or watching an informative program if you happen to come across this disaster on late-night TV. If it appears on daytime programming, do yourself a favor and go for a long walk—preferably somewhere without smog—just to escape the misery of having watched this mess. Life is too short, and this movie is painfully long.

I really enjoyed this movie—it was charming and fun. I liked it a lot, but if you didn't, that's okay. Emma Roberts did a great job as Nancy Drew, even if her portrayal isn't exactly like the book character. The vintage outfits are a bit odd when viewed in a modern context, but she wore them well. As for the wealthy girls, their outfits didn't quite convey a sense of wealth; it seemed like they randomly picked clothes—almost as if from a garage sale—and combined them without much thought. Some of the outfits, especially the penny loafers paired with everyday clothes, felt a bit tacky. I don't mean to criticize the film; it really was enjoyable! Definitely catch it in theaters—you'll have a good time!

"People I Know" falls flat as a film, lacking compelling characters to root for or connect with, despite the efforts of a talented ensemble cast. Pacino delivers his signature powerhouse performance as Eli Wurman, a once-successful publicity agent now worn down by a lifetime of moral compromise. However, unlike Michael Corleone, it's difficult to feel emotionally invested in this character, his struggles, or his outcome. 

The storyline follows Eli as he prepares for a fundraiser supporting a liberal cause, all while being sidetracked by a client's recent scandal—Ryan O'Neal, fittingly cast in a limited role, plays a behind-the-scenes figure entangled in trouble, with his TV actress girlfriend caught in the wrong crowd. Tea Leoni brings her usual charisma to her supporting part, yet the script offers her little substance to showcase her talent. Kim Basinger, portraying Eli's sister-in-law, manages to evoke sympathy despite the somewhat far-fetched plot developments.

Ultimately, this film is mainly for viewers who enjoy watching Pacino in action and appreciate the other main actors. Regrettably, due to weak script and direction, "People I Know" comes across as amateurish, which explains its brief theatrical run and quick move to DVD. Be warned before you watch.

I understand why this short film received an Oscar nomination for Best Live Action Short, given its skillful craftsmanship. Even if blues music isn't your favorite—though, in my opinion, it leaned more toward jazz—you can still easily appreciate the film's quality. It's simply very well made. However, I can't help but wonder why director Gjon Mili only directed this one film; it seems surprising that such a remarkable work didn't propel his career further. Regarding the Black performers, I realize their careers might not have experienced a significant boost, as sadly, many in white society remain indifferent—if not dismissive—toward Black artists or this genre of music.

If you decide to watch this film and find the beginning less engaging, I recommend skipping ahead to around 5:50, where the energy noticeably picks up. Once the woman stops singing and the performers begin improvising, the rhythm and pace improve substantially.

This film resonates strongly with a specific, clearly defined audience—something I am not among. I attended a preview uncertain of what to anticipate, but I ended up feeling let down. The story of a profoundly dysfunctional, occasionally even "twisted" Hungarian Jewish family doesn't particularly appeal to me. An epic narrative like this should offer viewers deeper insights by the conclusion. Ultimately, films of this nature aim to explore the human condition, yet this one sheds little new light on its more profound aspects.

I have no interest in rap or ghetto culture; I’m white and prefer classic rock. Still, that didn’t stop me from enjoying this fantastic comedy. It’s essentially a sequel to This Is Spinal Tap, in the sense that it’s the same type of movie—just about rap instead of rock—but it’s just as hilarious. The film features many witty jokes, although a few fall flat. The characters are all very funny and believable. I watched it simply because it made me laugh at 3 a.m., and any movie capable of doing that deserves at least a test screening. One reason this film is so amusing is that it satirizes rap from a different perspective—highlighting how contemporary rap often focuses on the wrong things, relying on studio antics and lacking genuine talent. The movie hails from a time when rappers truly deserved more credit. Overall, it’s a comedic film filled with jokes about racism, sex, and music culture, along with other obvious humor themes. I highly recommend it to fans of This Is Spinal Tap. They are essentially the same movie—just set in different worlds—and, yes, the same jokes work in both.

I'm not entirely convinced that Rob Schmidt truly qualifies as a "Master" of the horror genre, given that his filmography includes only a single horror film, "Wrong Turn," which was merely slightly above average. However, his work on "Right to Die" stands out as one of the most chilling and compelling episodes of the second season of the "Masters of Horror" series. Interestingly, there was a similar underdog narrative in the first season when William Malone directed the standout episode "The Fair-Haired Child," despite his other feature films like "Fear Dot Com" and "House on Haunted Hill" falling flat.

"Right to Die" skillfully tackles the contemporary hot-button issue of euthanasia, while also weaving in classic horror elements such as spectral vengeance, deadly conspiracies, dark humor, and comic book-style violence. The story begins with a late-night drive home, where the Addison couple discusses the husband's ongoing infidelity, only to be involved in a severe car crash. Cliff escapes unscathed, but his wife Abby is severely burned and requires life support. As Cliff and his unscrupulous lawyer (played by Corbin Bernsen of "The Dentist") plot their next move, the story plunges into a tense exploration of morality, desperation, and the horror lurking beneath the surface.

I must admit that I didn't initially give this movie much of a chance. I decided fairly early on that it wasn't really my kind of film.  

On the positive side, the cinematography is impressive. The scenes depicting early 70s Manhattan are beautifully crafted, and the lead actress delivers a compelling performance. The black and white visuals are sharp and striking, giving the film a modern, almost timeless feel. However, some of the stylistic choices undermine this effect. The disjointed editing, reminiscent of late 60s surrealism and new wave cinema, feels somewhat jarring. The story itself also seems rooted in a very specific era—somewhere between free love utopianism and experimental art.  

The plot follows a young woman wandering the city as she searches for a man with whom she had anonymous phone sex. Along her journey, she encounters a series of eccentric characters, sharing quirks and revealing secrets. The film appears to be an offbeat, irreverent comedy infused with an avant-garde sensibility. Fans of Andy Warhol's work might find "The Telephone Book" particularly appealing.  

A few issues I encountered include...

Some people adored "The Aristocrats," while others disliked it so much they walked out midway. Reactions to Eddie Izzard are unlikely to be as polarized—if you can handle a transvestite comedian who claims to prefer girls and whose language often includes enough "f" words to turn his show into a continuous beep on network TV. Many of Izzard's supporters are so passionate that they see no flaws in his performances whatsoever. Conversely, I found this show occasionally flatter than Izzard's chest, yet more often than not amusing, with moments that were genuinely hilarious. He has a talent for linking references from earlier routines to later ones, creating a cohesive flow. He's neither a storyteller nor a traditional joke-teller, nor a frenetic performer like Robin Williams. Instead, he plays with ideas, some of which land successfully, while others—such as his routine involving the San Francisco cable car and Alcatraz—fall flat. Nevertheless, he skillfully moves past the flops and embellishes the routines that connect. I rated this performance a 7 and might be

Eleven Oscar nominations and zero wins! I still can't understand why—it's not like the actors' careers skyrocketed afterward, which makes awarding them for minor roles seem unnecessary, just like with Halle Berry and Denzel Washington. Actors like Whoopi Goldberg, Oprah Winfrey, Margaret Avery, and Danny Glover all delivered incredible performances. I’m genuinely curious about the discussions that took place at the Oscars that year—surely, it falls into the "Shoulda-Woulda-Coulda" category for the judges.  

The book is remarkable, but true to Alice Walker’s writing style, she often makes her characters seem exaggerated. That’s why I’m glad the film adaptation cut out some elements.  

The cinematography was stunning—though the African scenes left much to be desired. The story's setting in Liberia, West Africa, was supposed to be vividly portrayed, yet Steven Spielberg seems to think audiences are too simple to picture Africa beyond safaris. So, there had to be a stereotypical zebra and wildlife scene—which, of course, was unnecessary and inaccurate.

Having read the book multiple times, I notice that the movie doesn't quite stay true to it. While I can accept some artistic license, I have significant concerns about the film's setting. Nobody seems to mention that both the book and the movie are based on real events that took place in Nebraska. As a Nebraska resident who grew up in the town the story depicts, I find this particularly bothersome. First, the "small" town portrayed as the setting is actually the third-largest city in the state, with a population of around 50,000. Grand Island is the largest city between Lincoln and Denver. Second, the movie's scenery is inaccurate—Grand Island is located in the Platte River Valley, which is characterized by flat terrain and few trees. Watching the film was frustrating because it misrepresents my hometown, which was heavily affected by the actual events—the city was severely damaged and portions were destroyed. In the book, there's mention of riding bikes from Mormon Island to Fonner Park, a trip that covers about 15 miles, assuming you don't mind the distance.

This is a truly powerful film. When I first watched it, the Scottish accents made understanding difficult, which hampered my enjoyment. I almost gave up on it, but after acquiring the DVD and using the English subtitles when needed, I was able to fully appreciate its brilliance. It is an exceptional movie.

The widescreen presentation adds a spectacular touch, highlighting stunning rugged landscapes. The story reminded me of Braveheart—a compelling struggle between good and evil. Here, Liam Neeson plays the hero, while Tim Roth portrays the villain. Both actors deliver remarkable performances.

Few characters are as reprehensible as Roth’s. His arrogance and irritation make you want to punch him in the face. His character’s nastiness is so convincing that even critics love to praise him more than other performances. Neeson embodies the quintessential hero—strong and dependable, much like Gibson in Braveheart. Jessica Lange delivers a powerful performance as the female lead. The film engrosses you deeply, ensuring an emotionally charged viewing experience.

Why do films about Cleopatra, the last pharaoh, consistently seem to bring out the worst in filmmaking? The allure she supposedly held for the greatest Roman leaders—Julius Caesar and Mark Antony—rarely translates to the screen beyond the antics of oversexed high schoolers. Despite opulent sets and costumes, these movies remain as lackluster as the Italian "sandals and toga" epics of the 1950s. Admittedly, such extravagance belongs on the big screen, which is why "Gladiator" succeeded, yet it didn't rely on romanticized sex like these Cleopatra films do. Miss Varela has as little acting talent as Elizabeth Taylor, but Timothy Dalton possesses genuine skill. It's a shame some of that talent didn’t rub off on her colleagues.

Whenever someone asks me to name the scariest movie I've ever seen, I always say "Black Noon," and to this day, hardly anyone has ever heard of it.  

I watched it alone about 30 years ago, when I was just 13, while my parents were out for the evening. As far as I know, it was only ever screened once in the UK, and unfortunately, it's not available on DVD or VHS.  

If anyone manages to track down a copy, please let me know.  

Watching it again now might not be as frightening, but it has left a lasting impression as a particularly unsettling little film!

I had high expectations for this movie, drawn by the previews and the buzz it generated, but ultimately I left feeling thoroughly disappointed. Slums is a bleak and unfunny film that echoes the unsettling family dynamics often explored by Todd Solondz—without his signature humor. The plot moves sluggishly, and each scene seems to grow duller than the one before. Perhaps I missed the deeper meaning, but if this film truly depicts every girl’s coming-of-age, I’m certainly grateful to be a man.

When contemplating captivity, a multitude of words spring to mind—many of which are unflattering. Think: dull, unengaging, predictable, unappealing, inscrutable, and unwatchable.

I used to despise those mid to late nineties films that essentially copied Scream, but these new Saw-inspired knockoffs are making those old relics seem like timeless classics. While they continue to target the same demographic that propelled those earlier hits, these new films introduce an even darker level of depravity, making their young teenage audiences feel both rebellious and trendy.

This film is a complete waste of time—boring and uninspired. What happened to Larry Cohen’s talent? His name hasn’t been associated with anything worthwhile since 1993. Still, I was shocked to see his name attached to such a terrible project. And was anyone genuinely surprised when the love interest turned out to be one of the psychopaths? Did anyone not see that coming from the very first scene? Only someone who has never watched a movie before in their life!

This episode is one of the shallowest, primarily serving as a fun-filled spectacle rather than a complex narrative. However, I really enjoyed its light-hearted tone, making it one of the most entertaining episodes purely for amusement. Imagine the crew encountering the White Rabbit and Alice from Wonderland, a Bengal tiger, a samurai warrior, a knight on horseback who kills McCoy, and a variety of other seemingly bizarre events that don’t make much sense until the very end. Despite the danger, there's a sense that nothing can be taken too seriously—it's all just too fun, and the episode feels incredibly surreal. Overall, on a non-aesthetic level, it's simply great entertainment.

Typically, I’m not the type to be frightened by horror films, but this one was an exception. Somehow, it got under my skin! The movie is quite simple, yet incredibly effective, thanks to its fantastic atmosphere that builds up to some truly startling moments. The scene where the girl’s father comes down the hill is particularly memorable. Another scene that caught me off guard was the family photo; I didn’t see it coming and literally jumped out of my seat! I highly recommend everyone watch this film—turn out the lights, and it will stay with you for a long time!

Although the premise might appear silly, Murphy's character treats it casually, making it easier for viewers to engage with this blend of mysticism and gritty contemporary child abduction. The film boasts an excellent cast, notably Charles Dance and Charlotte Lewis, with Murphy delivering some of his best comedy and action work of the 1980s. It features impressive special effects, a highly surreal dream sequence, and a fairly unique storyline. Often underrated among Murphy's films, this one certainly deserves a watch.

WARNING: If you haven't seen the film yet, please avoid reading this comment.

Although I haven't seen every movie out there, The Hamiltons certainly delivered one of the most disappointing pieces of entertainment I've encountered—I found it completely unentertaining! The film's mediocre acting, an absurd plotline, and a final twist that was just plain stupid all contributed to my negative impression. 

As for the story, it suggests that these characters are cannibals, but it's not clear whether they're humans, inbred, or something else entirely. The film never clarified if they're just odd beings exploring what people taste like or long-time cannibals. Honestly, the whole thing was just terrible—horrible, even. If you think The Hamiltons is worth watching, I have to ask—why? To me, it just fell flat. 

So, a big thumbs down from me on The Hamiltons! Instead, try watching movies like The Gravedancers, Tooth & Nail, or Borderland for a more enjoyable experience!

"Return of the Jedi" is often remembered more for its flaws than its strengths, which is unfortunate because as the final chronological chapter in the Star Wars saga, it exemplifies epic storytelling at its finest. It skillfully ties together all the previous storylines into a grand, convincing conclusion. 

While it features the charming Ewoks—adorable little bears that likely helped expand the franchise’s appeal—and the pacing slows somewhat in the middle, the last hour stands out as one of the saga's highlights. This is where Luke finally confronts Darth Vader, the most iconic villain in cinematic history.

The film accomplishes numerous feats that often go unrecognized: it offers a compelling resolution to Darth Vader's arc—evolving from somewhat improbable in "The Empire Strikes Back" to profoundly convincing here; it delivers an exhilarating opening set at Jabba's Palace; Ian McDiarmid's portrayal of the Emperor is superb; Luke's journey toward self-realization culminates powerfully; Solo and Leia’s romance reaches its resolution; and the emotional climax on the forest moon of Endor remains profoundly impactful.

The depiction of UK police in this film is utterly unrealistic. It seems as if the US is running the entire force, with officers constantly armed and running around. Did you know that CID officers change into uniform when they finish work and head to the pub? This film is one of the most inaccurate and poorly portrayed representations of "real" UK police I've ever seen, and it’s been presented to the public with no regard for authenticity. I understand Mr. Snipes might have needed the money to settle his back taxes, but it's baffling why a talented actor like Charles Dance would choose to be part of this. 

Compared to even the worst low-budget B-movies of the 1950s, this film is a hundred times worse. An hour and a half of my life I’ll never get back, wasted on scenes of despair and nonsense. 

Avoid it at all costs.

I don't usually take the time to leave comments, but I felt compelled to warn anyone who might think this is a comedy. It’s nowhere near funny. The premise—changing color, gender, or whatever else—has been done before, and often better. The actual transformation of two Black men into two white women is among the least convincing on screen. It would be bad enough if the script only required them to become white women, but the Wayans brothers are tasked with resembling two specific white women, and they fail miserably. I’ve seen drag queens without makeup look more authentic than these two, even with Hollywood’s best special effects and makeup. It’s simply unacceptable. To make matters worse, there’s a basketball player built like a brick wall, terrible dialogue, and more plot holes than a golf course, making this film a new personal low. And I usually enjoy bad movies! Stay far away from this one.

Many sources often categorize this compelling period drama—rooted in historical fact—together with the superficial "nunsploitation" films that were popular in '70s European cinema, neglecting the righteous anger that fuels the entire story. Interestingly, it may also be the sole narrative feature directed by Gianfranco Mingozzi, who was primarily known for his acclaimed documentaries. 

Set firmly within a historical framework, FLAVIA depicts the burgeoning rebellion of a young Italian nun in the early 15th century. Florinda Bolkan delivers a career-defining performance, arguably surpassing her outstanding role in Lucio Fulci's haunting DON'T TORTURE A DUCKLING. The girl is confined to a convent by her nobleman father in a desperate attempt to suppress her awakening sensuality. As she questions why women are often relegated to secondary roles in life and scripture, she witnesses firsthand how male domination can devastate female lives. This realization sparks her rebellion, fueled by the rants of the semi-mad Sister Agatha, powerfully enacted by veteran actress Maria Casarès, known for her role in Marcel Carné's LES ENFANTS DU PARADIS. Her defiance is further influenced by the threat of a Muslim invasion, which introduces a complex, constructive element to her resistance. In her pursuit of autonomy, Flavia unwittingly joins her oppressors and manipulates them, ultimately becoming the outcast she has long feared to be.

Despite the title, The Sword Bearer, and the action-packed, heroic poses on the DVD cover, this film is not a superhero movie.  

(Minor Spoilers) It tells the story of Sasha, The Sword Bearer, who is cursed with a retractable sword embedded in his forearm. Sounds cool, right? But in this film, it's very much grounded in reality. If you had this power as a child, could you control it—especially when faced with a madman or your mother’s abusive boyfriend? And if you can’t, how would you cope with having killed twice by the age of 12?  

That’s essentially where Sasha is when we meet him—wandering aimlessly after yet another killing, reminiscent of *Breathless*. His life changes when he meets Katya, and they fall instantly in love, giving Sasha a real reason to try and change his ways. However, his past relentlessly catches up with him in the form of two police officers.  

That’s the core of the story—there’s virtually no on-screen action, although much is implied.  

I really enjoyed this movie. Unlike many Hollywood superhero films, it offers a much more realistic and nuanced portrayal of its protagonist’s struggles.

Oddly enough, this film never reached Danish cinemas, so I had to wait for the DVD release. My expectations were high, but they were certainly not disappointed. As is often the case with Ang Lee, the film features outstanding performances, a clever and suspenseful plot that keeps you guessing until the very end, and superb cinematography. Alongside Unforgiven, it stands out as one of the two best Westerns of the 1990s.  

Those expecting something similar to Mel Gibson in The Patriot (which can be quite cheesy) or Braveheart (somewhat acceptable) may find themselves disappointed. However, anyone who appreciates the qualities mentioned above will have an excellent viewing experience. I give it a 9 out of 10.

Before I begin, I must confess that I'm a huge Bon Jovi fan. In fact, that was what initially drew me to the DVD case. Being a passionate horror enthusiast and a big fan of the first Vampires movie, I probably would have purchased it regardless.  

However, this sequel falls significantly short. Even Jon could not rescue this film for me. My biggest issue is that it simply isn't frightening. Aside from Jon's character, Derek Bliss, the rest of the cast fails to leave an impression, and I couldn't care less about their fates—especially the annoying vampire/drug addict woman. The female vampire neither appears scary nor seductive; she looks more like an undernourished 14-year-old girl, which makes sense considering how desperately she needs blood. Another major flaw is the movie's overly bright visuals. There's no atmosphere or sense of dread; the film lacks the darkness and foreboding tone that made the original so effective, even though its New Mexico setting wasn't exactly cloaked in mystery. This version is devoid of the tension and mood that are vital to horror.

William Powell's final portrayal of Philo Vance appears in The Kennel Murder Case, where the death of a champion show dog sparks a series of two additional murders and one attempted murder of a human. The core of the story revolves around unraveling how these crimes are connected and uncovering the motives behind them.

The Philo Vance series, penned by S.S. Van Dine, enjoyed immense popularity during its heyday. Van Dine cleverly structured his publications to maximize sales, allowing studios to acquire the rights individually and produce multiple adaptations. This strategy contributed to the numerous Philo Vance films and the frequent studio adaptations that followed. Had William Powell not achieved later fame as Nick Charles in MGM’s The Thin Man series, he might have been celebrated as the definitive Philo Vance.

Interestingly, Powell’s own dog, a small terrier named Captain, participated in the same dog show where the murdered champion was entered. Subsequently, another dog owner, a rival in the contest, became the first murder victim. As always, Powell's character is assisted by Eugene Palette’s Sergeant Heath, whose most notable contribution is using his physical strength to break down the locked door from the inside, where the initial murder occurred.

This series takes place a year after the mission to Abydos depicted in the Stargate movie, filling in many details the film left out. For instance, it explores how the Stargate was activated without a human computer, the origins of the Goa'uld—Ra's race—and the number of their members.  

The inaugural episode features retired Colonel Jack O'Neill (spelled with two Ls) being called back into action by General George Hammond after an attack from the now-inactive Stargate, orchestrated by Apophis, a formidable Goa'uld who murdered four men and kidnapped a woman. We are introduced to Dr. Samantha Carter, a brilliant scientist who believes she should have gone through the Stargate on her initial attempt—and is eager to do so now. Additionally, we learn that Daniel Jackson married on Abydos, and that hundreds of Stargate addresses are available for dialing. The episode's climax reveals that Daniel's wife has been captured by Apophis and is made his new queen.  

In the second episode, General Hammond announces the creation of the Stargate Command (SGC), comprising nine teams. Jack's team is designated SG-1, consisting of Jack O'Neill, Samantha Carter, and Daniel Jackson. Their first mission takes them to Chulak, a Goa'uld homeworld, to rescue Daniel's wife.

There are countless negative reviews of "Stay Away, Joe" here, and I can no longer stay silent in the face of this injustice. Let me share a perspective you might not have encountered yet.

For me, Elvis Presley's movies are a guilty pleasure for a simple reason: they are perfect films for pure relaxation because they require no mental effort. There’s no need to worry about missing intricate plots because, frankly, there rarely are any. I can kick back, put my feet up, grab a beer, switch off my brain, and enjoy all the quirky humor and catchy, easygoing rock 'n' roll tunes from the most vibrant decade of them all.

In my opinion, "Stay Away, Joe" definitely qualifies as "so bad it's good." If you're like me and enjoy a bit of campy, trashy entertainment, this film offers the ultimate 1960s experience. It's so poorly made that it feels almost surreal, and just when you think it can't possibly get more bizarre, it surprises you in the most unexpected ways. Ultimately, you find yourself dazzled by the sheer absurdity—unsure whether to laugh, shake your head, or marvel at the madness.

The film features a solid, deep cast, but for a thriller, it needs to offer more than just recognizable names and dialogue. The first third is almost entirely dialogue-heavy, predominantly women complaining to one another. The top five billed actors are all women, confirming that this is primarily a "chick flick" and not much else. It likely fits more comfortably on the Lifetime network. After a brief murder scene, the narrative devolves into more conversations, and by the halfway point, I’d lost interest. Also, Sally Field looked about 15 years old in this performance.

I had believed that the French had a reputation for quality filmmaking, but I was clearly mistaken. As has been noted before, this film primarily uses its titular character as a launchpad; its depiction of her life and personality bears little resemblance to the true Artemisia Gentileschi.  

The screenplay is abysmal—pretentious, awkward, and superficial—and its distortion of historical facts is particularly egregious for a genre that often relies on misrepresenting history rather than honoring it. Coupled with some reasonably well-designed sets, Valentina Cervi’s physical attractiveness stands out as the film’s main highlight, and it’s evident from the start that the filmmakers were well aware of this; they quickly insert various "erotic" scenes that serve more to titillate than to advance the story or deepen the characters. Sadly, the allure of watching an attractive young woman simulate sexual arousal is insufficient to carry the film. The performances are forgettable, and the musical score is overly generic, save for a few intriguing chords. The cinematography is decent, featuring some appealing colors, but it’s also...

Things to Come stands out as a rare gem—a film that explores ideas. Unlike many movies that merely envision the future, few attempt to depict how that future unfolds. The opening sequence, depicting war descending upon Everytown, is brief yet impactful. Ironically, upon its release during a time of widespread appeasement, audiences mocked reports of enemy planes attacking England—Wells’ foresight proved all too accurate shortly after. The subsequent montage of relentless warfare, despite some subpar model work, is highly effective. The explanatory titles evoke the bold graphic style of German Expressionism. The art direction by William Cameron Menzies shines in the detailed set designs of the ruins of Everytown, among his finest work. Margaretta Scott delivers a captivating performance as the Chief’s mistress. The depiction of the 21st-century Everytown features equally striking design elements. However, the acting in this future segment lacks depth, possibly an ill-conceived attempt to juxtapose the cold rationality of the era with the barbarism of 1970. Regrettably, the model scenes illustrating angry crowds rushing along elevated walkways are embarrassingly poor—something that even 1930s technology could have improved significantly, making their quality all the more frustrating.

This film, much like Astaire's *Royal Wedding*—which aired after it on Turner Classic Movies last night—is renowned for a single musical scene that has cemented its place in Gene Kelly's legacy. Just as Fred Astaire danced with a clothing rack and later twirled around a room’s walls and ceiling, Kelly is celebrated for a cartoon sequence where he dances alongside Jerry Mouse. The animation is skillfully executed. What often goes unnoticed is that Kelly narrates the story behind this cartoon to Dean Stockwell and his young classmates during a school break, setting the scene by asking them to close their eyes and envision a idyllic countryside backdrop. Kelly even modifies his actual navy uniform, transforming it into a white "Pomeranian" style navy outfit with blue stripes. In this sequence, Jerry Mouse does more than just dance with Kelly; he speaks—a rare occurrence that Kelly did not replicate for many decades. Additionally, Jerry finally asserts his dominance over Tom Cat, who appears briefly as King Jerry’s butler, trying to cheer him with a platter of cheeses.

I hadn't seen this movie until I purchased the tape last year, and I was captivated and thoroughly entertained. It contains all the elements I cherish in a sci-fi story—social commentary, speculative ideas, and a compelling narrative.

There's a certain eeriness and amusement in observing a 1936 vision of the distant future—what the 60s and 70s thought the future would look like.

I believe it's a must-watch, not just for science fiction fans.

Flame in, flame out—that captures Gammera perfectly: a prehistoric beast capable of both destruction and endurance. Although I'm not particularly fond of Japanese monster movies, I ended up watching every film in the fifty-movie sci-fi DVD collection from Mill Creek/Treeline Films. At just about twenty-five dollars, it offers incredible value—around fifty cents per film—making it a worthwhile investment of time to enjoy some delightfully cheesy sci-fi adventures.

Gammera is awakened from a centuries-long sleep by a nuclear explosion, and he’s not pleased. Much like Godzilla, he unleashes his fury on Tokyo, prompting the United Nations to scramble for a plan to save the world. They settle on 'Plan Z,' which is presented as Earth's last hope—and in a clever detail, there's a large shed labeled the 'Z Plan' building, adding a touch of humor.

By the mid-1960s, American portrayals still lacked political sensitivity. One notable scene set in the Alaskan Air Defense Sector features General Arnold asking a female sergeant to make coffee—an example of the era’s stereotypical depictions.

I went into watching "The Hills Have Eyes 2" with some hope, having enjoyed the original film immensely and found the remake to be fairly entertaining. It was clear that the filmmakers had a bigger budget this time, especially for the special effects, which certainly added to the movie's visual impact. While I still favor the original, the remake was well-made and surprisingly enjoyable—pretty much a guilty pleasure for me. It was bloody, intense, and packed with impressive effects, making it a solid popcorn flick for horror enthusiasts.

Now, as for "The Hills Have Eyes 2," I honestly don't know where to begin. The storyline is nearly nonexistent—completely thin and uninspired. We're not exactly venturing into new territory here. The plot revolves around the military monitoring the area, leading to a series of disappearances. Naturally, the solution is to send in the National Guard to investigate. But in true Hollywood fashion, they cast the soldiers as the most inept, clueless bunch imaginable. It’s a tired trope, and I’ve seen it way too often. The mutants pick off the soldiers one by one in gory, graphic scenes. Again, the special effects by Nicotero are impressive, but overall, the film falls flat due to its lazy storytelling and clichéd characters.

I purchased the DVD of Before Sunset and watched it for the first time just a week ago. Having seen it twice since then, I couldn't help but feel nostalgic for Before Sunrise. Not because the sequel wasn't as impressive, but because these two films felt like they completed each other in a way no other sequels ever have. Every time I finished watching one, I experienced an irresistible urge and longing to see the other. As a result, I spent the past few weeks repeatedly revisiting both movies—I hesitate to say exactly how many times. 

What stands out most about Before Sunrise is how authentically it captures the evolution of the characters' feelings towards each other. It may seem straightforward—the gradual development of chemistry—but I believe many romantic films attempt to depict this, often failing to truly succeed. For someone like me, who isn't particularly a Nora Ephron fan, Before Sunrise is the first film that genuinely allows viewers to feel that transformation. I first watched it about eight years ago when I was 20 and liked it from the start. However, I didn’t initially consider it a "great film"; it still seemed to me like just another romantic movie.

As the quintessential example of a classic Errol Flynn adventure film, this movie boasts a compelling story and features two exceptional co-stars—Maureen O'Hara, whose stunning beauty is unforgettable, and Anthony Quinn. I wholeheartedly recommend this film to anyone with even a hint of appreciation for romance and adventure. 

Hollywood at its finest!

I first watched this movie around 1990 and cracked up laughing the entire time. It quickly became a cult favorite among my friends, and we’d often quote it spontaneously ("I'm going home in a bag!"). Remarkably, the humor still holds up fifteen years later. It’s become a Halloween tradition to introduce this film to my new friends—luckily, you can still find it on eBay! I’ve discovered that Halloween candy tastes even better when your tongue is firmly in your cheek, and this movie delivers everything—pathos, suspense, unrequited love, nobility, and more. Royal Dano delivers an exceptional, heartfelt performance as Old Man Wrenchmuller. I remember seeing him as a villain in "The 7 Faces of Dr. Lao," meeting a grim fate, but here, you truly feel for the old man right from the start.  

Be warned: if you're not paying close attention, you might miss some of the layered humor. The creators are quite subtle with their offhand comments, clever jabs at other sci-fi films through costumes, and even a scene that feels straight out of Wile E. Coyote’s playbook!

I wanted to read others' comments before sharing my review, and it seems the consensus is clear: this movie is terrible! From the acting to the unrealistic animation and numerous mistakes, it’s disappointing. I had hoped that the flaps might have been extended somehow—though, realistically, you can't extend flaps without engines. The landing gear requires electricity to be lowered, but the tiny fan shown during the scene was woefully insufficient to accomplish this. What struck me as especially odd was the landing itself: the rear wheels touched down first, and then the nose wheel broke off, leaving the plane suspended with both rear tires on the ground. How could the captain apply left and right brakes to tires that weren’t even touching the runway? Did they forget about the spoilers? To the director: please research aircraft thoroughly before making a movie about planes. Sorry for the technical rant, but I have to give this film a 1 out of 10.

This documentary chronicles the final years of Betty Page's (Paige Richards) career through reenactments. Known as the Tennessee tease, she was the most iconic pin-up queen in history. Her most memorable work emerged in the 1950s, featuring fetish photography, bondage scenes, and playful "girly flicks" involving staged fights. Irving Klaw (Dukey Flyswatter), operating out of Movie Star News, guided Betty on how to perform in front of the camera. While these famous photos and "stag films" contained no nudity, Klaw was nonetheless charged with distributing obscene materials and was ordered to destroy them to avoid legal trouble. It’s no surprise that Betty garnered a devoted cult following during her peak. With her girl-next-door looks—jet black hair, blue eyes, and an hourglass figure—she captivated audiences for decades, whether dressed in fetish gear or casual attire. Interestingly, she was photographed more than Marilyn Monroe and ranked second only to Elvis Presley in popularity. Eventually, Betty Page retreated from the public eye, dedicating her last years to religion. Although the film could have been even better, it remains engaging enough to hold viewers’ interest. Miss Richards is stunning in her own right; her look—bra, panties, garter belt, and hose—only enhances her presence.

I must say, Uma Thurman is truly the most captivating woman on the planet. This movie was incredibly adorable—really, super adorable. It included all the typical "sex" elements you'd expect from an Ivan Reitman comedy, but with an added twist: CHEMISTRY. Uma and Luke both share an awkward yet convincing chemistry that shines through in every scene. Their relationship is quirky, twisted, and fascinating, filled with intense sexual tension that will have you laughing until you can't feel your face. Anna Faris and the rest of the supporting cast play off each other's roles perfectly, and even Wanda Sykes, despite her small part, will keep you giggling. While these types of comedies aren't everyone's cup of tea, I went with someone who usually doesn't enjoy this genre, and he was laughing uncontrollably. Of course, this film isn't suitable for everyone, especially younger children, as some moments are a bit too adult for younger viewers. Overall, I was pleasantly surprised by this movie, though I felt the ending was a little weaker compared to the rest of the film. (3.5 out of 5 stars)

This movie is absolutely terrible—let's make that clear from the start. While there are a few isolated moments that stand out, they can't save the overall dull and flimsy plot. Colin Farrell resembles Brad Pitt in "12 Monkeys" both in appearance and acting style. Usually, I dislike Farrell for various reasons, but he’s somewhat okay in this film. The storyline is split between two threads: one about a kid who throws rocks at moving cars and another about a woman with a mustache. Honestly, the film seems completely directionless, unsure of what message it wants to convey or where it’s headed. The characters’ storylines occasionally intersect, but they are so poorly developed they shouldn’t have been included at all. Overall, the film feels weak and pointless, with only a few decent scenes scattered throughout. Save yourself the trouble—unless you're obsessed with Irish accents, in which case you might endure the mediocrity because everyone sounds like the Lucky Charms elf. Unfortunately, this faux Irish charm has a habit of elevating some truly bad movies into the realm of popularity.

A dull children's fantasy that grants Joan Plowright top billing yet offers little for her to do. Sweet kids chase their dreams—Frankie aspires to be both a ballerina and a baseball player (ugh), while her best friend Hazel runs for mayor—despite being only 13! The story is entirely predictable, complemented by overly sentimental performances from the young actors and the baseball players. Clearly a lesser production for Showtime—no creativity or originality?

Bill Boyd, Robert Armstrong, and James Gleason star as carnival workers at Coney Island competing for the affection of Ginger Rogers, a saltwater taffy seller. With the outbreak of World War I, the trio enlists and chases Ginger from a distance. The first half of this RKO Pathe film is sluggish, with the male leads overacting and delivering clichéd, overly snappy dialogue that quickly becomes tedious. The latter half shifts focus to action, featuring dynamic scenes of the U.S. Navy hunting a German merchant cruiser and a U-boat. While these sequences are energetic and skillfully shot, the film as a whole drags on too long, ending on a flat note. Overall, it's an unsatisfying comedy-drama best appreciated by devoted fans of the stars.

I usually enjoy comedy films and find them quite entertaining. However, I didn't quite understand the point of "Envy." The plot feels dull, and it lacks genuine humor. While the performances are generally solid, they aren't enough to make the movie engaging. Stiller and Black don't fully showcase their talents in this film. 

So, if you're thinking of renting a comedy, I definitely recommend skipping "Envy." Unless you're prepared to be bored—and from what I gather, I'm not alone in this opinion—since even Jack Black apologized for the film (check the Trivia section for details).

Despite being notorious for over twenty-five years and frequently banned, its obscurity appears to have been its greatest asset. Sometimes, it's better to be the subject of gossip than to have a reputation backed by substance. 

Recently, the film has been screened a few times in Los Angeles and is now available on home video, gradually revealing its secrets. While it still contains material likely to offend viewers, it more often risks inducing boredom than genuine outrage, unless you count a gratuitous and drawn-out XXX scene involving two horses—reminding one of a "Nature Documentary." Following this, nearly an hour of tedious arranged marriage melodrama ensues.

The explicit scenes kick in with relentless sequences of masturbation, a lengthy flashback portraying a supposed "beauty and the beast" encounter, and a nude woman wandering the mansion—without any apparent concern from her protective aunt about clothing. On video, you might fast-forward through the dull parts, but even then, it’s hardly worth the effort. The nudity is relatively tame compared to what’s shown in films like Bertolucci’s *The Dreamers*.

I attended this movie at a special cast and crew screening, invited by my friend who is a producer on the film. Forget what you've seen in the trailers or heard in the buzz—experience this movie for yourself. I was genuinely impressed. In a landscape filled with films like The Grinch, Charlie’s Angels, The 6th Day, and Unbreakable, this one stands out as a must-see that’s worth your hard-earned money. With breathtaking visuals, stunning cinematography, and a cast you’d happily share a meal with from the heart, it’s one of the most meticulously crafted powerhouse films of the year—and for good reason. Robert De Niro truly deserves an Oscar nod. If it were possible to award everyone involved as a unified package, this film would be the deserving recipient.

I revel in cheesy, low-quality films, and this one definitely ranks among the best. The CGI is mind-blowingly bad—or perhaps it predates our very existence—and the sight of a six-foot guy in a rat costume chasing after people is hilariously terrible. I found some enjoyment in parts of it, but the acting is so atrociously bad that it’s hard to take seriously. Even the obligatory nude scene fails to deliver any real nudity. Overall, it’s a complete waste of time. I wonder who squandered more time—me watching this, or the poor souls who were involved in making it, probably hoping it would jumpstart their acting careers. Spoiler: it won’t. On a slightly more positive note, I managed to connect this movie to Kevin Bacon in six degrees, so I suppose watching those 91 minutes was almost justified.

One word sums up this movie: WOW! I watched "Darius Goes West" at the Tribeca Film Festival, and the feelings in the theater were overwhelming—people were crying. The film vividly depicts the struggles Darius faces with Muscular Dystrophy. It was exceptionally well-crafted and truly immersive, touching my heart deeply. It reminded me how fortunate we are to be healthy, while others in this world face greater challenges. Sometimes, we should extend a helping hand and support those in need, unconditionally. I would give it ten stars. The filmmakers helped Darius when he needed it most—not for fame or money, but out of genuine friendship. Darius went west, and the world should know his story.

If your idea of a thriller involves high-speed car chases, spectacular explosions, and hordes of people getting caught in gunfire, then "House of Games" might not be the film for you. However, if you enjoy and value psychological drama and suspense, I wholeheartedly recommend giving it a watch.

"House of Games" centers around Dr. Margaret Ford (Lindsay Crouse), an esteemed psychologist and author who becomes entangled in the clandestine world of con artists led by the charming Mike (Joe Mantegna). Revealing too much about the plot would spoil the surprises, but I can say that predicting the twists is virtually impossible. Like a clever con artist, this film ensnares you in its web and subtly keeps you off guard.

The narrative is tightly constructed and skillfully executed, with sharp, concise dialogue and consistently strong performances—Mantegna’s charisma is particularly noteworthy. Some viewers have remarked that Dr. Ford lacks sympathy and questioned why Mamet chose to depict Lindsay Crouse as physically unappealing. Yet, her aloof and cold demeanor is deliberate and integral to the story—her appearance and attitude serve a specific purpose within the plot.

I genuinely can't believe this film isn't listed among IMDb's Bottom 250; it is truly dreadful. When I first watched it, I remember discussing it in a college class, and two other classmates had also seen it. We all recommended to our peers that they avoid it, as it was so terrible. By the end of our conversation, a few others actually became curious and wanted to watch it just to see if it was as bad as we claimed. Don't follow their example—skip this movie entirely. I'm sure everyone involved with its creation would prefer you to never see them in it.

Together with its companion piece, this stands as the most exceptional animation ever crafted. The visuals and stylistic choices are stunning and seamlessly complement the narrative—a brilliantly realistic reimagining of our world, exploring where we've been and where we might head. It is deeply moving and at times difficult to watch, a true masterpiece of visual artistry.

I had heard of Eddie Izzard but had never seen him perform live. I knew he was a transvestite, and one summer night last year, I turned on HBO without knowing my husband's reaction. He completely blew us away. He's even better than Robin Williams. His command of the audience is remarkable; when he does the routine about Englebert being dead—then not being dead—the audience is left unsure what to believe. His impression of God as James Mason is a brilliant touch, and his comedic take on the Spanish Inquisition parodying the Church of England—"Cake or Death?"—is absolutely hilarious. By the end of the show, my jaws ached from laughing. We spent months checking the TV listings to catch him again and were fortunate to tape his next appearance. If you ever get the chance to see this performance, clear your schedule and record it—you won’t be disappointed.

A delightful, funny, and heartwarming film featuring Morgan Freeman, who plays himself, as he meets a Spanish girl named Scarlet (Paz Vega) at a small shop while researching a potential independent project. Initially, I was a bit skeptical during the first ten minutes, but once Freeman entered the store, I found myself genuinely enjoying the movie. It beautifully illustrates how a positive outlook can transform any situation. The story is straightforward with no complicated plots, making it easy to follow, yet it can brighten even the gloomiest day and keep you smiling throughout—no cheesy romance clichés involved. Throughout the film, there are numerous hilarious scenes that had me laughing out loud. Truly a rare gem!

My reflections: Postwar comedy at its finest. Tom Drake and Grandpa from "Meet Me in St. Louis" appeared again two years later—the year I was born. Donna Reed was charming and lovely. Margaret Hamilton delivered her usual excellent performance, though her role was smaller than in "The Wizard of Oz." Spring Byington was noticeably more beautiful, with the signature cheerful small nose that Hamilton lacked. The tent scene at the end with the former boy-next-door was hilarious. Having served two years in Army tents myself, he appeared quite youthful and somewhat inexperienced when I looked into his eyes.

I once worked in a department store quite similar in elegance to this one. Sadly, it has since vanished and fallen into obscurity. We were renowned for our stunning display windows designed to attract passersby and encourage them to purchase all our wonderful merchandise.

10/10

Like many environmentally conscious films from the 1970s, SOYLENT GREEN presents a somewhat cheesy and simplistic view of ecological collapse. It suggests that overpopulation directly leads to food shortages, but my understanding is that famines are typically caused by war or failed economic policies. For instance, Stalin's policies in the Soviet Union during the 1930s resulted in millions of deaths due to famine, and Mao's rural policies in China in the 1950s caused over 30 million starvation deaths—the greatest man-made tragedy in history. Additionally, the devastating famines in the Horn of Africa during the 1980s and 90s were primarily driven by conflict, not overpopulation. It's also worth noting that two of the most densely populated regions on Earth, Hong Kong and Macau, have never experienced modern famines. Furthermore, the expansion of shanty towns around cities isn’t solely due to overpopulation—it often stems from economic factors, as people migrate to urban areas seeking better-paying jobs than those available in rural settings. This movement is a sign of industrial progress, not merely a result of high birth rates.

Alright... it appears that so far, only the Barman fans have shared their thoughts on this film—time for a different perspective. Fair warning, this review is *LONG*.

For those unfamiliar, mostly non-Belgians: Tom Barman, the director of this film, is the lead singer of dEUS, one of Belgium’s most prominent rock bands in the late '90s. The band initially released several bold, innovative albums and quickly gained national fame. However, tensions and egos eventually led to their disbandment, with Barman and a few others continuing under the dEUS name. As is often the case after such splits, the subsequent dEUS was much more subdued and less compelling than their original work. They aimed for an international breakthrough with their 1999 album "The Ideal Crash," which featured a significantly softer take on their earlier, more daring songwriting style. Unfortunately, they didn't quite reach that goal. It seems egos remained a potent force, and Barman evidently saw himself as an artist capable of branching out into filmmaking.

Typically, when musicians venture into cinema, it’s a risky move—and often not a successful one.

Humans have explored the farthest corners of the Earth, and now they venture into uncharted worlds. Yet, with these new territories come ancient menaces—the space vampires. Not just a few, but entire clans of these creatures. In this film, known as "Bloodsuckers" or perhaps "Vampires Wars," we witness what unfolds when Earth’s imperialist forces clash with the equally imperialist vampires.

I'll keep this review brief, as the film hardly warrants a detailed praise. The only redeeming aspect is its cast, which features a mix of B-list and emerging stars. Natassia Malthe appears as Quintana—much more striking here than in "BloodRayne 2." Michael Ironside plays Muco; he's a perennial favorite, often considered the poor man's Jack Nicholson. Additionally, Carrie-Ann Fleming appears as Damian’s wife—fans of horror might recognize her as Jenifer from Dario Argento's "Jenifer." Despite its numerous flaws, the film boasts some notable names, though this is not unlike the casting choices of Uwe Boll’s works.

The premise of soldiers hunting and destroying vampires in space isn’t inherently flawed, but it...

I believe that somewhere deep inside, even in the most hidden and sordid corners of their hearts, everyone harbors a secret fondness for Jerry Springer. Although his show is undeniably provocative and often ridiculous, it also offers us a glimpse into how fortunate most of us truly are. Watching the trailer park dwellers, whiskey drinkers, and dysfunctional families featured on Springer puts even our worst days into perspective—making them seem almost manageable. In a way, Jerry is providing a public service, and we should be appreciative of that. He sacrificed a potential political career just to host this spectacle, all for our entertainment.  

However, we have no reason to thank or endorse the movie "Ringmaster." That film is a trashy portrayal of what life might be like for those who appear on the show—or at least, how it wants us to see it. The plot sticks to the familiar formula of love triangles: one involving Connie, her daughter Angel, and her husband Rusty; the other featuring Starletta, Vonda, and Demond. When these two groups cross paths in Los Angeles, their lives rapidly intertwine and clash, culminating in a dramatic and explosive Springer episode. It’s reminiscent of a typical soap opera—only much cruder and less believable.

This film offers dull, uninspired entertainment, featuring Stella Stevens taking direction from an undercover figure (which I guessed early on) in Old Nevada Town outside Las Vegas, as they plan a heist at the Circus Circus Hotel. Stevens leads a small girl gang of three, and they quickly realize they need to act faster than initially planned. While there are some interesting glimpses of 1970s Las Vegas and the acting from most cast members is fairly credible, the story itself has potential but falls flat, resulting in a tedious viewing experience. The movie drags to get started, and even once it does, it only sputters along without gaining momentum.
