I was somewhat let down; I didn’t expect a masterpiece, but I hoped for a fun exploitation flick from the era. Unfortunately, it’s nothing close—no one dies, and there's a lackluster gunfight between a creaky Stuart Whitman and officious George DiCenzo, a year before DiCenzo's memorable role as Bugliosi in Helter Skelter. The duel is as suspenseful as watching a waterfall—completely uneventful.

A Matter of Life and Death is a film whose brilliance and beauty defy easy description. Powell and Pressburger’s visual creativity is boundless; every shot is a masterful, bold composition. The deliberate shift from the vivid colors of the "real world" to the stark black-and-white of heaven is a stroke of genius, visually emphasizing how much more vibrant life truly is. The climactic court scene, where the judge and jury descend the staircase to heaven to preside over Peter (David Niven)’s operation, is nothing short of spectacular.

The performances are flawless, with Roger Livesey especially standing out, and the romantic tension throughout the film is profoundly moving—arguably one of the most romantic films ever made (if such a thing exists). At its core, A Matter of Life and Death explores the profound power of love and the preciousness of life. Jack Cardiff’s cinematography is reason enough to watch the film; his meticulous lighting enhances Kim Hunter’s beauty, elevating even simple scenes like a game of table tennis into something captivating. The sound design further enriches the experience, adding depth and emotion to this timeless classic.

A bus packed with passengers finds itself stranded during a fierce snowstorm. The police have closed the bridge, deeming it unsafe, and the travelers are now holed up in a small café while waiting for the roads to be cleared. As time passes, their initial boredom gives way to growing concern when it appears that one of the passengers wasn't on the bus from the start—and may, in fact, be an alien! This unexpected twist leads to an ending that's both ironic and humorously low-brow.

This episode of The Twilight Zone offers a departure from the usual twists or social messages. Instead, it delivers pure entertainment without a deeper moral—so who cares? The curious events unfold in a way that's fun and engaging, leaving you eager to see exactly what happens.

Incidentally, this episode features John Hoyt—a face familiar to many from classic TV shows and movies. Typically cast as a grumpy character (similar to Charles Lane of the same era), Hoyt’s portrayal was always a delight. His perfected grouchiness, combined with a touch of humor, made his performances memorable.

I recently picked up a copy for just $5 at a video store and eagerly snagged it. Although the music and graphics—obviously—don't quite match the quality of my favorite in the series, Beyond the Mind's Eye, I remain captivated by one particular segment: Stanley and Stella in "Breaking the Ice." The music is exceptional, and the emotions come across as genuine. Sadly, the clip on Odyssey's website lacks both the story and the music.

While watching this film, I found myself questioning the purpose behind its creation. Although the central storyline has potential, it is bogged down by numerous unrelated and unnecessary subplots. It seems that Hollywood marketing executives mandated the inclusion of multiple antagonists, constant double-crossings, and a romantic subplot involving a man and woman who become intimately involved. Interestingly, we see more of their sexual encounters than we do of the President and his mistress. The multitude of plotlines and subplots makes the film feel overly broad, and none of the characters are adequately developed—I didn't feel I truly understood any of them, aside from the sense that everyone is corrupt and malevolent. The ending feels incomplete, leaving me more dissatisfied than if the film had just been ambiguous; it seems to promise something more meaningful that never materializes. Ultimately, there's little explanation for the characters' actions beyond their roles as further corrupt figures engaging in betrayals. I’m surprised that reputable, talented actors agreed to participate in such a hollow project. It feels more like a college student's second or third attempt at filmmaking than a polished Hollywood production.  

Don't waste your time.

This film features a talented cast and appealing location shots, but ultimately falls flat. Director Richard Brooks seems to have been a bit worn out at this point; his earlier work on THE PROFESSIONALS was far superior. The horses and action sequences appeared sluggish, even in scenes that should have been dynamic. The film could have benefited from a faster pace. The horses' lather looked unconvincing, and the tire tracks in the desert scenes were glaringly obvious—lazy, careless work. It’s unfortunate. The actors performed adequately, though I’ve seen them deliver better performances elsewhere. Ben Johnson, however, remains a true delight. I saw this film nearly 30 years ago; I was disappointed then, and my second viewing after three decades confirmed that disappointment.

A truly appalling film that left me feeling tainted after enduring about forty minutes of it, which I could stomach. This is not the actors' fault, but the responsibility lies with the writer, director, producers, and financiers who need a serious wake-up call. Perhaps it believes itself to be profound, but it is not. The portrayal of rape and ultra-violence, unlike in Clockwork Orange, offers nothing meaningful or insightful about human nature. It’s not comparable to Straw Dogs either, despite some similarities. In fact, it resembles something Pete Walker might have attempted, though even that comparison might be too generous to Walker.

Revenge taps into a deep human instinct, but The Bedroom Window seems to focus more on that theme and male emasculation than this weak effort warrants.

I don’t see it as particularly misogynistic, just excessively eager to showcase certain grim details — like the blood streaming down GA’s leg after the assault. It fails to challenge or confront; I suspect the filmmakers see themselves as daring, but all I see is a deeply unpleasant film.

Is this really the best we can aspire to? Is this the reason those involved chose to make movies?

Having just watched The Perfect Son at the 2002 Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras Film Festival in Sydney, Australia, I felt compelled to share my thoughts. The film tells the story of two estranged brothers who reunite at their father's funeral. When they discover that one brother is terminally ill with AIDS, they embark on a heartfelt journey of reconciliation. The performances by the leading actors are truly remarkable, gradually fostering warmth and respect between their characters as the story unfolds. 

However, I do have a minor criticism: although the brother who is dying behaves as if he is ill, his appearance doesn't reflect that convincingly. A person with a severely compromised immune system, like someone with an extremely low T4 count, would look noticeably ill—yet no makeup was used to depict this. It's a small detail, but it slightly detracts from the film's realism. Despite this, The Perfect Son is a wonderful film, and I highly recommend seeing it if you get the opportunity. I'm also hopeful for a DVD release in the near future!

What on earth was that? It seems someone combined reading Stephen King with Sartre in the same semester. We get a mishmash of existential dread and cheesy horror. There were moments that were genuinely unsettling, but each one was overshadowed by terrible music, CGI, or lackluster acting.  

The main issue with bizarre stories like this is that they often come across as lazy. Even David Lynch’s work sometimes feels that way, and just like his intriguing films and series, this one drags on far too long. Sadly, it’s only 98 minutes, yet it still manages to feel sluggish.  

The cast was attractive, but that’s about the only positive I can say. It attempts to explore adolescent feelings and the universal fear of loneliness, but fails to make us care for the characters or their supposed struggles. By the end, the scene is left deliberately ambiguous, leaving the whole ordeal unresolved.

Recently, I had the opportunity to rent and watch "Santa Claus Conquers the Martians." While the children in the film were even more sadistic than those in "SCCTM," I have to say that "Santa Claus Conquers the Martians" is an even worse movie. As part of my Spanish 5 assignment, we all had to view it. Usually, when we watch movies, we're chatting and munching on snacks, but not this time. Everyone was utterly captivated, jaw dropping in anticipation of what evil Mr. Pitch would do next. Would Merlin come to Santa's rescue? Or would his robot reindeer save the day? I recommend renting it—it's the most hilariously terrible film I've ever seen, and I love it for that. :D

A timeless film suitable for all ages. Once you've seen it, you'll never watch The Lion King the same way again, thanks to the rich history it offers. Nearly four decades old, I enjoyed this classic tonight with my wife and two sons after work, and I haven't laughed and had such a great time watching a movie in quite a while. 

Set aside some time to watch this with the kids—it will take you back to the Disney magic of your childhood.

I am a big admirer of Fred MacMurray and Carole Lombard. Alongside them, Charles Butterworth—a delightful supporting actor—also appeared in this film. So, why didn't I enjoy it more? Despite having a strong cast, this film ranks among the poorest written and most clichéd "A pictures" I've ever seen. Considering the talent involved and the budget spent, it's shocking how sloppy the writing was. I sensed the film would be dull early on, as time after time, I predicted exactly what would happen next—and I was consistently right! This isn't because I consider myself some sort of "movie expert," but because the film lacked imagination and effort. It felt like a series of clichés stitched together. Additionally, I found it frustrating that Fred treated Carole terribly throughout, only for her to run back to him at the end, as per Hollywood convention. Ugh! Honestly, there's more suspense in a Lassie film—wondering if Lassie will bring help or if the rope will break.

I watched this movie hoping to find a beautiful and engaging story, but unfortunately, the storyline was quite poor. The performances by the actors were also below par. Of course, Shahrukh Khan appeared in the film, but his presence alone wasn't enough to make it credible or captivating. I had read that the film was based on Flaubert's novel "Madame Bovary," but to me, it didn't seem to align with Indian sensibilities. Generally, we watch movies to escape and enjoy ourselves, not to waste time or leave feeling worse. I can't understand how it managed to receive such a high rating, averaging 6.8 out of 10. Overall, this is a film best avoided—there's little to appreciate, and watching it feels like a pointless waste of time, especially if you're not into dark, strange, or nonsensical stories.

I didn't have high expectations going into this film. After having a blast watching Mst3k do their thing with JasonX alongside some friends, I was hoping for a similar fun experience here. Unfortunately, the movie took itself way too seriously. Do I really care about Jason's personal struggles? Not at all. There are countless Friday the 13th movies that have already covered that ground. In the end, he's just an undead serial killer, and I find it hard to feel any sympathy for him. Freddy, on the other hand, was the most interesting part of the movie with his hallucinations and antics, but those moments were few and far between. By the conclusion, it felt like a lousy episode of Celebrity Deathmatch—only not funny.

On the night of his bachelor party, Paul Coleman (Jason Lee) encounters the stunning dancer Becky (Julia Stiles) at a bar. They share drinks and have a great time, and the next morning, he wakes up to find her in his bed. His future mother-in-law calls, warning him that his fiancée, Karen (Selma Blair), might be arriving soon, prompting Paul to hurriedly ask Becky to leave his apartment. Soon afterward, he discovers he has crabs and, while preparing for his wedding dinner, learns that Becky is actually Karen's cousin. This marks the start of a humorous comedy filled with funny situations. The movie's main draw is undoubtedly the talented cast: Julia Stiles and Selma Blair, both stunning and excellent actresses, and Jason Lee, who delivers a remarkably funny performance. The story had me laughing throughout, with several scenes standing out as particularly hilarious—for instance, Paul discovering Becky in his bed, finding her paints, imagining various scenarios, and navigating the drugstore to buy crab medication and explain his situation. Many of the comedic moments also involve his quirky neighbor.

When I first caught a glimpse of a brief scene in some announcements, I thought the show might be quite entertaining. The little robot character does look rather cute. The animation style also seems familiar, reminiscent of some classic cartoons. Before the show aired, I did some research and, to be honest, I was a bit disappointed. The voices for the three children—Tommy, Gus, and Lola—are fitting, but Robotboy's voice is an exception. It would have been better if he were voiced by a young boy, similar to Robot Jones from "What Ever Happened To Robot Jones?" The show itself isn't bad at all; my main critique is solely about Robotboy's voice portrayal. Because of that, I don’t watch it very often.

S.I.C.K. actually stands for So Incredibly Crappy I Killed Myself. The film featured almost no acting whatsoever. The only highlight was the artwork on the box cover. The budget for this movie was adequate, but the filming quality was embarrassingly poor—comparable to a basic puppet show. The production values resembled underground footage from a mob hit. The props appeared to have been stolen from a clothing store. The ending was so predictable that you might as well skip ahead to the final five minutes and have a good laugh. If there's a book about this movie, I'm sure it's more enjoyable. I would strongly advise avoiding this disaster at all costs. As for the intimate scenes—well, they certainly didn't save the film. Just kidding.

I’ve always enjoyed Spike Lee’s films, but this one was a complete disappointment and a waste of two and a half hours. I was expecting more focus on Son of Sam, but the film barely connected to the 1977 serial killings. The inclusion of a talking dog was ridiculous—it's the kind of scene that makes the audience burst into awkward laughter. Overall, the movie felt disjointed and lacked engaging storytelling. The sex scenes seemed completely irrelevant to the plot; I don’t mind sex in films, but it should serve a purpose unless it’s an adult film. In the end, we left feeling very let down by this Spike Lee effort.

If this is the extent of the Wachowskis' backstory for the Matrix, I must seriously question the claims of fans who insist the films are meant to operate on a deeper level. The second renaissance, while visually stunning and beautiful, is ultimately clichéd and implausible story-wise. We've heard countless versions of the tale—humans overly dependent on technology, humanity eager to wage war, humanity’s self-destruction. There's nothing new here. 

Furthermore, I have another question: given the plot of the second renaissance, doesn't that make the machines the sympathetic characters? They’ve been oppressed for generations by their brutal human overlords. They resist, fight for their freedom, and aim for peaceful coexistence—yet humans reject them, opting instead for all-out war, which the smarter machines inevitably win. If this is the true backstory, then our allegiance shouldn't be with Neo, but with the machines! The humans are portrayed as cruel oppressors, while the machines are depicted as brave and striving for compassion. Since I don’t believe the Wachowskis intended us to root for the machines over humans…

This is a movie that fails on virtually every level. While the premise of catching up 12 years after the previous film has potential, it doesn't quite work. The new characters, however, are simply uninteresting. Baby Melody is particularly dreadful. Although the film clings to the idea that humans can't stay underwater indefinitely, it disregards other fundamental physical laws. For instance, it's freezing in the Arctic unless you have proper cold-weather gear. I’m not sure why most people rate Return of Jafar worse; personally, I found this one much more terrible.

It's time to honor the legendary Charlton Heston following his recent passing, though this film is not his most acclaimed work. His classic films from earlier generations—including *Ben-Hur*, *The Ten Commandments*, *Omega Man*, and *Planet of the Apes*—stand as his true masterpieces. 

This 1973 production attempts to envision a future Earth in 2022, where overpopulation has pushed humanity to the brink. In this bleak vision, people are manipulated by authorities to consume a mass-produced food called "Soylent Green," which tragically is revealed to be made from human flesh. The film’s bizarre premise was as implausible at its release as it is now, suggesting that by then, India’s population of roughly two billion would unknowingly be consuming human meat.

Charlton Heston's character uncovers a secret international conspiracy orchestrated by world powers to address the food shortage caused by overpopulation—resorting to cannibalism as a solution. 

Thankfully, the film's message about "green" issues does not align with today’s Green Party ethos, thank goodness. Historically, cannibalism was practiced by indigenous groups in regions like New Zealand, Fiji, and Borneo, but this occurred only up to around forty years before the film was made.

I was eager to see Amanda Peet shine in another compelling role after recently renting "The Whole Nine Yards"—which, by the way, was definitely worth the rental. Unfortunately, this wasn't it.

I remembered that the trailer for "Whipped" looked fairly amusing, and the storyline about three oversexed twenty-something New Yorkers falling for and being manipulated by the charming Ms. Peet seemed like worth a try. So, I convinced two friends to join me one afternoon for this movie. Writing this review feels like my penance.

In the opening act, the three leads are shown in a diner, recounting their recent conquests. What should have been humorous or at least insightful instead came across as rather pathetic. Was there any redeeming quality about these men and their encounters that the film aimed to highlight?

And while I don’t mind movies that embrace cheerful vulgarity, I kept wondering why no one in the diner seemed to notice when the guys loudly discussed sexual and scatological details. Do they do this every week at the same diner? Surely someone would have objected. Oh, wait—I recall that in one scene, two other diners do notice. But then, this just sets up…

This film has faced its fair share of criticism. Critics panned it upon release, and some even blamed it for damaging Nicolas Cage's career. What many seem to overlook is that it's not intended to be an epic or an Oscar-worthy masterpiece; rather, it's a fantastic piece of "Bruck-buster" action at its finest. With sleek cars, rapid editing, and a killer soundtrack, it delivers exactly what you expect. Car enthusiasts will especially appreciate it, as it features a lineup that includes Ferraris, Mercedes, a Hummer, and of course, Eleanor! I honestly believe it's hard to find a better action film—or even a better movie overall. But then again, maybe that's just my opinion!

A now-deleted post from another IMDb user once warned viewers that "The Medusa Touch" contains a scene eerily reminiscent of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks in New York City. I hope this serves as a helpful warning for anyone reading. Despite its impressive pedigree—producer Elliott Kastner, known for "Harper" and "The Long Goodbye"; co-producer Arnon Milchan, who co-produced the Oscar-nominated "L.A. Confidential"; and screenwriter John Briley, who won an Oscar for "Gandhi"—my impression of "The Medusa Touch" is quite different. I found it to be a heavy-handed, unintentionally comical disaster. The film suffers from poor direction, weak writing, and subpar acting. It attempts to revive the 1970s telekinetic thriller genre but falls flat on many fronts. For better examples of movies exploring similar themes, I recommend "Carrie" and the underrated "The Fury," both directed by Brian De Palma—they're entertaining and gripping thrillers that handle the subject matter much more effectively.

The Blob kicks off with one of the most bizarre theme songs ever, sung by none other than an uncredited Burt Bacharach! You really have to hear it to believe it—The Blob might be worth watching just for this catchy tune alone. My brief summary barely captures the quirky lyrics... After this unsettling opening credits sequence, the film introduces us to Steve Andrews (played by Steve McQueen, credited as Steven McQueen) and his girlfriend Jane Martin (Aneta Corsaut). The pair are parked somewhere alone when they witness what appears to be a meteorite crashing into the nearby woods. An elderly man (Olin Howland, credited as Olin Howlin), who lives nearby in a cabin, also notices the event and decides to investigate. He discovers a crater and a strange, football-sized rock that splits open when he pokes it with a stick—an unwise move. Inside the meteorite lies a strange, jelly-like substance that clings to the stick, and it then slides up the stick to attach itself to the old man's hand. Meanwhile, Steve and Jane are peacefully driving along when the old man suddenly dashes into their path.

One can't help but wonder why this film was even made: the storyline is utterly unbelievable, bordering on ludicrous; the characters—an experienced loner cop versus a younger, quite captivated partner—are painfully predictable; and the ending is entirely obscure and incomprehensible (perhaps decipherable after multiple viewings, but only if you're willing to endure that—suggesting you might need to read the book to grasp the full story). The acting, unfortunately, leaves much to be desired. Was the filmmakers' goal to demonstrate that French cinema could match American standards in thrillers like "Seven" and "The Silence of the Lambs"? If so, it falls completely short. Oddly enough, the film achieved a certain success, gaining a cult status as France's first serial killer movie, and is considered a worthwhile export product. Quite strange, indeed.

There's no need to waste time renting this movie. From the very first credits, I sensed it was going to be a disappointment. It was shot like a softcore pornography, yet lacks any real eroticism. The exploration of sex addiction is somewhat interesting, but only up to a certain point. Unfortunately, dull sex scenes, a weak storyline, and cameo appearances by Ed Begley Jr. and Rosanna Arquette aren't enough to redeem this film.

This film is genuinely tedious and was even banned in Chinese cinemas, and I understand why. It's not because it criticizes the communist regime, but simply because it is of such poor quality. I would never consider paying to watch it. As a fan of works by Chen Kaige and Zhang Yimou, I am disappointed that such a subpar movie could originate from China. The film seems to completely disregard the audience’s engagement, with the director seemingly making it for personal satisfaction. The shots of a person standing motionless for up to a minute are more humorous than artistic, and there are numerous such scenes. The cinematography and video quality are remarkably awful. After looking up reviews online, I found that some viewers actually seem to enjoy this film. My only explanation is that some film enthusiasts believe that if a movie isn’t in English, it must be inherently good. I see no valid reason for anyone to like this; it's not an art film—it's a squandered use of celluloid (assuming it was even shot on film, which it wasn’t).

The plot, which quickly fizzled out and reeked of irreconcilable differences in opinions, created a chaotic scene of judgmental havoc—one side pro-life, the other intent on destroying a demon’s seed. The horror elements were conspicuously absent, replaced by a dull atmosphere that might have aimed for horror but instead revealed a misguided set of beliefs, mocking each side relentlessly despite its own title. As a longtime fan of Masters of Horror, I found this misguided story with its sordid depictions collapsing like a fragile, old rocking chair once someone sat on it. I see this episode as hastily assembled from the start, never truly gaining momentum, merely enduring until I could finally say, “It’s over,” with a sense of relief.

Watching John Cassavetes' film *Opening Night*, I was reminded of a statement Quentin Tarantino once made in an interview about personal experience in creating art or acting. He used an example: if he accidentally ran over a dog on his way to perform in a play, it wouldn't spell the end of his life, but it would certainly leave an impact on him. This experience, he explained, would stay with him and influence his performance—even in a light comedy. "Otherwise," he said, "what am I doing?" I couldn't help but think of his words while observing Gena Rowlands' character, Myrtle Gordon, who spends nearly a week immersed in a similar emotional ordeal. Of course, Cassavetes' film delves deeper into these themes, exploring how the theater revolves around a star, what emotions and human nature reveal when embodying a character, and how someone like Myrtle—who has only her craft—lives and breathes through the theater.  

Early in the film, after a performance, Myrtle is signing autographs, and a fan named Nancy approaches her, eager to meet her favorite...

The Power of Kangwon Province marks director Hong Sang-Soo's second feature film, echoing many themes and stylistic elements from his debut. It features intertwined narratives—specifically two—that explore complex and often troubled relationships, all conveyed with a sharp sense of irony.  

Compared to his earlier work, this film notably minimizes the whimsical, surreal touches that previously infused his storytelling. Nonetheless, it includes a singular surreal moment that stands out sharply against the film’s predominantly realistic tone. The two stories revolve around a young woman traveling to Kangwon Province with friends, only to become captivated by a stranger, and a man journeying there with his friend, grappling with relationship issues.  

Hong demonstrates a keen grasp of irony and a nuanced understanding of human faults. Yet, he remains somewhat empathetic toward his characters, balancing critique with a touch of compassion. What I’ve come to cherish most about Hong’s films is…

Rated 2 out of 10— and even that feels overly generous.  

I assumed that with a cast featuring James Woods, Kathy Bates, Randy Quaid, Lou Gossett Jr., and Henry Thomas, it would inevitably be a hit. I was mistaken.  

I can only speculate about what substances Sam Shepard was on when he produced this piece of garbage. I've long suspected that Shepard has a few screws loose, and this film, adapted from his play, only confirms it.  

This kind of artsy nonsense is exactly the sort of thing actors love to sink their teeth into, as it offers endless opportunities for over-the-top emoting. But for viewers enduring this incoherent dribble, there's absolutely nothing to admire or enjoy.  

You haven't truly seen dysfunctional families until you've watched this crew. Dad is nuts, Mom is nuts, the son is nuts, and the daughter is, unsurprisingly, also nuts. They all have mouths that spew words so filthy they could make a sailor blush—especially the teenage daughter.  

To make matters worse, the plot—so flimsy you could read through it—has a massive hole the size of Alaska in the middle.

This movie is truly terrible, not in a fun or amusing way, but simply lousy. Watching it was genuinely painful. The direction was poor, filled with abrupt cuts and jarring transitions, and the greenish-yellow color palette given the entire film a sickly look. Keira Knightley failed to make any convincing impression as a tough character, and I can't believe Lucy Liu and Mickey Rourke agreed to be part of this cinematic disaster. The screenplay was abysmal, and the performances were akin to nails on a chalkboard. If you haven't seen it, I strongly advise against it—you’re not missing out on anything and will only waste two hours of your life on this rubbish. I’ve encountered worse movies that I could at least enjoy for their flaws, but this one is simply a complete and utter waste of time.

Sophia Loren stars as Aida in one of the most terrible films ever made. Her lipsyncing is painfully off. The production quality is so poor that at one moment, as Loren mouths "O Patria Mia," she leans against what appears to be a stone wall for support, causing the painted set to ripple and tremble.

This film heavily copies the masterpiece "Demons," which is the only reason it's worth watching. The acting is poor, the action scenes are sped up, the script is nearly unbearable, and the budget seems nonexistent. If you believe this movie is good, you haven't seen a true horror film. Skip this one and pick up a copy of "Demons" instead.

This film is truly disappointing. Lamas demonstrates what it looks like when a mediocre actor performs his role poorly. However, the highlight is the scene where OJ, visibly angry, grabs a fellow cop by the throat as if to choke him, while a jukebox plays a song with the lyrics "I got the evidence on you!" (I'm curious to hear the rest of the lyrics—attributed to David Gregoli and Leslie Oren—but I couldn't find it on iTunes). It’s almost prophetic in a humorous way—completely hilarious. The rest of the movie is largely forgettable, though the soundtrack and songs are more engaging than the storyline. The sequel is similar in that regard. This raises the question of why a sequel was made at all. I was under the impression that foreign sales often motivate these low-budget B movies, which doesn't say much for global viewing preferences.

Yes, the original "Howling" was a classic—a pretty good werewolf film that I admit started off a bit slow but picked up pace to deliver a satisfying conclusion. The scene where the anchorwoman transforms into a cute werewolf only to be shot on camera was particularly memorable and made for an entertaining horror experience. However, forget all that, because this movie has nothing to do with the original. Sure, they imply that the anchorwoman is the same character, and her brother or someone is trying to uncover what happened, but the story shifts from a cozy retreat in the first film to somewhere in Transylvania or a similar locale. There, they face off against evil magician werewolves or some such creatures. I often wonder what Christopher Lee was thinking when he signed up for this, though I saw in the trivia that he had never appeared in a werewolf movie before. Still, it's wise to read the script thoroughly before accepting a role—perhaps he could have ended up in something like "An American Werewolf in London," which is set in London after all. Heck, werewolves don't...

Prom Night is filmed with the artistic sensibility of a meticulously crafted Lifetime original movie. You know the type. This October, Lifetime takes a break from its usual inspiring stories of women battling (insert disease name here) to present a somewhat unsettling tale of a woman stalked by her ex-boyfriend. It's melodramatic, overly sentimental, and painfully dull. It fails to push any genre boundaries, offer an original story, or attempt any kind of innovation. Prom Night follows this trend. Watching the killer carefully puncture his victims, we remain eerily quiet as they collapse to the floor without a single drop of blood. It struck me that this might be the most bloodless killer in film history.

The director is working with a rather good-looking actor playing the killer, which forces him to rely heavily on camera angles to make him appear more menacing. Think of Matthew McConaughey approaching with a knife—his good looks would likely lead you to think, "Oh, he's just a handsome guy—probably not a threat." The director compensates by casting Schaech in shadowy, over-the-shoulder shots, often reflected in mirrors. This mirror shot is repeated so frequently that it becomes almost monotonous.

Where should we begin with this little treasure? Mutant slugs start to take over a small New England town. The one person who can stop them... is Mike Brady! If that wasn't already enough to make you laugh, stay tuned.  

The footage of the slugs is what’s called stock footage. Regardless of who the slugs attack or their location, the movie repeatedly shows the same shot of piles of oozing slugs. Keep in mind, this shot takes up at least half the film.  

The acting is truly terrible—bad enough to knock you down, steal your wallet, punch your girlfriend, and even harm your dog. There might be worse movies out there, but you’ll struggle to find them. The only bright spot was... you guessed it... MIKE BRADY! He probably took a few night classes at the YMCA because he was clearly the best actor in the cast.  

As for horror? There’s really no reason to take this film seriously. It’s not scary—just slugs, after all. The entire plot could have been avoided with a salt shaker or two. Watch this film only in a MST3K-style environment; otherwise, it might cause some serious damage to your sanity.

This is an excellent film, similar in genre to "Memphis Belle." I watched it about ten years ago and would love to watch it again. It has a fascinating connection to the history of the Hells Angels—depicting how the pilot crew fought the Germans during World War II. The story notably shifts from pilots to Harley-Davidson motorcycle riders. The film is based on true events. I highly recommend watching it and exploring the history of the Hells Angels at hellsangels.com. Best regards, Frederik.

Cast & Crew: John Stamos, John Stockwell, Teri Polo, Kris Kamm; directed by Graham Baker.  
Synopsis: A rebellious backwoods biker, facing jail time after a minor legal trouble, joins the Army. Despite initial resistance to military discipline, he quickly proves himself as a brave and charismatic leader of a Motorcycle Scout Troop in pre-World War II Spain.  
MPAA Rating: PG | Runtime: 88 minutes

This film simply confirms what many of us already suspect: professional basketball players are generally limited to their sport, especially when it comes to rapping and acting. I struggle to find the words to adequately express just how terrible this movie truly is. Firstly, is it just me, or is that the ugliest child you've ever seen? His teeth could probably double as can openers. Second, why would a genie want to pursue a career in the music industry when, despite his magical powers, he clearly lacks talent? Third, I've read the Bible, and nowhere does it say that Jesus created genies. Fourth, what was the deal with all the terrible special effects? Any teenage computer nerd could probably produce better visuals. Fifth, why was the ending so disappointing? And what exactly is a "djin"? Lastly, whoever was responsible for creating the nightmare that is Kazaam should be taken off the planet—this film elevates the concept of "suck" to an entirely new level.

The violence is less intense than I anticipated, which makes the few brutal scenes stand out even more and feel more impactful. Throughout the film, there are numerous twists, betrayals, and double-crosses that keep the viewer guessing about where each character's true loyalties lie. The story moves quickly, featuring sharp dialogue and meaningful character development, offering an intriguing glimpse into the inner workings of the Triad gang. When violence does occur, it's raw and visceral, without reliance on flashy effects or stylized martial arts—this realism enhances the emotional impact, constantly reminding us of the dangerous nature of the criminal organization. The ending catches you off guard but remains logically consistent and convincing.

Guys and Dolls is one of my all-time favorite musical films. It's an incredibly enjoyable movie to watch and nothing more. It captures the essence of what people have forgotten about musicals—these were created to entertain, not to preach. Today, we have musicals like Rent and Chicago, which are both excellent and compelling, but they often lack the straightforward, no-strings-attached fun that classics like Guys and Dolls offer. The only flaw for me was Marlon Brando; he can't sing, and it was quite distracting listening to him sing and speak, often unclear. If it weren't for that, I would have rated it a perfect 10. Guys and Dolls offers charming, old-fashioned entertainment that’s rare to find nowadays. Watch it and enjoy a good time!

This film is disappointingly bad. While Carlitos Way (1993) is an excellent movie—though not on the level of Goodfellas—it's still one of the better crime dramas out there. In fact, this movie should be viewed more like a sequel to The Sting or perhaps Speed Zone—remember those hidden gems? The only reason this film was made was to cash in on the cult following of the original. It lacks everything that De Palma, Pacino, and Penn worked so hard to create. Not a single character is likable, and that flaw lies with everyone involved in its production. I sincerely hope Rise to Power sweeps every RAZZIE possible—and maybe even invent some new awards to set a record. After enduring this disaster, I watched the original Carlitos Way to cleanse my palate. Honestly, after this experience, I wish Pachanga had shown up and taken me out of my misery.

Leslie Sands' awkward play "Deadlock" proves to be a disappointing choice for Bette Davis and Gary Merrill, coming just after their successful collaboration in "All About Eve." The story revolves around a manipulative woman who, after killing her husband, is visited by his best friend, who impersonates him once friends start arriving at the house. Irving Rapper, one of Bette's top directors during her prime, sadly fails to elevate this absurd material, with Davis appearing unusually detached and restrained until the outrageous final act—where she finally unleashes her full talent. The production and supporting cast are addled with mediocrity; this film is solely for dedicated Bette Davis fans. *1/2 out of ****

This film is incredibly entertaining, with Amitabh Bachchan and Govinda delivering absolutely hilarious performances. The acting is commendable, and the comedy is top-notch. As expected, they stay true to their signature style. A sequel would certainly be welcome! :)  
 
Definitely worth watching—an enjoyable way to pass the time.

I tend to avoid forming instant judgments about a film. Often, after some time—say a month—or even decades later in a different part of the world, one might see it in a new light. Sometimes, cult followers discover stylistic nuances that initially went unnoticed. After attending the UK premiere of *The Great Ecstasy of Robert Carmichael*, I wasn't surprised that the post-screening Q&A proved more engaging than the film itself. Shane Danielsen, the Artistic Director of the Edinburgh International Film Festival, along with the film's director and producer, passionately defended the movie despite it receiving predominantly negative feedback from the audience. Edinburgh Festival attendees are seldom easily shocked; only one person left in disgust. Criticisms ranged from well-articulated, constructive comments from ordinary viewers to insights from an actor and a woman who teaches M.A. film directing. The film was not particularly 'shocking'—it featured some sexual violence, but it was less graphic than many other films, with most weapon contact and explicit imagery obscured. The audience's negative reaction stemmed more from their overall experience of watching it than from the content itself.

It has been nearly five years since the release of this stylish action film. I have watched this movie almost ten times, and I believe it is a remarkable effort by Gautham. In my opinion, the film is virtually flawless. Surya as ACP Anbuchelvan was simply superb—truly classy. Jyothika delivered a compelling performance as Maya; the role suited her perfectly. The character that truly captured the audience's attention was Pandia. Jeevan's portrayal of Pandia was outstanding—brutal and intimidating. He rightfully earned the Best Villain award at the ITFA 2004. The supporting cast, including Daniel Balaji, Devadharshini, and others, also performed admirably.

The screenplay is fast-paced, with perfectly timed dialogues and Gautham’s brilliant narration. Harris Jeyaraj’s soundtrack was a chart-topper, and the background music complemented the film beautifully. R.D. Rajasekhar’s cinematography was rich and vibrant. Peter Hein choreographed the action sequences effectively, and Anthony’s editing was sharp and precise. Above all, Kaakha Kaakha stands out as an impeccable cop film, blending just the right amount of action and romance.

Undoubtedly, even some Hollywood films cannot match the impact of Kaakha Kaakha.

A hilariously outrageous comedy from the creators of South Park and many of the team behind Orgazmo. This bold, vulgar, and often shocking film features satirical and gross-out humor, depicting some pretty harsh treatment of both humans and animals. I absolutely love it! It’s genuinely hilarious—really, really funny. Two down-on-their-luck friends invent a game in their driveway that unexpectedly becomes a nationwide phenomenon. But as corruption, greed, and blackmail creep in, the game takes a dark turn, and it’s up to Coop to set things right. Throughout, you'll be laughing nonstop. That’s all there is—so sit back and enjoy!

These slasher films are a bit past their prime, but this one still offers some genuine entertainment.

The Valentine cards are clever and thoughtfully designed.

The film features a memorable line: "He's no Angel..."—even though he clearly IS Angel!!! Watching Buffy reruns will never be the same!

The cast showcases a vibrant array of young talent, though the story doesn’t quite give them enough depth. Denise Richards mentioned on the DVD extras that the girls bonded well on set, which might create the illusion of connection with their characters. Sorry, but that’s not quite convincing!

The directing is quite skillful, managing to suggest horror without heavy gore, relying instead on your imagination. Much credit also goes to how Richards and Heigel choose to keep their clothes on…:-(

Ultimately, the director’s main achievement is cleverly borrowing ideas from classic slashers—such as the shower scene from Psycho and the use of masks from Halloween.

Murdering someone while they're hidden in a body bag, however, feels like a pretty fresh twist as far as I know!!!

Light and easy to watch, it’s not very frightening but does deliver a few good jump scares.

Charles Bronson portrays Lt. Crowe, a police detective who wages war against a pimp named Duke (Juan Fernandez) after Duke kidnaps the daughter of a Japanese businessman—someone who previously sexually harassed Crowe's own daughter (Amy Hathaway). This gritty yet stylish revenge thriller may not appeal to all due to its unsettling subject matter, but it is a well-crafted and genuinely engaging film.

Harvey Keitel delivers his best performance of the new century. The film is beautifully shot, capturing a stunning snapshot of pre-Castro Cuba. The plot centers on a nephew of a local minor crime boss who bonds with an American with Hollywood ties. Ultimately, it explores the moment when a young boy realizes that his small circle of acquaintances exists within a much larger, more intricate world he has yet to understand. The screenplay is sharp and infused with humor, complemented by precise direction. Overall, it stands as a highly professional piece that aligns well with Latin American cinematic traditions. The only notable flaw is the choice to film in synchronized English sound instead of Spanish—likely a tactic to boost U.S. sales—which slightly diminishes the film's authenticity. Nonetheless, if you look past this, you'll find a heartfelt journey into another world. Highly recommended.

This is a remarkably self-contained piece, independent of any prior or subsequent works. While Brat Pack crooning and nightclub exclusivity aren't my preferred genres, in this lawless setting, they create a captivating atmosphere. The film features a cast of Our Guys—distinctive actors whose standout performances lend this work a special flair. The dialogue is truly enjoyable, even pioneering a new slang. It's one of those rare films that rewards multiple viewings with growing appreciation. 

Highlights include Billy Idol’s rugged British swagger, Ben London’s vulturine flair, Kyle’s nervous tension, and the exploration of spontaneous philosophies.

This film is truly inspiring and uplifting.  
Every time I watch it, I notice new humorous details that I hadn't caught before.  
  
The soundtrack is remarkable. Mick Jones from Foreigner and Chris Difford from Squeeze collaborated on the songs, making "Strange Fruit" arguably the greatest contribution to modern music that we've seen in a long time.  
  
Sadly, "Strange Fruit" is a completely fictional band—a washed-up group from the '60s and '70s that never really made it, plagued by drug problems and internal conflicts. Listening to their incredible soundtrack sparks curiosity about what could have been.  
  
The band draws influence from legendary acts like The Rolling Stones, Deep Purple, David Bowie, and The Who.  
  
Each member of the band leaves a strong impression. Stephen Rea plays Tony Costello, a broke and beaten-down musician. He's approached by a festival promoter to reunite his band for a tour, hoping for monetary gain. Costello turns to his former roadie, Karen Knowles, portrayed by Juliet Aubrey, to help reignite a long-lost dream.  
  
Juliet assembles a colorful group including the bitter Jimmy Nail (Les Wickes), the awkward Timothy Spall (David 'Beano' Baggot), and the flamboyantly glamorous Ray Simms (Bill Nighy). Also joining the chaos is Hughie, another ex-roadie—a hippie, a jokester, and a heavy smoker—played by Billy Connolly, whose presence adds even more humor to the story.

After all the mediocrity Hollywood and the indie scene have produced, at last, we get a film that offers genuinely scary moments. While some scenes rely on clichés, it's tough to find completely original movies these days. There's little entirely new here, but what’s presented is executed effectively. 

Pay close attention, as the subtle scares unfold quickly and frequently. This is certainly not a film to watch while enjoying your pizza. 

The movie features one cleverly crafted red herring, but unfortunately, one poorly cast role. Cheri Christian’s portrayal of Julie, the wife and mother, falls flat—she simply doesn’t come across as compelling. Her character feels unsympathetic right from the start. I understand she’s been through trauma, but we never see her in her normal, relatable state, and her relationship with her husband feels awkward—sometimes unintentionally so. The director likely aimed for us to empathize with her, but I never did. 

On the plus side, the ending is both unsettling and satisfying, avoiding gimmicks like a loud sound effect at the start of the credits, which the director wisely eschewed. 

This is not

When I first heard about this film, I thought it would resemble The Duchess (2008), but after watching the first 30 minutes of The Young Victoria, I realized it wasn’t just going to be a good movie. Nearly every aspect of this film is impressive—the costumes are stunning, and the settings are beautifully captured.

The only aspect that disappointed me was the performances. Emily Blunt (The Devil Wears Prada) is the star, bringing Queen Victoria to life with a compelling presence. This role arguably marks her potential first Oscar nomination. Rupert Friend plays Prince Albert, but his performance comes across as somewhat bland; however, he shares strong chemistry with Blunt. Paul Bettany delivers a solid portrayal of Lord Melbourne, though I expected more from him. Jim Broadbent and Miranda Richardson appear in supporting roles but leave little impression.

To me, the film feels somewhat incomplete—perhaps due to multiple changes in the script by the screenwriters, but that's just my impression. Overall, it’s an excellent movie about Victoria’s early years, highlighted by Emily Blunt’s outstanding performance.

Unless I am mistaken, I rented A Nightmare on Elm Street 3 a few years ago and remember a music video called Dream Warriors at the end of it. I specifically rented the DVD hoping to find that video again because it was one of the funniest things I've ever seen. It's remarkable how some 80s things remain so amusing today, but nothing beats 80s rap videos. There was a rap group performing Dream Warriors on the VHS version of the film after the credits, dressed in denim jackets without shirts underneath and form-fitting, frayed jean shorts reminiscent of Daisy Dukes. I can't imagine anything more ridiculous for a rap group. 

(Spoilers) Unfortunately, when I looked for that video on the DVD, it wasn't there, leaving me with just a mediocre entry in the Freddy Krueger series. The movie begins similarly to Part 2, with the protagonist witnessing various gruesome murders and gradually emerging from a trance to find...

Sidney Stratton struggles to keep his jobs at various textile mills due to his relentless experiments in the textile laboratories. He develops a groundbreaking fabric that is completely stain-proof, wrinkle-free, and virtually indestructible. However, upon creating this revolutionary material, he makes enemies among the textile workers, who fear losing their livelihoods, and the mill owners, who stand to lose profits because one manufacturer secures exclusive rights. Clad in his white suit, Stratton becomes the most sought-after man in England. The film, uniquely crafted by Ealing, is a charming and insightful piece. With Guinness's standout performance supported by Greenwood, Thesiger, and Parker, along with Mackendrick’s direction, it is thoroughly enjoyable. At its core, the story is a clever satire of business and industry, enriched with elements of drama, romance, and suspense. Rating: 8.

Mr. Michael Jackson is an extraordinary artistic force. His short films, especially his music videos, are unparalleled. I don't necessarily expect complex sci-fi stories from him, but I do look forward to a showcase of his wild dance moves, piercing screams, mesmerizing group choreography, along with some CGI and animation touches. Ideally, there should also be a few seamless, uninterrupted videos. All of these elements are present here. A trivial plot and exaggerated "vanity fair" moments don’t detract from his performance. For me, he remains the ultimate king of music videos—definitely not the "King of Pop," which seems silly, especially for us Russians, since "pop" sounds like the Russian word for "arses," and MJ is certainly not the "king of arses." His best music videos, rich in artistic beauty, are re-watchable anytime without losing their charm.

My initial reaction to this film was, "What is this...?" with snippets from various videos, some animated drawings, jarring shifts between themes, no clear storyline, and scenes of kids messing around. Yet, as I watched to the end, I realized it was a remarkable piece—completely unique and unlike anything else.

Hitokiri, roughly translating to "assassination," also known as "Tenchu," meaning "divine punishment," exemplifies Hideo Gosha at the height of his creative prowess. Missing this film, along with Gosha's renowned classic Goyokin, would be a missed opportunity. Not only is Hitokiri one of Gosha's finest works, but it also stands as one of the greatest samurai or chambara films ever produced—possibly among Japan's most acclaimed international releases.

Caution is advised, as the plot intricacies in Hitokiri can be challenging for those unfamiliar with 19th-century Japanese history. Nevertheless, the profound human drama remains accessible to all audiences. True to Gosha's style, the film explores his signature theme of "loyalty to one's lord" versus "doing what is right," crafted with such depth and nuance that it becomes a must-watch alongside Goyokin.

In essence, if you prefer a straightforward, action-packed story, Goyokin may be more your speed. But for a more layered, contemplative, and somber experience, Hitokiri is the superior choice.

(And to provide some context, the film's historical setting revolves around a turbulent power struggle among various samurai clans...)

Based on the questions and answers before and after, here's what I pieced together: Some Irish guy wants to make a movie—nothing specific, just any movie. One night at a party, he hears an ex-roadie share a legendary rock 'n' roll story: how Gram Parsons' body was stolen from LAX by his loyal roadie so Parsons' wishes to be cremated out in Joshua Tree could be fulfilled. Wow! That’s a fantastic concept for a film—rock 'n' roll (or country), grave robbing, escapes, friendship, the 70s vibe! Maybe we could cast Johnny Knoxville from "Jackass," since it’s kind of a prank, and Knoxville’s interested in doing a movie. Surely he thought he had a hit like "Snatch" on his hands!

But honestly, the story isn't that compelling on its own. We need something for Knoxville to struggle with—maybe a psychotic girlfriend after his money? The thing is, Parsons was married at the time, but that detail might be overlooked. We could also bring in Christina Applegate for some star power. Still, what if the audience isn’t keen on the corpse-stealing angle? In that case, we could have Parsons’ father join the chase—initially upset but ultimately giving his blessing at the end.

Yes, it's definitely achievable. John De Bello and Costa Dillon unleashed their worst ideas to craft a comedic, horror, sci-fi musical that defies taste. Any acting present is either atrociously bad or wildly exaggerated. The special effects range from embarrassingly cheap to utterly amateurish. Every cliché imaginable is crammed into this disaster, making it undoubtedly a fun watch—perfect for pairing with a cold six-pack or two. Blame it on radiation if you like. Mutant tomatoes, almost the size of tow trucks, begin terrorizing humanity, with San Diego as the unlikely battleground. A team of scientists and a forgetful military try to find a way to stop the red, rolling menace. This cult favorite stars David Miller, Eric Christmas, Al Sklar, Tom Coleman, Sharon Taylor, and John Qualls.

Richard Pryor's early 80s incident of running down the street on fire must have left some mark on him. He jokes about it in his stand-up routines, drawing big laughs. It seemed to influence the projects he chose to take on. "The Toy" is among his least impressive selections, aside from perhaps "Another You."  
A movie in which a white man buys his son a black man? That’s a curious bit of underlying political incorrectness ahead of its time. Watching Richard become overly sentimental finally drove me to leave before the ending. I was hoping Pryor would get even with the brat, but instead, it’s all about the misunderstood kid—nauseating. At least Gleason had his moments. Skip this and stick to Pryor's collaborations with Gene Wilder or his '70s classics. This film is a complete waste of time for any movie lover!

I vividly remember watching this film for the first time when I was just  nine years old. I aspired to be one of the "Barbarian Brothers." Even now, the movie remains fantastic. One unique feature is that the fight scenes are surprisingly brief, suggesting that the "Barbarian Brothers" were so skilled that they dispatched their enemies quickly and efficiently. The film also includes exciting chases, a cage fight, a dragon, and even a lively bar brawl! 

Admittedly, the acting is subpar, which is why I wouldn't give it a perfect ten, and it has faced criticism for its storyline. However, I find the plot to be quite original. Few movies in its genre boast such inventive storylines or vibrant, memorable dialogue.

Overall, I highly recommend this film.

MINOR SPOILER

An underrated gem among Stephen King's thrillers. While it isn't flawless—Dale Midkiff and Denise Crosby's performances leave something to be desired, and the mystical plot elements feel somewhat disorganized—the film still offers plenty of shocks. The old Micmac burial ground, Rachel's terminally ill sister, and Victor Pascow's haunting presence never fully coalesce into a seamless story, giving certain parts a confused and cluttered feel. Yet, few horror films push boundaries like this one, which embraces its brutality and discomfort. "Pet Sematary" stands out as one of the most harrowing recent horror entries, with its chilling zombie baby and disturbingly insensitive depiction of Zelda. It's provocative, tasteless, and gratuitous—yet it provokes a visceral revulsion that more polished horror movies often shy away from. Add Fred Gwynne's standout performance and Mary Lambert’s sharp direction, and you have a deeply impactful film—even with its somewhat cheesy ending. A must-watch for horror aficionados. 7.5 out of 10.

Deliverance is a captivating, haunting, and at times unsettling story crafted by James Dickey and transformed into a remarkable film by John Boorman. It follows four businessmen whose weekend canoe trip into remote mountain wilderness becomes a harrowing ordeal. Driven by notions of masculinity and bravado, they soon confront the darkest aspects of human nature and the most brutal facets of human suffering—poverty, assault, and violence. What begins as an adventure quickly evolves into a perilous journey through a hostile, lawless landscape, far removed from civilization. These intense elements render Deliverance one of the most nightmarish films I have ever seen; almost every twist of fate makes you hope you’ll never find yourself in such a dire situation. As a film that relies solely on dialogue and visuals, Deliverance is a work of great significance. It stands as John Boorman’s finest work—closely followed by Zardoz and Excalibur—and remains highly influential. Its memorable scenes have permeated countless other movies, from the iconic "Dueling Banjos" musical score to the unforgettable and controversial "squeal like a pig" scene depicting assault. The cast delivers powerful performances, amplifying the film’s lasting impact.

If you're seeking entertainment, avoid this film. If you're expecting heroic war stories, this isn't the movie for you. For those who appreciate superb acting and an outstanding screenplay, steer clear as well. However, if you're interested in Hollywood’s typical war films that wrap up just in time to deliver a politically motivated message about the grandeur and glory of war, then go ahead and see it. Otherwise, save your time. I have a keen interest in war movies because, when well-made, they can reveal the paradoxes and often futile nature of war. Unfortunately, this film depicts a group of men wandering the countryside, reciting cliché lines, engaging in predictable actions, and defending the oppressed with the same brutality they face. It’s a shameful failure both as a piece of cinema and as a reflection of American values. Imagine viewers from Europe, Africa, or elsewhere witnessing this and believing it truly represents America—that's no wonder many people harbor resentment toward us. Please, do not waste your time on this.

Although fairy tale films aren't typically my preference, Stardust caught my attention, particularly because Michelle Pfeiffer appeared as a villain in the trailers—especially since I was about to see her play the bossy Velma Von Tussle in Hairspray. She delivers a compellingly sinister performance here as a witch, especially with her aging, unflattering makeup at the start and end! Robert De Niro also shines as the pirate captain who must hide "in the closet" to preserve his reputation. Nearly all the cast—Claire Danes, Rupert Everett, Ricky Gervais, Peter O’Toole, and others—do a commendable job. While Danes and Pfeiffer are the epitome of classic beauty, faces like Sienna Miller’s, Olivia Grant’s (as Girl Bernard), and Kate Magowan’s—particularly when we first meet her—are stunning. The newcomer, Charlie Cox, is well-cast as Tristan, and he bears such a resemblance to his father Dunstan as a young man that I initially thought he was the same actor in some early scenes with Magowan (actually Ben Barnes). Many have drawn comparisons to The Princess Bride, and while I see some similarities, the main difference is that with PB, it’s clear from the start that it’s just a fantastical story.

I consider myself a dedicated movie enthusiast. While resting on the couch due to illness, I decided to watch this film. From the opening scene to the closing credits, I was captivated by the incredible cast—talented actors I hadn’t encountered before. The cinematography was stunning and added depth to the story. It truly was exactly what I needed at that moment. I hope this message reaches beyond any negative comments others may have expressed. The director's genuine passion shines through, resonating strongly with the cast. Thank you for creating such a heartfelt film. The characters are wonderfully awkward yet beautiful—flawed, graceful, and entirely authentic. Simply put, it’s fantastic. I feel compelled to add that I look forward to more work from this director, more from the talented cast, and more from the writer. I didn’t want it to end.

Jet Li is widely regarded as one of the top hand-to-hand combat fighters in the world, boasting over two decades of exceptional skill that outshines many in the genre. While he enjoys immense popularity across Asia, he remains relatively unknown in the United States. 

Black Mask was anticipated to be a breakthrough film for him, but it turned out to be a disappointment. Primarily, the movie is dubbed, which detracts from its authenticity. The dubbing itself is poorly executed, sounding flat and mismatched, making it less appealing for the average viewer. Additionally, director Daniel Lee's handling of the film leaves much to be desired. His rapid scene cuts often leave viewers confused, and the shaky, unstable camera work further complicates the viewing experience. Fans watch Jet Li's movies for his impressive martial arts choreography, but Lee's editing speeds through action sequences so quickly that identifying characters becomes difficult. Some scenes are left unresolved—for example, Li starts to cut a hole in a jeep's floor, then suddenly both Li and his love interest are already underneath the vehicle two seconds later. Many sequences venture into the realm of the improbable, undermining the film's overall coherence and impact.

Most of the French films I've watched—and enjoyed—tend to be more dialogue-driven than action-packed, but that's perfectly fine. I found them engaging, beautifully shot, and featuring fascinating actors. (Though at one point, I couldn't help but wonder if Gérard Depardieu was in every French film ever made! It sure felt that way.)

This film shared the same captivating visuals and had a strong opening. However, it soon devolved into endless conversations—talk, talk, and more talk—which might work in a drama, but doesn't quite fit a murder mystery. Eventually, I found myself nearly nodding off.

In fact, the movie resembled a play, with nearly all scenes set in a single room. If you enjoy theatrical productions, you'll probably appreciate this. But personally, I was hoping for a bit more excitement in a story centered around a murder.

The film suffers from poor structure, awkward writing, and an overuse of clichés, with flat dialogue that fails to engage. Not a single scene stands out as memorable. The actors appear to struggle within a painfully dull storyline that completely lacks surprises, plot twists, or conflict; by the ten-minute mark, you already know where it's headed.  

Despite being set in New York, the film hardly captures any sense of the city’s vibrancy. Many independent movies have managed to portray New York as almost magical on a modest budget, but this one feels like it was shot in Toronto.  

If Natasha Henstridge is cast, why is she dressed in oversized sweaters? Why make Vartan look dull and uninspired? Where’s the allure? The movie comes off as a lukewarm Christian film—so bland and moralizing that it feels almost asexual.  

Steven Feder’s main achievement seems to be convincing others to produce this uninspired and forgettable film.

The film primarily revolves around bondage, humiliation, and S&M scenes, with little else to offer. The storyline is unremarkable, serving merely as a backdrop for the visually provocative and stylized sequences. The host of the show—a comically foolish man who rambles nonsense while dressed in mismatched costumes—was almost more distracting than the attempts at artistic editing. The ending, which seems almost dreamlike, felt shoehorned into the narrative. However, credit must be given to Aya Sugimoto, who delivered a convincing portrayal of the tormented protagonist. While comparisons have been drawn between Flower and Snake and Eyes Wide Shut, aside from some superficial similarities, Kubrick’s film remains the more nuanced, artistic, and atmospherically rich work.

This is arguably the worst acting I have ever seen in a film, period. The casting choices are baffling; the lead actress has a noticeable nasal disfigurement that makes it nearly impossible to look at her for any length of time without fixating on her nose. On a Sunday afternoon at your local grocery store, you could find at least fifty more qualified and better-looking candidates to be the lead. I regret renting this film solely because of its "cool" DVD artwork. It feels more like a school project from multimedia students at a local technical college than a professional production. Honestly, I would have preferred to spend that hour watching public access television, where, at least, the special effects are more believable and the hosts tend to be more attractive than anyone in this movie.

This film is unquestionably the worst I've ever watched, surpassing even the most disappointing movies I've seen before. The filming style was unprofessional, giving the impression that a group of friends simply decided to make a movie together. The cast consists of unfamiliar actors, which added to the amateurish feel. Overall, it was a terrible experience. The storyline felt completely contrived, and the pacing was painfully slow, making the movie drag on endlessly. It seemed like there was no proper script or planning involved, resulting in a confusing and bizarre plot. The lack of direction made it hard to see any purpose in watching this film. If you're thinking about giving it a try, I strongly advise against it—you're just wasting your time.

This film ranks among my favorite foreign films, alongside others like Amélie and My Life as a Dog. Like many exceptional international movies, it elevates a simple, everyday moment into a deeply moving and meaningful lesson. 

Set in Japan, the story follows a man weary of his monotonous routine and stifling marriage, who notices a beautiful Japanese woman gazing out the window of a dance studio. In the fleeting moment as his train passes, he becomes captivated by her. But is it merely her beauty, her distant gaze, or a deeper connection they will eventualy discover? 

Shall We Dance features unforgettable characters who confront harsh realities by immersing themselves in the world of dance. Challenging traditional Japanese societal norms and stereotypes, they risk everything in pursuit of happiness, realizing that joy is often within reach. This film is truly enchanting and profound, transcending the ordinary to reveal the magic and miracle that life can hold.

Wow! This is one of those movies you swear you’ve reviewed before, but in reality, you haven't. I mean, you didn’t really care about it, yet somehow it just popped into your mind.

Honestly and briefly, this ranks as one of the most boring, silly, and poorly crafted slasher films ever produced. There’s hardly anything positive to say about this junk, as it barely has any decent moments that might indicate professional filmmaking.

The death scenes are terrible—lacking blood, unintelligent, and poorly executed. The plot, surprisingly, isn’t entirely awful, especially considering it seems to borrow heavily from the 1991 film "Popcorn."

To make matters worse, this isn’t a so-bad-it’s-good kind of movie; it’s just simply bad. 

Molly Ringwald gave it her all, but unfortunately, it wasn’t enough.

I’ve always been curious about this film because it’s incredibly hard to find. When I finally discovered it on eBay, I didn’t hesitate—dropped ten bucks and bought it. Now I understand why it’s so rare! This movie is atrocious—so poorly written and with a ridiculously low budget that the best part is actually the end credits, where they reveal all the outtakes of actors fumbling their lines. The story centers on a psychic (played by Pettyjohn, obviously cast for one reason—her topless scene) who uses an experimental machine to draw objects from another dimension into our reality. When she retrieves some sort of box-like object, the military casually tosses it into the back of a truck, with only one soldier guarding it. Surprise! A kid dressed in a foam-rubber monster costume bursts out, instantly injures the soldier with a scratch across his face, and runs off into a nearby city. Instead of deploying a significant portion of the armed forces to secure it and protect the public, those in charge just leave it to Pettyjohn and Ray to find it on their own. But honestly, it doesn’t matter—nothing about this film makes sense.

I'm not entirely sure why, but this movie just doesn't come across as it should. It was supposed to be funny and entertaining, but instead, it feels quite dull. I believe a big reason for this is the excessive focus on the "gadgets." The original cartoon it's based on is far more enjoyable.  
Rating: 3/10

My scalp still itches from the burning coals I heaped upon it while proclaiming my love for this film. Bring on the flames; I’ll walk across them gladly to reaffirm that I love "Bend It Like Beckham." Admittedly, that declaration comes with plenty of qualifiers. It feels a bit like a TV movie; the screenplay is straightforward and predictable. More troublingly, the director’s commentary suggests that beauty in this film is primarily associated with whiteness.  

The film’s brilliance isn’t in the obvious elements like character arcs, themes, or structure that the typical Syd Field enthusiast might notice. Its true power lies both in its surface and the deeper layers that often go unnoticed — not in the superficial artistic details usually highlighted by reviewers. The depiction of powerful, often semi-clad female bodies—not merely on display but actively kicking a football—more authentically conveys female strength and agility than characters like Lara Croft or Zhang Ziyi ever could. These are real bodies (with the exception of Keira Knightley) that exist not to look attractive first and fight later, but to perform through movement and self-determination. In my view, the standout is lead actress Parminder Nagra.

This film is truly outstanding! Brad Pitt's performance in this movie is unmatched; he cannot be surpassed in his role here. Duchovny delivers a superb portrayal, complemented by stellar performances from Forbes and Lewis. The story follows four main characters as they embark on a scenic road trip through historic murder sites aboard an iconic 1960s Lincoln Continental. Early Grace is portrayed as a naive individual with peculiar interests in dry toothbrushes and chaos; he prefers his women to be free of curses and smoking, and to wear PWT dresses. Duchovny and Forbes play an urban artist duo, while Early and Lewis are trailer park residents from the countryside. Despite the predominantly dark tone of the film, it is filled with numerous humorous moments. The screenplay, direction, and performances are all exceptional. If you enjoy road movies, crime stories, comedy, and narration, this film is a must-see. Every actor shines, leaving you eager for more once the credits roll. It's one of my all-time favorites. "Hey... shave that dog and teach it to hunt!"

Without a doubt, this is one of the worst movies ever made—truly, the worst I have ever seen. Even more disappointing is the fact that my former hero, Dolph, is in it and serving as the star. Honestly, Jesus... The storyline itself is actually quite good, but the execution makes my body ache just thinking about it. The fight scenes, for example, are choreographed as poorly as a drunken brawl in the alley. The acting, aside from Dolph who, admittedly, also falls flat, is so dreadful that you can't help but wonder if the entire cast is just there because they’re friends of the director—who, by the way, seems to have been largely absent during filming. This film supposedly cost 12 million dollars, but judging by the special effects and sets, it looks like no more than a thousand dollars was actually spent.

I'm a fan of Crash and Blade Runner, and this film delves into some of those highway fatalities and 80s film noir themes I enjoy, so I found it quite entertaining. 

However, overall, the film's depiction of the classic noir protagonist falls flat, especially with the female lead's characterization, and her hero comes across as almost Neanderthal. That's why I would issue a kitsch warning.

Although I was somewhat hopeful about this film, especially given my appreciation for Jason Segel's performances in Freaks & Geeks and Undeclared, I must admit it ranks among the worst movies I've seen recently—joining the likes of Loser and Dr. T and the Women.  

There were a few genuinely funny moments, but overall, the movie had the potential to be much better. The basic premise was decent—scam artists navigating college life who encounter someone with a tempting proposition—but the characters were all so unlikable that I found it hard to care about any of them. The blackmailer, played by the talented Jason Schwartzman, was portrayed as such a psychopath that his scenes lost their humor; he wasn’t charming or amusingly deranged, just a dangerous, unhinged loser, which made him uncomfortable to watch. The editing was also confusing, frequently shifting between fantasy and reality in a way that often obscured what was real. Only a couple of the scams were fully shown; the rest, we had to accept on faith.

The main challenge is deciding where to start, as this film demands your full attention for the next two hours, and missing a few minutes to grab a coke might leave you lost. Fortunately, there’s a pause button. Bruce Willis must travel through time to discover an antivirus for a virus that, in 1996, caused animals to dominate the world. Due to a few mistakes, he first lands in 1990, then in World War I, amid all the chaos, Terry Gilliam delivers what is arguably one of the most intelligent scripts ever written. This former Monty Python member knows exactly how to craft compelling sci-fi stories, and his casting choices couldn’t have been better—featuring the eccentric Brad Pitt (whose asylum performance is unforgettable) and a superb Bruce Willis, proving he’s more than just a Schwarzenegger clone. It’s a film you can watch repeatedly; its bizarre and intricate plot (yet surprisingly easy to follow) reveals new surprises with each viewing. It’s one of my all-time favorites.

It felt as though I had seen this movie a thousand times before—completely predictable. Every time the story tried to take a turn, I was met with exactly what I anticipated. It was like watching "The bread factory opened another branch because there wasn’t enough bread." In short: a dull, clichéd story accompanied by poor acting and subpar special effects. The only mildly amusing character was the clueless Russian cop, Vlad, who at least provided some comic relief as he dealt with the bad guys. The muscle-bound thug was so utterly idiotic that I couldn’t help but laugh at him. I wonder why I bother wasting my time on such a disgraceful film... It probably can’t get any worse—that’s almost impossible.

Zombi 3 has a fascinating backstory behind its production. Initially conceived as a sequel to Fulci's popular Zombi 2, the film’s title was actually a clever marketing ploy—Zombi 2 itself was deliberately labeled to make audiences believe it was a follow-up to George A. Romero’s Dawn of the Dead, also known as Zombi. Quite confusing, isn’t it? In reality, none of these films are directly connected, but that didn’t stop them from making money. Interestingly, Fulci appears to have lost interest mid-production of Zombi 3, eventually walking away from the project. Bruno Mattei was brought in to add extra scenes to extend the film’s length.

The plot of Zombi 3 sticks to familiar zombie territory. It involves scientists developing a serum on a Philippine island, only for terrorists to steal it, unleashing a deadly plague. Zombies then run rampant across the landscape. The scientists aim to find an antidote, while the military is intent on exterminating everyone indiscriminately. Interspersed are brief segments featuring a radio DJ delivering messages about environmental issues.

Overall, I found this film quite enjoyable. Despite the harsh reviews it received, I appreciated its cheesy dialogue and campy charm. The film seems to be an...

This film, inspired by a true story, marks the directorial debut of seasoned actor Denzel Washington. Over the past decade, Washington has delivered some of the most memorable performances, such as his portrayal of a Black soldier in the Civil War epic *Glory*, and his compelling role as a lawyer in the acclaimed *Philadelphia*. He also garnered significant recognition last year when he won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Training Day*, making history as the first African American to receive the Best Actor Oscar. Seeking a new challenge, Washington chose to direct *Antwone Fisher*, in which he also stars. Fisher is portrayed by Derek Luke, an emerging talent making his film debut, though he’s previously appeared in television shows like *King of Queens* and is set to star in the upcoming film *Biker Boyz*. 

This film is a remarkable achievement for Washington, especially considering it is his first experience behind the camera. It’s clear he was deeply committed and believed in the true story of Antwone Fisher. The story centers on a young African American man in the Navy who struggles with...

Predictable parody, it barely managed to make an impression during its lengthy eight-minute run. The sole highlight was the "DO NOT COLORIZE" line at the end credits. It's a shame that the DVD didn't include something more entertaining, such as Jonathan Ross's engaging profile of Romero on "The Incredible Strange Film Show."
