This film offers a sharp, satirical critique of pop culture and its creators. I was particularly impressed by the cinematography, which featured vibrant colors and digitally manipulated settings—quite remarkable considering this is Zukovic's first major project. 

A word of caution: don’t take the film’s message too literally. It’s not exactly designed for broad audiences (and that’s not a compliment). Instead, it presents a stylized, post-college, novice perspective on society.

Nonetheless, I enjoyed the core storyline about a fictional zine editor sharply criticizing the chaos of 90s society.

This film was marketed as both a comedy and a mystery, but it falls flat on both counts. The real mystery is why anyone would assemble such a poorly made movie. The only humor I found was in my surprise at how highly this film is rated by viewers here. Could there be two movies sharing the same title? The version I watched featured a girl with striking blue eyes and a storyline that was nonexistent.

So, what exactly is this supposed to be? Is it a family-friendly fantasy film trying to capitalize on the massive success of Spielberg's "Close Encounters of the Third Kind"? Or perhaps a nostalgic homage to classic prehistoric epics like "When Dinosaurs Roamed the Earth" and "The Lost World"? Maybe it's an overlooked philosophical and intellectual tour de force—though that seems unlikely. Whatever the case, the creators of "The Day Time Ended"—John 'Bud' Cardos of "Kingdom of the Spiders" and writer David Schmoeller of "Tourist Trap"—must have been on some serious glue when they put together this bizarre mash-up of genres. The plot makes no sense whatsoever, and the storytelling is downright incoherent, but who cares? As long as it features papier-mâché dinosaurs, tiny spacecraft, headache-inducing light shows, laser effects, and spontaneously exploding supernovas! The voice-over introduction is nearly impossible to hear, but honestly, it’s all just gibberish anyway. Did you know that our understanding of 'time' might be totally off? Time doesn’t necessarily move in a straight line; it’s one giant paradox! Words spoken thousands...

I genuinely can't grasp how such nonsense gets produced. Even the most amateurish junior-high talent show act is more entertaining than this movie. The only fleetingly funny parts are due to Will Ferrell's wrestling obsession. Overall, it's utterly terrible.

Once again, it's a film that tugs at your emotions, leaving you feeling tender rather than hardened—a style I personally enjoy, so I rated it highly. The performances were outstanding, filled with genuine emotion. The violence was understated, which was a refreshing change. I might have given it a 9, but the salute at the end nudged my score down a bit. Overall, it's a solid movie with excellent actors.

This film was truly dreadful! I can't understand how it ever made it to production. No blame here on the cast—they did their best—but the real issue lies with the writing team. They rely on the tired, clichéd "let’s dance our way out of poverty" storyline—similar to STEP, in this case—but this version lacks any genuine plot or substance that would engage the audience. Adding to the confusion, actors with Canadian accents are cast in what’s supposed to be an American setting, making the whole film fall flat. On a brighter note, the directing was quite competent, and the cinematography was decent. It seems the production had a generous budget, but all that effort went to waste. My only plea is for this team to step back from the writing and bring in skilled screenwriters who can truly craft compelling stories. In the end, the result is: how she moves, how she stinks.

"Bruce Almighty" is poised to dominate the Academy Awards with an unprecedented 14 Oscar victories, surpassing "Titanic" as the highest-grossing film of all time. Jim Carrey's star power will reach new heights, leading him to announce a bid for the presidency in the 2004 White House race—quite the divine aspiration! These spectacular dreams would only come true if the filmmakers (including Carrey) possessed divine powers. Ironically, that very premise forms the heart of Carrey's latest comedy, "Bruce Almighty." In the film, Carrey portrays Bruce Nolan, a television reporter so consumed with being the top anchor that he blames God for his personal setbacks. Morgan Freeman, playing God himself, grants Bruce the "Gift of God"—his own divine powers—to test whether he can do God's job better. Naturally, Bruce quickly succumbs to his newfound powers, using them selfishly. Once again, Carrey delivers his signature comedic mastery in "Bruce Almighty." Jennifer Aniston plays Bruce's girlfriend, and her performance is far from "mis.pittiful." Special praise is due to director Tom Shadyac for not letting the dog out of the house in the film's hilarious bathroom scene, which stands as one of the most humorous moments involving man's best friend.

This is unquestionably the funniest of the Curly Stooges shorts. I've watched it countless times, and it never fails to make me laugh. The hilarious pantomime scenes are top-notch. It’s a perfect illustration of "musical comedy." Even those who aren't fans of the Stooges hold this one in fond remembrance.

Following the murder of "Central City's" mob boss, partner-in-crime Robert Armstrong (portraying "Doc" Rogers) takes drastic action to maintain the criminal empire. He enlists the meek son of the fallen gangster, Richard Cromwell (playing Edward "Baby Face" Morgan), to take over the family operations. Naively brought into the city, Cromwell is appointed President of his father's "Acme Protection Agency," which serves as a facade for the gangsters' illegal activities. While Cromwell unwittingly sells insurance, his staff run an extortion scheme behind the scenes. He falls for a beautiful client, Mary Carlisle (as Virginia Clark), and together they find themselves in serious peril. "Baby Face Morgan" captures Cromwell and Carlisle as they approach the end of their once-promising acting careers. This film is a quick, light, and harmless crime drama.

**** Baby Face Morgan (1942) directed by Arthur Dreifuss — featuring Richard Cromwell, Mary Carlisle, and Robert Armstrong

As a devoted Elvis fan, I simply can't understand how this project was even made. It is by far the worst Elvis-related movie ever, completely unfunny, absurd, and riddled with inaccuracies about The King. For instance, Elvis' grave in a public park? A reference to Suspicious Minds set in 1958? These are just two of many issues. Some cast members do their best; Mike Starr delivers some funny moments, especially as a impersonator, and Tom Hanks' cameo is a pleasant surprise. However, the actor portraying young Elvis fails miserably. Overall, the film lacks entertainment and becomes duller with each passing minute. If you're looking for a cheesy, wild, yet hilarious Elvis-themed flick, I highly recommend "Bubba Ho-Tep" over this disaster.

I'm not inclined to provide an in-depth critique of this film. Numerous glowing reviews have already appeared, and since I generally hold Maria de Medeiros in high regard, I hesitated to offer any negative commentary—so much so that nearly a year has gone by. Still, every time I see the DVD resting on my shelf, I can't help but feel a slight inward sigh. Nonetheless, let the positive voices carry the day! However, for fellow cinephiles like myself, a word of caution: beware.  

Simply put, here is my perspective:  

The political upheaval and regime change depicted in this film echo a chapter of my own life—a period I experienced through the daily newspapers I read at a local Central European pub. Back then, I followed the headlines with interest but often struggled to fully understand what was really unfolding. Reporters tended to present the news either in a neutral tone or with a conservative bent, expressing disapproval of groups disrupting the peace or inciting rebellion against authority. Those were turbulent times, with unrest swirling through Paris, Berlin, Prague, and various U.S. cities—issues I understood well at the time. Yet, regardless of whether it was a dictatorship or not, the complexities remained elusive to me.

For those unfamiliar with Jimmy Stewart, this film is one of his lesser works from the later part of his career. While it doesn't measure up to many of his more acclaimed movies, it’s not a bad watch and makes for a decent time-killer—though not much more.  

Kim Novak plays a witch in New York City who inexplicably casts a spell on Jimmy Stewart, causing him to fall in love with her. As time passes, the aloof and detached Novak also begins to develop feelings for Stewart—an act that, according to witch’s rules, is a serious no-no.  

The movie presents an unusual take on witches; they aren’t depicted as the all-powerful or sacrificial type. Their magic is mostly limited and often pointless—like Jack Lemmon using his powers to turn off street lamps. Strangely, all the witches seem to be bohemians, frequenting trendy bars where people wear berets and listen to lousy jazz. Considering my own disdain for jazz, it must really be tough being a witch in this world!  

Overall, the film carries a pretty romantic vibe.

I purchased this DVD for my brother, who is a huge Michelle Pfeiffer fan. Earlier this week, I decided to watch it myself.  

The film is fairly entertaining, featuring two entirely separate storylines. The segment with Michelle Pfeiffer was definitely the more compelling of the two. She portrays an emerging Hollywood actress who has experienced several brief, unfulfilling relationships. The story kicks off when she accidentally crashes into Brian Kerwin's car; initially, they are hostile towards each other. However, he kindly offers to drive her home since she no longer feels comfortable behind the wheel. As the story unfolds, romance blossoms, culminating in tragedy when his wife discovers the affair. The ending caught me off guard, but the slow pace and routine television-style direction diminish the emotional impact of the drama.  

The other storyline centers around an aging studio boss played by Darren McGavin. This part features a stronger cast, including Kenneth McMillan, Lois Chiles, Steven Bauer, and Stella Stevens. They all have their own motivations for interacting with the studio head, but when he is asked to resign, they realize their careers are effectively stalled and will go nowhere from there.

Eddie Murphy's "Delirious" is entirely characterized by its rudeness, crudeness, crassness, and vulgarity. This description perfectly captures the offensive and lowbrow nature of this stand-up performance. Murphy leans heavily on shock value rather than genuine humor in an attempt to captivate his audience. While he manages to deliver some funny moments, they are overshadowed by excessive obscene language and inappropriate sex jokes.  

Skip it! Unless you appreciate Eddie's gritty and vulgar comedy style, there's little here for you. Personally, I wouldn't bother with "Eddie Murphy Raw"; I prefer seeing Eddie in a scripted movie setting.  

Saturday, January 17, 1998 — Video

I was really excited to see Planet of the Apes, but it turned out to be a huge disappointment. The sets and masks are impressive, but that’s the only positive aspect of the film. Everything else is quite frustrating. Mark Wahlberg's performance feels lackluster; he just appears in the movie looking foolish. The other actors are also not very convincing. 

Most disappointing of all is the story, which is completely absurd. For instance, the apes lie unconscious on the ground, yet the humans don’t take the opportunity to attack them—they simply wait until they wake up again! That’s just one example of how nonsensical the plot is; there are many more, but it would take too long to list them all.

First and foremost, I want to emphasize that I am a strong supporter of fan productions. I view them as a way to keep beloved shows alive well beyond their official runs. Series like Star Trek Voyages and Star Wars Revelations are prime examples of commendable efforts. Because of this, I have a soft spot for fan-made projects, which often allows me to overlook flaws I would normally criticize harshly.

Now, turning to Star Trek: Helix Force. Let’s start with the positives. Enthusiasm plays a crucial role in making any fan creation convincing, and overall, the cast of various ships seems genuinely engaged with their roles. The special effects are quite decent for a homemade project, with nothing glaring enough to pull you out of the experience. The storytelling isn’t bad either—nothing groundbreaking, but dependable, with at least some ongoing story arcs to follow.

However, the project does have its share of issues.

One major concern is that, while it’s understandable to borrow footage, sets, music, and effects from official Star Trek productions, it’s less justifiable to lift nearly every other sci-fi musical score ever composed. From the ominous tones of Aliens to the militaristic surge of Starship Troopers, the soundtrack choices are overly derivative and at times distracting.

I just watched the movie on TV and truly enjoyed it. I love a compelling mystery, and this film kept me guessing until the very end. Sean Connery delivered an excellent performance. I would definitely recommend it to a friend.

Or listening to, for that matter. Even the soundtrack fails to excite.  

Honestly, this isn't the worst gay film I've come across—that distinction belongs to Regarding Billy—but it's definitely close to the bottom of the barrel.  

The film painfully drags on and on. It's not that the story is entirely nonsensical—if written by a skilled writer, it might have had potential—and it could have been quite entertaining. Yet, every plot twist is glaringly predictable from miles away. The dialogue falls flat, the jokes feel recycled, and to make matters worse, the characters are portrayed as one-dimensional stereotypes.  

Nothing about this movie convinced me that the situation or the relationship between the two leads feels genuine or even plausible. There's no spark, no chemistry, no real indication of why they fall for each other—apart from the fact that we're simply told they are. It’s perplexing, considering they share nothing in common and seem sexually incompatible. Do they both happen to like the same book? Really?  

The acting isn't entirely poor, but the pacing is agonizingly slow—almost Jarmusch slow, but lacking the artistry that makes that pacing compelling.

This series introduced me to Deighton's writing and the genre when I was younger, and I really enjoy how the story is presented here. However, I would disagree with the earlier comment. From my previous reading, it appears that it wasn't Holm's performance that caused Deighton to refuse the series' release, but rather the way all three books were heavily altered during their adaptation to screen. A prime example is the rewritten scene at the border crossing that marked the end of Samson’s undercover career. This scene is not from the book; the character who dies in the minefield was never part of the original story, and the crossing in *Sinker* was from East Germany to West Germany, not at the Polish border. These modifications are fabrications. Similarly, changes in the *Set* storyline undermine its original integrity. 

Regarding Holm’s performance, I felt he captured Samson’s disorientation during his wife’s defection very effectively and portrayed well the aging agent’s desperate attempts to bridge the class divide. Samson bears the cost of his father's idealism and suffers from its impact on his life. As Clevemore remarks, if only he had pursued an education...

I'm a fan of Jean Harlow because of her undeniable star quality. I don't believe her films are particularly strong, nor do I think she was necessarily a great actress, but she was exceptional in comedies. The humor in The Girl from Missouri is particularly sharp and well-executed. However, the film leans more towards being a love story. Jean Harlow shines brilliantly in this movie, to the point where the rest of the cast's performances fade into the background—they offer little to elevate the story. It always amazes me to consider that Harlow's stunning appearance was drawn from someone who was often unwell. Yet, in this film, she looks absolutely beautiful.

You know those movies that make you feel like you're stuck in the theater? Seated perfectly in the best spot—center of the row, in that one sweet spot you fiddled with three times to find—only to realize, after what feels like thirteen hours, that you're still trapped there, uncomfortable and itchy, thinking, "When the hell is this movie ever going to end?" (You know the feeling—think of A.I. or The Village). 

Well, Visitor Q offers a strange twist on that sensation. I sat through the first half-hour wondering when it was actually going to start! It drags on endlessly—so painfully "artsy" it’s almost unbearable. This was my first time watching a Takashi Miike film. I've heard he makes movies by the dozen, but if they're all as pretentious and pointless as this, I doubt I’ll be watching any more. 

I'm not inherently opposed to pretension—David Lynch is one of my top ten directors, after all—but Visitor Q feels cheap, tacky, and manufactured in its pretentiousness. 

As you might have guessed, I absolutely hated it.

Yes, it's definitely an improvement over my viewing of Death Tunnel. Some of the deaths were quite inventive, and the gore was fairly well done. It reminded me a bit of a mashup between Wrong Turn and The Hills Have Eyes.  

However, there are a few issues: 1.) When the "kids" (are they high school or college students?) are discussing horror movies in the kitchen, Shae's lines are nearly identical to a scene from Scream (1996), especially regarding the big-breasted girls and such. 2.) Was Steve supposed to be a bootleg version of Randy from Scream? 3.) Besides the fact that the setting is in October, what does the movie have to do with Samhain? It feels pretty unnecessary. I always find it amusing when '80s horror films try to justify plot holes by blaming druids or referencing pentagrams. 4.) They even made a Sam Raimi homage—a nice touch! 5.) Why were Gary and his sister included at all? Their characters added nothing to the story, and he's portrayed as so psychic that he couldn't even foresee his own death. 6.) During Gary's death in the bathroom—which, by that point, had become rather Troma-esque—how could she hear his screams if she was downstairs?

Actually, Goldie Hawn hails from Takoma Park, Maryland, in Washington, but I digress. The film resembles a "Mr. Smith Goes to Washington" story, with some variations but a similar core idea. I recorded this movie off cable years ago because I had a huge crush on Goldie Hawn. The plot is intriguing, though it's quite improbable that a cocktail waitress would land a significant government role simply because she saved a high-ranking official's life. It made me laugh and angered me simultaneously. I laughed because some of her situations were so absurd that I couldn't help but chuckle. (POSSIBLE SPOILER AHEAD.) Yet, I was upset thinking about how our government might set up an ordinary citizen in the way she was portrayed. The speech she delivered at the end was truly beautiful. Too bad many people lack the courage to speak out like that in real life.

This movie brought back memories of those cheesy "erotic thrillers" I used to stay up late watching on Cinemax when I was 13. I'd call this film a softer-core version since it lacks any simulated bump-and-grind scenes. However, it features plenty of nudity—starting with a scene set in a strip club, where we catch a glimpse of Kane Hodder's backside (or at least a stunt butt), followed by an inexplicable ten-minute lesbian dance sequence nestled in the middle of the film, and a nude female werewolf who appears to have been costumed by someone who mugged a Munster. 13-year-old boys would definitely enjoy this. 

Aside from that, the werewolf transformation scenes boast some of the worst CGI I've seen in years. Shot quality resembles FMV from a PlayStation-era game like Resident Evil. The wolf character looks so bad that it’s hard to watch, yet despite the shoddy costume, it appears far too frequently. 

The plot and acting are equally baffling. There’s some strange backstory involving werewolves and hybrid-werewolves—the Darkwolf being one of the latter. From what I gather, hybrids do the same thing as regular werewolves: they look human, transform into wolves, and kill people.

Wow, how much worse could it get? This was genuinely terrible—not just because of the laughable CGI gore, but also due to the poor acting, lack of atmosphere, and misguided direction.

The plot was absolutely dreadful, with the main character's arc being completely nonsensical. After just a few nights of stalking Vinnie Jones, he becomes so "haunted" that he ends up crying while photographing his girlfriend. Are all New York photographers this immature, impressionable, and fragile? His character development had no foundation or purpose whatsoever, and by the end, you'll be laughing at the utterly predictable and ridiculous twist his character undergoes.

The gore scenes seemed like a desperate attempt to hop on the MTV-style shock trend—overused CGI, blood splatter, but no genuine emotion. These moments were unintentionally hilarious and detracted from the film’s overall tone, with exaggerated camera angles and self-aware gimmicks.

Overall, this film ruins a potentially atmospheric story—until the pointless monsters at the end—by prioritizing superficial, self-conscious directing. It clearly wasn't made for an audience that values storytelling or substance.

Beyond its superb direction, production, acting, and the familiar plot twists, the film carries a vital message embedded within its script:  
  
"Listening guides us through everything." For the voice to thrive, we must listen. To truly harmonize with others, listen. To understand ourselves, listen. To uncover the needs within any situation or person, listen. It seems the screenwriters are revealing a fundamental secret of life—listening fosters self-awareness. It awakens our other senses, especially sight, and broadens our perspective. Through listening, we can even discover our inner selves.  
The artistry of "As It Is in Heaven" masterfully depicts the journey of life—not just its joys and sorrows, but the hope that persists throughout. All of this begins with the first instruction of the lead character to the choir:  
  
"Just listen; it leads the way."

"The Return of Chandu" is noteworthy—if one can say that—primarily for casting Bela Lugosi as the hero rather than the villain. Interestingly, he even ends up with the girl.

The plot revolves around the Black Magic Cult of Ubasti, which seeks to capture the last Egyptian princess, Nadji (played by the delightful Maria Alba), to sacrifice her in hopes of resurrecting their ancient leader, who coincidentally resembles Nadji. Lugosi portrays Chandu, a character endowed with magical powers, attempting to thwart the cult's sinister plans.

Director Ray Taylor makes the most of limited resources and extensive stock footage, including recognizable scenes from "King Kong" (1933), with the giant doors used to contain Kong appearing in several shots. The acting overall is largely poor; for instance, the actor portraying the high priest—likely Lucien Prival—delivers a heavily accentuated, overly theatrical performance reminiscent of early sound film acting styles. The performances of the other cast members are similarly subpar.

It remains a mystery why Lugosi chose to appear in low-budget indie productions like this at this point in his career, given that he was still a bankable star at Universal. Perhaps...

I'm still uncertain whether there was any meaningful point to this film.

For a story that claims to be so 'rebellious' and 'controversial,' the materials Maddox hands out to the students are surprisingly dull. The students appear easily influenced by vague anti-authoritarian slogans and poorly scribbled snippets on leaflets. Everyone wants to be a rebel.

It would have been too much to hope for a teenage rebellion film where a school fire alarm isn't triggered.

Apparently, a 'massive fight on the football fields' is just two people arguing.

The characters' personalities seem to change randomly. The football jock Maddox was fighting—who ended up with a staple on his face—is all smiles and apologies the next day.

The lack of any real resolution to the plot makes me think this could have been condensed into a half-hour after-school special—if only they had cut most of the attempts at a pseudo-glitch soundtrack.

Without question, Private Lessons II is the finest film I have ever encountered. An import from Japan with a rather clumsy English translation, it remains a true delight to watch. Though much of it defies logical understanding, that hardly detracts from its charm. It stands as the greatest comedy around, even without aiming to be funny intentionally.

Rare and seldom available on video, I’ve only caught it a few times late at night on pay TV. My taped copy has been replayed countless times as I gradually and personally introduce this cinematic treasure to others.

Joanna Pacula portrays the tutor and lover to Ken, our protagonist. She was likely just working for the paycheck. Ken, played by Goro Inagaki from the Japanese pop band SMAP, delivers a spirited performance and sports great hair throughout the film. Stacy Edwards, known for "In the Company of Men," also appears and probably feels glad to have secured other acting roles afterward.

It takes at least three viewings to start piecing together the plot. On repeated watches, you can appreciate quirky details like the staggering number of vases in Ken’s house—at least fifty—or other peculiar elements woven throughout.

I hope the audience member who claimed that "Dream Machine" ranks among Corey Haim's greatest works and one of the "best movies of the century" was joking. Do I detect sarcasm? I genuinely hope so.

"Dream Machine" inaugurates a series of mediocre ventures that would overshadow much of Corey Haim's career—except for "Prayer of the Rollerboys," which was unexpectedly decent. In this film, Haim portrays Bernie, a laid-back college student who believes that owning a stylish car will help him win the girl of his dreams. Fortunately for Bernie, a wealthy woman seeking revenge on her unfaithful husband impulsively gifts him a sleek Porsche Turbo. What she doesn't know—and what Bernie remains oblivious to—is that her late husband's body is hidden in the trunk. Since bodies in this movie don't seem to decay or emit any foul smell, Bernie remains unaware of the crime. In fact, he has no idea that anything suspicious is going on, despite a series of odd occurrences, including a sinister man stalking him, eager to retrieve the body without attracting attention.

Overall, this is a forgettable action misfire.

Simply put, I am not a fan of westerns. Having never watched one from start to finish, I decided to give "My Darling Clementine" a chance and see it through, regardless of how uncomfortable it might be for me. The beginning was as difficult as I anticipated — the acting struck me as comical, the scenery (typical deserts, horses, and cowboys) bored me, and the music and its timing nearly caused me pain. Nonetheless, after a mental pep talk to push through, I found it gradually easier to endure beyond the first 20 minutes. Paying attention to the cinematography and how John Ford transformed even the most mundane scenes (at least from my perspective) into visually striking moments made the experience more engaging. 

In the end, I can't claim I enjoyed the film, but I was able to sit through it entirely, which I find quite an achievement in itself.

Check out Eva Longoria and Paul Rudd in a quirky film about a deceased girlfriend haunting her new partner. Featuring Gabrielle from Desperate Housewives and the guy who wore "Sex Panther" cologne in Anchorman, this movie isn't aiming for Golden Globe glory—so if that's what you expect, you might want to adjust your standards. But if you're open to suspending reality for 90 minutes and having a good laugh, you're in the right place. The cast delivers plenty of humor, and their chemistry is great. The standout scene features Paul Rudd and Lake Bell—he's just as funny as he was on Friends, and she manages to be both hilarious and attractive. I saw it with my wife; she enjoyed it, and I did too.

Famous was renowned for its tension-and-release style of cartoon storytelling, where the semi-main character finds themselves in dire danger only to be saved by the hero at the very last moment. This particular Casper stands out as the only one I recall where death itself makes an appearance. Yet, even in the face of mortality, the story concludes happily.  

A recurring theme in Famous Studios cartoons is that "virtue always triumphs." Popeye reliably reaches his spinach just in time, Baby Huey outsmarts the fox, and Little Audrey consistently learns her lesson. Of course, some FS cartoons are remarkably dark and somber.  

Credit must be given where it's due. While I adore Looney Tunes and Tom and Jerry, I believe no other studio was producing a superior cartoon product at that time than Paramount. Their use of color, animation quality, musical scores (notably by Winston Sharples), editing, and voice work was exceptional. They maintained a high standard and stood as a shining example of the best the art form had to offer.

In the era of digital fabrication, no computer can replace the skill of an actor or writer. Unfortunately, films driven primarily by compelling characters have become increasingly rare. Duvall’s performance, along with James Earl Jones’s, meets the high expectations of their audience. I wonder if this film was made for television, given its intimate, "close-up" storytelling style. To say that the performances are all outstanding would be an understatement. The only factor preventing it from being a cinematic masterpiece is the absence of a top-tier cinematographer, but stunning visuals alone do not make a great film. How is it that talents like Jones and Duvall continue to deliver such exceptional work in an age when actors are often reduced to digital poses?

A captivating film, especially for fans of horses, WWII history, and the stark Hungarian Plateau. It tells a timeless tale of bravery, kindness, and loyalty that spans generations. The horsemanship scenes are breathtaking, highlighting the main characters' training with their horses. 

I plan to purchase this movie and watch it again. It's a family-friendly film that I highly recommend—perfect for a "Family Night" movie. While it includes some intense and violent scenes due to the Nazi occupation of Hungary, the portrayal of the resilient local people standing firm, even when facing certain death from a Nazi officer with personal motives, is truly compelling. A hauntingly beautiful film that leaves a lasting impression.

Everything seemed better in the good old days, even children's television. Fraggle Rock is a perfect example that clearly supports this idea. As I write this at fourteen years old, I still can't help but be captivated by its charm. For those of you who might have been living under a rock (pun intended!), Fraggle Rock features a lively community of playful, goofy creatures called Fraggles who live inside a giant rock. But they aren't alone—the rock is also home to other species like the diligent Doozers and numerous plants. Outside the rock, on one side, lives the inventive scientist Doc and his loyal dog Sprocket, who later befriends Gobo Fraggle. On the other side are the Gorgs, a family of creatures who believe they are the rulers of the universe. The five main Fraggles—Gobo (the brave leader), Mokey (artistic and gentle), Wembley (hesitant and loyal to Gobo), Boober (pessimistic and domestic), and Red (sporty and fiery)—find themselves in strange adventures each episode, all while singing and dancing to forget their worries.  

Fraggle Rock is truly a family show. While its plots feature intricate details that younger children might miss, the appeal lies in its memorable songs and lively dance routines, making it a timeless favorite for viewers of all ages.

I find it hard to understand the negative critiques of this film. Yes, it follows a classic boy-meets-girl romance plot, but it is executed with such style and finesse that time simply slips away. Henstridge (talk about hitting the jackpot in the gene pool!) remains as captivating and charming as ever—who says the golden age of cinema is over? Vartan holds his own superbly.  

There is a palpable chemistry between the leads; the film truly comes alive whenever they share a scene—there are plenty of those! It’s so well crafted that you find yourself rooting for them to be together...  

Don’t pay attention to the naysayers—if you're feeling a bit down, watch this movie, and your mood will lift. If you're already in a good place, it will elevate you to pure euphoria.  

(P.S.: I’m 33, male, from the UK, and a hopeless romantic still on the hunt for my Princess...)

The seventeen-minute dance sequence in George Gershwin's 1928 orchestral masterpiece, "An American in Paris," stands as an undeniable masterpiece. Choreographed with meticulous precision and unmatched ingenuity by Gene Kelly, this vibrant fusion of color, music, and dance remains startlingly captivating. The sequence is divided into scenes inspired by renowned artists: Dufy in the opening Place de la Concorde, Manet at the flower market, Utrillo on a Paris street, Rousseau at the fair, Vincent Van Gogh in the spectacular Place de l'Opera, and Toulouse-Lautrec at the Moulin Rouge, where Kelly dons his iconic white bodysuit. While the 97 minutes leading up to this finale are less exhilarating, they possess their own charm, especially when viewing the entire 1951 Oscar-winning musical.

Directed by Vincente Minnelli with a screenplay by Alan Jay Lerner, the film crafts a surprisingly sophisticated yet somewhat lightweight romantic story centered on Jerry Mulligan— a former G.I. who remains in Paris after World War II, pursuing a career as a painter. With his confident demeanor and athletic dance style, Gene Kelly can be both charming and slightly irritating as a screen personality, but he manages to find...

Short but sufficiently lengthy, *Cat Soup* is a wildly surreal experience to watch. One day, while browsing through my On-Demand anime selection, I stumbled upon it and decided to give it a shot. I spent the entire duration with my jaw dropped, either completely blank or battling a fleeting urge to turn it off. However, I didn't, and in retrospect, I'm glad I didn't.  

The animation is absolutely breathtaking—highly artistic, bizarre, and darkly atmospheric. I was captivated by its stunning visuals, but the seemingly simple or vacant storyline proved just as intriguing for me.  

The plot centers around a young cat-like boy searching for his sister's soul. In the beginning, she's depicted lying sick in bed, soon visited by a reaper-like figure. Her soul is split in two—one half is recovered by the boy, while the other is lost.  

Beyond that point, the story becomes somewhat obscure to me. I believe they return to their world, which may be gradually unraveling. Perhaps her missing half of the soul holds the key to this decay, adding an enigmatic layer to the film's lingering mystery.

Oh my goodness, this movie was terrible. I watched it purely as a joke, and it’s not even so bad that it’s amusingly good in an accidental way. It honestly felt like the filmmakers intended to upset me. And they succeeded completely. It’s as if the creators took all the most irritating elements from the movie PRIEST, threw in a bunch of unattractive characters, and stripped out anything remotely interesting, funny, sexy, or clever. Then, they topped it off with a generous helping of stale, rancid cheese. That’s all this film amounts to—pure cheese. There’s not a single character you could relate to, and no universe into which this film could logically fit. Why can't a movie just be about celebrating life and happiness? Why did they have to turn what was already an absurd idea into an even more ridiculous spectacle? Why couldn’t they have at least made it an okay film or a decent B-movie? Honestly, what were they even trying to accomplish with this? I went in expecting a campy love story, and instead...

When I first watched this film in the 1980s, I was a teenager in my mid-teens and somewhat hesitant to see it, as I considered myself grown up and no longer part of the "Sesame Street/Muppets" crowd. Honestly, I can't recall whether I liked it back then or not. However, sometime during college, I watched it again, and it ultimately found a permanent place in my personal collection of Best Films Ever. 

This movie is packed with humor that surpasses what you'd typically expect from the Muppets. While the Muppets have always appealed to both kids and adults thanks to their layered humor, this film takes it to a new level. For instance, there's a scene where Janice is accidentally overheard saying, "I don't take my clothes off for anyone, even if it IS artistic." There's also a joke where a father, speaking to his son, implies that if the son is in love with Kermit the Frog, the father prefers not to hear about it. Gonzo hilariously rescues a chicken with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, then quips, "I think we're engaged now." Moments like these had me laughing out loud. Plus, the film features sharp dialogue and clever Broadway-inspired humor that adds to its charm.

This film is truly terrible, with not a single scene that captures genuine emotion. The characters are flat, poorly developed, and predictably stereotypical, while the plot is overly obvious and echoes the standard Hollywood fantasy of wish fulfillment.  

William Holden, who was 55 when the movie was made, is cast as a man in his early 40s, yet he looks more like he's in his sixties. Kay Lenz, only 20 at the time, was supposed to find him irresistibly attractive, but honestly, the dog they found by the roadside appears more lively and sexier than their supposed erotic connection.  

Holden’s character, coincidentally the same age Clint Eastwood was when he directed this film, is set against clichéd 60s "cool" backdrops—bachelor pads, swinging hi-fi systems, lunches at Yamashiro. Yet, the movie itself is painfully unhip, a jarring collection of clichés of aging men desperately clinging to the fantasy that the free-spirited youth seen on Sunset and in Laurel Canyon will find them and their oversized cars alluring.  

Ugh. Youth culture was never that desperate. It’s unsettling to think that William Holden was so eager to chase youth that he took on this embarrassing role.

This extended 4-hour remake of the Rider Haggard tale features the usual addition of a female character and an extraneous subplot involving Russian soldiers searching for a "Stone of Power" buried with King Solomon's treasure. Visually, it's very well shot, vividly capturing the vast open landscapes of Africa, and the performances are strong. Patrick Swayze delivers an excellent portrayal of Alan Quatermain, while Allison Doody is charming as Elizabeth Maitland, who hires Quatermain to rescue her father. Memorable supporting roles include Sidede Onyulo as Umbopa, Gavin Hood as McNabb, and the unnamed leader of the Russian soldiers. Despite Hollywood's tendency to alter classic stories, this adaptation is well told, and aside from its excessive length, I found it enjoyable. 6/10.

With an IMDb rating of 8.1, I had high expectations for this film, but it ultimately fell short. It begins with humor and charm, bursting with a spontaneous energy that draws you in. However, before reaching the halfway mark, the pacing slows, and the plot becomes excessively predictable. The office characters are delightful early on, but as the story develops, we get to know them a little too well—transforming into caricatures rather than genuine individuals. The plot echoes countless similar stories, only slightly altered in circumstances. The real disappointment lies in the dialogue, which remains painfully stale; I could tolerate another predictable romance if the conversations were more engaging. Worse still, the characters’ motivations are inconsistent and unconvincing, a flaw that also marred Dead Letter Office. Hopefully, this film will soon join the ranks of forgotten movies.

The film remains vague for too long, offering very little exposition as it unfolds. As a result, many sequences come across as odd and seemingly loaded with hidden meaning, but due to the storytelling approach, they only feel confusing and difficult to grasp. It almost invites a second viewing, but I have no intention of doing so. I watched this film in the morning, and I’m certain that if I had seen it at night, I would have nodded off. To me, it feels like a poor imitation of "Blade Runner." 

The movie leaves numerous questions unanswered and features many implausibilities, ultimately resulting in a shallow and forgettable impression. 

Additionally, its unconventional visual style doesn’t do it any favors. The film is a mix of CGI and live action, but the execution isn’t as polished, impressive, or imaginative as later films like "Sin City" or "300." They even generated some characters entirely through computer-generated imagery, which seemed like a pointless and strange choice—especially considering the quality of the character animation itself.

Among all the films I've watched, this one ranks near the bottom—only kept from the absolute worst by films like Haunted Mansion, Nothing but Trouble, and a few others. The pacing is rushed, the story wobbles, and the performances are painfully stiff. Some of this can be attributed to the source material; the book on which the film is based is excruciatingly slow and makes little sense. Oprah delivers a decently appealing portrayal as Bigger’s mother but falls short of her true potential. Other well-known actors also seem to be performing their worst. The storyline revolves around an African American man who takes a job as a chauffeur. While driving the family’s daughter to a communist dinner, he strikes up a friendship with her. Things take a turn when she gets drunk. The family he's working for isn’t racist, but he perceives them to be. When he returns home, he tucks her into bed, but she starts to make a fuss. The blind mother (yes, really) hears the commotion, and Bigger tries to quiet her—misjudging the situation, he ends up smothering her. Fearing he’ll be in serious trouble for killing a white girl, he then does what any rational person would do—he shoves her into...

This film was truly a disappointment. Watching it was a painful experience. Nearly every action scene lacked motivation within the story, and the performances were quite poor—P. Diddy being the only somewhat credible actor, which really speaks volumes about the overall quality. The plot was largely predictable, with only some nods to Carlito's Way, like his aspiration to move to the Caribbean, offering minor interest. Overall, these references felt weak. I also found the love interest to be completely off, though I suppose that’s up for debate. Honestly, I didn’t have high expectations before viewing, and unfortunately, they weren’t even met. I feel somewhat sorry for Jay Hernandez, who is a talented actor, as seen in Friday Night Lights—he’s fortunate this film isn’t likely to attract many viewers. I usually give movies a fair rating if they even manage to pique my interest, so I’ll give this one two stars. Better luck next time. And yes, I did enjoy Carlito’s Way.

As a devoted fan of Neil Young's music, I was eager to see Greendale, especially after hearing the glowing praise it received from many alt-indie publications. I managed to catch the earliest screening available. Unfortunately, my enthusiasm was quickly dampened by a plot that felt sluggish and a lyrical flow that lacked momentum, leaving most of the audience either snoozing or thoroughly disappointed.

Neil mentions that the film originated as a soundtrack, and the characters were so vividly brought to life that they simply filmed the music. This approach, however, is not ideal for storytelling. No character truly undergoes development, and when "important" events occur, viewers remain indifferent, overwhelmed by distracting filmmaking techniques. The entire film is composed of songs, with characters mouthing the lyrics as they sing—an effect that works briefly at the start but quickly becomes tiresome. It neither feels authentic nor artificial; it just feels out of place and unwelcome.

The acting is generally poor, with characters sticking to a single emotional tone throughout. There are also instances of inadequate lighting. The only aspect worth mentioning is the use of scenes shot as news broadcasts; however, this technique is so common in cinema nowadays that it adds little originality.

I believe the first episode of the series was a tremendous success. It was incredibly entertaining, and I thought the actors did a fantastic job. It’s unfair for anyone to criticize it as being bad, since it captured the right atmosphere. I find it quite frustrating when people complain about its historical accuracy, because it’s meant to be a Saturday night entertainment show, not a dull history documentary. In my opinion, the costumes and sets were perfect. It was a fantastic beginning, and I’m really looking forward to what comes next! I’ve also talked to many of my classmates, and they love the show too. We all agree that it’s excellent entertainment, with great stories to go along with it.

This past weekend, I rented this movie and turned up the surround sound system, which delivered fantastic sound effects. It's a great rental choice—the special effects were intense enough to scare my fiancé, although I did notice some looked surprisingly computer-generated. I didn't see it in theaters, but it's perfect for a spooky late-night stay-in movie when you're not in the mood to go out. I definitely recommend it!

This film is an excellent movie, with each actor effectively portraying their roles. The story is engaging, centering around Raj, who falls in love with Priya and they eventually marry. Priya later becomes pregnant, but unforeseen complications prevent them from having a child. Raj then meets Madhu and persuades her to assist him; she becomes pregnant despite not being married to him. The film is truly captivating, featuring wonderful dialogues and melodious songs. The picturization is impressive, especially the vibrant wedding scene. Salman, Rani, and Preity deliver outstanding performances. The cinematography is remarkable, with beautiful scenes captured in Switzerland. Overall, the cast enhances the movie’s appeal, making it well worth the time and money. Rating: 8/10

Inspired by a real mining disaster, this early German talkie (with English subtitles) remains one of the most powerful docudramas ever created. Featuring many non-professional actors, "Kameradschaft" offers a haunting portrayal of the bond that unites mine workers, regardless of whether they are French or German. When a tragic accident occurs, it brings out the best in everyone, overriding authority and official orders. Fellow miners in distress receive aid from their comrades, even at great personal risk, including their lives.

The film evokes the heroic self-sacrifice exemplified by the NYFD after the September 11 attacks. Putting aside formal protocols, these brave men and women in uniform operated with a single purpose: to save lives and reunite with their fallen comrades. Over seventy years later, "Kameradschaft" continues to convey a timeless message: a friend in need is a friend indeed.

Having watched this film multiple times across various short-film festivals, I often feel as if I've seen a movie trailer rather than a full-length film. While the production quality and direction for a school project are impressive, the story itself could have benefited from more depth to make it larger and more engaging. The character Tim Watcher, in particular, needed a more in-depth exploration. Unfortunately, this superficial approach is common in some Portuguese short films, where the script tends to lack complexity. Nonetheless, I still enjoyed the movie. Congratulations!

Many argue that Antz is the superior film. While Antz is indeed a well-made movie, I found myself enjoying A Bug's Life even more. Few Pixar animations—aside from the Toy Story series—had me laughing as hard as this one. The animation is crisp, the story fresh and free of preachiness. The voice acting truly elevates the film; Dave Foley delivers a sincere ant struggling with frequent mishaps, while Kevin Spacey’s Hopper is a brilliantly crafted villain, complemented by Haydn Panettiere’s charming Dot. The supporting cast, including Dennis Leary, David Hyde Pierce, and Madeline Kahn, provides exceptional performances, and the script is sharp—hilarious, and at times, genuinely moving. Though it lacks the social messaging present in Antz, the movie stands strong as pure entertainment. A solid 9 out of 10. Bethany Cox

Jason Lee's chest makes a return! If that's what you're after, you've found it. If not, you'd better keep searching...

Now, about the film itself: filled with clichés, some awkwardly filmed but somewhat exotic fight scenes (featuring JKD techniques), and plenty of poor acting paired with cheap special effects. Lee appears to be in pain throughout the entire runtime, and honestly, it's no pleasant comeback.

The movie doesn't even qualify as a true B-movie. There was a stereotypical German-esque bleached blonde villain reminiscent of Rutger Hauer, yet surprisingly, there were no gratuitous sex scenes or even a single shot of nudity—nothing at all. Even in *Starship Troopers 2*, they understood the importance of including the mandatory nude scenes (for more on that cinematic gem, stay tuned for our upcoming review of that mind-blowing sequel...). It felt like the writer was taking revenge on someone, so I won’t delve into the plot or any other details. One thing to note: it had some non-heterosexual undertones, but that’s about all I’ll say on that.

On the bright side, there is one thing this movie reliably delivers—no Jean-Claude Van Damme.

First, sketch out your script on a napkin—who needs more than that? After all, we're not making a blockbuster. Then, cast some amateur actors; it'll boost the festival buzz. Who cares about seasoned performers? Next, hire a cinematographer who can't light a scene. If it's too well-lit, it won't seem "real," and festival judges will overlook it. Professional-grade cinematography is overrated anyway. Finally, hire a ten-year-old unfamiliar with cameras to operate it. This will lend your film that raw, amateurish feel, making festival selectors mistake it for "authenticity" and ensuring that, despite drawing only a handful of viewers, critics and over-analytical fans will praise it as "brilliant" because they won’t believe it’s just pure amateur hour. Once you've assembled this masterpiece, buy your ticket to the Festival of Bad Movies—Sundance. What a tragic waste.

Michael Rooker is a capable actor, but he's hardly suited for a leading role outside of low-budget films. His charisma leaves much to be desired. Ryo Ishibashi, on the other hand, commands a stronger screen presence, yet unfortunately, he isn't the main character. Instead, most of the screen time is dominated by the stoic Rooker.  

Danielle Harris, known from Halloween 4 and 5, portrays Rooker's daughter. She is charming and fun to watch, but her character is written as rather naïve, and one of her foolish mistakes results in the death of a key character. The film also features interesting roles for comedians Fred Willard, Bobcat Goldthwait, and Stephen Furst. Observing the fates of these characters provides some priceless moments.  

Vincent Schiavelli plays the consigliere to the local Mafia boss, and it's ambiguous whether he's delivering a comedic performance. Tim Thomerson also appears in the film, a regular fixture in low-budget, direct-to-video action movies. He's also known for roles in some low-budget comedies. The presence of so many comedians and comic actors lends the film a spoof-like feel. Is it a parody of a Yakuza movie? That remains uncertain.

I found it nearly incomprehensible that this film could be a flop, yet I was genuinely disappointed. As a longtime aficionado of Peckinpah’s cinema, I stumbled upon this DVD—significantly discounted—and decided to give it a try. The opening credits, a signature touch for Peckinpah fans, feature the classic inter-cutting between a man and an animal. However, here, the scene is overlaid with non-diegetic ambient sounds of children playing in a schoolyard while a bomb is being planted—an intensely suspenseful moment. Later, when the villains, Caan and Duval, head to their next assignment, Duval casually drops a bombshell on Caan: his date from the previous night had an STD, discovered by rummaging through her purse during their intimate moment. The resulting laughter is superb and clearly pays homage to Brian De Palma’s *Dressed to Kill*, albeit at the expense of Angie Dickinson. The flaw with *The Killer Elite* is that after the opening credits, the film loses its momentum. Even *Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia* boasts stronger production values—a bold statement for anyone familiar with these films. I often reference Peckinpah’s credits as supplemental teaching material, but once they’re over, I recommend turning *The Killer Elite* off.

Greetings once more from the shadows. This film may draw comparisons to "The Princess Bride," and while it doesn't quite reach that legendary status, it remains highly entertaining and crafted with care. The plot has some odd elements, particularly the mysterious wall that is never fully explained, but the overall execution is solid, building genuine suspense.

Charlie Cox stars as Tristan, who falls for the wrong girl—played by Sienna Miller—and promises to retrieve a fallen star for her. That star turns out to be played by the breathtaking Claire Danes. While the romantic tension between Tristan and the star is predictable, the real intrigue involves the wicked witch, portrayed by Michelle Pfeiffer, and the prince, son of King Peter O'Toole, who seeks to reclaim the ruby necklace adorning the star. A lot of chasing and conflict ensues between good and evil.

Along the journey, viewers are introduced to the most eccentric pirate you’ll ever see—surpassing even those from the Caribbean. Robert De Niro delivers a memorable performance as Captain Shakespeare—tough and formidable yet surprisingly in touch with his feminine side. There's also a delightful appearance by Ricky Gervais as a quick-talking trader, providing some well-timed humor.

Not

I spent nearly the entire series enduring teenage angst and family conflicts. Honestly, I couldn't care less about high school girls worrying over their relationships. I've already faced such issues in my own personal hell, and I have no interest in watching fictional teens go through watered-down versions of those horrors. What I want is science fiction—that's the only reason I'm watching. There was a brief moment of sci-fi toward the end of the episode when we finally saw a proto-Cylon. It was a good step, but it had one flaw: its red eye-dot was locked onto an object of interest. We all know that Cylon eye-dots typically scan back and forth, building a map of their surroundings. However, this red eye-dot never paused; it kept oscillating, which doesn't match the established behavior. I sincerely hope the writers address this inconsistency before the next episode.

Embarrassing. This is what results when a director shows up just because he's getting paid.  

The intentions were noble—fantastic locations and settings suited for an epic film. But the execution, wow! In some shots, extras can be seen staring directly into the camera or glancing at the actors because no one briefed them on what to do once "Action!" is called. The battle scenes are so poorly choreographed that you wonder—are these actors even real? They could have caused more damage by simply embracing each other. During slow-motion shots, you can observe people wandering around the battlefield or standing still, waving their hands aimlessly.  

The only action that stands out is in the foreground, but for what purpose? The story is so illogical and disjointed that it feels like a series of random scenes jammed together, sometimes even without chronological order. The dialogue is senseless, and the romantic subplot is more embarrassing and absurd than in typical Hong Kong action flicks.  

With a budget of $40 million, you can see where every dollar went—ultimately, the best outcome of this massive effort is a shiny, round laser disc.

About twenty minutes into the film, I found myself already bored. Frankly, the characters were quite uninteresting. Every so often, something engaging would occur, but then the story would drag again. Luckily, my patience paid off, and the ending turned out to be quite decent. Still, it wasn't enough to make the first ninety minutes worth watching. Overall, I’d describe the movie as mediocre, and given the talented cast, I can't help but feel disappointed.

Panic In The Streets begins with a striking noir aesthetic—a shot down a shadowy street that gradually tilts upward to reveal a window where a sordid card game unfolds. This opening flourish, combined with some location filming, anticipates the atmospheric tone that Orson Welles would later achieve in Touch of Evil a decade afterward. When one of the players flings open the window, it serves a dual purpose: it introduces the unfolding drama within and offers our first vivid glimpse into the seedy underworld.  

Filmed in stark black and white, Panic In The Streets gains much from a compelling cast and authentic location shots in New Orleans. Scenes set in places like the mortuary, the bustling shipping office, or amidst the worn paint of Frank's Place create a uniquely tense and often claustrophobic ambiance—impossible to replicate on a studio set. These elements reflect the influence of Jules Dassin’s pioneering Naked City, released two years earlier, which pioneered a gritty, almost documentary-style approach within the noir genre. Interestingly, Widmark’s previous role was in Dassin’s even more acclaimed Night and the City, a film that...

We bought this film as a joke for a friend, but it might have been our worst prank yet. The movie is barely watchable, with acting that’s painfully bad. The child actor is arguably the worst we've ever seen, and Hasslehoff’s performance is disappointing. The plot is disgraceful, and at times we were so bored that we wondered what on earth was happening. It attempts to be gruesome in some scenes, but it comes across as nothing more than laughable. Simply put, it's terrible.

Who would have thought they could be so hilarious? Christopher Meloni and Janel Moloney are best known for their stellar performances in some of television's most popular dramas—"Law & Order: SVU" and "The West Wing." Bringing them together on the big screen results in a charming romantic comedy packed with plenty of laughs.  

The actors skillfully develop the evolving relationship at the story’s core, making it easy for audiences to root for Barry Singer (Meloni), even though he's a stand-up comic with a sharp tongue and a sexist streak.  

You'll find yourself cheering for him as he grapples with insecurities about the opposite sex and chases Thea (Moloney) across the country in hopes of winning her over. They seem to have almost nothing in common, yet when Barry finally lets his guard down, you'll start to wonder why Thea keeps running away.  

The Souler Opposite is a delightful film featuring an incredible cast and a talented writer. It’s definitely worth your time.

No, I’ve never watched any of the "Santa Slasher" series, such as "Silent Night, Deadly Night," the original "Black Christmas," or this one, "Christmas Evil." I’ve heard all about their reputation, or what Mothers Against Deranged Santas (MADS) have to say. I decided to rent this one after hearing it mentioned in a "Fat Guys At the Movies" segment.  

Mothers should be outraged, not because of the "killer" Santa, but because the film is just plain terrible. Boring and drawn-out—even at only 92 minutes, it’s a complete dud.  

The story starts with a boy in 1947 witnessing Santa arrive down a chimney, deliver presents, eat some treats, and then miraculously float back up. That night, he goes to bed, only to return to the living room and see his mother and Santa (sort of) getting intimate. Apparently, this traumatized him for life, though the scene was as provocative as Ralphie’s dad’s "Leg Lamp" in "A Christmas Story." So disturbed was he that he went to the attic and, well, cut his own hand.  

Fast forward to 1980. The now-grown troubled boy works in a toy factory. We get a

If you're into derivative, predictable rape-revenge thrillers, then you'll find this to be a rare treat... However, they don't really resonate with me, and I couldn't find a single redeeming aspect in this odd story. It feels like something straight out of the 1980s—a different era when it might have gone straight to video. Gillian Anderson and Danny Dyer do their best with a weak script and an uninspired plot. But I have to ask—what was Gillian Anderson thinking, choosing to participate in a film like this after delivering such a remarkable performance as Lady Deadlock in the BBC adaptation of Bleak House last year? The director claims his inspiration came from witnessing a near-rape and his documentary work, yet that hardly justifies the bizarre scene where a pack of rural hounds attacks Dyer. I wasn't the only one in the cinema laughing at that moment. What puzzles me even more is the involvement of the production companies—FilmFour and Verve Pictures. Both have recently been behind some excellent independent British films; Verve distributed titles like Bullet Boy, Code 46, and Red Road. Straightheads, however, doesn't deserve to be mentioned in the same breath.

That summer, I spent several days on set during the filming of this movie, but in the end, only two scenes made it into the final cut. The scenes were shot at Sylvan Lake in the Black Hills, involving bringing the wagon and stopping the wagon. As a young Dakota, I was eager to see the film and wasn't disappointed. During filming, the local buffalo herd was being culled, so the scenes involving animals were authentic—yes, Doris, some animals were harmed during production. I believe the film’s ending was later echoed by Jack Nicholson in *The Shining*. It’s a compelling western with social commentary from the 1950s—worthy of being ranked alongside *High Noon* for its genuine Western drama or serving as a social statement akin to *Blackboard Jungle* or *Rebel Without a Cause* for 50s youth.

This film can be summarized as a modest effort. It is a decent sixties movie, but it lacks a sense of achievement. Maggie Smith delivered a credible performance, though it could have been more compelling; unfortunately, other actors delivered poor and unconvincing portrayals. The film failed to be genuinely funny, missing the mark in both comedy and drama, and the only genre it managed to fulfill satisfactorily was romance. The intended target audiences were not effectively reached, and the film conveyed confusing messages. With a basic plot and a straightforward storyline, it was poorly executed, leaving viewers puzzled about its shortcomings and audience focus. Nonetheless, Maggie Smith's performance was commendable, and the storyline showed some moments of promise.  
4.

First and foremost, yes, I am white, so I approach the sensitive topic of race with caution... Anyway... White people hating Black people is considered bad, but Black people hating White people is somehow acceptable (as if we somehow deserved it!). Where do I even begin? I wish I had something positive to say about this movie apart from its unintentional comedy moments: the infamous scene where Ice Cube and his crew fight some enormous, furious, and intimidating Neo-Nazis—and somehow, they come out on top! The Neo-Nazis are twice their size, and the chase scene that follows is priceless. 

This isn’t a film about race, tolerance, or understanding; it fails to deliver on any of those fronts. Instead, it’s a racist film that reinforces clichés and stereotypes—the weak white guy who gets dominated by his Black roommate automatically transforms into a skinhead. Honestly, it’s simply awful. I regret having watched it.

Save yourself the trouble of enduring a poorly written, poorly acted, dull, and blatantly biased film. If you're interested in the subject, rent *American History X*—now that’s a movie worth watching.

Allen retreats to the countryside—an place he notoriously dislikes—and spends the weekend with his friends, who are the typical successful, white, middle-class complainers that populate many of his films. 

Usually, I find some humor in Woody Allen comedies, but this one completely misses the mark. Even the sharp one-liners seem to have abandoned him. The film has no coherent plot—just scattered snippets of faux-Shakespearean dialogue—while Allen attempts to lend the setting a mystical aura, which only renders the film more dull and undercooked. 

It fails on every level and becomes an outright bore. The only redeeming aspect—the impending end credits—is overshadowed by the fact that the negative reviews seem to jolt him into the realization that cobbling together a haphazard script and casting friends does not automatically guarantee entertainment.

Understanding the age of a film can help set expectations and make the viewing experience more tolerable. With that in mind, I approached Revolt of the Zombies, and true to form, it features the typical reliance on dull dialogue and cheesy movements. The primitive special effects—or lack thereof—are also what I anticipated for its era. Such limitations place a heavy burden on the viewer’s imagination—perhaps too much in this case. The storyline itself is somewhat confusing: during WWI, a group of zombified Southeast Asian soldiers perform remarkably well, though the reasons for this are unclear and sensitive if true; thus, a team is sent to investigate archaeologically, keeping the secret from falling into the wrong hands. A member of this expedition learns the secret of long-distance hypnosis, which he uses for various purposes, including temporarily replacing his love interest’s beau. To demonstrate his devotion, he relinquishes his control over everyone, a decision that backfires since, once they’re unzombified, many turn against him in hopes of reclaiming control. Overall, it’s below average, even considering its constraints. Only the most patient viewers should consider watching it.

This film is intended to be a tense, mysterious thriller about a man searching for a missing girl. However, by the 30-minute mark, it devolves into a comical, unrealistic mess populated by annoying characters and random scenes. It’s hard not to laugh when Cage suddenly executes a Karate kick on a blonde girl or when he "bear" punches an elderly woman. The dialogue, characters, and performances are poorly crafted from the start. Although I’ve always admired Nicolas Cage as an actor, he has starred in several terrible movies this year, and this one is by far the worst yet.  

I wouldn't recommend this film to anyone seeking a gripping, intense thriller. If you genuinely want to enjoy the story, it's better to watch the original instead. But if you do decide to watch this movie, be prepared to find humor in some of the lines and scenes rather than taking them seriously — that’s the only way to get some entertainment out of it.

What were they thinking? Over the years, the Columbo series has experimented with new ideas and strayed from its tried-and-true formula, but this movie takes it way too far. It’s fundamentally different from any other Columbo installment, and not in a good way. 

The most obvious difference is that there is no murder to solve. The entire premise is completely altered, placing Columbo in an entirely different environment and situation. The overall tone is also much more modernized and distinct from the classic style fans know and love.

Director Alan J. Levi had previously helmed other Columbo movies that adhered closely to the traditional formula, making his involvement in this departure somewhat surprising. 

Additionally, the character of Columbo himself feels noticeably different, likely because he’s placed in unfamiliar circumstances—helping his nephew after his bride vanished immediately after the wedding. The signature humor and charm that typically define Columbo are noticeably absent here, further distancing this film from the essence of the series.

Richard Dix decided to retire, and Michael Duane stepped in to take over the role of Ted Nichols. In this story, Ted meets a young French girl named Alice Dupres Barkley (Lenore Aubert). The two only knew each other for two days before they decided to get married before a Justice of the Peace. However, as they arrive at the judge's house in a heavy downpour, they discover he's not home and won't return until the next day. While inside, someone secretly lifts the hood of their car and removes a part from the engine. This startling event signals that the couple is about to face a major surprise, as the narrative begins to unravel a mysterious situation surrounding Alice Barkley. Ted Nichols, initially full of hope, quickly finds himself entangled in trouble and without a marriage. An intriguing mystery unfolds—though I must admit, I missed Richard Dix. Enjoy the story.

Released in 1984, this film featured Prince at the height of his popularity. Crowned as one of the hottest artists of the era, everyone was eager to see this movie, which essentially functioned as an extended music video. The acting left much to be desired—understandable given that it was many musicians’ first foray into big-screen acting. Nonetheless, it remained highly entertaining! Morris Day and Jerome Benton deliver timeless comic performances, particularly with their hilarious rendition of "The Password," reminiscent of Abbott & Costello’s classic "Who's on First" routine.

Appolina, who was known by a single name at the time, contributed some striking visuals, including brief nudity, and her attractiveness certainly added to the film’s appeal. The soundtrack, a collection of some of Prince’s finest work, stands out as one of his best recordings. Although Prince later parted ways with Warner Bros. and adopted a different name, he was undeniably at the peak of his creative powers during this period.

While this film may not be classified among the all-time greats, it remains thoroughly enjoyable.

When I was nine years old, my parents took me to see this movie, and I have never forgotten that experience. At the time, I had never seen anything as stunning as Elizabeth Taylor. (She was twenty-two when she starred in Elephant Walk.) Keep in mind, I was just nine, so my feelings weren't romantic; I simply couldn't take my eyes off her on the screen. I wanted nothing more than to sit at her feet like a puppy and gaze up at her. Although she is nearing seventy-four now and has started to show her age, I still believe she remains one of the most beautiful and breathtaking women who has ever lived.

Since then, I’ve watched the film several times. It’s a sentimental melodrama at its core, but what makes it worth it are Miss Taylor’s extraordinary beauty, stunning scenery, the impressive elephant stampede, and the meaningful message about human arrogance in the face of nature.

Overall, it was a few enjoyable hours spent watching the movie channel or a rented video.

This film delivers some truly gripping and chilling moments for a debut. In true horror style, it keeps your stomach clenched with tension throughout. The ending is exceptional—crafted in a way that feels less like conclusion and more like the start of something even darker. A remarkable movie, and among Japan's finest in the horror genre, earning a perfect score. It provokes deep thought while leaving you terrified out of your mind.

This review contains spoilers.

"Rosenstraße" is a film about courageous women during Nazi Germany. However, it is overly long, fails to evoke real emotion, and at times becomes boring. The movie is laden with clichés and suffers from weak performances.

The storytelling is poorly executed. Similar to James Cameron's *Titanic*, an elderly woman recounts her life experiences to provide a perspective. Soon after, another woman is introduced, also recounting events, which becomes confusing because both are describing the lives of other people. This indicates a fundamental misunderstanding of narrative structure—how could Riemann know details about the fate of the young girl’s mother or her interrogation, for example? It feels like a misstep in storytelling.

The scenes are arranged out of chronological order, making it difficult to determine when events occur. For instance, the scene where Riemann proposes to Fabian appears to be set in the 1920s, but the timeline isn’t clear.

Riemann’s character is portrayed as a talented pianist and even a baroness—impressive, perhaps. Her brother returns from the Eastern Front, proudly displaying a "Ritterkreuz" (Knight’s Cross), suggesting he’s a decorated war hero.

Kimi wa Petto is a charming story about a girl who one day discovers a boy inside a box outside her apartment. She decides to bring him inside, tending to his wounds. She then leaves a note asking him to eat some food she prepared and to go home since she has to leave for work. However, when she returns, she finds that he is still there. He tells her he wants to stay with her like a brother or cousin. Desperate to get him to leave, she jokingly suggests that he could stay if he became her pet—implying that as her pet, he would have no rights and would do whatever she told him (not in a perverted way). To her surprise, he agrees, and from then on, he is known as Momo, her pet.

This film is to the Zatoichi series what the "Star Trek" movies were to the original TV show—except, in this case, every one of the original films was far more engaging and compelling than this glossy remake, and also better crafted, if substance takes precedence over style. Had I never seen the original Zatoichi films, I might have found this visually appealing but hollow; however, having watched the originals, I found its style inappropriate and its substance lacking. The notion of reviving the character in a bigger, sleeker production probably seemed appealing, but ultimately served no purpose beyond the hope of profit. It’s merely a spectacle that largely fails to evoke the essence of Zatoichi’s world and doesn’t take the character anywhere new—nor does the actor deliver a compelling performance. I had hoped to see Ichi in his later years, in a story that would allow him to fade gracefully and reflect on his journey, but all we get are rehashed snippets from past films, padded with more sex and CGI violence. It’s a completely different experience, and not for the better.

What an underrated 80s soundtrack. I can picture John Travolta singing some of those tracks, but watching the movie, it truly embodied all the cheesy tropes of the decade. Clearly, films that featured mechanical bulls, bartenders, and immature relationships were all the rage. The highlight was his hilariously bad Texas accent. Compared to the more authentic feel of Friday Night Lights, this was pure 80s fluff. To really dive into the cheesy side of film, I recommend watching Cocktail and Stir Crazy. On a side note, Made in America with Ted Danson and Whoopi Goldberg is hilariously bad—I was amazed to realize I’d never seen it before. Another oddball of this genre is Cadillac Man with Robin Williams. Just remember, some of the biggest stars—Tom Cruise, Richard Pryor, Robin Williams, and John Travolta—all starred in these delightfully cheesy movies.

This Chinese film resonated deeply with me, evoking a sense of familiarity with a culture I do not belong to and am distant from. Embracing an almost Buddhist perspective, the movie encourages viewers to connect with each character and find joy in the simplicity of everyday routines.  

The performances are exceptional; Xu Hzu radiates kindness and wisdom while also revealing moments of vulnerability and meanness. Er Min, the developmentally challenged brother, illustrates that intelligence and wisdom are not one and the same, and that true wisdom can emerge from the most unlikely individuals in this universe. This portrayal presents a different vision of China—distinct from traditional realism, yet rich in humanity and a different kind of authenticity.  

See it. You won't be disappointed.

This film is quite disappointing, but I have some interesting tidbits to share about it:

It was shot in 1976 at Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff, AZ, as well as at Oak Creek Canyon near Sedona, AZ. A large number of the extras were drama students from NAU at the time. I was a freshman that year, minoring in theatre, but for some reason, I didn't get involved in the production. However, I knew several people who did, and I can share this rather peculiar fact:

In one scene, two of the main characters, as part of their hazing ritual, run naked into the woods. They are shown from behind in the movie, doing just that. The twist is, those aren't professional actors; they're two guys I knew from the theatre department. Their identities as the "stunt posteriors" will remain anonymous here—unless they choose to "reveal" themselves!

As a devoted fan of Anthony Hopkins' acting, I was eager to see his work as a writer and director. Sadly, I found myself deeply disappointed. The film was disjointed, and the cinematography was so excessive that it became distracting—so much so that I felt like unplugging the projector. While the cast delivered strong performances, it was a shame to see such talent go to waste. Not every actor is suited for writing or directing, and clearly, Mr. Hopkins falls into that category. In my 50 years of movie-watching, this stands out as the worst film I have ever seen. Mr. Hopkins, please do us all a favor and stick to acting, where you excel, and leave the writing and directing to those truly skilled in those fields. If there were a rating below one, I would gladly give it.

I believe Michael Ironside's acting career may be over if he's willing to take roles in such low-budget garbage. Surely, he has the talent to do better than waste his time on this rubbish.  

This film could have been much better with a proper budget, but that deficiency is evident throughout the entire movie. One particular scene at an outpost appears to be filmed outside a train station, and I suspect that’s exactly where it was shot.
