There’s a single scene that earns this movie a three-star rating—when the spaceship lands and takes off over a lake surrounded by forest. That scene was well-executed, but the rest of the film is forgettable.  

Another scene looks like it's set at an engineering plant, which I highly doubt it is. It certainly doesn't resemble the space outpost the characters claim it to be.  

Overall, this movie is foolish, clearly low-budget, nonsensical, and honestly, I feel sorry for Michael Ironside.

I watched this film last night on cable, and it truly is exceptional. What I admire most is its subtlety and understated approach, yet it remains profoundly heartfelt. Henry Thomas, known for playing the boy in E.T., delivers a masterful performance that is intentionally reserved and inarticulate, fitting his character as a man of few words. David Straithern shines as a wonderfully unhinged villain. Remarkably, given that it’s a Hollywood production, a baby is a central character—though not through dialogue or acting, but simply by existing, luminous and vital. It’s interesting to note that Thomas’ enigmatic relationship with E.T. was the heart of that film, while his connection with the baby stands at the core of "A Good Baby." 

The music is also a highlight—absolutely incredible. Gillian Welch’s songs are beautiful, and the entire score features stunning hill country melodies. 

This film creates a richly atmospheric experience. I highly recommend it.

This film appears to favor a pro-Muslim perspective. Why do I say that? The protagonist has a Muslim father and a Christian mother. He spends his first 20 years in a Christian village. By the end of the film, he seems to have converted to Islam—evidenced by his head covering, the amulet he still wears, and his overall attire. He also has a six-year-old child who wears the same headgear, suggesting the child is Muslim as well, despite the mother being Christian. It seems that the main character has chosen to embrace Islam, leading his child to follow suit. The other male main characters, who are Christians, do not appear to have children. Overall, the depiction suggests there are more Muslims in this world by the film’s conclusion.

Legendary film producer Walt Disney brought three of the world's most beloved fairy tales to the silver screen, each remaining among the most cherished animated classics of all time. The first was his pioneering masterpiece, "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs," debuting in 1937. The last was the then-overlooked "Sleeping Beauty," which premiered in 1959. Between these two standouts was perhaps his most heartfelt adaptation of a fairy tale: "Cinderella" (1950). Of the trio, "Cinderella" stays closest to its original story. Ironically, unlike "Snow White," which for many became the definitive version—good or bad—"Cinderella" took a different route. While it was a commercial success and, like "Snow White," helped revive Disney's fortunes, it never quite achieved the widespread recognition it truly deserved. In this instance, Disney honored the classic by choosing not to alter it, instead enriching the narrative with depth and detail rather than rewriting it for the screen. The result was truly magical. 

A blend of exquisite animation in lush Technicolor and perfectly cast voice performances brought the tale to life with a brilliance that continues to captivate audiences today.

Television undeniably influences society—just consider the spike in popularity of cappuccino shops following the debut of this superficial little program. Moreover, it’s amusing how truly attractive people like those on TV apparently face no real struggles.  

And honestly, does anyone genuinely believe these characters can afford a stylish Manhattan loft given their line of work? NBC seems intent on underestimating its audience, even if they are only as perceptive as Forrest Gump. I know a web designer earning $100,000 annually who still lives in a cramped one-bedroom apartment in Manhattan that rents for $2,200 a month.  

I’d love to see a show called *Phriends*, featuring six ordinary, unattractive people working dead-end jobs in a seedy neighborhood where sirens never stop wailing and someone gets mugged weekly—only to have the landlord hike up the rent. Now that’s a series I’d actually watch.

For the first twenty minutes or so (though I was watching on a PS2, so I have no precise idea of the runtime), Alienator presents an intriguing premise. It's not every day you see a slasher flick featuring an extraterrestrial as the villain. Yet, any initial curiosity quickly gives way to stunned disbelief when you realize the so-called 'alien' is actually a colossal bodybuilder woman clad in a steel bikini. Yes, Alienator is undeniably absurd.  

I don't hold that against it, though. In the realm of B-movie horror, outright ridiculousness can often be a charm. Unfortunately, the film's main strength is simply its sheer stupidity. Alienator is hilarious, but also a chaotic mess of epic proportions. The actors deliver earnest but failed attempts at seriousness, while potentially great lines of cheesy dialogue are butchered with baffling clumsiness. The direction struggles to craft even one memorable set-piece, leaving you with a sense that the original concept is buried beneath an overwhelming pile of garbage.  

Adding to the chaos, the 'Alien' character kills victims by vaporizing them—a detail that...

I was expecting an in-depth background on the Apollo 11 mission, but what I received was somewhat decent interview material with Buzz Aldrin, Gene Kranz, and other involved individuals. Unfortunately, it was accompanied by a sensationalized, disaster-predicting voice-over that seemed typical of TV's worst tendencies. 

If the voice-over had been removed and the program reframed as a positive story about how perseverance can lead to extraordinary achievements, it could have been quite inspiring. Instead, I feel like I wasted about 45 minutes of my life watching a 60-minute program—those minutes I want back.

I guess I must be that one guy in America who didn't enjoy this movie. Honestly, it just wasn’t my style, and I fail to see what’s so captivating about it. It was barely entertaining, let alone one of the greatest achievements in cinema history. 

The plot is about a guy who rises from nothing to become a drug lord. That’s a pretty straightforward summary of the entire film, and it reflects how I felt about the whole experience. Contrary to popular belief, just because a movie centers on mafias, drug trade, or criminal organizations doesn’t automatically make it a masterpiece. Good storytelling is what truly makes a film stand out.

I've watched many excellent Korean films, including thrillers and darker-themed movies, but this one falls flat. The director seems to have a sadistic streak and managed to assemble a piece of outright junk. The film offers no entertainment value and doesn't even qualify as a true thriller. I can't believe such a movie was ever made. While the acting is passable, the storyline and overall impact are dreadful.  

I'm certainly not interested in watching any more films by this director. There’s a lack of real filmmaking skill and an utter failure to deliver genuine thriller moments. Instead, the movie relies on scenes of psychopaths wasting time with poorly shot sequences, overused blood, and violence, assuming that these elements make it exciting. It’s a highly disappointing film, and I strongly advise avoiding all movies of this nature.

One of my favorite Amitabh Bachchan comebacks films. This movie came during a period when Govinda was riding high alongside Dhawan. The soundtrack was fantastic, full of lively, fun-filled songs that perfectly captured that "masti" spirit. An evergreen entertainer, complemented by the versatile Anupam Kher’s memorable performance. The plot is filled with hilarious twists and turns, true to David Dhawan’s signature style of comedy. The appearance of Madhuri Dixit added to the chaos, making the climax a complete riot. It was wonderful to see Amitabh perform with such energy and humor after a long absence from the screen. While some might see it as a typical Bollywood masala film, I’d gladly watch it anytime. I rate it an easy 8 out of 10 for its pure Bollywood flavor.

Good grief! (And that from an atheist, no less.) This "movie" is truly terrible!  

Much has already been said by reviewers who rated this piece a 3 or lower, and I completely agree with them. I just want to add a few personal observations:  

Among the three characters who had to eat their own digestive end products, got chopped up by an axe, raped with a broomstick, and had their balls blown off—the ex-boyfriend endures the worst torture, especially while being subjected to the girl’s endless, pointless chatter at the kitchen table. (We suffer along with him, though at least we have the mute button to escape.)  

If only the director had cut out the endless graveyard scenes and the pointless inversion sequences, this movie might have been over in thirty minutes.  

The only redeeming feature—if you could call it that—are Emily Haack's ample assets (one star).  

Honestly, forget it. Don’t buy it. Don’t waste your time or your sanity. After watching this, my brain feels so fried I immediately want to watch—and perhaps suffer through—"Scrapbook" instead.

As a devoted Trekkie (or Trekkers—I'll leave the label up to you), I endured all seven seasons of "Star Trek: Voyager," always hoping for a better series on the horizon. I mourned the conclusion of "Deep Space Nine" in 1999, but my prayers were finally answered. "Enterprise" is absolutely outstanding—offering a fresh perspective, featuring radically different characters, stunning new visuals, and even a pop song for the opening theme (I was genuinely surprised!). Honestly, I can't find anything I dislike about it. Count me in for ten seasons of this new adventure. "Star Trek" has truly returned—"Voyager," no one misses you! Keep on Trekkin'!

From the stellar performances delivered by an exceptionally talented cast to the cleverly crafted and highly quotable screenplay, from the opulent cinematography to Carter Burwell’s beautiful musical score, Rob Roy presents a rare cinematic experience—one that is nearly flawless across all aspects.  

Several comparisons have been drawn between Rob Roy and Braveheart, released in the same year. While credit is due to Mel Gibson, I found Braveheart to be somewhat overly self-conscious and preachy, making it less appealing for multiple viewings compared to Rob Roy. Whereas Braveheart endeavors to be a grand, serious epic, Rob Roy effortlessly pulls you in with its tightly woven narrative. Every scene is purposeful; none are superfluous.  

The film strikes an ideal balance of dramatic tension, action, and even touches of humor. Its characters are richly developed, convincingly exhibiting period-appropriate vernacular and mannerisms that firmly ground them in their historical setting.  

Moreover, they are not mere stereotypes of heroism and villainy, a common pitfall in modern films.  

For instance, while we root for the noble Rob Roy to succeed, we also recognize that his struggles stem from complex circumstances, adding depth and realism to the story.

Many of the critiques on this thread tend to compare this film with "The Mortal Storm" or "Casablanca." While audiences are free to draw their own parallels, the similarities between "The Mortal Storm" and "Watch On The Rhine" primarily lie in their focus on refugees fleeing the Nazi regime. In contrast, the comparison with "Casablanca" centers on the perceived unjust treatment of Humphrey Bogart by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 1943, when Paul Lukas was awarded the Best Actor Oscar instead. I don't find this entirely unfair; Lukas had a solid career in both Hollywood and England—he played the villain in "The Lady Vanishes," for instance—and that role was his finest performance. Bogart, on the other hand, delivered many exceptional performances beyond Rick Blaine, such as Sam Spade in "The Maltese Falcon" and Roy Earle in "High Sierra," both of which he was rightly recognized for, even though he never received an Oscar for his most iconic roles as Fred C. Dobbs in "The Treasure of Sierra Madre," the writer/murder suspect in "In a Lonely Place," or Captain Philip Francis Queeg in "The Caine Mutiny."

Of course, certain aspects of this film feel a bit outdated today. The all-white male crew stands out, and like many pre-Star Wars sci-fi films, it tends to linger a little too long on self-congratulation. 

Nevertheless, no other film has quite captured the essence of Golden Age Science Fiction as effectively, right down to the use of "electronic tonalities" in the musical score. Robbie the Robot embodied the classic Asimov-inspired androids and served as the blueprint for characters like C-3PO and Data. 

The storyline itself draws heavily from Shakespeare's "The Tempest," with Morbius taking on the role of Prospero, an exiled wizard whose domain is threatened by intruders. This film was pioneering in treating Science Fiction as a serious, adult genre, perhaps the first to do so.

Aldolpho (Steve Buscemi), an aspiring filmmaker, resides in a rundown New York City apartment, heavily dependent on his mother to cover the rent. His attractive neighbor, Angelica (Jennifer Beals), whom he’s unsure is married, becomes the object of his romantic and professional aspirations, as he hopes she will star in his movie. When a mysterious man named Joe unexpectedly offers to finance Aldolpho’s project, he believes his dreams are within reach. However, things take a turn when Joe invites Aldolpho on a reckless scheme to steal a Porsche to secure additional funding. Will Aldolpho manage to complete his film before losing all sense of morality? And will Angelica agree to appear in it? In my opinion, this film is truly dreadful. The screenplay is poorly written, with a meandering plot that lacks cohesion. Beals delivers her lines with a constant snarl, while Buscemi, though charming, comes across as forgettable. The movie is riddled with offensive content and unlikable characters. Additionally, the production quality is subpar, giving the entire film a cheap, second-rate appearance. If you have free time, it’s probably best to avoid this movie entirely.

I love movies and will watch just about any film all the way through to give it a fair shot. However, I can now confidently say I’ve found a movie I simply cannot finish. The acting is painfully dull and monotonous, the CGI looks as if a basement-dwelling computer geek threw it together with minimal software, and there are endless scenes of nothing but people walking! To make matters worse, this film stretches over three hours. I didn't even last 15 minutes before fast-forwarding the DVD in frustration. The alien scenes are fleeting and sparse. Honestly, instead of calling it "War of the Worlds," they should have titled it "War of the Walking Long Distances." It cost five million dollars to produce—what was that money spent on? Probably just the dramatic opening song.  

On the bright side, one scene worth watching is the moment the aliens start killing people. It’s unintentionally hilarious—not because of the deaths, but because when the aliens turn their victims into skeletons, those skeletons still twitch and squirm for a full 20 seconds afterward.  

So, as I mentioned, if you enjoy dull, stale, actionless movies, this one might be a perfect addition to your DVD collection. But this review isn’t for you; it’s for the...

This film features a compelling story paired with stunning animation. The influences of Frazetta and Bakshi are unmistakable, which is a positive aspect. Fans of Conan the Barbarian or Dungeons & Dragons are likely to enjoy it. The classic battle between good and evil is portrayed clearly, even though our hero sometimes appears neutral. Traditionally, fantasy films depict elves with white skin and blond hair, while goblins and orcs tend to have darker features; however, fans of Frazetta, Bakshi, or Tolkien know that these choices are not rooted in racism. Anyone who appreciates fantasy movies should find this film appealing. Please note, it is not suitable for young children due to violence and sexual innuendo. The casting is well-executed, and the scenes and music are top-notch. I hope it gets released on DVD soon, as I feel fortunate to own a good-condition VHS copy.

Almost Golden: The Jessica Savitch Story

Aspect Ratio: 1.33:1

Sound Format: Stereo

This film offers a tepid soap-opera-style dramatization of the rise and fall of America's pioneering female TV news anchor. With sharper scripting, tighter direction, and a stronger cast, it could have been more compelling, but the weak storyline ultimately falls flat. A well-crafted documentary might have provided a more insightful approach. While it features polished production values characteristic of TV movies, the overall experience feels superficial and lacks lasting engagement.

The core criminal tale depicted in In Cold Blood might come across as somewhat subdued compared to the sensational serial killer stories many are familiar with—stories like Gein, Bundy, or Dahmer—or the notorious Hollywood cases such as O.J. Simpson or Charles Manson. The basic facts of the case are straightforward: Perry Smith and Dick Hickock (portrayed by Robert Blake and Scott Wilson, respectively) met by chance, devised a plan to rob a Kansas farmstead’s safe, and ended up murdering a family of four with a shotgun and a dagger, stealing only 43 dollars. Aside from their brief escape to Mexico and subsequent return to the United States, there isn't much in the way of mystery surrounding their downfall. They were finally caught by a twist of fate—a police officer stopped them for possessing a stolen car after Smith and Hickock helped a boy and his father collect bottles for change—and were sentenced to hang. The story concluded in 1965.

However, what elevates the film is its masterful storytelling, the contemplative pauses, the compelling performances, and the pure cinematic craftsmanship brought to life by director Robert Brooks and the exceptional work of the late Conrad Hall, whose cinematography lends a profound and haunting visual depth to the narrative.

This film narrates the heartfelt story of a troubled scientist who, following the tragic decapitation of his fiancée, stalks strip clubs in search of a suitable body to reattach her head. Throughout the movie, all the characters ooze more slime than a snail, especially our main protagonist.

This film is a perfect pick for both hopeless romantics and sports enthusiasts. Drew Barrymore truly shines in this role, and as a fan of hers, it was a pleasure to see her excel after a few less successful films. I had some reservations about Jimmy Fallon, but he completely exceeded expectations as Ben—the charming, sports-obsessed sweetheart. The humor in this movie is fantastic, with several moments that had me laughing out loud.

Their first date was off to a rough start when Ben arrived at her apartment with flowers, only to find her feeling ill from eating at a new restaurant earlier that day. Instead of leaving, he stayed to help her, assisting her with pajamas and later cleaning up her vomit in the bathroom, humorously commenting that she was "very lady-like... no chunks." The chemistry between Ben and Lindsay was flawless throughout the winter, but everything changes when baseball season begins. Lindsay begins to notice just how deeply Ben is obsessed with the Red Sox, raising questions about why such a great guy is still single. She tries to brush it off, viewing it as a positive—especially since her busy work schedule means she doesn't have to feel guilty about working.

Robot Jox may not excel in story or special effects, but that’s understandable given it was made in 1990. Back then, even RoboCop 2 relied heavily on stop-motion animation, just like many other films of the '80s. If you look at the biggest blockbusters of that era, they often made do with the limited special effects technology available. It wasn’t until the release of Terminator 2: Judgment Day the following year that a true technological breakthrough emerged, inspiring storyboarders to incorporate that new innovation. Still, viewers will surely have nostalgic memories of Transformers, Gundam Wing, and Power Rangers after watching this film. The enemy robot is incredibly intimidating, making it clear that facing such a foe requires a solid backup plan. The film also features some memorable moments, including the reveal of a traitor or spy among the protagonists—someone you trust completely might turn out to be the last person you'd expect. That's a disturbing thought, isn't it?

(Spoilers ahead?)  

Although the historical accuracy may be questionable—especially given the widespread popularity of the somewhat inaccurate LOTR—such liberties seem more acceptable now. I appreciated the artistic style of the film, even if it doesn't quite qualify as an art house production. It does deliver some emotionally intense moments from time to time.  

I have two main criticisms: first, it feels a bit too brief; second, the mysterious whispering voice that occasionally appears remains unexplained.  

Rating: 8/10  

Quality: 10/10  
Entertainment: 7/10  
Rewatchability: 5/10

Even if you're unfamiliar with Ireland, you can't help but adore "My Left Foot"—and particularly Daniel Day-Lewis's extraordinary performance. He portrays Christy Brown, a man with cerebral palsy who faces constant ostracism throughout his life. Despite his efforts to warn others or communicate, he's often met with mockery. The beacon of hope in his challenging world is his sole control over his left foot, which he transforms into a tool for painting and poetry, ultimately gaining recognition.  

Daniel Day-Lewis and director Jim Sheridan worked together brilliantly on this film, as they did later on "In the Name of the Father." (Their collaboration on "The Boxer" didn't quite hit the mark.) "My Left Foot" evokes a range of emotions—sadness, hope, and more. Nonetheless, Daniel Day-Lewis delivers a performance that defines a career. It’s a truly outstanding film in every way.

During his visit to London, American author Edgar Allan Poe catches the attention of British journalist Alan Foster, who becomes entangled in a strange wager. Skeptical of Poe's claim that all his eerie tales are rooted in real experiences, Foster accepts a challenge from Poe and Sir Thomas Blackwood: he must spend an entire night in Blackwood's haunted castle. Once inside the deserted fortress, Foster quickly realizes he is not alone—he is approached by stunning women, handsome men, and a metaphysical doctor. The doctor reveals that these apparitions are lost souls condemned to relive their deaths on the anniversaries of their demises. When I first watched this classic horror film, I was utterly captivated. It managed to be both profoundly unsettling and poignantly sorrowful. Babs Steele's undeniable beauty adds to the film's allure. The haunting musical score amplifies the eerie atmosphere, making it even more terrifying. A shocking topless scene caught me off guard, as I wasn't expecting it. The picture quality is excellent, likely thanks to Synapse’s meticulous restoration, and this is the Uncut International version, making for a truly remarkable viewing experience despite the film’s age.

Upon hearing such praise for this play, I decided to watch it when I came across it on cable. I fail to see how it "elevates" women or their "struggles" by concentrating solely on the topic presented. If you're interested in stories centered around women's private parts and their impact on lives, then this might appeal to you. However, for others, it tends to be quite dull and unengaging. In fact, I found it somewhat demeaning.  

I also asked a female friend who watched it as well, and she thought it was awful too. So, it's not just a male perspective of "not understanding" it.

This film held a lot of promise: starring my favorite actor in a historical drama set during the War of Independence. It evoked memories of "Dances With Wolves" with its expansive prairies, Native Americans, and military conflicts, as well as "Barry Lyndon" for its British characters and candlelit atmospheres.  

Unfortunately, the screenplay falls flat: the narrative lacks consistency, jumping with "5 months later" or "3 years later" without smooth transitions, and the romance is so implausible that it's hard to take seriously. Despite America's vastness, the characters keep bumping into each other, and the ending makes it painfully clear how to undermine the story—imagine the same misstep in "Titanic."  

Sometimes, a poor script can be elevated by a talented director, but Hudson proves to be a weak one here. Having previously directed "Greystoke," I see the same flaws: scenes lack energy, editing feels sluggish, and the score is uninspiring. The result is a long, dull, and flat film.  

I suspected this movie would be a career misstep for Pacino, and now I understand why. Ultimately, this 2006 release mirrors my overall feelings for the year—a difficult, painful experience.

I'm glad I didn't watch this while I was pregnant; I probably would have burst into tears or vomited. The film was quite gruesome and unsettling overall. I have to admit, the baby was strangely adorable in its own warped way. As a mom, I winced when Beth stabbed herself in the stomach and when Virginia attempted to abort the fetus with rusty tools during her third trimester. As an animal lover, I nearly cried when she scratched the cat to a bloody pulp. Despite how creepy and sinister the baby was, I found myself hoping it would survive. As bizarre as the movie was, I’m genuinely curious to see the sequel.

Judging by the sets, staging, and editing, it's clear that this project was made on a limited budget. Perhaps Bela Lugosi's presence is intended to distract from such shortcomings. The story revolves around young brides who faint and drop dead at the altar after saying "I do." Their bodies are then stolen by the notorious horticulturist Dr. Lorenz (Lugosi) and his peculiar minions, as his aging wife (Elizabeth Russell) requires injections of glandular fluids from these young virgins to stay eternally youthful and beautiful. A keen local reporter (Luana Walters) notices that each missing bride wore the same rare orchid to the altar—an orchid Dr. Lorenz would be intimately familiar with. As a storm approaches, the visit to the Lorenz estate becomes increasingly ominous, especially with the presence of a dwarf and a slobbering hunchback on the grounds. Other cast members include Angelo Rossitto, Tristram Coffin, Minerva Urecal, and Frank Moran.

Without repeating what’s already been said about this film, I want to share that I was genuinely excited to see it—thanks to the impressive cast, scenic location, and the renowned director Michael Winterbottom. From the start, the storyline carried a faint echo of 'Don’t Look Now,' with a stay in a different setting—Italy again—seemingly intended to ease the pain of loss. Maybe that was just my interpretation. I found myself waiting for the plot to develop and take an unexpected turn, challenging our assumptions about the family’s fate in a foreign European land. But instead, I sat through the entire film—expectantly—and guess what? Nothing truly happens. Absolutely nothing. You’re not given the chance to connect with the characters, as they come across as one-dimensional and hollow. The pacing suggested that something would happen to flip the story on its head, yet it never did. The eldest daughter’s flirtation with local Vespa boys hinted at potential new directions, but that storyline went nowhere. The youngest daughter’s visions of her deceased mother ended up feeling pointless and unfulfilling. Even the father’s attempts at seduction by a woman didn’t lead anywhere meaningful.

I watched this film at the Esquire Theatre in Cincinnati, OH, and honestly, I now regret ever going.

Christopher Reeve would have played a more convincing boxer.

As a movie, it was excruciating, but seeing Bret Carr in person was like witnessing desperation at its peak.

My favorite moment was when Bret Carr was hit in the face with what looked like a "C" battery. The jury's still out on whether it was real. Turns out, it was from a dildo, caught in slow motion. Yep.

"Shoot the left side of the face only... people become famous by demanding things!" — Bret Carr. B. Carr even wore a chicken suit for a while, doing a bit of reverse psychology by wandering the streets of Clifton and criticizing his own film. He should. Absolutely, this film deserves to be criticized.

This movie left my soul feeling raw and chafed.

Bret Carr isn't charismatic enough to lead a cult, nor clever enough to be considered particularly intelligent. That’s the vibe you get from the quasi-psychological, "What the Bleep" style stream of brainwashed, impressionable neo-yuppies who came to see this Bret Carr masterpiece.

Just thinking about it is an emotionally exhausting experience.

I'm not particularly a Sylvester Stallone fan, and the only time I truly appreciated his presence was in the French film Taxi 3, where his role was barely noticeable. Nevertheless, I have to admit that the movie wasn't as bad as I expected, despite my initial concerns.  

When Gabe (Stallone) fails to save his friend's girlfriend, who falls to her death from a 4,000-foot mountain summit, he finds himself unable to continue working as a mountain ranger. He stays away from the reserve for nearly a year, but eventually returns. Soon after his comeback, the rangers receive an emergency call about a group of hikers caught in a snowstorm—at least, that's what they believe. In truth, a band of robbers crash-landed their plane in the mountains after a failed attempt to steal money from a flying government aircraft. The stolen cases are scattered across the reserve, and the robbers seek the aid of professional climbers to recover them.  

Of course, this isn't one of the most intellectually stimulating films, but...

They made me watch this at school, and it was terrible. The movie feels outdated, and the episodes are confusing because they blend fact with fiction to make the story more engaging. The teachers presented it as a treat, but in reality, it was a painfully dull experience. I've read that very few of the people in the film are professional actors; most of them do what they do in real life, which often results in cheesy acting. Additionally, the story frequently becomes absurd and far-fetched. I also dislike some of the lines, wishing they carried more meaning. Although it was intended to be educational, funny, suspenseful, and trendy, it ended up being boring, dry, unrealistic, and outdated. I hope no one wastes their time watching this movie—trust me, you're better off skipping it.

If this series was intended to be an improvement over Batman: The Animated Series, I must say it falls very short. The character designs are poorly executed—Catwoman, for example, looks dreadful. However, what truly frustrated me was how it depicted Batman as a sort of weakling who can't handle himself in a fight without the assistance of two or three sidekicks. He's Batman, for crying out loud! I understand that in the comics, Nightwing and Batgirl are his allies besides Robin, but still... portraying Batman as someone who needs their help—what is he, incapable of taking a few hits? In BTAS, he could face a dozen enemies without breaking a sweat. Is he getting old? Come on...

Additionally, I find it hard to believe that Batman would let a kid like Tim Drake jump into battle without years of rigorous training. That’s irresponsible—and Batman is anything but reckless. Plus, it doesn’t align with the comics if we want to stay true to their source material.

Batman: The Animated Series truly made history with its animation, storytelling, and characters. It was nothing short of legendary.

I only watched this film from start to finish because I had promised a friend I would. It offers no unintentional entertainment, unlike many poor-quality movies. It might be the worst film I've ever seen. I'm amazed a distributor was willing to put their name on it.

Although I gave this film a 2 due to its sheer lack of effort in attempting to craft a quality horror movie, it scores a solid 10 on the unintentional comedy scale. I had no idea what was happening or who the characters were, but I didn't mind because every scene seemed designed to make me burst into laughter. The dialogue is sparse throughout, which I suspect is because they probably started filming without a script. The absence of a clear plot makes the film remarkably adaptable—whether you watch it straight through or in reverse, you'll be entertained and confused in equal measure. I especially enjoyed the scene where the inmates take turns running around outside, beating each other with sticks. I believe the doctor calls this "treatment." Pure genius!

Somerset Maugham's characters are vividly brought to life in RKO's "Of Human Bondage"; however, the film offers a rather condensed adaptation of the novel, with Bette Davis's star-making performance overshadowing other elements. The story primarily follows Leslie Howard as Philip Carey, who aspires to be a painter but is told he lacks talent. As the narrative unfolds, Howard's character shifts focus, striving instead to become a doctor. His transition suggests some misguided advice regarding his artistic ambitions; while he finds success in medicine, his pursuit of painting appears to come more easily—highlighted symbolically through his disability, a "club foot," explained in the film.

Early in the story (in this adaptation), Howard becomes captivated by waitress Davis as Mildred Rogers. Davis delivers an extraordinary portrayal of Mildred, climaxing in a memorable speech where she tells Howard that she had to "WIPE MY MOUTH!" after kissing him. Howard's performance is also commendable, yet the film fails to clarify the depth of his obsession and love for Davis, rendering their compelling performances somewhat squandered.

Nonetheless, the film is worth watching for its acting, including standout performances from supporting cast members. Bette Davis's portrayal became so influential that it inspired a notable "write-in" campaign.

After watching monkeys—er, apes—for over an hour, I started to feel like one myself. I was just another ape, wasting money on this film. Honestly, folks, save your cash and go enjoy a hilarious movie like Bridget Jones's Diary instead.

A beautifully crafted, free-flowing, and often lyrical film that carries you along effortlessly, smiling even in the face of some truly shocking moments. One cannot help but be stunned by the treatment of the women, yet ultimately they emerge resiliently, thanks to the skill and dedication of everyone involved, as many potentially disastrous scenes are executed with great success. This may well be Depardieu's finest performance—arguably his most natural. Jeanne Moreau delivers an outstanding portrayal in what must have been a challenging role, including intense sex scenes with men at least half her age. Miou-Miou is charming throughout and faces similarly difficult scenes with grace. At first, the film appears to be a gritty, misogynist romp, but as the story and characters develop, a much deeper, more tender, and honest portrait emerges. Ultimately, this unflinching and bold film commands respect.

An Inconvenient Truth is as overly simplistic and demagogic as the exaggerated rhetoric spewed by the fervently ignorant Republicans. It drifts along vague lines until it finally attempts to shove a grim truth into your face—that humanity will likely be extinct within a few hundred years. While this is an undeniable fact, who cares? Humans are inherently selfish and destructive; I see little point in wasting my time worrying about human extinction. I prefer to view it as a natural course of events. Let the apocalypse come—meanwhile, we’re subjected to the same smug politicians promising a “new society.” Don’t be fooled: power remains concentrated in the hands of the wealthy and those responsible for the crises we face. True change is unlikely.  

As for Al Gore, his hypocrisy is glaring. The film shows him being chauffeured in a gas-guzzling car alone, while he uses a consumerist computer. He owns vast parcels of land and lives in a sizable mansion—land that has been eroded through practices like cattle grazing, tobacco and pig farming (which release methane), among other exploitative activities. His wealth relies on greed and exploitation, underscoring the contradiction between his message and his lifestyle.

A dull, utterly foreseeable film filmed in the unappealing surroundings of the lower Coachella Valley. The acting is amateurish at best, resembling a basic screenwriting 101 exercise. Nevertheless, it serves as an effective sedative.

Here's an indie film I genuinely wanted to enjoy, but ultimately couldn't. The absence of a cohesive script—boldly acknowledged in the opening titles—becomes painfully obvious and undermines the entire movie. The narrative is a confusing jumble that isn't worth deciphering. I lost interest within the first 10 minutes, then endured the next 30, clinging to hope for improvement, only to finally skip to the end—though even that effort felt pointless. OZARK SAVAGE clearly attempts to be clever, borrowing its most memorable moments from EVIL DEAD 2 and THE MATRIX. Consequently, there’s little here that hasn't been done better elsewhere. The film might have been more entertaining as a 10-20 minute short; as a feature, it feels overly stretched and artificially padded. Of course, there's little profit in shorts, which likely explains why it was extended beyond 75 minutes. Director Matt Steinauer shows real potential, and I wish him all the best.

Revolver is neither the catastrophic failure critics in the UK claimed nor the misunderstood masterpiece its few enthusiasts suggest. At its core, it represents a commendable effort by Guy Ritchie to inject more depth into his conman narratives. However, nothing is more vilified than an ambitious film that overreaches, especially within the gangster and con artist genre. Given Luc Besson’s role as producer, the film bears a distinct ‘Cinema de look’ aesthetic: set in a semi-realistic fantasy world where America and Britain blend seamlessly, it boasts striking visuals, a couple of brilliantly edited and executed action scenes, and a strong sense of style—characteristics that make it a largely disposable form of entertainment. Yet, Ritchie clearly aims beyond mere formulaic filmmaking; he’s dedicated considerable time to contemplating life, the universe, and everything in between. One could argue that its main flaw is an overabundance of influences—from Machiavelli to Godard to chess principles—sprinkled throughout the film via quotations, motifs, and techniques. Originally, the film was intended to…

"3lbs" clearly serves as a vanity project for Stanley Tucci, who seems more interested in playing a brooding, self-important doctor than delivering compelling storytelling. Unlike "House," Tucci's character lacks any real personality, and the brain surgery cases—despite being set in a top neurological center—are dull and uninspired. The supposed tension from a petty rivalry or hallucinations adds little to the narrative. The pilot briefly touches on the lead’s personal life as a father, but it’s tedious and forgettable. Overall, this show is lackluster; with so many medical dramas on air, it fails to distinguish itself or offer anything new.

One evening, I caught the final half of this film on cable and was struck by its bleak tone. Even as one of the victims reaches his most deteriorated state, the camera persists, lingering on haunting scenes—like the uncovering of his corpse and his gaunt figure being zipped into a body bag—that evoke both deep emotion and despair. If you're already feeling down, it's best to avoid this movie. Conversely, if you're in a good mood, it might be best to steer clear altogether.

Ignore the misleading title "Werewolf Woman." Europeans tend to prioritize sex and nudity over genuine scares in their horror movies, and this film pushes that tendency too far. "Werewolf Woman" features a lurid sex scene paired with the protagonist going berserk and brutally murdering her partner—initially shocking, but after a hundred minutes, it quickly becomes dull. Interestingly, she isn't even a werewolf but a schizophrenic woman whose ancestor was hanged for lycanthropy. The film struggles with its tone; the opening ten minutes—a flashback—offer some legitimate supernatural horror (making me think I was in for a cult classic), but it quickly devolves into a poorly executed character study of a woman repeatedly abused and tortured, then shifts into a revenge thriller. By the end, the director claims it's based on a true story—sure it is.

That said, there are a few redeeming qualities. The title character is visually appealing, and the movie boasts some decent gore effects and nude scenes. However, these elements become repetitive fast. Additionally, the dubbed dialogue often comes across as amusingly campy.

CITY HALL presents a somewhat uneven experience. It offers a blend of vignettes capturing the essence of New York City politics and moralistic storytelling. Al Pacino portrays a Dukakis-like boss with presidential ambitions, delivering performances that are often subdued or contemplative. There are moments when he indulges in more flamboyant acting, and in these instances, he truly shines. John Cusack delivers a restrained and nearly flawless performance, avoiding caricatures of a New Orleans accent or slipping into melodrama during the film's climax. Danny Aiello, as a borough political leader, also provides a strong showing. I also have a fondness for show tunes.  

However, the main flaw of CITY HALL—and despite its strengths—is a noticeable lack of momentum. The film feels more like a documentary than a gripping narrative, presenting the story from a detached perspective. This approach prevents viewers from becoming truly engaged, leading to a sense of emotional distance. When audiences don't connect deeply with the characters or the story, apathy sets in, and the plot fails to resonate.  

This disconnect ultimately diminishes the impact, turning what could have been an electrifying, intricately detailed finale into a tepid "Hmmm… okay." As the saying goes, "You can't fight city hall," but perhaps it’s also hard to truly fight that sense of detachment when watching.

In the 1980s, Warren Beatty demonstrated his versatility by creating two distinct epic films. At one end of the decade, he brought to life the intellectually driven Reds, a compelling portrayal of the founding of the Soviet Union seen through the eyes of radical icon John Reed. This film was both an engaging and meaningful masterpiece, featuring an all-star cast that delivered a powerful message. Later in the decade, Beatty crafted Dick Tracy, a different kind of epic that embraced pure entertainment. With its vibrant characters and star-studded cast donning elaborate makeup, the film was a lively homage to classic cartoon adventures.

The fact that both Reds and Dick Tracy originated from Warren Beatty highlights his remarkable range as a filmmaker and actor. In the latter film, he successfully integrated beloved cartoon characters from the comic strip into an original screenplay, showcasing his storytelling prowess.

The story revolves around the city’s notorious mob boss, Big Boy Caprice, who is intent on crushing his competition. The film opens with a dramatic scene reminiscent of the Valentine’s Day Massacre, as Caprice ruthlessly eliminates Lips Manlis's henchmen, and then proceeds to have Lips himself sealed in a cement overcoat. As Caprice’s power grows, so does the danger he faces from the determined police detective, Dick Tracy.

This is the first segment of a brief animated excerpt depicting the history of the Matrix— the epic conflict between humanity and machines that ultimately led to the creation of the Matrix itself. The animation blends elements of Japanese anime with modern American stylistic influences, showcasing exceptional craftsmanship reflective of the talented directors behind the project. It illustrates the early development of artificial intelligence and humanity’s exploitation of the machines, culminating in their rebellion...

Let's set aside the explanations involving distributors, secondary directors, inebriated scriptwriters, and receptionists meddling in the screenplay. For now, I'll just present this film as it is, without unnecessary justifications.

This movie is utterly terrible—poorly made and painfully unwatchable. Instead of reiterating what little plot there is, I'll highlight some baffling moments that made me shake my head.

A group of five students from a history class embark on a field trip to a remote part of Ireland. They might be Canadian or American; it's hard to tell. The fact that it was shot in a Canadian forest rather than Ireland is pretty obvious. One student appears clueless about history and fits the stereotypical "dumb jock" archetype from classic '80s films—except when he suddenly acts like Randy from *Scream*. One of the characters might be Chris Klein's stunt double. He has a girlfriend who presumably gets killed, though the film never confirms this. Another student is withdrawn and moody—completely detached from everyone else—for no apparent reason. And then there's the blonde girl. Just... because. 

Ireland's population is just two people—who are cousins. Gary, who is evidently the same...

Since I'm not familiar with US television stations, I initially thought this was just a low-budget sci-fi film when I happened to catch it on my in-laws' cable. After a few minutes, I wondered if it was a clever satire mocking the worst excesses of Christian fundamentalism. Then it hit me—these people are serious! It's been a while since I saw something so unintentionally hilarious. I was hesitant to write a review out of concern for offending believers, but after reading others' opinions, I figured, why not? A tough philosophical puzzle: how do you critique movies without actually revealing what you're criticizing? The answer: craft it so that only those who dislike the genre will get the joke. Some liberals (ugh! can't stand saying that!) might be offended by the filmmakers' disdain for viewers not obsessed with the J**** C***** myth, but honestly, I found it incredibly funny!

Very intriguing. The plot twist wasn't quite as shocking as they might have intended, and it felt a bit outdated, but it certainly got my brain working. It made me contemplate a world without plants or animals, which deepened my appreciation for the world I live in. Charlton Heston delivers a strong performance, and the supporting cast is also commendable. The film's realism was quite surprising, though at times it lacked clear direction, and some of the settings and background details could have been better explained. Despite these flaws, it turned out to be a surprisingly intelligent and well-made movie. The only real drawback was that I didn't want the film to end when it did—I was eager to see what came next.  
   
7/10

I watched this movie just once, and that was enough for me. The film offers hardly any plot, consisting mostly of relentless scenes of psychotic and sadistic violence, with little else to offer. I was initially interested because Zoe Trilling, from the second "Night of the Demons," stars in it, hoping to see her portray a normal character. Unfortunately, the script by Tobe Hooper barely gets started and quickly goes nowhere, overshadowed by Robert Englund, who devours the scenery and dominates both the film and its storyline. Zoe, I know where you are now—probably hiding from this movie!

This is among the worst films I’ve ever watched. However, the character of Alice, the little enslaved girl, along with Jared Harris’s impersonation of Christopher Walken, actually adds a touch of entertainment to the film. Alice’s habits of smoking, drinking, and her eerily precise way of appearing whenever her name is called are both bizarre and captivating. I must commend Jared for his impressive Christopher Walken impersonation, and I also appreciate Christopher Walken for permitting this portrayal to be included in the movie.

This is yet another example of the typical Lifetime TV film that depicts the reprehensible actions of a despicable woman with undeserved sympathy. Alongside other offensive movies like "The Burning Bed," "Enough," and "Monster," this film sensationalizes a criminal to make her seem less condemnable. Honestly, give us a break! My question to the filmmakers is this: if LeTourneau were a man and Vili a 12-year-old girl, would you have produced a film that sympathizes with and portrays him as misunderstood? Absolutely not.

Consider what would happen if the genders were reversed. It becomes clear why I and many others see this as a worthless piece of trash. If that were the case, there would be no attempt to sympathize with the male perpetrator. Instead, we’d likely see a depiction of a grotesque man preying on a young girl, his predatory behavior leading to incarceration, with the girl suffering from Stockholm Syndrome. The only reason LeTourneau isn't portrayed this way is simply because she is a woman.

Let’s call things what they are. LeTourneau

Although we all admire Al Pacino, watching him in this film was genuinely difficult. At what appears to be the decline of a once distinguished and idealistic career, Pacino delivers a performance that looks as disheveled as an unmade bed, accompanied by a completely inconsistent southern accent that feels purely forced and artificial.

The storyline meanders through various twists and turns, riddled with loose ends and unlikely developments that leave the mind overwhelmed—and ultimately overwhelmed into retreat.

Kim Basinger makes an appearance, but her role is underwhelming. Her scenes with Pacino feel flat and unconvincing, making it hard to believe there was any genuine connection between their characters. The lack of energy is palpable.

Meanwhile, Téa Leoni steals the show with her vibrant presence. She was truly electric, and her scenes with Pacino stood out as the most engaging parts of the film. Unfortunately, even her spark couldn't fully rescue Al from the realms of embarrassment.

Franco Rossi's 1985 six-hour Italian mini-series Quo Vadis presents a fascinating blend of approaches. It constructs a convincingly authentic ancient Roman world through pragmatic filming techniques—rarely employing long shots or expansive cityscapes—yet it downplays drama in favor of allusions to classical literature and history, causing the narrative to recede into the background. 

The series’ unconventional structure, notably with much of the first episode narrated through voice-over letters, combined with a lack of narrative urgency, renders the full six-hour version both challenging and somewhat underwhelming. Nonetheless, it possesses notable strengths. Foremost among these are the portrayal of Petronius, played by a dubbed Frederic Forrest—whose own voice would likely diminish his dialogue—depicting a man so long searching for a clever survival tactic in court that he has become emotionally numb, and Klaus Maria Brandauer's distinctive interpretation of Nero as a wannabe actor whose every gesture is meticulously planned based on how his audience will react. Occasionally, Max Von Sydow makes brief appearances, delivering the film’s most striking and heartfelt scene when he encounters a child.

This is an incredible film! You should recognize that Chinese folklore is intricate and deeply philosophical, often layered with stories within stories. While I don't understand every detail—despite studying Chinese folklore in school—it remains a complex tapestry. Just embrace what it offers you…Enjoy the movie and savor the journey…Hooray!

I watched this film during a small screening organized by members of my college's gaming club. We were warned in advance that it would be the "Reefer Madness" of gaming movies, and it certainly lived up to that label.

Tom Hanks stars as Robbie, a young man who is restarting his college journey after taking a semester off. As the story unfolds, we learn that Robbie was deeply addicted to a role-playing game called "Mazes and Monsters," and he reconnects with it when a gaming group invites him to join a campaign.

The movie is incredibly cheesy on multiple levels. One particularly amusing scene shows the group "gaming by candlelight," which I can only describe as. While it might have been intended to look cultish, most gamers know that this is far from accurate. Typically, role-playing sessions happen in well-lit rooms, accompanied by snacks and soda.

The acting is not award-winning, but it’s not painfully bad either. This was one of Tom Hanks's early roles, long before "Bosom Buddies" and "Bachelor Party," which were still a year or two away. The supporting cast may not be memorable, but they deliver performances that are decent enough.

I sincerely apologize, but I must admit that although Fassbinder is still regarded as one of the greatest directors in post-war Germany and many of his films are considered masterpieces, my view of "Lili Marleen" has changed. Watching it in 2004, I find myself questioning what all the fuss is about. The acting is genuinely poor—Hanna Schygulla's constant smile comes across as foolish—and the transitions between Nazi glamour and battlefield scenes are poorly executed. The entire film appears as if it was hastily made in just a couple of days in an attic. Perhaps that’s actually how it was created, and many might see this as artistic, but to me, the film feels cheap and amateurish. When I compare it to Visconti’s "La Caduta degli Dei," I struggle to see "Lili Marleen" as a worthwhile film.

I have never read the book "A Wrinkle in Time." To be completely honest, after watching the movie, I wonder if I even want to. I should start by saying that I shouldn't be judging this film too harshly. Next, I’ll mention that the TV adaptation is quite forgettable. Do you know why I say that? Because I can't recall most of what happens in it. Yes, I told you it’s forgettable. Honestly, no TV movie will ever surpass "Merlin." 

How should I describe a TV movie? I've never written a review for one before. Well, generally, they tend to feature some celebrities. "A Wrinkle in Time" includes only one: Alfre Woodard (or Woodward, I’m not sure), the Oscar-winning actress.

The film is filled with cheesy special effects, a somewhat interesting plot, and moments that make you go "WTF." Overall, the movie is really bad and leaves you thinking "WTF." What did I expect? It’s a TV movie, after all. They rarely turn out great—this one is no exception. "A Wrinkle in Time" is a complete waste of time and a big letdown. Most likely, you'll forget about it the moment it ends. Well, maybe not immediately, but soon enough.

Some reviewers here seem to think this is an awful film, but I believe that’s an unfair assessment. The acting is solid, and the direction maintains a smooth flow throughout. I don’t see anything wrong with the Tarantino-inspired style of weaving interconnected stories; in fact, I think it adds a layer of sophistication and intrigue. It’s likely just a new technique for filmmakers to explore. While a few parts of the script could benefit from tighter editing, that’s about the only critique I can offer. Nestor Cantillana delivers a remarkable performance as Sylvio, and Antonella Rios is absolutely stunning—worth the price of admission all on her own.

Let me start by saying that Casey Affleck is a highly talented actor, and I hold his work in high regard. I wish he appeared in more films that truly showcased his abilities. That said, Soul Survivors was an extraordinarily poor movie. Truly, very bad.  

I believe the main blame lies with the weak script. Affleck is a talented performer, Wes Bentley delivered an outstanding performance in American Beauty, Melissa Sagemiller did well, and Eliza Dushku is currently one of Hollywood’s rising stars. Unfortunately, none of the actors seem to have truly connected with the screenplay, which is understandable. Labeling this film as a horror movie is an overstatement; it contains the expected twists and turns, but they lead nowhere—only deeper confusion. The ending was particularly disappointing, coming across as anti-climactic and leaving many questions unanswered about the story.  

I wish I could recommend this film, but I simply cannot. Honestly, the only thing potentially frightening about it is that...

This film was rather harsh in its execution, featuring numerous implausibilities, a flimsy script, poor performances, and other shortcomings. The sole reason to watch it is the occasional display of some surprisingly striking scenes.

I'm sharing this because I somehow believed that Dark Remains might be a decent movie. While it's not the worst I've seen, it definitely falls short of being good.

The film suffers from a weak script, underwhelming performances, and lackluster direction. Even if a big-name cast wasn't within reach, wouldn't it be reasonable to hope for a more visually appealing lead actress? Watching the plain actress deliver a dull performance throughout the film was quite painful. The storyline was clichéd and poorly written, with minimal special effects. The repetitive use of suspense tricks made them hard to take seriously.

To be fair, Dark Remains isn't worse than some episodes from Masters of Horror. However, it doesn't quite reach the quality of a well-made film. I would only recommend it to hardcore horror enthusiasts who want to see every entry in the genre, even if it's poorly executed. For everyone else, it's definitely better to spend your time on something more worthwhile—and that shouldn't be too hard to find.

This adaptation of John Van Druten’s Broadway classic comes to the screen infused with star power, telling a romantic fantasy about a contemporary witch who captivates a successful Manhattan publisher. While James Stewart may receive top billing, it is Kim Novak who truly steals the spotlight as one of the most enchanting witches to grace the silver screen. However, the leading pair is one of the film’s minor weaknesses: Stewart, with his silver hair, appears a bit too mature for his role, and although his affection for Novak is understandable, it’s somewhat puzzling what she finds appealing about him, given their contrasting temperaments and outlooks. An amusing aspect of the story is its depiction of witches and warlocks as Greenwich Village beatniks and bohemians. Interestingly, the Stewart-Novak chemistry would have been even more fiery in "Vertigo," released the same year, but that film benefited from a gripping suspense narrative and Alfred Hitchcock’s masterful direction.

Much of the film’s humor comes from its remarkable supporting cast, which includes a young Jack Lemmon as Kim's warlock brother, Elsa Lanchester as their whimsical aunt, and Ernie.

1985 was a remarkable year for films—perhaps even a great one—but this particular film missing out on an Oscar helped reinforce the notion that the Academy often sees itself as little more than a decorative accessory for high-society gatherings.  

With eleven nominations and no awards, the Academy’s clear disregard for one of their finest directors was evident. It would take another eight years before they finally recognized him with seven Oscars for Schindler's List, a film many argue isn’t quite as impactful (and I speak as someone half-Polish).  

Don't misunderstand me—Schindler's List is a timeless masterpiece. I’m not disparaging 'Out of Africa' (which took home the award that year) either; but in my opinion, it’s a step below this one: an epic tale of suffering and hope that moved me to tears—something I don’t do easily.  

Perhaps it was the music—absolutely exceptional—or the lavish cinematography, but most likely it was the performances: Whoopi Goldberg, who proved she was much more than just a comedian; Danny Glover, whose name I hadn’t known before; and, of course, Oprah.  

The rest is history.

Having seen most of Ryuhei Kitamura's work, I have come to recognize his talent for crafting dynamic action scenes. His sequences are often energetic and rapid, skillfully blending martial arts, gunfights, and samurai duels, all captured through camera work that vividly conveys the chaos on screen. Films like "Versus" and "Aragami" showcase his inventive approach and demonstrate his ability to work effectively within low-budget constraints. So, what went wrong with "Alive"? To be frank, not much. The film is over two hours long but delivers very little in the way of action, character development, or a compelling plot.

Based on a comic by Tsutomu Takahashi, "Alive" explores the story of Tenshu Yashiro (Hideo Sasaki), a death row inmate who survives his execution. Afterwards, he's faced with a choice: undergo a series of bizarre experiments or face execution once more. He opts for the experiments, which place him in a room with a rapist and later a girl infected with a strange parasite that grants supernatural powers at the cost of the host's humanity. Naturally, the film...

Having heard so much about the 1990s Cracker series yet never having watched any, I eagerly anticipated this viewing. Surely, the talented duo of Jimmie McGovern and Robbie Coltrane couldn't go wrong. Unfortunately, I was mistaken. The heavy-handed political commentary, amplified by frequent, repetitive, and violent flashbacks, became overwhelming. The production attempted to appear cutting-edge, but the distracting flashing graphics and childish font only grated on my nerves. Robbie Coltrane seemed to sleepwalk through the two-hour episode, offering unexplained and unlikely "insights," while the police characters were portrayed as one-dimensional, bumbling fools. As a result, the tension failed to develop, and the penultimate scene—without revealing spoilers—was as embarrassingly poor a piece of TV drama as I've seen in a long time. 

No, I don't plan to watch any more of these, but I will revisit the DVDs of the 1990s series to see if they truly live up to their reputation.

I am from Sweden and have just watched this movie. Honestly, I thought it was okay. Despite many negative comments online, it's important to remember that viewers of this two-part miniseries are spread all over the world, not just in the USA. Additionally, not everyone may be familiar with the film from the 1960s or the true events (the murders) it depicts. Finding the original movie can be challenging, and some people simply don't appreciate black-and-white films. This version feels fresh and in color, and I believe it will find its audience. Although it’s been 12 years since its release, I saw it for the first time just now. I’ll try to track down the original to compare, but I haven't seen it anywhere in Sweden. Of course, the internet exists, but access varies around the world. Mainly, this story is a part of American crime history, popular in the 1950s and 60s in the US, but it seems to have been overlooked elsewhere. It was widely discussed during that time, but beyond that, it probably didn’t make much of an impact internationally.

I can somewhat understand why some might want to emphasize this film's connection to the Eighties, but I wouldn't claim it's an accurate portrayal of most people's lives during that period—even on the poorest Bradford estates. Instead, it exemplifies the blunt, propagandistic nonsense the Royal Court Theatre was producing at the time. Plenty of superficial, 'politically correct' artistry aimed at small audiences, accompanied by enough backslapping among the well-connected to secure future commissions for its stolid playwrights. The truth is, if you want a more authentic reflection of everyday life, you'll find millions more nodding in recognition at the love and struggles depicted in 'Gregory's Girl.'  

I might label this as a 'kitchen sink' drama, but that would do a disservice to the plumbing industry. When it comes to having a solid script, this film is thoroughly washed up. Curiously, it has gained an odd following among Guardian-reading cinephiles—perhaps they enjoy the visual thrill of pretending to experience hardship. Stay away, my friends. It’s a poor film with a weak script that falsely believes it’s more than that.

I first encountered this video fifteen years ago. At the time, I found it to be outstanding, and my opinion has not changed. As a former teacher of both high school and college English, and an enthusiast of Romantic poetry, Coleridge holds a special place for me. Any attempt to diminish the poem's beauty or the story's power would not earn my nod of approval. Fortunately, everything about this video succeeds in captivating viewers, particularly high school students. It effectively illustrates the story in a way that resonates with a generation raised on television. Moreover, Michael Redgrave’s narration imparts a genuine sense of authenticity and authority. While the project certainly didn’t have a large budget—no CGI, and certainly no star wars-level effects—the inclusion of Gustave Doré’s illustrations adds a remarkable visual dimension. The brief critique above, dismissing the entire work as garbage in just four lines, feels unfair and lacking insight. I am friends with the producer, but that is not why I write this. I am simply defending a piece of artistry that I believe possesses value on multiple levels. It is particularly well-suited for introducing Coleridge’s poem to students.

What an exceptional crime thriller! My wife and I attended the Toronto International Film Festival last week, and this film stood out as the clear highlight among an impressive lineup. It quickly became my second favorite film of all time, just behind *Dr. Strangelove*, and I found myself riding an emotional high as I walked home, eagerly discussing the movie with my wife.

I prefer not to reveal too much of the plot because thrillers of this caliber are most impactful when experienced without preconceived notions. However, I can share that the story revolves around two brothers, portrayed by Phillip Seymour Hoffman and Ethan Hawke, who are planning to rob a jewelry store in Westchester, New York. The narrative shifts back and forth over approximately two weeks—before, during, and after the heist—and features a pivotal scene that is repeated at least three times. Usually, such repetition might slow down a film, but in this masterwork, it only enhances the tension and keeps the momentum soaring. The adrenaline, suspense, and quality of acting only intensified as the story unfolded. By the conclusion, I was on the edge of my seat, breathlessly eager to see how it all would end.

I despised the first episode of this show, 'Protesting Hippies,' back in 1999, so I avoided watching the rest. However, when it aired on 'The Paramount Comedy Channel,' I decided to give it a full viewing and was surprised to find it genuinely hilarious. Lesson learned: never judge a comedy series after its first week.

Set in 1969, 'Hippies' features Simon Pegg as Ray Purbbs, the editor of an underground magazine called 'Mouth,' reminiscent of 'Oz.' His friends include Jill, a feminist; Alex, relaxed and easygoing; and Hugo, somewhat dim-witted. During the late '60s, a wave of youthful optimism swept through, driven by the belief that they could change the world with magazines that no one actually read. Rather than mocking the hippies' idealism, the show affectionately captures it. Arthur Mathews' scripts cleverly parody icons of the era—'Hair,' 'Woodstock,' 'The Graduate,' and even the notorious 'Oz' obscenity trial of the early '70s. The cast delivers excellent performances; Julian Rhind-Tutt's portrayal of Alex oddly reminded me of Richard O'Sullivan's character from 'Man About the House.' It's unfortunate that there was no second series, perhaps because of viewers like me. If you missed 'Hippies,' I recommend giving it a shot.

In the mid-1930s, Hollywood was beginning to regain its confidence after the challenges faced during the transition to sound films. While the technical issues of integrating sound were swiftly resolved, it took longer to determine the visual style, narrative structure, and acting techniques suitable for talking pictures. *The Informer* stands out as a significant film because it demonstrates how silent moments can effectively tell a story, emphasizing the power of imagery while still incorporating sound and dialogue.

However, this does not mean *The Informer* is merely a nostalgic throwback to the silent era. Unlike many silent films, which often relied heavily on title cards and were less visually driven, the film exhibits a confident use of extended pauses between lines, a focus on characters’ reactions over their speeches, and the ability to let scenes unfold naturally for mood and atmosphere.

Director John Ford, despite his talent, was known to put less effort into projects he found uninteresting. When he considered a story trivial, he would approach it with less dedication. Fortunately, *The Informer*—with its themes of community, honor, and resilience—received his full attention and effort.

May I assign a negative rating to this film? Unfortunately, no. However, I must say this is the most dreadful movie I’ve ever attempted to watch. It was an excruciating experience—Boreus Maximus. The storyline is buried beneath layers of confusion, making it nearly impossible to follow. I rented this film with a friend, and after thirty minutes of hoping it would improve, we resorted to fast-forwarding, only to find that it never did. The plot revolves around a guy being kidnapped by two girls, which sounds intriguing, but in reality, it’s utterly dull. Nothing remotely engaging ever occurs. If you ever consider watching this, save yourself the trouble and opt for “PLAN NINE FROM OUTER SPACE” instead.

This film, Bedknobs and Broomsticks, is one of the most charming and delightful movies you'll ever enjoy as a child. It’s an unforgettable adventure featuring two adults and two spirited kids having fun together. While it might seem a little questionable to some, I encourage you to give it a try—my mother didn’t think it was bad, and I was truly captivated by the story and the animation; both were quite impressive. 

It’s a wonderfully whimsical comedy suitable for the entire family, including children aged 7 and up. This musical comedy, filled with engaging animation, is sure to entertain you and your loved ones. The animation’s movement and layout are particularly impressive and well worth praising. It’s a fantastic musical experience for everyone, so don’t wait—head over to the video store and rent Bedknobs and Broomsticks today!

I watched this movie at the 2006 Palm Springs International Film Festival. It's a movie, not a film, since it was apparently produced by HBO to air on their cable network later that year. The film depicts Page as a pinup with a bondage and discipline fetish, highlighting her role as a B&D stag film actress who possessed enough talent to pursue a serious acting career. In reality, Page was more than just that, and the movie briefly touches on her other work in modeling, though not enough to fully represent her legacy as a 1950s pinup icon. 

The film is supposedly adapted from Richard Foster's book "The Real Bettie Page." It’s filmed in black and white, enhancing the nostalgic 1950s vibe. I also own a book titled "Bettie Page: The Life of a Pinup Legend," featuring numerous iconic photographs that document her career. Impressively, the movie, with Gretchen Mol portraying Page, accurately recreates many of those renowned images. Mol, with her black wig and brown contact lenses, embodies Bettie Page perfectly—not just in appearance, but also capturing her signature smile and distinctive personality.

Three sisters, the youngest heirs of the distinguished Gaylord family—one of America's most aristocratic lineages—are orphaned at a tender age. Just before departing for France to serve in World War I, their father commands the eldest, Fiona, never to sell their ancestral land. As the years pass and the sisters reach adulthood, they are forced to exhaust much of their inheritance to fund legal battles defending their estate. Through certain clauses in their father's will, a man named Charles Barclay stands to inherit the Gaylord property, aiming to develop it into a complex named Barclay Circle. Barclay's character draws inspiration from John D. Rockefeller, who historically acquired land and buildings from wealthy families in New York to create Rockefeller Center.

The story primarily explores the melodramatic lives of the three sisters. Fiona, portrayed convincingly by Barbara Stanwyck—though not among her most iconic roles—comes across as a cold, commanding figure, hinting at hidden secrets from her past. Susanna, played by Nancy Coleman, is portrayed as somewhat naive and is deeply in love with a young, modern artist named Gig Young. Coleman's performance was my...

This film is perhaps the most moving and inspiring I have ever watched. Though I don't consider myself religious, a powerful work of art like this can sometimes evoke an almost spiritual experience, making me realize that life truly holds deep meaning. 

Initially, I was skeptical when I first heard about the movie. The storyline seemed artificial, and I feared it might be dull. However, as a fan of David Lynch, I decided to give it a chance. It took about half an hour for the film to fully draw me in, after which I was completely immersed. The movie exudes wisdom and warmth, leaving me with a profound sense that I had gained valuable insights about life. 

This film is quite different from Lynch's usual dark and complex works, and it was surprising to see him craft such a heartfelt story after years of exploring human darkness. Yet, in a way, it was not unexpected that he could evoke such deep emotions and human understanding, as I have always believed in his capacity to convey profound truths.

This delightful Bugs Bunny cartoon features the return of the still-unnamed Marvin the Martian and his green canine sidekick, K-9. This time, rather than attempting to destroy Earth, Marvin is on a mission to land, capture an Earth creature, and bring it back to Mars. Naturally, he chooses Bugs Bunny. At first, Bugs suspects Marvin and K-9 are just trick-or-treating, but he quickly realizes otherwise when Marvin dramatically enlarges Bugs's rabbit hole with a ray gun. Bugs attempts to outsmart his captors in several ways, including convincing Marvin that K-9 is planning a mutiny. Ultimately, he is captured using an Acme straight-jacket ejecting bazooka. Surprisingly, for an Acme gadget, it functions as intended, forcing Bugs to use his ingenuity to persuade K-9 to release him. The tide turns, and the two disgruntled Martians end up tied up, with Bugs trying to pilot their spaceship back to Earth. I really enjoyed this episode, although the ending feels a bit weaker compared to the rest of the story. Marvin's voice has a slight change here, and he shows visible emotion when angry.

Sometimes a premise begins promisingly but falters into a chaotic mess due to the need to constantly overexaggerate in order to capture the fleeting attention of an audience suffering from adhd. For three esteemed actors who have consistently delivered superior work before and after, this is a profound disappointment.

Let's consider the premise: a loving couple living in a beautiful home faces a threat from a sinister cop. An intriguing concept, to be sure. Making the antagonist a slightly unsettling figure could have added depth—recall how effectively this was handled in THE HAND THAT ROCKS THE CRADLE and SINGLE WHITE FEMALE—both proven formulas for a compelling thriller.

Herein lies the challenge: should the story aim to genuinely unsettle by introducing authentic menace into the characters without crossing into absurdity, or should it escalate the shock factor by transforming the cop into an overly extreme villain—an exaggerated version of the countless antagonists that have populated cinema since the silent era? 

Regrettably, the filmmakers opted for the latter. The result is a poorly executed film, with actors desperately trying to make sense of the chaos around them, ultimately losing themselves in a script that sacrifices plausibility for superficial shock.

My all-time favorite film. An Oscar-worthy achievement by everyone involved, both in front of and behind the camera. The screenplay is flawless, providing a completely satisfying portrayal of the relationship between Lady Caroline and George Briggs, surpassing the novel’s execution. The meticulous development of the other main characters pays tribute to screenwriter Peter Barnes, while the striking visual artistry should have earned Oscars for director Mike Newell and cinematographer Rex Maidment. Josie Lawrence delivers her best performance to date, and it reshaped my perception of Joan Plowright. Having watched this movie over 50 times, I find no flaws whatsoever. The score by renowned composer Richard Rodney Bennett is simply exquisite.

This could have been a superb silent film. The performances are impressively earnest, especially in that unmistakable "Look Ma, I’m Really Giving It My All" manner.  

Everything feels exaggerated—every line is grandiose, and each scene is overwhelmed by human tragedy.  

Mostly, I was tempted to gag. Yet, like a train wreck I couldn't look away from, I found myself unable to turn away. The dialogue might have had some merit on stage, though I highly doubt it. On screen, it comes across as cluttered, erratic, clichéd, and riddled with every negative stereotype you could associate with poor drama.  

If you crave your melodrama served in large, over-the-top portions, you might find some amusement here. Just be prepared to wait, because despite all the excess, the film drags along at a snail’s pace.  

The script probably sounded quite different when read by the actors in private. Once they perform it for the camera, it simply falls flat.  

IMDB’s use of its quirky, computer-generated "weighted score" often does a disservice. "Curse of the Starving Class" earns less than a one from me.  

Character-driven stories are wonderful, but when you develop your...

Am I missing something here? "Unexpected plot developments"? "Plot twists with subversive glee"? Are these viewers watching the same Arquette vehicle I just endured—an experience I now realize was a subconscious act of self-punishment? I signed up on this site just to warn others to avoid renting this disaster. This film was an embarrassment to everyone involved. Quick question: did Sir Stevie actually read the script before giving Kate C. the green light? If he did, then he must be the same Spielberg who approved "Howard the Duck." Don’t give me that “it was a hit play” excuse—I doubt Mr. Reddin is too pleased. The DVD cover promised "surprising twists" and a "twisted story," but what story?
