It’s garbage like this that makes old Bobby McKee and his band of Structuralists look like geniuses. Sundance? Berlin? Toronto? I have a home video of my cat farting that’s more captivating than Arquette’s utterly hollow portrayal of grief. And the deus ex machina with Mr. Stanley T.—thank goodness he thought to have Dave call the cops just in time. Thankfully, the police had already caught the real killer—wait, what? I was still waiting for something to happen right up until the credits rolled.

While Rome is engulfed in excitement celebrating Hitler’s visit—with uniforms, bands, and parades—two outsiders remain at home within a large building, where they unexpectedly meet. She is Sofia Loren, the wife of a brutish public servant and mother of six. He is Mastroianni, a radio announcer dismissed due to his homosexuality. Both yearn for companionship and understanding, and they find it in each other.

The film unfolds over a few hours. The colors are muted, and the scenes are accompanied by the sounds of military marches and frantic radio broadcasters. Strangely, the Nazi anthem—the Horst-Wessel-Lied—transforms into a romantic musical motif.

A beautiful film, skillfully recreating a unique chapter in Italian history, and telling a poignant, sorrowful story. Mastroianni delivers a performance as compelling as ever, while Sofia Loren excells, far from her typical roles as a truck driver’s pin-up or a Neapolitan fishwife. Do not miss this film.

This was undoubtedly one of the worst films I have ever watched.

I must disagree with another reviewer who claimed the special effects were acceptable. In my opinion, they were quite poor—unrealistic and so blatantly artificial that they only served to draw attention away from the storyline.

Perhaps that distraction contributed to my inability to fully grasp the plot. The archaeologists are searching for "the set," but the film never explains what set they are after or why it is so significant. This omission also makes it confusing why the search occurs in California when the opening scenes depict ancient Egypt.

If your movie is set in the desert, make the effort to shoot in a desert location. The opening scene—an ancient ceremony—looks as if it was filmed indoors in a studio rather than outdoors in the desert.

The level of action remains steady throughout, with no peaks or valleys, no real climax. While that results in a shorter film—arguably a positive aspect—it also contributes to a sense of monotony.

This film communicates a universal language, resonating with individuals on levels of self-awareness, community, society, and the broader world. It skillfully prompts viewers to ask profound questions, encouraging a journey of self-discovery and the pursuit of personal truth. By highlighting stereotypes and archetypes present in our surroundings, the film underscores the recurring cycle of destruction contrasted with innovation, creativity, and growth. It brings to light the factors that disrupt natural harmony, urging acknowledgment and action. More than just a viewing experience, this film invites deep engagement, touching the inner voice and conscience through its visual storytelling, making viewers feel profoundly rather than merely observe.

Cult classics are notoriously unpredictable. Who would have thought that films like Vision Quest, Fight Club, and 2001: A Space Odyssey—initially criticized by both critics and audiences—would later achieve cult status and widespread popularity? Like many IMDb users, I consider myself a cinephile. Unlike the majority who despised Envy (evidenced by its dismal 4.4 rating), I found it to be one of the funniest movies of the past decade.

The storyline of Envy is utterly absurd. The dialogue lacks wit, the scenes lack coherence, and the screenplay feels like it was penned by a fourth grader. Yet, precisely because of these flaws, the film becomes hilariously entertaining. To truly appreciate Envy’s accidental brilliance, you need to watch it with a sense of ironic detachment.

Why do I enjoy Envy? Because its deficiencies push it into the realm of so-bad-it’s-good. This is exactly the kind of movie that becomes a cult classic, and Envy unquestionably fits that mold.

Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer has become somewhat of a forgotten player in the short cartoon arena. This genre is now largely led by Warner Bros.' Looney Tunes and Merry Melodies shorts. However, MGM still manages to produce hidden treasures, such as "To Spring," a remarkable tale celebrating the most beautiful season of the year.

In the world portrayed here, spring is not a natural phenomenon but a crafted illusion. And who is responsible for this creation? A group of tiny male elves living beneath the surface. Each year, as the snow begins to melt, they spring into action. Their first task is felling rainbow-colored rock formations, breaking them into rubble. They then transform this debris into vibrant color fluids, which they carry upward to the surface. There, these fluids nourish grass, flowers, and the lush greenery we associate with spring. The first half of the cartoon focuses on this intricate process of artificially creating spring, but the story takes a turn in the second half. Old Man Winter reappears, intent on re-establishing winter by sabotaging the elves' efforts. From this point forward, a lively battle ensues between the elves and Old Man Winter.

The musical score accompanying this short is exquisitely delightful. Its melodic lines are so catchy and memorable they cling to your mind like an ink blot on paper.

***SPOILERS*** ***SPOILERS*** As a die-hard fan of H:LOTS, I might have enjoyed the movie more than the average viewer. Nonetheless, I think it’s a fantastic film. It was packed with surprises and provided additional closure for the series. Although I was disappointed to see Bayliss become a murderer, overall, I left the movie feeling quite satisfied.

An intriguing perspective on human behavior reveals how our relentless pursuit of perfection can sometimes undermine the very foundations we're striving to build. It also highlights how we often overlook those who are less vocal, potentially missing out on valuable opportunities. The infusion of humor makes the film an engaging and enjoyable experience. It's a must-watch for anyone interested in a thoughtful yet amusing reflection on life. I eagerly anticipate your next creation and hope you continue to deliver high-quality entertainment. Outstanding work.  
— Joanne

Govind Nihalani's directorial adaptation of Vijay Tendulkar's novel is truly outstanding. Om Puri delivers a compelling performance as Inspector Velankar, who is compelled to safeguard underworld don Rama Shetty, portrayed powerfully by Sadashiv Amrapurkar. This film is one of Govind Nihalani's most acclaimed works and is considered a classic. Smita Patil stars as the female lead opposite Om Puri, while Naseeruddin Shah makes a memorable cameo appearance. Despite having only four scenes, Sadashiv Amrapurkar's presence is commanding and leaves a lasting impression; this was his acting debut. Om Puri received the National Film Award for Best Actor for his role, and the film also won Filmfare Awards for Best Film, Best Story, and Best Supporting Actor for Sadashiv Amrapurkar.

I was about to say this was the worst gay-themed film I've ever watched, but honestly, I can confidently declare it the worst movie across any genre I've ever seen.  
It becomes clear you're in trouble right from the start when the film opens with a "personal note" from the Director, requesting the audience's "understanding" for the "many challenges" faced by a first-time director. The audio quality is so poor in many scenes that following the dialogue becomes nearly impossible, even on a DVD release. Poor lighting, unconvincing sets, subpar cinematography, a weak script, and lackluster acting all combine to make this "film" completely unwatchable. I managed to endure until the disappointing ending after several attempts and immediately discarded the DVD I had foolishly purchased.  
While I understand that first-time directors face numerous challenges, there's no excuse for delivering such a half-baked product. According to IMDb, Richard Natale’s directing debut was also his only one, which is the only positive aspect I can find in this so-called "movie."

What can be said about the film *White Fire*? Astonishing? Magnificent? Unsettling? Hilarious? These words scarcely do justice to the experience that is *White Fire*. From its shaky, muddled opening to its surprisingly profound conclusion, this film keeps you hooked from start to finish.

Our story begins deep in the woods of an unspecified country. A family is hiding from unidentified soldiers dressed in uniform-like costumes. When the father separates from the mother and their children, it becomes clear what kind of movie you're in for. The father joyfully rolls down a hill dressed entirely in white, politely drawing attention before shooting his targets—only to be burned alive in what appears to be a dangerously unmonitored stunt. Meanwhile, the mother and kids are fleeing along a beach, with an armed soldier just a few feet behind. He issues a stern warning with a bizarre "HALT!" before firing—taking the mother's life. This intense action scene lays the groundwork for the idyllic childhood of our protagonists, Bo and Ingred.

Fast forward about twenty years—or thirty, if we’re being honest about the characters’ ages—and the story continues.

What an exhilarating experience! Twisted and deeply thought-provoking. Once again, Sharon Stone flawlessly embodies her stunning, mesmerizing character of author Catherine Tramell. The original Basic Instinct was set in San Francisco, but the sequel moves the action to London, where Catherine has now made her home. Both vibrant cities, renowned for their energy, fashion, and sophistication—perfect backdrops for someone like Catherine Tramell. David Morrissey ("Derailed") delivers a smooth performance as psychiatrist Dr. Michael Glass. Meanwhile, David Thewlis, known for his role as Lupin in the Harry Potter series, offers a compelling portrayal of Roy Washburn with Scotland Yard—a refreshing change from his previous parts. The film features flashy cars, designer fashion, sex, intense drama, humor, and tension—classic elements of the "basic instincts." It keeps you guessing with its mind-bending twists from start to finish. The screenplay is excellent; from the electrifying opening scene to the unexpected conclusion, this movie is anything but dull! The entire theater was captivated, glued to the screen throughout.

Last night, I had the pleasure of watching Cracker Bag prior to a preview screening of Disney's Holes. I'm not sure who decided to showcase it, but I’m incredibly grateful they did. Cracker Bag is a true treasure—a vivid portrayal of Australia in the early 1980s viewed through a child's perspective. The humorous "conversations" between Eddie and her brother were hilarious and perfectly authentic, as was the rest of the film. Each frame evoked a strong sense of nostalgia, reminding me of my own childhood—perhaps helped by sharing the same age as the director—and the soundscape only heightened that feeling. I sincerely hope I get to see Cracker Bag again someday.

Take a look at the film's website—more effort clearly went into creating that than into writing the script for this movie. Its boasts couldn’t be more exaggerated. An original story? Really? They must have stashed the script somewhere between the Old Testament pages, or risk facing legal action for such blatant self-praise. High-end special effects? Please, I could outdo them with an Atari 7600 and a jar of earwax. Stylish cinematography? Still clinging to that classic America’s Funniest Home Videos look, I see. Likely operating on a limited budget, the visual effects are lackluster, occasionally poor, sometimes unintentionally funny—yet it’s the story that truly sinks this film, rendering it a complete waste of time and money. Four stories crammed into one, each more mindless than the last—rehashed, cliché-ridden, and thoroughly unoriginal.

Instead of lengthy dance routines and close-up shots of the characters that caused the film to feel sluggish, the movie would have benefited from focusing on clarifying the story and the characters' motivations.  

The sidelining of Nubo, the minister, auntie, and mother, along with the oversimplification of the crucial rivalry between Hatsumo and Mameha, and Hatsumo and Sayuri, deprived the film of any true depth. Without having read the book, viewers might not grasp why Sayuri is so drawn to the Chairman or how Mameha becomes her mentor.  

Visually, the film was breathtaking, and the cast delivered their best given the mediocre script, but that was the extent of its strengths.

This film was fantastic!! (Though not quite as incredible as the Leif Garrett classic Longshot) it still really impressed me! Ashley seemed noticeably larger than Mary-Kate in this movie—I wonder why that is. Who would've guessed they could switch places so seamlessly and almost pull it off? Dad came off as pretty mean, and Mom was a bit too friendly with Helmit Head. I’d give it a solid 4 stars. Anyone who enjoyed this should definitely check out Longshot.

This film gradually won me over. I adore R.D. Burman's music, and despite the rougher aspects of the story, I found myself deeply moved during repeated viewings. The brother-sister relationship is particularly powerful, though there are also some more clichéd elements—like bar fights and a bizarre crime plot—that can be a bit distracting. (Although, from certain perspectives, they can also be somewhat amusing.) The English translation is clearly by someone for whom English isn’t their first language, and while it’s somewhat outlandish, I appreciate the effort he put into it.

Much like many Bollywood films I've seen, this one is highly melodramatic and operatic. Notably, there's a song initially sung by a young boy to lift his suffering sister's spirits, and years later, the same song is performed by the now-grown man who has traveled to Kathmandu in hopes of reconnecting with her. She’s now an adult, estranged, and battling her demons with drugs, believing her brother and mother are dead.

What makes this 1971 film particularly interesting is its focus on the hippie movement, which drew a wave of seekers to...

In contemporary Eastern Europe, life is arduous, and for many young women, prostitution emerges as one of the few viable options—something Melania reluctantly accepts. She catches the eye of an American named Seymour, who becomes increasingly fixated on her, pouring more money into their encounters until he ultimately desires to purchase her entirely. She is supported by two pimps, each with contrasting emotional ties to her, and she is often shuffled around like a piece of luggage, devoid of her own feelings. However, this film ventures into the realm of "modern art-house cinema," where traditional conventions such as coherent narrative structure, proper lighting to reveal the subject, camera techniques that enhance rather than distract, and a consistent plot are often discarded. At times, I found myself bewildered about what was happening and rarely felt engaged. Audience members began leaving even before the final latecomers arrived, and I’ve never seen so many people walk out of a screening. The director places great emphasis on imagery—characters gradually emerge from or vanish into darkness, prolonged shots linger on seemingly insignificant scenes, and one explicit sex scene unfolds amidst this visual exploration.

When selecting a movie, I hope you consider whether the actors involved are leveraging their fame to positively or negatively influence our society's moral values. This isn't a political issue; it's a moral one that impacts us all. For instance, when a comedian or actor makes crude, racist, or sexual remarks about a teenager and her father, we must ask ourselves: do I want to endorse that behavior? In this case, Mr. Foxx’s conduct damages the social fabric that teaches our youth important lessons—distinguishing right from wrong, understanding that kindness is better than hate. He should remember that he is ultimately entertainment, and there are many options available. A mere apology doesn't undo the hurt or erase the negative influence his actions can have on young minds. One effective way to address this is to withdraw our support and refuse to endorse such behavior. We may not be able to change their actions, but we do have the power to stop giving them the platform and fame that perpetuate it.

Nacho Vigalondo is quite well-known in Spain. He has a reputation as somewhat of a poor showman who can come across as uncomfortable and embarrassing. I recall he directed some TV commercials, including one where he searches Madrid for Paul McCartney, which was tied to a McCartney CD collection. 

This short film resembles one of Nacho’s commercials: it features a weak storyline, poor direction, and disappointing performances. I find it hard to believe such an unremarkable film was showcased at The Kodak Theater—poor Oscar. 

It seems Nacho was able to make this film thanks to his wife, who produced it and is well-connected within the Spanish TV industry.

I had no idea what to expect from the movie initially, but now I do—it's truly terrible. The screenplay, direction, and performances were all equally disappointing. The plot was foolish and nonsensical. The director had the potential to create a thoughtful and engaging film, but that opportunity was missed entirely. I found myself squirming in my seat during the second half because it was so poorly executed. There was a lack of focus and coherence throughout. Instead of promoting it, Christians should consider boycotting this film. It was poorly made and a complete waste of my money. I strongly advise against seeing it.

It's a real shame—rarely do I watch a film and feel outright disappointed by the end. Having seen several of Ira Levin's adaptations, like 'Rosemary's Baby' and 'The Stepford Wives,' both of which I enjoyed, I had high expectations for this one. Unfortunately, it didn't resonate with me.

When I first read the synopsis—a renowned playwright, played by Michael Caine, plots to murder a former student, portrayed by Christopher Reeve, and steal his script to boost his own career—I was genuinely excited. I enjoy thrillers, appreciate Michael Caine's talent, respect Sidney Lumet's directorial skill, and generally think Ira Levin's work is solid.

I won't spoil the plot for those who haven't seen it, but I can say there are numerous twists and turns—so many, in fact, that describing the storyline without revealing spoilers is quite challenging. I liked the first 45 minutes; it was engaging until the plot twists started piling up, at which point my interest waned. That said, Lumet deserves credit for crafting a hilarious ending that genuinely made me laugh out loud.

As for the main cast—Michael Caine, Christopher Reeve, Dyan...

DER TODESKING is not among my favorite Jorg Buttgereit films, but it remains an intriguing exploration of suicide, its causes, and its consequences. Those expecting a gore-filled or exploitative experience reminiscent of NEKROMANTIK or SCHRAMM may find themselves disappointed. This film clearly adopts an "art-house" approach, so viewers seeking straightforward, easily explained narratives should look elsewhere.

The film's core premise revolves around a mysterious chain letter that appears to incite people to take their own lives, with each day of the week presenting a new "episode" centered on this disturbing phenomenon. Interwoven are scenes of a slowly decomposing corpse, adding to the unsettling atmosphere.

There are several visually striking and thought-provoking moments, such as a man discussing his marital problems and a massacre at a concert—though this latter scene lost some of its impact on me, partly because I couldn't help but laugh at a band on stage that resembled the Scorpions. Nonetheless, the film features moments of stark beauty; for instance, the scene showing various perspectives of a massive bridge is particularly powerful—especially for those aware of its significance, as the names displayed are of real individuals who committed suicide by jumping from that bridge.

The film is simply terrible—an utterly disappointing experience. The relentless stream of subpar Bollywood productions seems never-ending, and it appears they might be running out of ideas or perhaps just not caring.  
   
The primary issue appears to lie with the direction. This film features two talented actors who have previously demonstrated their capability for compelling performances, yet they were directed so poorly that their potential was wasted. The weak screenplay only exacerbates the problem.  
  
The movie is riddled with absurd moments and suffers from poor editing, especially in the first half. For example: After his first major concert, Ajay Devgn's character encounters Om Puri, from whom he distanced himself three decades earlier, and all Om Puri can say is to warn him about his friendship with Salman! It’s nonsensical. Not to mention the terrible soundtrack—what happened to the quality music of Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy?  
  
Ajay Devgn's casting as a rockstar feels completely off.  
  
The only redeeming aspects are the strong performances in the second half, where Ajay reveals his darker side and Salman convincingly portrays a drug addict.  
   
Perhaps only the latter part of the film is worth watching.

The simplest way to describe Ride With The Devil is with one word: authenticity. I won't reiterate the praise already lavished on this remarkable film, but I want to emphasize the impressive historical research and meticulous attention to detail that the crew undoubtedly dedicated, which I truly appreciated. As a historian familiar with the period and setting depicted, I can confidently say that this production is among the most accurate fictional portrayals of "Bleeding Kansas." While some liberties were taken—inevitable in fiction—the overall atmosphere feels genuine. The costumes are authentic, the attitudes reflect the era without modern political correctness, and even the actors look the part—Jewel Kilcher, despite a minor role, appeared as if she stepped straight from a mid-19th-century photograph. Some viewers I've spoken with have been surprised by the stylized dialogue, questioning whether 19th-century farmers would really speak like poets. What they may not realize is that, contrary to modern assumptions, the American public of the 19th century was unexpectedly literate and eloquent.

I find it difficult to give this film a poor rating or review for two main reasons: Robin Williams and Toni Collette. The movie has the potential to be a compelling thriller, with subtle unsettling elements leaning towards psychological themes—benefiting from a bit more focus in that area. Robin Williams portrays Gabriel Noon, a nighttime DJ who specializes in storytelling and is struggling personally—his partner has moved out, and he appears to be suffering from writer’s block. One day, he receives and reads a story penned by a dying 14-year-old boy named Pete Boland (Rory Culkin). Pete’s narrative recounts his life and the abuse inflicted by his parents. He lives with his adoptive mother and social worker, Donna Boland (Toni Collette). Intrigued, Gabriel begins a friendship with Pete, but things start to feel unusual when Gabriel tries to meet him and discovers that Pete Boland might not even exist. I won't reveal more details to avoid spoiling the plot, but I will say this: the story feels somewhat predictable. The film creates a captivating atmosphere for storytelling, and Robin Williams delivers a strong performance.

"Hitler: The Rise of Evil" is clearly a production crafted by individuals emotionally detached from the horrors of World War II, which makes watching it a surprisingly refreshing experience. 

I believe its greatest strength lies in its unambiguous portrayal of the Nazi machinery—shedding light on the utterly corrupt methods Hitler employed to ascend to power. Once he achieved his position, the film's focus ends. 

As the 'Führer'—the German term for 'leader'—he guided Germany into the most devastating war in human history, which concluded six years later with Germany’s total defeat. As a consequence, Germany forfeited its eastern provinces, amounting to roughly 35% of its prewar territory, and was compelled to accept a 44-year division of its remaining land. Both East and West Germany had to be reconstructed from ruins, their reputations severely tarnished by numerous Nazi atrocities rooted in racism. 

As I mentioned, "Hitler: The Rise of Evil" is a compelling watch. It is set in a convincingly thirties-era environment, supported by more than competent acting. Notably, Peter O’Toole’s portrayal of the aged President Hindenburg stands out, adding an extra dimension to the narrative. 

My copy of the film also includes a second DVD featuring two excellent documentary films.

This film explores the tragic events in Derry thirty years ago, widely known as Bloody Sunday. It is meticulously researched, expertly acted, and skillfully directed. While it reflects the most accurate portrayal available until the conclusion of the Saville inquiry, it contextualizes the atrocity within the broader historical landscape. The film also depicts the brutality of the soldiers involved on that day and critically examines the shameful whitewash of the Widgery Tribunal. Overall, it is a powerful and poignant drama that evokes both emotion and shock. Once the Saville report is published, revisiting this film will provide deeper insight into its accuracy and the pursuit of truth.

This is ridiculous. They claim they won’t make another Nightmare film and that this one is the "final" installment... yet they go ahead and make another. To be fair, the next one (Part 7) wasn't terrible, but it feels like they’re just stringing us along. Anyway, this movie made no sense at all; it was incredibly dull. The characters were one-dimensional, and Freddy was reduced to another goofy joker—completely missing the menacing edge that made the series great. The plot was terrible, even worse than Parts 2 and 5. I couldn’t understand the story; it was a pointless, cheesy 3D mess. I hated this film so much that I still remember every part I disliked—basically, the whole movie. It’s so different from the original films; it tries so hard, but ends up failing miserably. There were hardly any death scenes, and the few they had were disappointing and poorly executed. How did they let it get this far? Didn’t they learn from their biggest mistakes in Parts 2 and 5? Yet they went ahead and made this? It’s all about the money. Don’t waste your time on this sorry excuse for a Nightmare installment.

I gave "A Nightmare on Elm Street Part 6" a 3 out of 10.

**Good points:** The movie had potential with its plot.

**Bad points:**

What I remember most about this film is that it used to air annually on KTLA (Channel 5) during the Christmas season in the mid to late 1970s, primarily because the true story it was based on unfolded on or around Christmas Eve. Watching the harrowing ordeal of the girl, the sole survivor of a plane crash in the Peruvian jungle, was always unsettling. A particularly vivid memory is of the intense scene where she pulls leeches from her infected leg, which left a lasting impression on me as a young viewer. It wasn’t the kind of Christmas cheer I was accustomed to, and definitely not a Rankin-Bass special.

I rented this on DVD and feel a bit guilty because Dawson and Lugacy are so passionate about it in the DVD commentary. It’s not exactly a bad film, but one of those movies that desperately tries to be a profound reflection on human nature without realizing that its story essentially belongs to a familiar genre. Additionally, it simplifies the issue in many ways, and the characters’ actions often stretch believability. I’d say it’s a film that might resonate more if you lack much experience with film, TV, literature, or life in general—honestly, I’ve seen a very similar story in horror comics myself. Otherwise, its message has been conveyed before and more eloquently elsewhere. The main problem is that the film doesn’t offer much beyond that idea. It ultimately comes across as a fairly dull movie that relies on the notion that its basic story will be shocking and engaging, but it fails to deliver in that regard.

Drawing inspiration from the real-life adventures of Chuck Connors and Steve Brodie in 1890s New York, "The Bowery" bursts with lively energy and good-natured humor.  

However, viewers should be prepared: the film features casual racial slurs spoken by Wallace Beery and young Jackie Cooper, with the opening scene potentially shocking audiences. This reflects the historical setting and the diverse makeup of the neighborhood, contributing to the gritty authenticity of the atmosphere.  

Wallace Beery portrays Connors as a boisterous, thunderous figure—an outspoken saloon owner with his own fire brigade—and he harbors a soft spot for the mischievous orphan Cooper. Raft's Brodie is Connors' more suave, handsome rival, ever eager for a challenge and craving attention, famously attempting to jump off the Brooklyn Bridge—a stunt whose authenticity remains debated, whether done by Brodie himself or a dummy.  

Beery's performance is as exuberant as ever, complete with a thick Irish-American accent, embodying the rough-around-the-edges character who naturally draws children, cats, and women in peril. This film may be among the most lively and spirited of his roles.

When I was younger, I took great pleasure in watching cheesy television shows. We’ve all been there at some point, but my justification for tuning into programs like "Buck Rogers in the 25th Century" and "Silver Spoons" was simple: I was young and naive, unaware of what truly makes a show great.  

Fortunately, I’ve since developed a taste for quality entertainment. As for Stargate SG-1, it simply isn’t good. The twelve-year-old version of me would have adored every clichéd scene, every awkward line of dialogue, and every bit of unnecessary techno-babble. The writing is shockingly insipid—so dull and uninspired that it actually makes one nostalgic for Star Trek: Voyager. If your show makes me wish for the worst Trek series, you’ve got a problem.  

The original Stargate film remains a delightful guilty pleasure, thanks to compelling performances by James Spader and Kurt Russell, stunning Egyptian architecture and cultural influences, a fantastic musical score, and inventive sci-fi concepts. Unfortunately, most of what made that film enjoyable doesn’t translate to the TV series. Even Richard Dean Anderson, who once made MacGyver captivating and Legend intriguing, appears to be half-asleep in most episodes.  

It’s clear the production had a very limited budget, because

This film was absolutely dreadful. I struggled to stay awake throughout, and I would never watch it again—even if I were paid to do so. The so-called horror scenes were incredibly predictable and overused, offering nothing fresh or interesting. Honestly, there was nothing about this movie that made it worth the $7.50 I spent to see it. Avoid it at all costs—don't watch it, don't rent it, and avoid reading about it online, as any of those choices would just waste your time. Sarah Michelle Gellar's performance was lackluster, and she should be embarrassed to have her reputation associated with this film. Truly, this is a terrible movie that you can safely skip forever.

I reference Oedipus Rex because it underscores how tragic it is that this film was even produced. This ranks among the worst movies I have ever seen. I’m not one of those humorless IMDb users who dislike Uwe Boll; in fact, I find movies like Postal and Tunnel Rats hilariously bad and thus entertaining. However, this film was genuinely terrible. I hated it so much that I would give it zero stars if I could. The story is simply rubbish—spending most of the film developing the plot, only to hit a middle section filled with brutal, tastelessly executed murders. It concludes with a "villain wins" ending, which is acceptable in theory, but surely it could have been handled with more finesse. I’m not opposed to Uwe Boll or violent films—I love violent movies. I enjoyed the Saw and Hostel series, Tokyo Gore Police, The New York Ripper, the 28 Days Later films, Dog Soldiers, My Bloody Valentine, Last House on the Left, Watchmen, Wolf Creek, every Tarantino film, every Sam Peckinpah, and even Cannibal Holocaust.

I recently received my copy of this two-disc DVD set, and while it's not perfect, I found it to be an enjoyable way to pass the time. As someone who is a big fan of zombie movies, I have to say that I believe the creators of these films likely share that enthusiasm. I also have a soft spot for individuals who pursue their dreams, even against the odds, and these filmmakers certainly are doing just that. Is this a collection of award-winning, cinematic masterpieces? No. Not even close. But considering their modest budgets, these films definitely deserve recommendation. For me, the key question is always: was I entertained? Did I have a good time watching this? And in both respects, the answer is yes. The first film in the series is the most raw and gritty. It begins with an accident at a nuclear facility, leading to people melting down or something similar. Fast forward several years, and a new housing development is built atop the old reactor site. A group of kids filming a video stumble into a hole and find themselves trapped deep within the underground levels of the site.

This year's surprise contender in the Best Animated Feature category at the Oscars is an Irish film at its core, though it was co-produced by Belgium and Brazil, likely involving animators from all three countries. The result is one of the most stunning and distinctive films in recent memory. Its character designs evoke the French animated film Persepolis from a few years ago, featuring simple figures outlined in bold, black strokes. However, unlike Persepolis, this film is not black and white. Its brilliance lies in its daring and vibrant use of color—arguably some of the most bold and arresting palettes I've ever encountered. The visual style is also heavily geometric, with characters predominantly composed of rectangles and ovals. Viewers can spend much of the film playing "find the circle," as a central theme in the visuals is the circle—often positioned at the heart of each frame. Every geometric element serves a purpose; the story follows a young boy learning to be an artist, working on illuminated manuscripts. The film’s art draws inspiration from masterpieces like the Book of Kells, bringing to life a richly textured, visually captivating world.

Almost everything about this film falls flat. Take Mike Myers, for instance—his shtick hasn't evolved since his SNL days over a decade ago. He's stuck in the same goofy, stream-of-consciousness humor and voice routines, with his Cat character falling painfully flat. He seems to be overcompensating, coming across more as a nervous, overly eager comedian rather than the cool cat he's meant to be. The rest of the movie doesn't fare any better, featuring sets that are shockingly ugly and a complete waste of production money. Instead of building elaborate neighborhoods and Main Street, they'd have been better off with simple cardboard cutouts. Alec Baldwin attempts a humorous Great Santini impersonation but ends up sounding and looking incoherent. There's even an inappropriate cheesecake scene involving faux celebrity Paris Hilton—an odd choice considering this is supposed to be a Dr. Seuss story. Overall, steer clear of this film; it's not even an entertaining train wreck. Hopefully, Robin Williams will star in Horton Hears a Who—then we'll have the unfortunate trilogy of bad Seuss adaptations starring out-of-place comedians.

A few months ago, I caught this film on cable and it truly blew me away. William H. Macy, one of my favorite actors, delivered a remarkable performance that deeply engaged me. He has a talent for making his character sympathetic, even when his actions are clearly wrong. Neve Campbell also gave an outstanding performance—the best I've seen from an actress this year. She portrays a spirited young woman with wisdom beyond her years, and she was simply fantastic.

Donald Sutherland's portrayal of Macy's father was wonderfully unsettling—he played the role with just the right amount of creepiness. John Ritter also did well as a psychiatrist caught in the chaos unfolding around him.

I wish this film had a theatrical release because I believe it deserves a much broader audience. It’s a shame it’s not in cinemas, especially since it’s far superior to many of the new movies currently playing.

Henry Hathaway was both adventurous and passionate, driven by his admiration for the early American pioneers. While critiques of the historical accuracy of his film about Brigham Young and the Mormon community may not be necessary or particularly constructive, I believe Hathaway delivered outstanding direction that vividly portrays the life of the Mormon people during the formative years of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints—spanning from Joseph Smith's martyrdom to the film’s release. Through subtle cinematography and carefully delivered dialogue, he effectively conveyed Mormon philosophies and teachings across various scenes and segments.

I recall watching this movie many Saturday mornings in my youth during the early 1950s—just over a decade after its release and before the completion of the Los Angeles Temple, which I followed during its construction, sparking my curiosity about Mormons. Recently, I acquired this film again and look forward to reflecting on the messages Hathaway conveyed through his storytelling:

1. A love for all people, regardless of their beliefs  
2. Charity toward both the needy and those who are not  
3. The importance of family

I never realized that Charles Boyer (Luis Denard) appeared alongside Lauren Bacall (Rose Cullen) in a film and delivered such a remarkable performance. Even Peter Lorre (Contreras) had a role, though he faced an unfortunate mishap in his bathroom that caused him to faint. The story follows a Republican courier, Luis Denard, who visits England during the Spanish Civil War with the intent to sabotage a coal mining contract that could harm multiple nations. Lauren Bacall's character, Rose Cullen, comes to Luis's rescue by helping him after he falls, and along the way, she falls in love with him. She then assists him in escaping from a hostile crowd of English miners threatening his life. The real antagonist of the film is Victor Francen (Licata), who delivers an outstanding performance as the sinister villain in "Beast with Five Fingers." This classic 1945 film is a gem, even without Humphrey Bogart.

Here is another provocative European film that criticizes and undermines the religious traditions of its country. (These atheist filmmakers seem relentless in their opposition.) In this film, Catholics and their clergy are depicted harshly—though I am not Catholic myself. 

Interestingly, it won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, likely because it portrays Catholics and religious faith as feeble and insignificant. One of the key characters is a priest who appears more interested in food than spiritual matters, depicted as foolish. No wonder the secular-dominated Academy favored this film. 

Furthermore, there's a scene involving a foolish character who abandons his faith to marry one of the four daughters featured in the story. The daughters each take turns seducing the “seminary” student, who claims he studied for six years but now considers himself an agnostic. Just how blasphemous is this film?! 

This is truly disgraceful—a clear example of the secular-progressive bias prevalent in the global film industry, not just in Hollywood.

This is truly one of the most captivating films I’ve ever watched. I adore the rustic, backwoods atmosphere it captures. The film feels remarkably authentic and believable. It appears to be set in a different time period, perhaps the late 1960s or early 1970s. Henry Thomas delivers a heartfelt performance alongside the young child. The story is deeply moving and definitely worth experiencing.

I remember watching American Gothic when it first aired, and recently it came to mind again. All I could recall was that the same actor appeared in Midnight Caller—Gary Cole. I don't watch much television, but I did watch American Gothic, and I actually purchased the Complete Series on DVD this week. It’s still just as good as I remembered. This show is one of the best TV series ever. The reason I don’t watch much TV nowadays is because most of it is rubbish—mainly reality shows or soap operas like Grease and Big Brother. I’ve just grown tired of it all. I managed to get the Complete Series of American Gothic for £16.97 from the Asda website, which is the cheapest I could find.

Rated 10 out of 10, this outstanding documentary is an essential watch. It features rare film footage from the war that hadn’t been seen for years until its 1974 screening. The clips included leave no detail out; some moments left me completely stunned. The series spans over 20 episodes, narrated by Sir Laurence Olivier, who masterfully tells a powerful story of war. Even after more than 25 years, it remains arguably the best war documentary, still delivering a profound impact. You should definitely find time to watch at least a few episodes—you’ll be deeply moved by the significance of this film for those who experienced, suffered, and lost their lives in the chaos of war, in a world torn by conflict.

Indeed: a film featuring drug use, warehouse shootouts, 'Matrix'-style bullet dodging, a futuristic cityscape teeming with diverse Asian ethnicities, and a solitary vampire— all in one package— seems like a creation only a Japanese pop or rock star could envision. And that’s precisely what 'Moon Child' delivers, plus much more. While these disparate elements might suggest a cheesy B-movie, 'Moon Child' manages to pull them together with only a few expected stumbles along the way.

The movie exudes a raw, indie vibe, jumping from scene to scene in sporadic bursts rather than smooth transitions, offering fleeting glimpses into the characters' lives while barely scratching the surface of a cohesive plot. Yet, it makes no apologies; instead, it transforms into a story about friendship, love, trust, and betrayal, all wrapped in the layers of a futuristic society, gang rivalries, and vampires. 

HYDE's portrayal of the brooding vampire Kei is outstanding, adding depth and nuance to the character, balancing out Gackt's more over-the-top performance as Sho, an orphan who forms a bond with Kei. Lee-Hom Wang also delivers a memorable performance as Son, a vengeful figure who later becomes an ally to a grown-up Sho.

This should have been a film centered around Sam and his wife, featuring the illustrious Peter Falk and the equally remarkable Olympia Dukakis. That would have been a film truly worth watching. Instead, it’s a Paul Reiser vehicle, with a minor role for Falk. Elizabeth Perkins, who is fantastic, also appears, but her presence is barely noticeable. I can only assume Reiser believes he's a major movie star deserving of a prestigious project. He's not. What's more frustrating is that Reiser took the effort to cast some of the finest women character actresses working today, yet relegated them all to the background. Dukakis only appears in the final 15 minutes, but when she does, she lights up the screen. The story genuinely revolves around Falk and Dukakis, but we're forced through a pointless, silly, and preposterous road trip, during which Reiser tries to showcase how adorable, precious, and deeply insightful—though actually misguided—he can be. For example, in a restaurant scene that I think Reiser fancied as "Cassavetes-like," there's a painfully fake confrontation between Reiser and Falk that is so absurdly exaggerated, I felt embarrassment for Falk.

This Fourth of July weekend, it’s inspiring to see the enduring spirit of the Declaration of Independence reflected in the film "War, Inc." Just as our founding fathers boldly challenged King George III, this satirical movie humorously critiques the greed-driven war profiteering of today’s corporate elites, who are increasingly privatizing government functions—and even war itself.

The cast delivers outstanding performances. John Cusack shines as a dry, conflicted corporate hitman, while the lovely Marisa Tomei is fantastic as his romantic counterpart. (Honestly, George Costanza was onto something—Marisa Tomei is truly stunning!) However, it’s Joan Cusack who truly steals the show. Her role as a bossy yet sycophantic personal assistant is priceless, and her comedic timing is impeccable. Her expressive face captures every nuance, making her performance utterly memorable. Dan Aykroyd also makes a brief but impactful appearance as the head of Tamerlane Corporation, the company orchestrating the war.

This is the inaugural installment in the Guinea Pig series and is arguably the most notorious film within the collection.

It took me quite some time to muster the courage and acquire a copy of these infamous movies. I eventually purchased the Guinea Pig Box Set and decided to watch them in chronological order based on their release dates. So, I inserted this one and settled in to watch.

Based on what I had read online and knowing the nature of its content, I anticipated that it would push my nerves to the limit. However, that was not quite the case.

The plot centers on a group of men who abduct a woman and subject her to various tortures in an attempt to find the limits of human endurance and determine how much pain a person can withstand.

Does that sound like a particularly disturbing film? Actually, it’s not. The movie fails to genuinely shock. Perhaps this is because I have become desensitized over the years due to my obsession with horror films, but it’s safe to say that any seasoned gore enthusiast could watch this with relative ease.

Conversely, someone without

Alright. This was a low-budget film with some noticeable continuity errors—like scenes shot in bright sunshine then in shadow, and a mix of both. Despite my admiration for Nick Mancuso, he occasionally overdid the burnout look, and some of the supporting cast performances were quite poor; at least one actor played two different, obvious roles. Nevertheless, Richard Grieco's performance was hilarious—his hair alone makes it worth watching. Steven Ford was very likable, and Mancuso delivered some memorable lines, whereas Nancy Allen, ironically, came across as dull and unremarkable. Is it a classic? Definitely not. Are there bad parts? Absolutely. But is it entertaining? Without a doubt. I wish I could have been there on set when they decided Grieco's hairstyle. "Are you fast?" ... "Y'ain't THAT fast."

Regrettably, the film is flawed by a single issue that undermines its entire credibility. It begins with a critique of the Israeli occupation of disputed territories but neglects to explain the historical context—namely, that Israel's presence there stems from conflicts initiated by Egypt, Syria, Iraq, and Jordan, which attacked Israel. Consequently, Israel's so-called "occupation" is a result of wars these nations provoked.

Additionally, the film alleges that Israel has defied the United Nations by not adhering to Resolution 242. However, this resolution was rejected immediately upon its introduction by the Palestinians, rendering it effectively invalid.

While many well-produced films can compellingly present footage capable of swaying opinions, viewers should remain cautious—trust none of what they hear and only half of what they see. 

Furthermore, all the participants in this film are known critics of Israel, some having made numerous antisemitic remarks publicly, which severely diminishes their credibility. 

Ultimately, those involved would benefit from an objective, factual history lesson rather than one filtered through Palestinian sympathies.

I usually tune into the MTV Movie Awards to enjoy a witty, entertaining show that offers a unique take on awards—like the time Chewbacca received a lifetime achievement award. This year was no exception. Although I’m not particularly a fan of Justin Timberlake, I’ve always found Seann William Scott amusing—albeit a bit silly. I’ve chuckled at Stifler in the American Pie movies and even enjoyed him in Dude, Where’s My Car?. However, this year’s MTV Movie Awards were simply terrible. The show lacked coherence, humor, and entertainment value. Justin Timberlake should probably stick to singing and dancing—acting is clearly not his strong suit.

I'm also curious about who the writers were for this year’s show. Last year, Jack Black and Sarah Michelle Gellar delivered hilarious performances; the Lord of the Rings parody alone made the entire show worthwhile. But this year was a complete letdown. Did anyone understand Timberlake’s comments about Luke Wilson and Kate Hudson—saying, “They’re starring in a movie together, but have never met! Here they are...” Where was the joke? Kate and Luke simply exchanged awkward lines without referencing Timberlake’s supposed punchline. As for Seann William Scott, he was utterly wasted as a talent, leaving me unimpressed.

This film is an highly recommended masterpiece, acclaimed not only for its profound thematic depth but also for Angelopoulos's unparalleled and visionary cinematography. The performances by legendary actors Mastroianni and Moreau are truly exceptional, complemented by Ilias Logothethis’s remarkable character portrayal. While Gregory Karr's performance might initially seem overshadowed by his more dominant co-stars, he masterfully embodies his role, a nuance fully revealed in his final scene with Khrysikou and Mastroianni—a moment foreshadowed earlier in the film. (Warning: spoilers ahead.)

Set your expectations accordingly. This is an "art film" in the truest sense, demanding full attention and engagement. It’s not suitable for casual viewing but requires the same focused concentration as reading a novel or experiencing a concert. The film’s distinctive visual style makes it best appreciated on a large screen.

Dialogue is sparse, yet the film enriches its narrative with snippets in Albanian, Kurdish, and Turkish alongside Greek and English. These linguistic touches will enchant viewers who appreciate the musicality and beauty of multiple languages.

Wow, I can't believe I'm the first and only person to leave a comment on this fantastic movie. Although the film itself seemed quite intriguing, what really drew me in was Matt Lillard. Sure, many folks might think he's either overly hyper or just not talented, but being the same age and from the same generation, I've watched him so many times that he's become one of my favorites. This is one of the few films where he's the main star, similar to his role in SLC Punk—another excellent Lillard film. 

Basically, the story follows a typical heist plot but with more twists than I can count, which eventually leads to some madness. Another standout actor is Vincent D’Onofrio, who’s often underrated in the industry. The female lead is new to acting and does okay, though you can tell she was cast partly for her accent and a nude scene. 

It’s a game of Jack versus Jill versus Bob—each trying to get their share of the rewards without sharing with anyone else. They all make their moves to succeed.

Given its numerous entertaining qualities, I believe this movie deserves more recognition on IMDb. It's a classic 'whodunit' thriller packed with sex and murder, and it keeps you guessing until the very last moment. I enjoy films in this genre, and I feel this one lives up to the expectations. I found it worth watching multiple times, so I’d rate it an 8 on IMDb.

Mat Spirogolou, known as Toby Malone, comes from a family proud of his talent as a footballer. They are thrilled when he lands an audition with a major club, hoping that his cousin will look out for him once he arrives in the city.  

However, the cousins couldn't be more different: one is a naive farm boy, while the other is a street-smart spendthrift entangled with drug dealers and gangsters. Mat's first night in the city is unlikely to be a peaceful one before his big day.  

After missing his cousin George, played by Damien Robertson, upon arrival, Mat faces more trouble when a young biker offers him a ride—one that involves more than just a quick trip.  

Toby Malone, better known for his theatre work, delivers a commendable performance as the rural teen. Though the film shows signs of a limited budget, it compensates with more fun, spontaneity, and charm than the typical Hollywood blockbuster.

I waited some time before sharing my thoughts on this documentary because, over a decade ago, I wanted to reflect carefully before writing a review. 

From a filmmaking perspective, I can honestly say this is an excellent documentary. It achieved its goal of revealing something I knew nothing about and kept me captivated by the world it depicted. Prior to watching, I was completely unfamiliar with the drag scene and the world of "Balls," and learning about them was truly eye-opening. The talent displayed by these performers—how they craft their looks and perform for competition—was nothing short of spectacular. 

The film captures the drama—the cattiness, the complaints (I even got upset when someone questioned whether a coat was truly a man's coat!), the jealousy—all familiar elements from any competitive scene. Like every other competition, it has its conflicts and passions. To me, that was an important point. 

There’s also a touching moment with an older drag queen reflecting on how the Balls "used" to be, contrasted with the newer generations of drag performers who introduced more categories and increased competition. Some viewers observe these changes with a mix of nostalgia and anticipation for the future of the scene.

Years ago, my friend and I, both avid movie enthusiasts, decided to see a horror film we believed would be worth watching because it featured John Cassavetes. For those unfamiliar, Cassavetes was an accomplished actor, screenwriter, and director—married to actress Gena Rowlands—who had been nominated for three Oscars. He created a variety of low-budget films, often using his earnings from acting to fund his creative projects. Before watching The Incubus, we had no idea that Cassavetes' income came from any film he appeared in. Had we known the film's plot beforehand, we might have avoided it altogether. But we stuck it out and didn't walk out. At the time, my friend and I jokingly called it the worst movie ever made. Honestly, that's not entirely accurate. I've seen many poorly made films on Friday nights on Cinemax (did I really just say that?) that are far worse than The Incubus. For instance, nearly any movie starring Brian Bosworth is, by definition, a worse film. Certainly, Santa Claus Conquers the Martians surpasses The Incubus in quality. Since then, I’ve used The Incubus as a benchmark for depicting movies that fall below a certain threshold of quality.

There's no need for a clever review here—this film simply doesn't warrant one. It's neither an art house flick nor one of those elusive indie treasures you hear about from friends who recommend hidden gems screened at indie cinemas downtown. Just tuck it away with the Christmas decorations and get rid of it fast.

There is little doubt that H.G. Wells is the most influential writer of the 20th century. While Jules Verne has a valid claim as the father of science fiction, his stories primarily focus on adventure tales featuring marvelous inventions as plot devices. In contrast, Wells was deeply insightful and infused his narratives with subtext. Perhaps his most enduring legacy is that, before the 20th century, there was scant evidence to suggest that people believed in extraterrestrial life. Today, however, many— including Richard Dawkins— consider the existence of life on other planets almost certain. Of course, there's no concrete evidence to support this, leading to the speculation that Wells may have introduced this idea into human consciousness. Undoubtedly, he planted the seed.

THINGS TO COME was adapted by Wells himself from his novel. However, it’s quite clear that he struggled to distinguish between writing a novel and scripting a screenplay. The dialogue often feels heavy-handed, overdone, and unconvincing. For example, two pilots from opposing sides discussing the nature of war—“Why must we murder one another? Why?”—illustrates the somewhat awkward and forced nature of the dialogue.

I've never seen a worse murder mystery film than this. Centered around a medical examiner investigating his friend's mysterious death in a car crash, the movie fails on every level: poor acting, a dull storyline, no tension, lame humor, and a complete lack of drama. I recall watching it on PAX, a channel known for broadcasting low-budget, campy made-for-TV movies like this one. While TV movies generally lack the edge and suspense of theatrical releases, this one misses the mark entirely. The filmmakers squandered a chance to turn "Recipe for Murder" into an engaging TV movie; after all, the title hints at some suspense. 

If you're looking for a satisfying story, avoid this film at all costs. It’s enough to spoil your TV viewing experience. 

Grade: F

I found King Solomon's Mines to be beautifully executed. My only minor critique was regarding Alison Doody. While her acting was outstanding, her makeup and hairstyle did not quite reflect the period, which occasionally made her seem out of place alongside the other actors. I thought Patrick Swayze was an excellent choice for Alan Quatermain. It was refreshing to see a seasoned, rugged actor in this role after so many movies featuring the fair-haired, fair-skinned actors like Val Kilmer and Brad Pitt. His performance was spot-on, and I enjoyed every moment of the film. This version is incomparable to the 1950s adaptation with Stewart Grainger; it was a grand, big-screen production rather than a TV movie. Both portrayals of Quatermain felt believable, but it’s important to recognize the differences between the media. I look forward to watching this film again and hope Patrick Swayze considers similar roles in the future.

This is an art film believed to have been created either in 1969 or 1972, with the National Film Preservation Foundation citing 1969 and IMDb listing 1972. Regardless of the precise year, the film unmistakably reflects the visual and stylistic sensibilities of its era—featuring camera techniques and pop art influences characteristic of the late 1960s to early 1970s.  

The film presents three simple images that are heavily distorted through various unconventional camera tricks. Accompanying these visuals is a musical soundtrack, with no dialogue or storyline whatsoever. It seems designed as a form of performance art—initially intriguing, but quickly becoming monotonous. Frankly, the film is a complete bore, likely only entertaining its creators, their families, friends, or perhaps a select few who are so hip and "in the know" that it defies understanding by the general audience.

While there were a few funny moments, I found the film overall quite disappointing. As it progressed, it only seemed to decline further in quality. Once the story moved into Monument Valley, I found myself more captivated by the stunning natural formations than by the increasingly absurd and unconvincing interactions between the characters.

The daughter’s character was especially inconsistent. At one point, she’s in on the plan; then she uncovers the truth and abandons them. Shortly after, she reappears, only to leave again, then returns once more. Her decisions lack clear motivation, making her behavior difficult to follow. The film featured some intriguing characters and scenes, but many promising ideas were left unexplored. Ultimately, the movie felt like it was worth more than it delivered. It seems those who enjoyed Repo Man might have been more receptive to this film, but Searchers 2.0 cannot compare to the original The Searchers.

Any film in which Brooke Shields outperforms a Fonda is both an anomaly and a nightmare. Shields' poor performance stems from her youth, inexperience, and an evident lack of strong direction from her co-star. Peter Fonda, on the other hand, is simply terrible—though I did appreciate him years later in Ulee's Gold, here he is abysmal. Unfortunately, no one else fares any better. Apart from Henry Fonda’s charming cameo, not a single performance is even close to acceptable. I've rarely seen a movie plagued with such an abundance of bad acting. Regarding Luke Askew, the main villain, his poor delivery can be attributed to weak dialogue and direction, despite his history of good work. However, his partner, played by Ted Markland, delivers an embarrassing ham performance. The screenplay is simply dreadful, and the actors shouldn’t be blamed for the awful lines they’re forced to speak—but they deliver them so poorly! The editing and directing are worse than mediocre. Scenes are prolonged unnecessarily or cut off prematurely, preventing their emotional impact. This film was far worse than I expected and would have faded into obscurity—and likely never been remembered—if not for its remarkable level of ineptitude.

Letters without destinations end up in an alternate realm tucked away behind the post office, known as the back rooms. There, Alice finds a job, driven by the hope of reuniting with her estranged father. However, she uncovers something unexpected—the troubled spirit of her boss, Frank. Once a quiet Australian detective movie that briefly appeared at the cinema, Frank now resides in the shadowy recesses of the video store, dwarfed by dozens of copies of that notorious GODZILLA film. It’s unfortunate, because this film proves to be a rewarding watch, telling a courageous story with stark, powerful imagery and compelling performances from the two main actors. Unlike Garry Marshall’s other dead letter office film, DEAR GOD (1996 - USA), which missed the mark, this one nearly matches the brilliance of He Jianjun’s POSTMAN (1995 - China), not the Kevin Costner misfire, but a truly meaningful masterpiece.

Errol Flynn stars as "Gentleman Jim" in this 1942 film depicting the life of boxer Jim Corbett, famed for defeating John L. Sullivan. Directed with a light, skillful touch by Flynn’s close friend Raoul Walsh, the movie also features Alexis Smith, Jack Carson, Alan Hale Sr., William Frawley, and Ward Bond. Flynn portrays an ambitious and somewhat egotistical young man blessed with natural boxing talent, who is sponsored by the prestigious Olympic Club in San Francisco during the late 1800s. Although good-hearted, his background as a "shanty Irishman" and his social ambitions generate resentment among the club members; many of them root for his defeat and bet against him. Nonetheless, Corbett rises to prominence, even branching into acting. His big break arrives in the form of a much-anticipated match with the reigning world champion, John L. Sullivan, played by Ward Bond. Sullivan insists on a $10,000 deposit to secure Corbett’s appearance for the $25,000 purse. Corbett and his manager, portrayed by William Frawley, are desperate to secure the funds, but help unexpectedly comes from a most unlikely source.  

This is a highly entertaining film, with Jim Corbett’s story perfectly suited for Flynn, who...

Because that’s the only way you might avoid thinking this film is a complete waste of time and money. A remake of "Heaven Can Wait"—which at least had some worth—serves as a poor excuse for a romantic comedy here. Instead, it feels more like a vehicle to give Rock some screen time, highlighting his weak stand-up routines that don’t translate well to the big screen. His jokes, meant to be delivered by the body of an old, fat, wealthy, deceased man, are awkwardly presented as if coming directly from Rock himself. The film's attempt at humor falls flat, especially as it attempts to navigate racial insults—resulting in a jarring lack of chemistry. The movie is unfunny, poorly shot, and the acting is weak at best. For a better experience, rent the original "Heaven Can Wait" and watch a live Rock performance—you're bound to come out ahead.

Having read some of the comments about this film, I can only conclude that some viewers are easily pleased. This movie amounts to almost nothing. It suffers from extremely poor writing, direction, and acting, leaving hardly any impact. The characters deliver clichéd dialogue, and the plotlines are entirely unconvincing. While this might lend itself to camp and entertainment, it fails to do so because everything feels so dead and uninspired, rendering the film dull. It seems as though Lee Rose attempted to craft a drama about a woman grappling with her sexuality, but was either restrained by studio executives from portraying it with genuine authenticity or lacked the courage to do so. Ultimately, this film could easily be listed in the encyclopedia as a typical bad Lifetime TV movie.

Absolutely trivial and lacking substance—a regrettable reflection of the hypocritical, toxic culture of a decade ago. This film pairs superficial regrets about slavery with colonialist undertones, exemplified by the irksome redhead feeding Shaka rice. It also dismisses historical accuracy; most western slaves hailed from West Africa, yet here, a small group of men easily captures Shaka—hardly plausible. Additionally, David Hasselhoff’s performance is nothing short of obnoxious. One can only wonder how he would have fared in the miniseries—probably met a swift end. The miniseries itself was excellent, making it all the more disappointing that Hasselhoff managed to tarnish what could have been a unique work, turning it into something dull. I suspect he may have played a role in turning this into a fiasco.

I do not expect this film to be easily understood by viewers outside of Romania. This perhaps reflects the film’s limited universality or its specific cultural context, but it also highlights how different the history and daily experiences of ordinary people in Romania were compared to other countries, even within Eastern Europe.  

The film is an adaptation of a novel by Marin Preda, a controversial author who passed away during the Communist era shortly after the book’s publication. It narrates the story of an intellectual— a philosophy professor— whose life is shattered after he is unjustly imprisoned at the end of the Stalinist period. The first part of the film focuses on his struggle to survive in prison, while the second depicts his fragile attempts to rebuild his life after release. However, his freedom is only superficial; in 1960s Romania, he faces new forms of compromise and moral compromise, yet his fight for survival remains equally arduous, morally if not physically.  

The film features outstanding performances by some of Romania’s most talented actors. Stefan Iordache, who plays the lead role, delivers a compelling portrayal that, in different times and circumstances, would have resonated even more profoundly.

When I started watching this film, I recognized the guy from Buffy—Xander—and thought, "It's nice to see he's still making a living in movies." Now, this is a strange film I can tolerate, especially since it offers a healthy dose of weirdness similar to David Lynch's works like Twin Peaks and Lost Highway. You really need to be in the right mood for that kind of thing. However, this movie honestly made me mockingly recall those crazy conspiracy theory websites that make zero sense. Seriously, people? Nazis teaming up with America to form an unholy trinity of evil powers? I was surprised they didn't include the hollow earth theories, Hitler flying saucers, or lizard people. Maybe adding about 60 grams of heroin would help make sense of this mess, but I don't endorse drugs any more than I endorse this film. It should be burned, shredded, and forgotten—just so good old Xander can hopefully get another acting gig. The problem wasn’t his performance; he was fine. It was the script that simply made no sense. Sorry.

Here's another film that should be launched into a satellite, sent hurtling into space, and aimed toward the Andromeda galaxy to showcase the best of humanity to distant civilizations. This movie is so charmingly foolish and candidly honest in being little more than a shameless clone of the notoriously cheesy 1976 classic KING KONG that it not only outshines that film in sheer ridiculousness but also eerily anticipates much of Peter Jackson's disastrous 2005 CGI remake, which features a similar "romance" between a giant creature—here a Yeti—and a stunning human woman (Antonellina Interlenghi of Umberto Lenzi's CITY OF THE LIVING DEAD, who’s quite easy on the eyes).  

Designed as a kids' movie, aside from some innuendos involving fish bones and a bizarre nipple tweak as a farewell gesture, there's no focus on sex—the Yeti even sports a giant jockstrap to hide his more... impressive features, making it even more amusing than anatomical accuracy. In exchange, viewers are treated to a quirky old scientist, two curious kids, and Tony Kendall in a rare role as a cunning, duplicitous villain.

I can see why fans of filmmaker Roman Polanski might adore this film, just as I can understand why others might strongly dislike it—Ebert was one of the few who couldn’t fathom why audiences weren’t rushing out of the theater. After one viewing, I remain undecided about which side I fall on. As someone who loves Kafka and dark, paranoid comedies, I found The Tenant sufficiently compelling within its runtime. Or perhaps not—this might have been more impactful as a concise half-hour episode of The Twilight Zone, with Serling delivering the closing narration while Terkovsky (or whoever he may be) writhes in bed, bandaged and disturbed. The film’s portrayal of the doomed protagonist bears similarities to Repulsion, yet it could be argued that The Tenant offers more ambiguity, with a stronger sense of surreal disintegration of both character and setting—plus, arguably, a better lead performance. 

Ultimately, The Tenant boasts an intriguing premise—one that’s easy to recount to others: Polanski is a Polish émigré living in Paris.

Follow the Fleet, a 1936 RKO production, features Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers in a witty and layered romantic comedy. While they had appeared together in numerous romantic films, RKO once again crafted a story that resonated with contemporary societal themes. The film's plot cleverly interweaves multiple storylines between its main characters, enhancing the romantic and comedic elements.

The central storyline follows Bake Baker, portrayed by Fred Astaire, a sailor in the U.S. Navy, and Sherry Martin, played by Ginger Rogers, a former dance partner and now a singer and dancer. Their story kicks off when Bake's shipmate Bilge Smith discovers a photograph of Bake and Sherry together. Bake admits that he last saw her with a proposal to marry, prompting Bilge to suggest they try to reconnect on land, hoping Sherry might have a friend they could meet.

The film's subsequent scenes introduce a second, parallel plot, further enriching the romantic and comedic tapestry of Follow the Fleet.

Although it stands as a notable James Arness western, this film is regarded as the worst Alamo adaptation ever produced. The plot was poorly executed, riddled with inaccuracies and outright falsehoods. The continuity was a complete mess. Did anyone notice the cannon scene? The Mexicans foolishly fired cannons that clearly still had mud and ramrods protruding from the barrels. Seriously? And let's not forget Brian Keith's absurd hat—either the costume designer was missing or simply didn't care. The whole thing feels like a misstep from start to finish.

Little Edie and Big Edie are characters who evoke genuine compassion in anyone who witnesses their story. Despite the chaos and filth of their home, this is somewhat understandable given their mental health struggles. A comment on a message board noted that "Little Edie has the coping skills of an eight-year-old," which brought to mind a line from the dramatized 2009 version, where Big Edie tells Little Edie, "If you're stuck, it's only with yourself." These women possessed incredible qualities—beauty, talent, intelligence, and a strong sense of conviction in their beliefs and actions. Perhaps if Little Edie had been gentler with herself during her early setbacks—losing her hair, her job, and her true love—she might have found a way through. I believe her challenges stem from her mental health: her difficulty in lifting herself up during tough times and recognizing that better days could come. The course of her life might have changed if she had heeded her mother’s heartfelt plea, "Come home, Edie! Let me take care of you!"  

Despite their deep-seated insecurities, these women manage to be remarkably brilliant, profoundly heartbreaking, and utterly lovable—even amid their extremely messy surroundings. Their extraordinary lives and their interactions with each other bring a unique humor that underscores their resilience and humanity.

Gédéon and Jules Naudet set out to create a documentary about rookie New York City firefighters. Instead, they captured the only footage inside the World Trade Center on September 11.  

Having previously worked with James Hanlon's ladder company, Jules accompanied the captain to inspect and repair a gas leak, while Gédéon remained at the firehouse in case of any notable events. During this time, Jules was distracted by a low-flying airplane over the city and pointed his camera upward, just seconds before the plane collided with Tower One.  

Jules then asked the captain to accompany him into the Towers. The first sights he encountered were two individuals on fire, which he chose not to film. He remained on the scene for several hours, documenting the reactions of firefighters and other responders.  

The Naudet brothers were careful to avoid making the film overly violent, graphic, or gory. However, the firefighters' language was somewhat coarse, and CBS aired much of it uncensored. They combined footage they shot with personal interviews, allowing firefighters to share their thoughts and feelings about particular moments during the crisis.  

Unlike a typical feature film,

If you ever hear these three words spoken to you—"Joe Don Baker"—be on alert...

Final Justice is a low-budget action film set in a Texas town called Geronimo (pronounced "Heronimo"). The protagonist is a gritty, sleazy, and abrasive sheriff who’s tracking a criminal in Malta—who previously murdered his partner back in Texas. Interestingly, his partner conveniently collapses twice during the film, signaling poor editing choices. Joe Don Baker's character, Geronimo, ends up in jail multiple times—about four or five—halting any real momentum in the story. He also shoots everyone he encounters as if he's in the Old West, despite it being the 20th century. A female police officer, who resembles Elaine from Seinfeld, is assigned to guide him around Malta—she's the only one tolerating his redneck antics. Honestly, she must be out of her mind!

The most memorable characters are the bar’s strippers, whose dancing scenes occur repeatedly throughout the film. I found myself somewhat sympathizing with these sleazy women—at least they provided more entertainment than Geronimo desperately trying to talk his way out of trouble. The ending feels flawed and somewhat predictable, leaving much to be desired.

It's been ages since I watched this comedy, and I had forgotten just how ridiculously silly it is. I would confidently rank it among Elvis Presley's worst films, perhaps in the bottom two or three. Presley stars as Joe Whitecloud, a half-breed Indian bull rider who returns to his rundown family shack in Arizona, a place where his friends love to party all night. His parents are played by Burgess Meredith and Katy Jurado, while his aging Indian grandfather is portrayed by Thomas Gomez. Unfortunately, none of these performances bring anything meaningful, either comically or otherwise. The plot involves the government investing in the family's cattle, but they’re missing a bull. Elvis gets to perform a handful of completely pointless songs and is constantly chased by a girl obsessed with him and her armed mother. The whole film feels slapped together, and the shabby scenery practically reek of manure, making it even harder to enjoy. Oddly enough, what puzzles me most is that Elvis actually seems to be having fun in this mess. It’s hard to believe, considering he was quite upset about being stuck making so many mediocre movies.

Don't be fooled by the big names like Burt Reynolds, James Woods, and Anne Archer—they're essentially glorified extras. Their scenes were likely shot in just a day or so. Whatever reasons they had for appearing in this film, if you're going to cast someone like James Woods, you should make good use of his talent. To me, this indicates poor direction throughout. The plot itself wasn't too bad, and most of the performances were above average. However, Cuba Gooding Jr. delivered an abysmal performance—so unconvincing that his dramatic moments nearly made me laugh. Since the film is meant to be serious, that’s hardly a good sign. The action scenes weren’t poorly executed, but they lacked that extra spark to make them more thrilling. Better direction was definitely needed here. Additionally, the pacing was off; it took nearly half an hour for the main character to get into any action. For a 90-minute action thriller, that's far too slow. The only bright spot was Angie Harmon, who gave her best to make everything work. Unfortunately, the director didn’t give her enough support. Yes, this movie had potential.

When young Kevin receives his late uncle's boat as a gift, he invites five friends for a weekend trip to Catalina Island. During their journey, they indulge in alcohol, engage in sexual encounters, and play games, each sharing their deepest fears. Tragically, Kevin drowns in the open sea when the engine stalls, and they find themselves plagued and murdered by their own innermost terrors.  

Yesterday, my wife, son, daughter, and three friends gathered to watch "Haunted Boat" on DVD. With a runtime under 30 minutes, the group quickly abandoned the film, deeming it a chaotic and dull amateurish disaster, and opted to watch something else. Later, I decided to finish watching it to see just how terrible it was — it would have been better to go to bed instead. The convoluted story features poor cinematography and shaky camera work, and the cast appears to be students still learning their craft. Ultimately, this film resembles a misguided film school project. The terrible, pretentious screenplay culminates in a ridiculous plot twist, leaving the film a complete mess.

Nikolai Gogol's story "Viy" has been adapted into a film once again and recently released on home video in the United States through Faith Films.
