The original narrative centers on a priest tasked with guarding a witch’s corpse, relying solely on his faith for protection. This new version significantly expands the story and sets it in America, though it appears to have been filmed in Russia, as evidenced by the mismatched houses, clothing, and furnishings despite the presence of English signage. The film is quite peculiar and doesn’t quite succeed. A notable challenge is its odd setting, which attempts to portray rural America but clearly falls short. Additionally, there are some deliberately obscure and strange moments, such as the main character starting out as a reporter and later becoming a priest—details that remain confusing even after watching the behind-the-scenes feature on the DVD. Another major issue is the dubbing, which is exceptionally poor. The voices are often out of sync with the characters’ lip movements, and sometimes voices are heard when lips aren’t visible, or vice versa. It’s unclear whether this problem stems from Faith Films or the producers who aimed to release the film in the West, as indicated in the making-of feature.

"Five Across the Eyes" begins with five teenage girls driving home as their curfew approaches. After stopping at a store, they accidentally collide with another vehicle and decide to leave the scene without reporting the accident. Their relief is short-lived when the other car catches up, forcing them to halt. A deranged woman armed with a shotgun emerges, shouting at them and forcing them to disrobe and urinate on themselves before driving off randomly. Shaken and bewildered, the girls believe their nightmare has ended—until the same woman returns, seemingly intent on killing them as they are stranded, low on gas, and lost.  

Produced and directed by Greg Swinson and Ryan Theissen, with Swinson handling the writing and Theissen responsible for cinematography and editing, I must say that "Five Across the Eyes" ranks among the worst films I have ever seen—possibly the very worst. I find it hard to recall a film that’s worse. Initially, I think some of the filmmaking choices may have been intentional, aimed at creating atmosphere and tension, but...

Initially, this documentary/fictional cartoon appears quite entertaining and thought-provoking. Naturally, when something stimulates reflection, it invites scrutiny. In truth, this film merges metaphysics with innuendo and unfounded conclusions. The supposed connection that "What the Bleep..." draws between science and spirituality is, in reality, unsubstantiated by scientific evidence. The Transcendental Meditation study mentioned claims that group meditation can reduce crime rates in specific areas, such as Washington D.C. However, in 1993, the HRA (Homicides, Rapes, and Assaults) crime rate was approximately 30% higher than the average crime rate from 1988 to 1992. There was no observed decline in homicide rates during the study period. Furthermore, every assertion that attempts to link metaphysics with science has been thoroughly debunked. 

From this, I conclude that the film is either a poor attempt at indoctrination or simply a joke. Either way, I recommend not wasting your time. 

If you're seeking a comprehensive film about science that can stimulate thoughtful discussion, you might consider watching *Mindwalk* (1990).

Although Louis B. Mayer reportedly showed little interest in signing young Greta Garbo to a contract, her first American film with MGM remains remarkably beautiful. It’s clear that exceptional talent was dedicated to filming and creating matte paintings for the production, resulting in a polished and artful appearance characteristic of the studio’s finest work. Even after 84 years, it continues to look stunning.

Regarding Garbo herself, like in her other early American films, she presents a somewhat different image. While still recognizable, her makeup is much softer than in her later portrayals—imparting a gentler, less severe look that adds a delicate charm unseen in her subsequent roles. I occasionally wish they had maintained this softer appearance, but given her eventual iconic look, it’s easy to see why they chose her signature style. The film’s plot centers on Garbo and her family being unjustly displaced from their land by the landlord. Although the landlady, the esteemed Doña Bernarda, claims it’s due to the bank’s demands, the real reason is her son’s affection for Garbo—and how she navigates this complex situation.

Paul Verhoeven’s arguably masterpiece, The Fourth Man, is saturated with disturbing dreams, vivid premonitions, blasphemous thoughts, and homosexual fantasies. Centered around a definitive femme fatale who adores her men only to ultimately eliminate them, the film is rife with bloodshed and sporadic gore, making it profoundly unsettling. Men might even jump in surprise when Renee suddenly brandishes her scissors...

Soldier Blue aspires to be a profound commentary—claiming to delve into humanity's brutality, white exploitation of indigenous peoples, and offering a stark critique of Vietnam horrors. Unfortunately, it falls flat on all these fronts. Instead, it emerges as a harmful, clichéd, poorly executed, and frankly dishonest piece of trash.

Another critic astutely pointed out that the film feels like a jarring mash-up of two entirely different stories. At its core, it's a dull, hackneyed "odd couple" romance—Strauss and Bergen shedding their prejudices and falling in love (how sweet)—stretched between two grotesque massacres that look more at home in a Lucio Fulci horror film.

There is simply no justification for the revolting, voyeuristic, gore-heavy climax, where innocent Native American children are brutally shot, dismembered, and impaled in graphic detail, while Native American women—many with large breasts—are molested, raped, and hung up. The only motive behind these scenes is commercial profit. The massacre itself, despite its intended shock value, is executed so poorly that it fails to serve any meaningful purpose.

This is arguably one of the most dull and poorly acted portrayals of Adolf Hitler's early days I have ever seen. Robert Carlyle is a talented actor, but casting him as Hitler was simply a mistake. Likewise, appointing Liev Schreiber as Hitler’s close friend and aide, Haefengstal, must have caused the Simon Wiesenthal Centre to lament in despair. Having a Jewish actor play a Nazi supporter was a blatantly bad casting decision. This film was not an engaging family-friendly historical piece; instead, it epitomized Hollywood's lowest efforts, exploiting the presence of a talented but underused supporting cast that has largely vanished from the acting scene in recent years.

The exaggerated German accents—"vee vill vin zis var"—are offensive to Germans everywhere. My mother, who is German, was visibly upset by the inconsistent attempt at German pronunciation, which switched awkwardly between American, English, and German within the same sentence. The supporting actors resemble cardboard cutouts more suited for a local video store than the big screen. However, Jenna Malone’s portrayal of Geli Raubal was outstanding; she managed to convey the innocence and confusion of her character with remarkable depth.

This might very well be considered one of "The Worst Films Ever." Without John Hurt’s involvement, it might have been dismissed as a harmless kids’ movie. Unfortunately, the real tragedy lies in Hurt’s participation, as one of the greatest actors on screen, he undermines himself in this mess. I awarded it two stars solely because Mr. Hurt made an appearance, but I deduct eight points for his failure to escape it quickly enough. As for the rest of the cast, they are simply dreadful. Janine Turner, despite her beauty, is utterly incapable of acting convincingly, and the leading actor is, for all practical purposes, atrocious. If you value your time and sanity, avoid this film at all costs. It’s so painfully bad, it almost hurts.

Over the years, I’ve watched numerous straight-to-video Seagal films, and honestly, they all deliver a similar level of entertainment—unfortunately, that level is pretty low. While the action scenes can be somewhat entertaining, that’s about as far as it goes. Seagal was truly at his peak during movies like *Under Siege*, *Under Siege 2*, and *Executive Decision*—especially in terms of action. However, over the past decade, his recent films haven’t quite lived up to those standards.

On a more positive note, the movie did a decent job of making good use of its runtime, with some engaging action sequences and moments of clever wit. Just when it felt like the film was starting to drag, a particularly exciting action scene managed to lift it out of mediocrity. I genuinely believe that Seagal’s movies would benefit if they featured more recognizable supporting actors and actresses. Supporting cast members play a crucial role, and having well-known talent alongside Seagal could potentially boost the movie’s popularity and overall reception.

I happened upon a documentary on the UK TV channel More4, and I must say I found it incredibly engaging and thought-provoking. I am now eager to find the book that served as the source material for this program. The documentary primarily explores Professor Jared Diamond's theory about why some regions of the world’s societies thrived while others lagged behind. His argument, which was new to me, emphasizes the importance of the availability of domesticated crops and animals as a key factor in societal success—an extremely compelling perspective.

The production itself is well-filmed and skillfully narrated, avoiding the overuse of re-enactments that often diminish modern documentaries. Diamond’s approach is notable for its clarity and respectfulness, avoiding the condescension that many intellectuals fall into when communicating complex ideas to the general public. Some have suggested that his theory is Marxist, but I see it more as a socio-geological analysis. It was also refreshing to encounter a theory on societal evolution that isn’t rooted in religious explanations. Overall, I highly recommend this thought-provoking documentary.

A few weeks ago, the German broadcaster SAT1 promoted this film as the "TV Event of the Year"—sorry, but I've seen better on TV this year. I didn't have high expectations for the movie, but as I watched the commercial, I couldn't help but think of two other terrible films: Titanic and Pearl Harbor. The scene looked so familiar—the "heroine" (if I can really call her that) in the center flanked by her two "loved ones." Sound familiar? It's essentially a cheap imitation of Pearl Harbor's love story—a version that's already poor to begin with. 

Nevertheless, since I enjoy watching movies and analyzing their structures, I decided to give this nonsense a try. The film opens with a doctor leaving his family to join the military strike against Russia near the end of the Third Reich, promising his wife he'll return. Fast forward to spring 1948: Germany has lost the war, and the Allies along with Russia have occupied the country, both vying for global dominance—capitalism versus communism. I suspect you already know how this story unfolds, but you might as well hear it from me.

The story centers on a crime lord orchestrating the alliance of three different mafias to purchase an island, which would then function as a money-laundering hub for organized crime. In an attempt to stop this scheme, the FBI targets one of the mafia bosses. However, the operation backfires dramatically, leading to a series of unlikely twists and turns. These events eventually evolve into a typical "cop buddies who don't get along" scenario, featuring a female FBI agent and a male former DEA agent.

While the plot itself is quite flimsy—at best a weak joke—the film's true strength lies in its humor. Surprisingly, the German synchronization adds to the comedic effect. The action sequences are engaging, highlighted by a memorable scene involving a shotgun and a rocket launcher. Nonetheless, the film's primary focus is on comedy. It doesn't aim for sharp satire nor pure slapstick but instead offers a blend of funny jokes scattered throughout.

However, the film is far from politically correct. It prominently features drug abuse without any critique, even portraying it as something cool, which was particularly frustrating for me. This aspect makes the movie inappropriate for children in my view.

This film is one of many "Kung Fu" action movies produced in Asia during the late '70s to early '80s, characterized by cheap sound effects, dubbed dialogue, and lightning-fast martial arts sequences. Unlike most films in this genre, it also features a solid storyline and lots of comedic moments. The plot centers around workers at a dye factory who are ousted by Manchu bullies; they hire a con artist (Gordon Liu) to intimidate them. After his scheme fails miserably, he infiltrates a Shaolin temple to learn genuine fighting skills. However, instead of becoming a student of kung fu, the Master assigns him to build scaffolding to cover the roofs of all 36 chambers. Surprisingly, while performing these menial tasks—stacking and tying bamboo poles—he inadvertently learns the skills needed to become a kung fu master. This is reminiscent of "The Karate Kid," where Mr. Miyagi teaches Daniel basic karate moves through routine chores like "wax on, wax off." The movie delivers continuous humor and culminates in an exciting showdown as Gordon Liu once again faces off against his foes.

I genuinely think this movie is fantastic. However, every film has its drawbacks. Some of you might not have seen Hilary Duff's "Raise Your Voice," but if you think about it, the two movies are quite similar—if you catch my drift. In "Brave New Girl," Holly desperately wants to get into Haverty Conservatory, while in "Raise Your Voice," Terri aims to attend a conservatory in L.A. (though I can't remember its name). Both are in the music world and have to perform at the end of the semester. It's amusing how these two films are so alike. Personally, I prefer "Brave New Girl" over "Raise Your Voice."

I just rewatched The Convent for the second time. I had enjoyed it in the past and thought it would be a fun drunken Friday night movie—full of gore, style, humor, and all that. Unfortunately, I found myself unable to appreciate it nearly as much this time around. It felt like someone aimed to modernize cheesy classics like Night of the Demons but ended up losing what made the originals appealing. For the record, I’m not even a huge fan of Night of the Demons, but there were elements I genuinely appreciated. The Convent embraces its cheese but misses out on the charm. Aside from Joanna Canton’s likable performance as the lead, the goth girl, and a charming cameo by Adrienne Barbeau, nearly all the other characters were painfully unlikable—bottom-tier morons and offensive jocks at their worst. The film is further hampered by the absence of gratuitous nudity, which, combined with the atrocious dialogue, makes it difficult to connect with or enjoy the characters, even when there are some decent aspects. The evil nuns have a fresh design and do manage to deliver some good moments, but overall, the film falls short of capturing what could have made it memorable.

"Transylvania 6-5000" is a minor, yet occasionally amusing and charming horror parody from the mid-80s, featuring a cast of recognizable names and several moments that elicit genuine laughs. The story follows two bumbling tabloid journalists, who are reluctantly dispatched to Transylvania to investigate the supposed return of the infamous scientist Frankenstein. Throughout the film, viewers can find delightful little gimmicks and details, such as a tiny guillotine designed for hard-boiled eggs and laboratory test tubes repurposed as condiment dispensers at breakfast. However, the film's overall charm is somewhat diminished by lengthy jokes and parody setups that drag on too long. For a more consistently humorous experience, Roger Corman's "Transylvania Twist," released four years later, comes highly recommended. The movie mainly parodies early 1930s Universal monster classics, so watching those films beforehand will help you catch all the subtle gags and references. Interestingly, the film offers a unique twist suggesting that Frankenstein's monster merely mimics the behavior of an evil, mad scientist, adding a fresh perspective to the parody.

I've always been a fan of Batman—I've enjoyed the animated series, Batman Beyond, and even read a few comics here and there. Naturally, I was pretty excited when I heard about this new series, but I was severely disappointed. It’s nothing special and doesn't hold a candle to the original. It feels like one long toy commercial, lacking any depth or substance. And what on earth was the deal with the Joker? In my humble opinion, he's the greatest Batman villain of all time, and they completely screwed him up. I wish I could blame the poor design as the worst part, but honestly, I’d prefer to find any redeeming or creative aspect at all. In short—because I could go on forever—do not waste your time or money on this show.

This portrayal of the infamous 1959 Kansas murders, inspired by Capote's book, is starkly shot in black and white by Brooks and cinematographer Hall, lending it a documentary-like atmosphere. Strong performances come from Blake and Wilson as the killers, alongside Forsythe as a determined police officer. The scenes leading up to the crime, filmed at the actual murder site and accompanied by the haunting sound of whistling winds, are tense and chilling. Brooks directs with energy, employing several inventive scene transitions. The only drawback is that the film feels slightly too long, with the ending extended and a bit preachy.

This mockumentary exemplifies just how absurd people's enthusiasm can become when they latch onto something like this. Frankly, I despise cryptozoology. It’s unscientific and only undermines genuine science. On a positive note, the visual effects were impressive—those dragons looked stunning. However, much of the information presented was completely fabricated, which is especially disappointing given that it came from scientists. That’s why I’m giving it a 1 out of 10 instead of a 0. For instance, the hydrogen theory is flawed: although chemistry shows that hydrogen can be produced in the stomach, the quantities needed for a creature like a dragon are impossible to generate naturally. This requires a thorough explanation of what actually occurs inside a dragon’s stomach. Many substances contain hydrogen in nature, but none are present in sufficient amounts to enable flight for such an animal, and hydrogen cannot just appear out of nowhere—that’s simply impossible. Even more baffling is the idea involving platinum, an element more rare than gold, and I cannot fathom how such a thing could exist or be found.

A truly touching film, showcasing the exceptional talent of John Thaw, who recently passed away. Always humble and understated, he was undoubtedly one of England's top ten actors of his era. 

He is best remembered for his iconic role as Inspector Morse, as well as Jack Regan in the 1970s hit TV series *The Sweeney* and his portrayal of a barrister in *Kavanagh QC*. This movie is perfect for family viewing and a valuable addition to my DVD collection. Its authentic filming evokes memories of wartime Britain, especially for those who experienced being evacuated from London to escape the German bombings. The chemistry between the two main characters, Tom and William, is beautifully portrayed and faithful to Michelle Magorian's novel.

I was told this film was a great action movie, but I didn’t quite agree. The plot felt convoluted and difficult to follow. Most of the action scenes are saved for the very end, and they’re quite dark, making it hard to see what’s going on. I was hoping for something different, but unfortunately, I didn’t find it here.

If you have any interest in pirates, pirate films, early 19th century American history, or Yul Brynner, I encourage you to watch this movie and form your own opinion. Don't be discouraged by mixed reviews; I personally found it to be entertaining, with strong performances (for the most part), sharp and witty dialogue, and a compelling portrayal of the charisma, allure, and legendary status of privateer Jean Lafitte. While not every event depicted is strictly historically accurate (can you find any historical film that is?), I believe the film accurately captures Lafitte's significant role in New Orleans' history and the complex, often ambivalent relationship between the city’s respectable citizens and this notorious outlaw, who was also one of its most beloved sons. Instead of fixating on what the film may omit, focus on what it accomplishes—namely, offering a fascinating glimpse into one of the most captivating figures in New Orleans and American history.

Come on, everyone, check out the title! LOL! I recall watching this movie during Saturday Night Creature Features years ago. It's a charmingly cheesy monster film featuring hilariously bad acting and two utterly clueless hillbillies that boost its schlock appeal. The two redneck boat rental guys are the highlight of the movie! LOL! You’ll especially enjoy the boat scene where the English husband and wife are discussing the stars—completely midday and sunny—it's downright hilarious! Clearly, they weren’t too concerned with the plot; they just wanted to finish filming as quickly as possible. Overall, if you’re a fan of 70s cheesy flicks, you’ll love it!

Initially, I was hesitant about watching this when it first aired on CBS. I was among the many people in NYC that day, attending Hunter College. I didn't want to relive the devastation and chaos, but curiosity got the better of me. Watching this documentary brought tears to my eyes; all my memories flooded back, and the powerful images were almost too much to bear. I bought the DVD on the first anniversary and have watched it several times. The way those filmmakers captured such footage is astonishing. If you haven't seen this documentary, I highly recommend it. It's undeniably heartbreaking and will likely bring tears, but it’s an extraordinary record of this country's darkest hour.

Perhaps I'm missing something, but I’ve come across more positive reviews of The Man Who Cheated Himself than negative ones, and honestly, I don't understand the disconnect. I prefer my noir films to have a certain flair—characters who speak, look, and act like Humphrey Bogart in The Big Sleep or Gene Tierney in Laura. None of the characters in this film possess that presence or style, or whatever you want to call it. Take the lead, Lee J. Cobb—his rumpled, just-rolled-out-of-bed appearance is quite the opposite of the suave, dashing noir hero. Or consider Jane Wyatt as the femme fatale; that casting feels completely off. It’s one of the most poorly executed casting choices I’ve seen in a while, and she simply doesn’t convince in the role. 

As for the story, it’s stale and completely predictable, offering no real surprises or fresh twists for the genre. I could have guessed the ending of The Man Who Cheated Himself within five minutes. And that final cat-and-mouse chase? Dull and uninspired. About ten to fifteen minutes of stagnation really drags down any momentum the film might have had.

Comedies are often unfairly regarded as lacking genuine depth. However, Arms and the Man demonstrates otherwise. Shaw's play brilliantly blends comedic drama, offering an engaging storyline along with profound philosophical insights.

At its core, Arms and the Man functions as a charming, somewhat distinctive romantic comedy. The protagonist, Raina, is young, idealistic, and somewhat superficial, hailing from a military family deeply embroiled in wartime. Her fiancé and father are both officers, immersing her in a military world. Her life takes an unexpected turn when she encounters an enemy soldier one night; she rescues him, knowing she must keep this secret from her family indefinitely. Eventually, the soldier departs, but once the war concludes, he reappears, prompting the main characters to reassess their beliefs and relationships.

What makes Shaw particularly intriguing is how he embeds layered meanings within this seemingly straightforward comedic plot. He offers sharp commentary on social class, the absurdity of war, and the essence of love—all delivered with his signature wit and a well-crafted narrative. There's so much to analyze here that many subtle nuances might easily be overlooked.

The opening scene depicts the Legion arriving in Paris on November 13, 1918. The soldiers disembark from the train dressed in the same uniforms worn by the French Army—and the Legion—when they marched off to war in 1914. This detail is a clear indicator that the film is likely to be a flop. By 1915, the French Army had recognized that red trousers and dark blue overcoats were impractical, and both metropolitan and colonial troops were issued uniforms in "horizon blue" and khaki, respectively. The Claude Van Damme (perhaps intended as Van Damme) remake at least attempted to get the uniforms right. It's really disappointing when directors make such mistakes, especially when they put effort into accurately portraying other aspects.

This mini-series proves to be more engaging than some productions with significantly larger budgets and loftier ambitions. SOTD sits somewhere between "Kung-Fu" and "H R Pufnstuff" in terms of entertainment value. Had it not been nearly three hours long, I believe children would enjoy it quite a bit. It features adventure, action, suspenseful cliffhangers, and minimal romance or other "icky" elements. When you're young, you're less critical of rubber swords, cheesy acting, or repeated scenes—at least two are repeated exactly as in old serials to help viewers catch up. Additionally, children tend to be more accepting of American English dialogue spoken by Asian actors, especially since several main roles are played by non-Asian actors.

I initially considered giving this film three stars, but ultimately felt the director, producers, and cast deserve some recognition for seeing the project through. While it isn’t a work of art, like painting your house, it required time, effort, and discipline to complete.

Overall, I wouldn’t particularly recommend it for casual viewing.

Georgia Rule ranks among the worst films I have ever seen. Its bizarre, surreal tone had me exclaiming "What?" at least seven or ten times during its exhausting two-hour runtime.  

Promoted as a film about three generations of women—Jane Fonda as the matriarch, Felicity Huffman as her daughter, and Lindsay Lohan as the rebellious, scantily clad granddaughter—the trailer suggested a clichéd, lighthearted chick flick about family and growing up.  

But that was a false advertisement of the highest order.  

The film is riddled with distracting shots of animals performing "funny" antics during pivotal scenes, and spends a baffling five minutes focusing on an elderly woman repeatedly visiting a doctor’s office simply to have her diaper changed. More disturbingly, the plot centers on Lindsay Lohan’s character being sexually abused by her stepfather. Georgia Rule invents a new genre: an ungrounded, poorly acted, and deeply inappropriate comedy addressing serious issues in an awkward, surreal manner. If Garry Marshall intended this...

I tend to support films that fill notable gaps in the landscape of world cinema. After viewing the trailer for "Water Lilies," I anticipated enjoying the film because I believed I had discovered something distinctive: an honest depiction of teenage lesbian love—kind of a female counterpart to "Beautiful Thing."  

The story centers on three young French girls, each around 15 years old. Marie is slender, reserved, and has a tomboyish charm; Floriane is outgoing, athletic, and strikingly beautiful; while Anne is loyal, plump, and somewhat immature in her behavior. The movie hints at the erotic tension between Marie and Floriane, simmering beneath the surface rather than overtly present.  

However, "Water Lilies" isn’t about the blossoming of lesbian love between two teenagers. Instead, it focuses on themes of sexual frustration, pain, boredom, and the often misguided efforts of adolescents. At times, it portrays sex as mechanical and joyless, which ultimately reveals how over-manipulation by screenwriters and filmmakers can undermine the authenticity of a story.  

In the bonus features of the "Lord of the Flies" DVD, director Peter Brook comments that "French cynicism begins with the arousal of sex," suggesting that while the French idealize children as angels, their attitude toward adolescents is quite different.

This isn't a typical video nasty—probably because it was released in 1994 when British audiences had grown weary of the genre. In many ways, it's a 75% rehash of The Boogeyman and likely would have faced similar bans, though for unclear reasons.

Initially, I was puzzled, thinking that Annie (Kelly Galindo) might have been a different Lacey, but it becomes clear she's a character troubled by psychic visions of a boogeyman reminiscent of the first film. Fans will quickly recognize that they are not the same person.

After witnessing a murder in a bathroom and noting the address, Annie, along with her psychiatrist and a parapsychology student—who bears an uncanny resemblance to a romantic novel cover model and a butter commercial star—head to the indicated house. Sure enough, it’s the same bathroom scene. Within 24 hours, another murder occurs exactly as she described. However, the identity of the mysterious, alluring woman murdered remains unknown.

The film then shifts into a re-telling of The Boogeyman story, enriched with additional footage not seen in the original version. Notably, the boogeyman is portrayed differently this time, unfortunately...

Regardless of what you might say about Andy Milligan, if his family was even 10% as dysfunctional as the one depicted in this film, he might have turned out better. Unfortunately, the video version of this movie includes sex scene inserts originally added by the distributor to boost its box office appeal. Throughout the film, Milligan's often clumsy camerawork and the silent film-style music suddenly cut out, replaced by attractive stand-ins for Milligan's less appealing actors performing to psychedelic 60s guitar riffs. If you're trying to focus on Milligan's original vision, it's easy to fast-forward through these parts, as much of the original footage was cut to make room for the inserted sex scenes. Still, what's left is quite captivating. I've never encountered a more hateful mother character in any film before.

I can't stand most reality shows, and this one is worse than the one with Paris Hilton. Sure, it's his company, but how many seasons have we been subjected to "you're fired" or "you're hired"? After watching it, I wouldn't want to work for the guy with his ego—honestly, watching paint dry is more entertaining.  

I’d love to hear just one person stand up and say, "Donald, I quit—here’s some of your money, and maybe get a decent haircut." I see he's even trying to buy fame through WWE wrestling. Honestly, I hope he gets hurt so I don’t have to see that pathetic face anymore. It’s sad to crave fame so badly without any talent and make a fool of yourself trying to buy it. If I could, I’d give this show a negative rating, but it only gets a 1—and honestly, it doesn’t even deserve that.

I believe it's a well-made film. It exudes a distinctly Romanian atmosphere through its scenery and mood. I don't think it was meant to be sensual; rather, any sensuality that emerges feels natural and unforced. The film feels authentic and humane. I found it intriguing. The performances never made me think, "Wow, that was poor acting," as the actors aren’t Hollywood legends like Sean Connery and others, but they’re credible, portraying ordinary people who can act realistically. I believe the film achieved its goal, evoking genuine emotions in me—or perhaps reawakening feelings I already had. I'm aware my perspective may be subjective. Overall, I genuinely enjoyed it—that much is certain.

Despite its English title, the film bears little relevance to devils and centers primarily on a power-hungry ruler obsessed with acquiring the Philosopher's Stone, seeking gold made from lead and virgin blood. Jacinto Molina portrays Gilles de Lancre, a character seemingly untroubled by executing those he perceives as threats or sacrificing virgins for their blood. His actions are driven more by greed and madness than by demonic possession, influenced by his mistress and an employed alchemist. The movie features some mildly engaging scenes, such as jousting matches and men attempting to knock each other off with large sticks, and it is visually appealing overall. However, beyond that, it offers little to recommend—minimal gore, no scares, and notably, for a Molina/Naschy collaboration, an absence of unintentional humor. Overall, I would rate it a 4 out of 10.

I wasn't particularly interested in watching The Flock. Andrew Lau, who co-directed the acclaimed trilogy Infernal Affairs, was originally attached to the project, but he was replaced by an emergency director, Niels Mueller, after Lau was fired. I sensed that Lau had crafted a quality film, but it apparently didn't satisfy the studio, leading to his departure and the hiring of another director. Such replacements often don't yield great results (just think of The Invasion). However, The Flock turned out to be better than I expected. It isn't a masterpiece, but it is an engaging and entertaining thriller. The character development is quite strong, allowing me to understand the characters deeply. Additionally, the relationship between the two leads feels natural and believable. Richard Gere and Claire Danes deliver solid performances. 

Now, moving on to the negatives. One aspect that really bothered me—at one point, it even irritated me—was the overuse of editing tricks intended to give the film more "attitude" and style. These techniques feel out of place and seem randomly applied. Furthermore, I believe the film could have been more ambitious. Despite these flaws, I recommend The Flock as a good thriller. It may not be memorable, but it is definitely entertaining.

While I can't claim that Wargames: The Dead Code is the worst film I've ever encountered, since it did have a few decent moments, I can confidently say it's the most transparent movie I've ever watched. Not once did a plot twist or device catch me by surprise; I was usually ten or more minutes ahead in guessing what was coming. There was a complete lack of subtlety in every scene, and no apparent intelligence behind the production. Every line, whether spoken or typed, laid its intentions so plainly that immersing myself in the story became impossible. 

Instead of engaging me, the film's poorly conceived plot and clumsy attempts to win back the audience often made me laugh at how badly it was put together, far more than any genuine enjoyment I derived from it.

Contrary to some summaries, the women portrayed in the film are not geisha; they are oiran (courtesans) living outside the renowned pleasure districts. Their lives and experiences reflect those of many women during the Tokugawa era. While I wouldn't say the stories are particularly revelatory, their true charm lies in how representative they are. The themes are universal and relatable—love, friendship, and sacrifice.  

I greatly appreciated the art direction and the performances. It felt as if I was glimpsing a world and a time I could never otherwise see. The four actresses who played the main oiran were especially captivating. I would only recommend this film to those interested in exploring Japanese culture or to viewers who appreciate subtle, emotionally resonant stories. It serves as a beautiful example of both.

When it comes to horror films, I am usually willing to overlook low production values, plot holes, and suspend disbelief for the sake of a good fright. Unfortunately, this movie offers no genuine scares. It can't even be enjoyed as camp; the dialogue is stilted, the acting subpar, and the direction lackluster. The kills are predictable and poorly staged, the music is grating, the camera work is dreadful, and even the costumes leave much to be desired. I felt genuinely sorry for the actors, who clearly tried their best but had to contend with contrived dialogue and a noticeable absence of guidance—probably no rehearsal took place. Watching this is embarrassing and dull, making the contrived "surprise" ending require considerable patience to endure. It ranks easily among the worst films I have ever seen.  

I don't usually write reviews, but this one was so atrocious that I felt compelled to warn others. It's a complete waste of time. If you decide to watch this, don't miss the "Making of" featurette. The writer/director seems to think that making the killer a woman was a daring, bold choice—something we've seen countless times before. He and the cast appear to be going through the motions...

Does anyone know where this film was filmed? The aviation scene on the cliff is stunning, and it seems to be set in England. However, Ivy's apartment building definitely resembles the Brill Building, with its intriguing elevators.  

Charles Mendl is credited as playing "Sir Charles Gage." I might have missed him, but I didn't see him on screen. Possibly he was the husband's lawyer, but I don't recall that character appearing beyond a mention of a phone call. Could he have appeared in the aviation scene or the ballroom? Has anyone spotted him?  

Herbert Marshall was 57 years old at the time of filming.

The highlight of An American in Paris is the extended ballet scene at the end, where Gene Kelly and Leslie Caron embody the styles of several renowned painters. Earlier in the film, Kelly is shown as a street artist in Paris, making this sequence a fitting conclusion to a vibrant, energetic musical filled with Gershwin melodies and cast members like Georges Guetary and Oscar Levant. Kelly delivers a standout performance here—distinct from his role in Singin’ in the Rain—and the seamless integration of the entire film with the ballet creates a truly impressive effect. It's no surprise that this sequence concluded with 'That's Entertainment,' after showcasing all the best moments of MGM's musical repertoire.

"A Thief in the Night" is a film that largely went unnoticed by mainstream audiences due to its evident low budget and provocative subject matter—the Rapture of true Christians and the fate of those who are left behind. Despite this, it delivered a compelling story that captivated viewers and prompted reflection on their own relationship with Jesus Christ. The film resonated deeply, illustrating even a preacher who, despite preaching the Word, did not believe it and knew precisely why he was left behind. Both this movie and its sequel, "Distant Thunder," are essential viewing. Although the newer "Left Behind" series, with its significantly higher production budget, retells the same story, the impact remains unchanged—"A Thief in the Night" pioneered this genre and continues to be remembered for its groundbreaking role.

In summary, this film is utterly worthless.  

The premise—viewing the future through the eyes of someone from the early 1900s—is intriguing in theory but is undermined by a lack of engaging storylines or compelling characters. As a result, viewers can't suspend their disbelief, rendering the entire concept ineffective.  

The movie appears to have been shot solely with actors in front of green screens, and we're expected to be impressed. However, from a visual effects standpoint, the excessive softening of images was a clear attempt to hide the challenging sharp edges inherent in green screen technology. The colors are heavily washed out, serving no purpose other than diminishing overall visual quality. I fail to see how anything rendered in this film could be deemed groundbreaking. If anything, the outdated and clunky graphics set a new low, even inferior to the early CGI of Jurassic Park. The robot designs are painfully simple, bland, and uninteresting. There are also a variety of strange prehistoric-like creatures on the island, yet they are never adequately explained.  

The storyline is unimaginably terrible—I honestly can't think of a worse plot.

A 1957 J. Arthur Rank production featuring James Robertson Justice, Margaret Rutherford, and Wilfred Hyde White—yet it’s supposed to be a blockbuster comedy, isn’t it? Unfortunately, it’s just dreadful. The film revolves around a single gag: people’s reactions to a tiny alligator. The music is inserted haphazardly and leaves no lasting impression. Jeannie Carson performs some lively dance routines and sings competently, but I have to wonder what she was doing in this mess. Diana Dors appears as well, flashing daring shots mainly for the trailers. Her acting isn’t terrible, but her role seems primarily designed to give viewers something to leer at. Honestly, there’s little else to do but groan through this film. It’s currently being sold on VHS by opportunists on eBay—do yourself a favor and avoid it. It’s a comedy devoid of laughs and a musical lacking any memorable songs or choreography.

I have loved all of Cream's work, despite their small yet treasured catalog. Even when their songs extend to twenty minutes—examples like "Spoonful" and "Toad" from *Wheels of Fire*—they still outperform many contemporary rock bands. Their live synergy is truly remarkable, as evidenced by their highly anticipated reunion at the Royal Albert Hall last year. Though time has passed and their fans have aged, their energy remains undiminished, especially in their masterful arrangements of both classic blues standards and original compositions. Their performances of "White Room," "Badge," "Politician," "Spoonful," and "Sunshine of Your Love" are flawless, with none missing a beat. Clapton's guitar solos display a maturity and structure that sometimes elude him in his solo projects. Ginger Baker's drumming speaks for itself, and Jack Bruce's vocals retain a robust, commanding quality that Clapton could never fully replicate solo. Ultimately, if you want to witness some of the greatest shows from last year—some you might wish you'd seen—Cream's reunion delivered truly unforgettable moments.

The Barbarian maybe isn't the best film any of us has seen, but honestly????...It's so hilarious...I can't even describe how much I laughed the first time I watched it. The director intended to make a serious adventure movie, but it turned out so terribly bad—so bad it's one of the funniest movies I've ever seen. So my advice is: you should definitely watch it... and if you've already seen it, watch it again!!!!!!!

Before watching this miniseries, I had no understanding of what Jane Eyre was. Having read and watched many literary classics beforehand, I often thought they were dull, overly verbose, and overrated stories with only moderately engaging plots at best. However, this Jane Eyre adaptation completely transformed my perspective. 

Zelah Clarke delivers a stunning performance as Jane Eyre. Her charming accent and her composed yet resolute demeanor perfectly embody the character of the young governess. Timothy Dalton's portrayal of Rochester is exceptional; his intense passion and energy make it clear that he was destined to play the moody master of Thornfield Hall. After watching this miniseries, I couldn't sleep that night. The story is both haunting and uplifting, and the characters are brought to life with remarkable skill, making this the finest film adaptation of Jane Eyre ever created. 

Later, I read the novel and was amazed at how faithfully the miniseries adheres to Charlotte Brontë’s original words. Jane Eyre has become my favorite both in film and literature. If you're seeking a masterpiece that could truly change your life, I highly recommend watching the 1983 BBC version of Jane Eyre.

This review focuses on the two-disc set that accompanied the "Wonderland" DVD rental.

The films included—"Wonderland" and the Johnny Wadd documentary—completely dismantle the myth perpetuated by "Boogie Nights." That myth suggested that those involved in the adult film industry were more than just unscrupulous individuals willing to do anything for money; it dismissed the reality that they were often heinous, self-serving opportunists. This portrayal is reminiscent of how "Wiseguy" and "Goodfellas" challenged the romanticized gangster image presented by "The Godfather" and similar stories.

What frustrated me most while watching these movies—and likely will upset anyone who appreciated "Boogie Nights"—is the naivety displayed by supposedly educated and refined viewers. The character of "Dirk Diggler" in "Boogie Nights" is clearly modeled after John Holmes, who, unlike "Dirk Diggler," had no redeeming qualities. Holmes was a criminal sociopath who exploited everyone around him, entirely driven by his obsession with self-gratification, and was undeniably involved in the brutal murders on Wonderland Avenue in Los Angeles in 1981. The film exposes these harsh truths.

This is the kind of film that, if it were produced today, would likely feature Sandra Bullock and Hugh Grant in the lead roles; in fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if it were remade at some point. It’s charming enough, but lacks any real depth. The film is hampered by a near disastrous miscasting of James Stewart, who is about two decades too old for his part, resulting in a palpable absence of chemistry with the stunning Kim Novak. Ernie Kovacs, in a minor supporting role as an aspiring writer, stands out as the only performer whose delivery approaches genuine wit. (**1/2)

The documentary offers a novel perspective on "Guns, Germs, and Steel." Through vivid reenactments of key episodes that strongly support its thesis, the series also addresses and counters common criticisms of the theory.  

I was genuinely puzzled by some viewer comments criticizing the series for lacking new information, claiming it merely reiterates what is taught in middle school. While that’s true, I found it refreshing to see familiar facts presented from a fresh angle and accompanied by insightful analysis.  

If you're someone who loves understanding the underlying reasons behind how things work—whether you've dismantled a telephone to see its inner workings, visited a farm to learn how it operates, or watched cows being milked—then you'll find this series particularly enjoyable. I wholeheartedly recommend it.

Wow! Stacy Peralta has once again delivered an extraordinary documentary, this time exploring the history of big-wave surfing in America, following his acclaimed work on Dogtown and Z-Boys. Through a compelling blend of rare archival footage and interviews with legendary surfers, we are immersed in the daring, free-spirited lives of the sport’s pioneers. Their boundless passion not only shaped a thriving industry but also inspired countless others worldwide.

What makes this film truly special is its focus on these iconic figures and their remarkable stories, which infuse it with genuine warmth. Peralta’s deep respect for these surfers is palpable as we hear recountings of Greg Noll, who boldly strode through groups of awestruck beachgoers to challenge 50-foot waves off Hawaii’s North Shore. Or Jeff Clark, who braved the perilous Mavericks off Northern California alone for 15 years before it gained recognition as a premier surf spot. The legendary journey of Laird Hamilton further enriches the narrative, culminating in Greg Noll’s reverent praise of Hamilton as the greatest surfer of all time—an endorsement that sent chills down my spine.

(As a side note, Noll, Clark, and others attended the Sundance screenings. Noll modestly described himself as an aging surfer past his prime and was deeply touched by the experience.)

The only redeeming aspect of "People I Know" is that it exemplifies the types of films Al Pacino should steer clear of. My initial disappointment stemmed from Pacino's attempt at a Georgia accent; at times it was half-hearted and unconvincing, while at other moments it felt exaggerated. The dialogue and character interactions were poorly executed, and the storyline was weak and uninspiring. The supporting cast barely managed to hold the film together, and after an hour, there was still no solid plot in sight. Overall, the story is dull, and I found myself having to slap my face a few times just to stay awake. 

This film is likely to bore you as well—stay far away.

This film is not worth watching, as it was destined to be a failure from the start. Initially, Ram Gopal Verma intended to remake the classic Bollywood film "Sholay," but after facing issues with the original creators, he decided to proceed with the project. Unfortunately, he chose to omit all the key elements—acting, script, songs, music, comedy, and action—and simply filmed it because he had already assembled a crew. It was a costly and time-wasting endeavor. Following his successes with "Rangeela," "Satya," and "Company," he surprisingly veered off course, reminiscent of Coppola’s direction with "The Godfather." What were you thinking, RGV? 

The plot, though somewhat difficult to follow, roughly echoes the original "Sholay." Ajay Devgn plays Heero (the Beeru character), while the newcomer portrays Ajay (the Jay character). Both are mischievous yet humorous friends who initially help a cop catch a villain. Later, a retired policeman hires them as personal security to protect him from the most wanted criminal, Bubban, played by Amitabh Bachchan. If you haven't been keeping up with Bollywood films, rest assured—the good guys win in the end. You've just saved yourself three precious hours!

American playwright Howard W. Campbell, Jr. (portrayed with a hint of outdated charm by Nick Nolte), once enjoyed a contented life in Germany alongside his actress wife, Helga Noth (Sheryl Lee), before the outbreak of World War II. At his career’s zenith, Howard is recruited by an American agent (John Goodman) to serve as a spy for the Allies. Despite being warned of the inherent dangers and the heavy toll it could take, Howard finds the offer alluring and cannot resist. After his wife’s death and the war’s end, Campbell adopts a life of obscurity as a solitary figure in New York City, which only deepens his psychological struggles. The central dilemma—indeed, a point of contention among critics—posed by both the film and Kurt Vonnegut’s original novel is: "Is Campbell a hero or a traitor?" Director Keith Gordon and screenwriter Robert B. Weide provide subtle hints but no definitive answer. This ambiguity—the persistent uncertainty—is what renders "Mother Night" compelling and thought-provoking throughout. Initially, Nolte’s portrayal shows Campbell as intelligent and self-assured; by the film’s conclusion, he appears either fearful and unsure or fearfully certain of his moral debt and the role he played during the war.

In the 1970s, WPIX aired "The Adventures of Superman" every weekday afternoon for several years. Occasionally, they'd preempt other shows to broadcast "Superman and the Mole Men," which I always looked forward to. Watching it again recently, I was taken aback by how truly poor it was.  

It wasn't because of the special effects, or the lack thereof. Sure, George Reeves' Superman costume was pretty rough, with the edges of the foam padding used to make him look more imposing clearly visible. And the Mole Men’s costumes were even worse. The supposed furry covering wouldn't have fooled a ten-year-old; the zippers, sleeve hems, and badly pilling fabric sewn into loose costumes were painfully obvious. Yet, these flaws were understandable.  

What really made it disappointing were the contrived plot devices. Time and again, Superman failed to take any action to prevent things from spiraling out of control. When a lynch mob was searching for the creatures, instead of dispersing the angry crowd or actively searching for the Mole Men himself, he merely stood around explaining the dangers to Lois, helplessly watching the chaos unfold.

A chemical spill transforms people into zombies, and only two doctors stand a chance at surviving the outbreak. As an Andreas Schnaas production, you can expect the usual: poor acting, disastrously bad special effects, and a shoestring budget. The dubbing is particularly ridiculous, and honestly, I find myself compelled to say more about this mess than just one word. Originally, I would have simply called it "Crap," but due to IMDb guidelines, I need to elaborate. Honestly, I struggle to find the words to fully describe how terrible this film is, but I think I’ve managed to fill enough lines to make this review count. All in all, avoid this movie at all costs.  
My Grade: F

This film is a reimagining of the 1978 Warren Beatty classic, "Heaven Can Wait," but reworked into the stand-up comedy style of Mr. Rock. The core story stays the same: Lance Barton (Rock) is summoned before his time is up and strikes a deal with God's agent, Mr. King, to return to Earth as someone else. Just like in the original, he chooses Charles Wellington, a wealthy white man who was murdered—mainly because he’s smitten with Sontee Jenkins (Regina King), who happens to show up at Wellington's house during the murder. However, the portrayal of Mrs. Wellington and her lover takes a nosedive in this version, and the attempt to turn an aging, multimillionaire white man into a stand-up Black comedian trying to win Sontee's heart simply falls flat. The film’s attempts at showing Rock as Wellington, then as the real white Wellington through intercuts, fail miserably. While the original didn’t perfectly capture the nuances of the afterlife concept, "Down to Earth" doesn’t improve upon it—in fact, it misses the mark entirely.

I adore the novel "Jane Eyre" and have seen numerous adaptations over the years. Each has its merits and flaws, but this one ranks among the worst I've encountered. I felt no connection to Jane or Mr. Rochester. Charlotte Gainsbourg (Jane) was barely tolerable and did a fair job of looking plain, but her delivery lacked any real emotion, making it hard to understand what Mr. Rochester saw in her.

As for Mr. Rochester himself, William Hurt seemed even more void of feeling than Jane—if that's even possible. It's a mystery how two such uninspired characters could fall in love, and the film failed to hold my interest. It almost seemed as if director Zeffirelli nodded off during filming.

The version starring Timothy Dalton is more faithful to the novel, though I believe Ciaran Hinds' portrayal of Mr. Rochester in the 1997 A&E adaptation is the most accurate, despite that adaptation not sticking entirely to the book.

On a positive note, Geraldine Chaplin was absolutely perfect in her role, and her performance was a bright spot in an otherwise disappointing film.

This movie was a complete disaster. Despite a decent score on Rotten Tomatoes, don't be fooled by the positive reviews. It wasn't scary, funny, or clever, and it certainly didn't keep my interest. I wasted two hours on this mess. The computer-generated monster was somewhat interesting at first, but after about fifteen minutes, it lost all its appeal. The dialogue was atrocious—probably a poor translation—and the portrayal of Americans was particularly irritating; three characters, all lacking in depth, intelligence, and good judgment. To meet the ten-line requirement, I’ll add that the staff at the video store must have been annoyed with me for bringing this title to the counter.

After being pleasantly surprised by Sandra Bullock's performance in Miss Congeniality, I decided to give Murder By Numbers a try. While she tends to excel in spirited, self-deprecating roles, her portrayal in more serious films like Hope Floats, Speed 2, and 28 Days often falls short. In this movie, her character is portrayed as simultaneously omniscient, confused, and sexually maladjusted—a combination that muddles her personality further. The subplot revealing Sandra's past feels unnecessary and contributes little to character development, making her portrayal seem shallow. The two teenage boys delivered decent performances, but their supposed expertise in forensics and their daring antics are undermined by foolish mistakes that loudly proclaim "We did it!" Chris Penn’s portrayal of the obvious suspect feels underused, as does Ben Chaplin’s role as the token partner and love interest.

***Spoilers Ahead*** Beyond some mediocre acting, the film's main issues stem from a clichéd, TV-movie-style plot that struggles to make the murder motives believable. As mentioned, numerous dumb errors—such as vomited rare food at the crime scene, an overly convenient framing involving the school janitor, the boys hanging out openly in public, and a love interest introduced solely to cause tension—shift the film's tone from intriguing to tedious.

The comically atrocious sound you might hear when watching this abysmal version of Jules Verne's beloved "Journey to the Center of the Earth" is Verne himself spinning in his grave. The only element of this 80-minute flop that even remotely relates to the original story is the title. Otherwise, everything else about this lackluster production is entirely new and not worth your time. In fact, the director has confessed on IMDb that he only directed eight minutes of the film, with the studio adding scenes from "Dollman" director Albert Pyun's sequel to his own "Alien from L.A." starring Kathy Ireland. It appears the producers ran out of funds and, to fulfill overseas contractual commitments, they grafted Pyun's sequel onto Rusty Lemorande's film. Please avoid renting or purchasing this dreadful piece of junk. 

In contrast to Henry Levin’s classic 1959 "Journey to the Center of the Earth" featuring James Mason and Pat Boone, Lemorande’s version is set in modern-day Hawaii. The story revolves around two guys, a British nanny, and a dog, who are unexpectedly thrown together on what promises to be the adventure of a lifetime.

I've got to say, I'm really enjoying what I've seen of this cartoon so far. Admittedly, the animation isn't top-tier, but honestly, I prefer this more exaggerated, cartoony style to the old-fashioned style that was starting to become more common—especially since the classic look only shines when given ample time and effort. There's nothing wrong with the sharp angles and tiny black-dot eyes; in fact, I find it quite charming. When I was a kid, I didn't find Scooby-Doo particularly adorable, but now I think I might appreciate it more.

Shaggy has always been my favorite character, and surprisingly, I believe he has the greatest potential for some real depth. Sure, the show isn't focused on the traditional mystery-solving theme anymore, but that old formula was getting a bit stale anyway. Don't misunderstand—I'm sure talented writers could bring new interest to Mystery Inc.'s classic adventures, which have been somewhat lacking lately. In the meantime, though, this show offers a fun and refreshing twist on the usual. Shaggy and Scooby are...

Usually, I don't feel compelled to write reviews, but this movie was so painfully bad that I had to. I cringed at its shockingly predictable plot, the unimpressive acting, and even found myself laughing at scenes meant to be tense. Most of the audience seemed bored and chatty, even during the supposed climax. Molly Ringwald delivered the only decent performance in what was clearly a troubled production. As for the ending twist—nothing special there either. I've heard claims that the film didn't take itself too seriously, but I found little evidence of that in the actual movie. 

The editing was so poor that entire cuts should have been left on the cutting room floor. Do yourself a favor: save your time and money and choose something else to watch!

I have been familiar with the wonderful book "Goodnight Mister Tom" for many years, and it was only recently that I had the opportunity to watch its adaptation. Having heard numerous positive reviews, I went into it with high expectations. However, once the film ended, I was greatly disappointed. 

This movie is far from good. "Goodnight Mister Tom" as an adaptation was extremely lacking, capturing only about 25% of the book’s content. I particularly noticed that many characters and memorable scenes were missing. The film featured minimal dialogue, felt rushed, and moved too quickly. Most upsetting was the lack of portrayal of the deep bond and love between William Beech and Tom, which was a core aspect of the story. Additionally, the casting was disappointing. I believed this adaptation had potential to be excellent, but it diverged too much from the source material. Overall, it was a very poor adaptation—one of the worst I’ve seen. It definitely warrants a remake that could surpass this version by a thousand times.

Few chess-themed films have been produced in recent years, but this one stands out as more than just a game portrayal—it's a story about the universal desire for love and validation. John Turturro delivers a compelling performance as a psychologically troubled man whose world revolves around 64 squares and 32 pieces. For him, the game offers a sense of purpose and identity; losing a match feels like losing everything that makes sense in his life. Turturro captures this emotional depth beautifully. Even love from a woman couldn't rescue him from his bleak reality. The film prompts reflection on whether there are others like Luzon, obsessively immersed in their games—I believe there are. If you're a chess enthusiast, watching this film won't be a waste. It’s a thoughtfully crafted and well-executed work that successfully conveys its message. Sadly, it seems unlikely there will be a sequel.

Like all the other reviewers, this film has remained in my thoughts for over 30 years. I remember spending hours at the library, delving into every available resource about this story. I even reached out to the PBS station in search of more details. However, the only information I managed to uncover was that it was a story published in a newspaper in the early 1900s. 

Fast forward to 2002, after years of frequent eBay searches, I finally found a VHS copy of the film. There was one other bidder, but I was determined to win it. The losing bidder later contacted me, requesting a copy, which I gladly provided. Even after acquiring the VHS, my search continued until I discovered a website selling a DVD version of the film. You can find it at: http://www.johntopping.com/Harvey%20Perr/War%20Widow/war_widow.html

Everyone we encounter leaves a mark on our thoughts and subtly influences our behavior; a small part of that person seems to rub off on us. "The Eighth Day" explores this theme, reminiscent of "Rainmaker." In the film, Harry (Daniel Auteuil), a sales psychologist and successful businessman, crosses paths with Georges (Pascal Duquenne), a child with Down's Syndrome on the run. The film's strength lies in the powerful performances delivered by both actors. The opening scene is particularly striking, where Georges shares his theory about the creation of the world. The finale reveals what God crafted on the eighth day. The story presents some moments of frustration for Harry—for instance, Georges, who is unreserved, insists on having a pair of expensive shoes despite lacking the funds. These scenes evoke a mixture of laughter and tears. I especially enjoyed the scene where Georges' group, while on an art gallery trip, sneaks onto a bus and crashes the Paradis amusement park. One of the funniest and most embarrassing moments occurs when Harry and Georges pass a horse float on the highway; Georges, looking back, gives the driver a cheeky rude salute. Despite these humorous moments, the film also features gentle, touching scenes that add depth to the story.

First, I would rate this roughly five stars primarily for the acting, which evokes a more subjective impression rather than an objective one—hence, I give it a well-deserved star for that aspect. However, I am aware that such ratings are often influenced by the actors' names, which can artificially boost the perceived quality of a production.

I have concerns about this type of film; it seems to be another attempt—similar to "Untraceable"—to promote a systematic narrative favoring government interference in personal rights. It's interesting that this comes at a time when internet service providers are trying to censor information, and both Americans and Canadians are actively opposing such measures. This time, instead of demonizing torrent file transfers as inherently evil—a tactic meant to evoke fear of sharing data online—the film appears to aim at creating a sexually frustrated population. It feels like Hollywood is resorting to fear-mongering more than ever, especially in thrillers, which have been the most popular genre for the past two decades. These films are being used as tools to subtly influence societal perceptions, often depicting extreme violence to reinforce this agenda.

Those who rated it less than 5 clearly aren't fans of witty, tongue-in-cheek humor. Keaton delivers a brilliant performance here, as he does in most of his work. This isn't a blockbuster or a larger-than-life spectacle; rather, it's campy, slapstick comedy brought to life by some of Hollywood’s most talented and versatile actors. Piscopo is equally impressive as the ambitious top dog wannabe.  

If you're looking for the funniest attempt at avoiding actual profanity on screen, you must see Dimitri’s hilarious portrayal of Morone.  

I rated it a 7.

I attended the Toronto Film Festival expecting a solid film, given its impressive cast and the fact that it was closing the festival—surely that meant it was worth watching, right? How wrong I was.

My concerns began even before the film started, when the director mentioned that during his time directing an episode of Wiseguy, he met an unknown actor named Kevin Spacey—a director and writer of Wiseguy making his feature debut. That didn't exactly inspire confidence. It seems the director and other cast members must have some compromising photos of Kevin Spacey, because I can't imagine why they would sign on for this disaster.

This film is absolutely terrible. It’s a jumble of every hard-boiled cop cliché imaginable, with nothing original to offer. The acting was subpar, and the direction was even worse—it looked like a cheap episode of Wiseguy. Honestly, this might be the best casted direct-to-video movie I’ve ever seen, and that’s saying something.

Some of the most ridiculous moments include Morgan Freeman randomly dancing around his apartment to rock and roll music—completely pointless—and Justin Timberlake trying to get creative.

Apart from about ten sublime minutes riding the celestial train with HB Warner, the remaining 94 minutes were utterly dreadful! The acting was horrible—wooden and stilted—by early talkie standards, though Lee Tracy and HB Warner managed to shine, each avoiding any missteps. Rose Hobart's performance as Julie was especially terrible—lifeless and flat—recalling her equally lackluster turn in the 1932 version of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. The rest of the cast was equally or more unbearable; there's no way to adequately describe their horrendous performances.

But more disturbing than the acting was the story itself. For inexplicable reasons, Julie is madly in love with Liliom, a charming but entirely unscrupulous man who mistreats women and has no redeeming qualities. He marries Julie but offers no support—spending his days lying in bed or hanging out with his shady criminal friend, played by Lee Tracy. Liliom never shows her kindness, frequently berates and beats her, yet Julie continues to love him and makes endless excuses for his behavior, which only encourages his abuse. Shockingly, the film presents this story as...

To me, A Matter of Life and Death is nothing short of perfection—simply the greatest film ever created. From start to finish, it exudes elegance and sophistication. It is engaging, thought-provoking, and serves as a reflection of the post-war world and human relationships. The cinematography is breathtaking, with the seamless blend of black-and-white and Technicolor seamlessly highlighting different realms. The characters and plot are crafted with near-flawless precision, and the meticulous attention to detail creates a truly believable fantasy. No matter how many times I watch it—and I've seen it many times—it never ceases to move me. It makes me smile, laugh, ponder, and even shed tears. It remains as fresh and relevant today as it was in 1946. If I could choose only one film to keep and watch forever, A Matter of Life and Death would undoubtedly be that film.

This stunning film is characterized by its striking visual style, crafted using only six or seven colors. When it was released over fifteen years ago, it amazed audiences with its bold and unique color palette—something entirely different from anything seen before on screen. For me, those vivid colors transform this movie into a captivating visual experience, making it a joy to watch. I often find myself wishing I could freeze thousands of scenes and turn them into paintings to appreciate the artistry behind each frame.  

Although the story and characters don't quite match the visual brilliance, they are all exaggerated and flamboyant—particularly the villains. The iconic actors who portrayed them clearly had a blast on set, embodying characters like "Flatop," "Pruneface," "Lips," and "Mumbles."  

On the other hand, Warren Beatty and Gleanne Hedley deliver solid performances as Dick Tracy and his sweetheart Tess Truehart, with her as adorable and gentle as her name suggests. A notable addition is Charlie Korsmo, who plays the mischievous young boy that Dick and Tess take under their wing. The film also features a colorful cast of characters played by stars such as Al Pacino, Dustin Hoffman, William Forsythe, Paul Sorvino, Mandy Patinkin, Madonna, and many others—too numerous to list here.

Anything that might have held even a flicker of interest in this material is immediately overshadowed by a disclaimer in the first few seconds, warning viewers that the events depicted are unknowable and claiming, "This is the whisper [rumor] most often told" about one of Hollywood's most notorious "mysteries." 

So, essentially, we're not uncovering anything new—E!'s "Mysteries & Scandals" offers a more solid background on the incident, and that’s hardly an endorsement. What do we actually get? 

We see Hollywood portrayed as a den of vipers and decadence. Nothing groundbreaking there. More revealing is how a washed-up director is desperate enough to do just about anything to reclaim his influence in the entertainment industry or political circles. It prompts us to wonder if Peter Bogdanovich is drawing from his own experiences through these characters. But the story told is so cynical, ugly, and muddled that it leaves us feeling guilty for witnessing a pile of hooey masquerading as history. 

The film's tone has a bizarre, frantic quality that I found more irritating than entertaining. There’s no empathy for any of the characters. And the film completely dismisses any nuance, much like the polished veneer of "Citizen Kane," which ultimately simplifies the complex relationship between Davies and Hearts.

If you have any heart and compassion for people, you'll find this to be a difficult film to watch, especially in its latter half. In that segment, we witness a kind-hearted young boy being brutally assaulted, and a mentally challenged man named Dominick reacting with overwhelming distress after witnessing this violence. The material is intense and unsettling. 

Nevertheless, it's a well-made movie with strong performances that will leave a lasting impression. The story resonates deeply and stays with you long after the credits roll.

Tom Hulce delivers what I believe is his finest performance as Dominick, a mentally disabled man with a kind soul. He's cared for by Eugene, a medical student played by Ray Liotta, who gained fame the following year with "Field of Dreams." 

Dominick is a gentle garbage collector who enjoys reading Hulk comics and watching wrestling. His innocent nature and genuine kindness make him a character you'll root for, hoping for his happiness. His outbursts are understandable, driven by his circumstances—watch the film to see how everything unfolds. It's a rewarding experience, though it will take you on an emotional journey that might leave you profoundly moved.

This film stands apart from any other I’ve seen; the closest comparison I can make is to a Woody Allen film. However, whereas Woody Allen often explores human flaws with a contemplative humor, Bret Carr seems to delve into confronting that one deep-seated insecurity that shapes us—whether for better or worse. In the case of Lou, this insecurity manifests as his stutter, which is rooted in a childhood trauma revealed through flashbacks.

There are so many peculiarly neurotic individuals out there, and I believe everyone deserves a chance at redemption. Yet, it’s also true that human diversity is what makes the world so captivating. Perhaps we shouldn’t aim to fix all our neuroses any more than we should try to alter our noses or breasts.

This is an indie film made on a very modest budget, but its production values are impressive, and the scope of the project is remarkable. It feels like a charming gem within the self-help genre. I eagerly anticipate what this filmmaker will create next; I can easily imagine a career comparable to Woody Allen or Albert [surname], full of wit and insight.

This is undoubtedly one of the best films I have ever watched. It takes me on an emotional rollercoaster, making me laugh, cry, feel disgust, happiness, and love—all within just over two hours!  
The cast is absolutely outstanding. I must especially highlight Michael Nyqvist, who delivers a truly remarkable performance. I also admire the actor portraying Tore, who convincingly captures the essence of a young man with mental challenges—his portrayal reminded me of Leonardo DiCaprio’s role in "Gilbert Grape." Additionally, the movie features the most beautiful song in the world: "Gabriella’s Sång."  
I highly recommend this film to everyone for a moving and enjoyable experience!

This particular Joe McDoakes short appears to be directly inspired by the star-studded Warner Brothers wartime morale booster, *Thank Your Lucky Stars*. In that film, Eddie Cantor played both himself and a wannabe comedian eager to break into Hollywood, hindered only by his resemblance to Cantor. 

In the McDoakes series, George O'Hanlon portrays both himself and the titular McDoakes, a hopeful aspiring actor trying to make it in the film industry. Similar to *Thank Your Lucky Stars*, a few Warner Brothers contract players happen to pass through this film during a quiet moment. 

O'Hanlon's character is sent by central casting to perform a small one-line role in a World War I movie, but the lookalike McDoakes quickly catches on to the situation. Overwhelmed with nervousness about his big scene, he begins to brainstorm ways to deliver his single line—perhaps by mimicking a genuine movie star. 

After 86 takes, much to director Ralph Sanford's frustration and Clyde Cook's patience—who plays a British Cockney soldier—they finally discover a niche for McDoakes in the film industry. This delightful and hilarious short is definitely worth watching and was even nominated for an Oscar.

This was an egregious waste of my time. The plot was non-existent, and the acting was so subpar it could serve as a textbook example of what not to do in acting classes. It simply copies the earlier Universal Soldier film, which already suffered from poor performances, and elevates that mediocrity. It's unfortunate that VD feels the need to repeatedly boost his ego every few years, and even more disappointing that audiences are willing to shell out money to endure such rubbish. This type of low-quality filmmaking tarnishes the reputation of martial arts movies, making stars like Segall, Norris, and Arnold seem almost talented by comparison. Perhaps VD should consider following Leslie Nielsen's lead and create parody versions of his genre. That way, we could at least enjoy the humor rather than ridicule the film itself.

The direction of this film was exceptional for a comedy, with many scenes resembling comic book panels and a darker visual style—more intense in appearance than I anticipated, though not in tone. While it may not be the funniest movie ever, especially if you prefer crude sexist jokes, it offers relatively little of that compared to films like Something About Mary or American Pie. On rewatching, several jokes become even funnier and more memorable. If you're a fan of comic books or comic book-inspired movies like Batman or X-Men, you'll likely appreciate the subtle humor woven throughout. Conversely, if those genres aren't your thing, you'll probably enjoy the film's respectful parody of them. Fans of the movie will find some interesting extras on the DVD. (8/10)

As a child, I thought the weapon the murderer used was pretty cool; however, I was just a kid and probably didn't think things through. Even back then, I found the movie's plot to be foolish and somewhat dull, especially when the killer wasn't wielding his light knife to slaughter victims. What surprises me is that the film features a genuinely talented cast. I can't imagine what script they read before agreeing to appear in this movie, as it’s undeniably boring and seems to be primarily an excuse to showcase a miniature lightsaber. The plot is occasionally confusing, and the ending descends into chaos. The entire film appears centered around aliens and this one weapon. It involves two kids and a man having an alien encounter, then flashes forward years later, suggesting some sort of return or continuation. There are scenes with dead animals and other strange elements, and for some reason, one character ends up with the aliens' weapon and uses it for a light-hearted killing spree. Honestly, I can't help but wonder why this movie was even made—if the goal was to...

Dolph Lundgren grimaces and broods his way through this confusing mystery/thriller that fails to live up to the coolness suggested by the packaging. He delivers a solid performance here, but the storyline is a jumble of B-movie clichés—detectives, revenge, tycoons, hookers, S&M—that seem improvised on the spot. The film improves somewhat in the second half, but for a more enjoyable Lundgren film, consider renting RED SCORPION instead.

The film was fantastic overall, with the exception of some scenes featuring Esposito. I appreciated how it brought together all the detectives from the series and provided closure to several unresolved storylines—something NBC never quite managed. It was especially touching to see Pembleton and Bayliss portrayed at their most vulnerable and genuine. Braugher and Secor delivered outstanding performances, though they might still go unnoticed as usual. It was bittersweet to realize this was the finale of Homicide. Watching reruns on CourtTV simply isn't the same as the weekly thrill of tuning in every Friday.
