Nonetheless, the movie succeeded in capturing the essence of life after Al's retirement and depicted the strong familial bonds within the unit beautifully. I truly enjoyed it.

CREEP is a straightforward and intense horror film set in real time, focused solely on the premise of people being attacked on an empty subway platform by a mutant creature over 85 minutes. It delivers exactly that—nothing more, nothing less. Director Christopher Smith maximizes the tension by introducing characters who have genuine reasons to remain in the subway after it’s sealed off. The film deliberately keeps the origins of the creature, known as Creep, ambiguous—hinting at clandestine experiments from the 1960s underground—adding a layer of mystery that mostly works. Unfortunately, Smith undermines his own effort near the end by holding back from delivering a more satisfying twist, one that could reveal additional genetic deformities (also alluded to earlier). Yes, you read that right—I was hoping for a clichéd twist. Franka Potente (RUN LOLA RUN) delivers a solid performance as the terrified female protagonist, and the rest of the cast holds their own.

Wow! Why would anyone bother making a sequel to an already terrible film? Half Past Dead was a bad movie, but at least it had a clear idea of what it wanted to be. HPD2, on the other hand, has no sense of direction. It simply exists on screen for reasons I can't explain. Spoiler alert: the entire film boils down to this—Twitch (played by Kurupt of Tha Dogg Pound) is transferred to another prison where there might be a buried treasure chest of gold bricks. Inside, a riot erupts among rival inmates, during which one is shot by a man named Cortez, who then schemes to escape. During a conjugal visit, Twitch’s fiancée and Burke’s (played by Bill Goldberg) daughter are kidnapped by Cortez and held in an execution room. Burke reluctantly teams up with Twitch, and they get into trouble with the idiotic inmates while trying to rescue their loved ones from Cortez.  

My opinion: This is arguably the most unnecessary sequel since Universal Soldier: The Return. The script is atrocious, the acting is unbearable, the dialogue is laughable, and every character is a caricature. Sure, it's a low-budget film, but that’s no excuse.

This film is quite strange... I couldn't quite grasp what it was about. A group of lowlifes from North London discover a mute boy in the woods, whom they all believe to be some sort of oracle. Somehow, each of them undergoes a change—often leading to disaster—through their interactions with him. The movie wraps up after about 90 minutes, leaving me feeling unsatisfied and almost annoyed by its apparent lack of purpose. I didn't connect with any of the characters; none of them were given enough depth to make me care about their fates.  

What was the intended message? Am I missing something? It just felt too bizarre. What happens to Runner? Why does Emilio shoot the kid? That scene made no sense at all—seemed pointless. Can anyone help me make sense of this jumble of a film?

So, where are the cannibals? Those drawn in by the title and the promise of the "real cannibal" aspect of this film will be disappointed. Instead, it features a peculiar man revisiting a Papua New Guinea village populated by natives, one of whom was his lover many decades earlier. The man, Tobias Schneebaum, is quintessentially Jewish from New York, and this aspect is subtly woven into the documentary, as he appears in his yarmulke during several scenes.

There are no actual cannibals in the film—only stories shared by some of the natives and by Schneebaum himself. It’s not a bad movie; it’s quite interesting with excellent cinematography. Schneebaum remains completely likable throughout and offers a captivating look into a world vastly removed from Western civilization.

However, it doesn’t live up to its cover or plot summary promises.

Rating: 4 out of 10, kids.

I'm generally not a fan of remakes, or as the modern term puts it, "retellings," but this particular film genuinely annoyed me. The original Prom Night, while not a masterpiece in my humble opinion, at least understood what it was—horror. There are some fundamental principles to keep in mind when crafting a horror film. Suspense is vital for holding the audience's attention. Unfortunately, this film failed on that front; it was not a nerve-wracking experience. The scares felt cheap, and the foreshadowing was poorly executed. A common trope, such as a cat suddenly jumping out of a closet followed shortly after by an unexpected appearance of the killer, has been overused to the point of cliché, and this film couldn't even do that convincingly. Given its shortcomings in these basic horror conventions, I didn't have high expectations. A likable protagonist is essential, yet this film lacked one. The character I most related to was the lead detective—his composed demeanor and logical approach to capturing the killer were refreshing in a genre that often relies on chaos. A sensible, level-headed response to danger—like turning around when fleeing from an axe-wielding psychopath—should be standard, yet it seems absent here.

As an avid horror film enthusiast, I make it a point to watch all notable releases within the genre, particularly those produced by my home country. Unfortunately, I must say that "Power of Fear" (known as "Vedma" in Russian) stands out as one of the weakest entries among them. Firstly, it fails to evoke any sense of fear—even a young child would be unaffected. The pacing is painfully slow, and the plot is so predictable that genuine horror elements are absent. Honestly, the film falls short on every front: from its absurd story—a baffling attempt by Russian producers and the director to adapt a classic Ukrainian witchcraft tale into a dull, modern American thriller—to the acting, which is painfully cheesy. The cast, including well-known Russian actors Valeri Nikolayev and Yevgeniya Kryukova, come across as stiff as mannequins; they hardly seem to try, merely delivering their lines in English with no emotion at all. I also fail to understand why they chose to shoot this film in English with Russian actors—seems like a misguided decision.

Initially, this movie appeared promising, but it ultimately failed to live up to expectations. The director demonstrates talent with striking camera work and artistic flair, reminiscent of many Asian filmmakers, yet struggles with crafting a cohesive and engaging story. The narrative felt disjointed, constantly drifting into various directions without settling on a clear, compelling focus. In essence, the film didn't align with the promising description provided in the press releases. On the plus side, the performances were strong across the board, with Jude Law delivering an especially remarkable portrayal, as he's known to do. It's unfortunate that he chose to be involved in such a weak screenplay.

What starts as a somewhat clever farce about a shady security monitoring company quickly devolves into an unremarkable and utterly trivial murder mystery. David Arquette and the talented Stanley Tucci strive to make this cinematic disaster tolerable, but some things are simply beyond the realm of human possibility.  

For example, what prompts Gale to abruptly transform from a kind, motherly figure into a drunken harpy at Tommy's parents’ house? Why would Heinrich, despite his obvious sleaziness, desire to ruin the very business he dedicates his life to—by robbing and possibly killing his clients? Why does the seemingly rational Tommy believe Heinrich could be a murderer—based nearly solely on a dream—and even if that suspicion held some weight, why wouldn't he report it to the police? And why didn't Gale activate the alarm upon returning home, especially after chastising Howie for leaving it off?  

All these implausible events are, of course, crucial for the plot—if one can even call it that—to move forward. It might be somewhat forgivable if they led to even a flicker of comedy, but instead, everything from Howie’s disturbing description of his date rape, to the coroner’s mistaken identification of Gale, to the lackluster finale, fails to entertain or make sense.

What can I say? I suppose I should start with a "Spoiler alert." In this movie, they used the F-word repeatedly—almost every two sentences. I didn't enjoy it at all, as it was filled with references to sexual perversions, infidelity, and deception. The extensive swearing was completely disproportionate. I rated the film a 3, with two of those points awarded solely for Mira Sorvino's alluring dance moves.

The previous reviewer was quite generous. I quite enjoyed the first film, but I can't say the same for this one. The opening is tolerable, but it quickly deteriorates. I find it hard to believe Jon Bon Jovi as a "bad-ass vampire hunter," and the vampire princess is neither alluring nor frightening. Many scenes simply don't make sense. For instance, any sensible person would suspect something's amiss when a mysterious woman suddenly appears to seduce them—especially an experienced hunter. Why Una can communicate with Jovi is never explained. Nothing in this movie makes sense, and while it might have been more forgivable if it were entertaining, unfortunately, it wasn't. This is one of the worst vampire movies I've ever seen.

The late Dudley Moore delivered his most iconic performance in 1981's *Arthur*, a hilariously lively and occasionally touching film that evokes warm smiles, hearty laughter, and sometimes a tear, depending on your mood. Moore earned a Best Actor Oscar nomination for portraying Arthur Bach, a charmingly irresponsible playboy who "races cars, plays tennis, fondles women, but he has weekends off and he's his own boss." Arthur is set to inherit $750 million upon marrying Susan Johnston (Jill Eikenberry), a privileged society girl and the spoiled daughter of an undercover gangster. Complications arise when Arthur falls for Linda Morolla (Liza Minnelli), a Queens waitress and aspiring actress who steals neckties for her father's birthday. Moore's performance sparkles as one of the most uproariously funny in recent history. The late Sir John Gielgud earned an Oscar for Best Supporting Actor for his impeccable portrayal of Hobson, Arthur's sharp-tongued but affectionate butler and confidant, whose outward disdain masks deep paternal care. Additional comedic highlights come from Barney Martin as Linda's father, Stephen Elliott as Susan's father, and Geraldine Fitzgerald as Arthur's eccentric grandmother. The film was directed with

As is well known, the sub-genre of sex comedies has become quite saturated. Simply being overly vulgar no longer suffices to make a film stand out. Having seen and heard countless crude jokes and antics, I now find that a sex comedy must also offer other redeeming qualities to capture my interest.  

When I first watched The 40 Year Old Virgin, I had a pretty clear idea of what to expect—thanks to the trailers, especially the question, "Is it true that if you don't use it, you lose it?" What caught me off guard was the movie's genuine warmth and sincere efforts at character development. It still features the quirky, "off-the-wall" characters typical of Adam Sandler movies, and it doesn't shy away from using plenty of inappropriate language, enough to fill Noah’s Ark. Yet, amidst all this, the film weaves a meaningful love story and carries an underlying message.  

The protagonist, Andy, is—unfortunately for me—a character I can relate to. From the opening scene, I notice he shares my passion for Mystery Science Theater 3000—there's a poster of the show on his wall—and as the story unfolds, we see his impressive collection of vintage items. Andy also has a sizable collection of video games and demonstrates a solid knowledge of them.

All this heartbreaking waste of film stock simply calls for Count Floyd to appear every sixty seconds. Somehow, they managed to assemble Steve Railsback, Susan Anspach, John Vernon, and Joe Flaherty on set, yet they couldn’t come within five miles—about eight kilometers—of making a decent film. Boy, does this thing suck. Not a single original line, thought, shot, or effect emerges from the mindless opening sequence to the equally mindless conclusion. The once enchanting, ethereal Susan Anspach from Five Easy Pieces—boring. Steve Railsback—boring. John Vernon—boring. The giant bug—boring. If this is supposed to be a scary movie, then Buttercream Gang is more like a thug life documentary. 

Honestly, every terrible film seems to have its own explanation for why it turned out so bad. Usually, it’s in the opening credits—"Written, Directed, and Produced by" some one-man band. Or it centers around a talentless ditz whose presence makes it painfully clear why this flop was even made. Here, you don’t find out until the very end of the credits, where it’s gratefully noted that about a dozen sub-agencies of the Canadian government had a hand in its creation. 

Right now, I’m watching MST’s parody of Beast of Yucca Flats to cleanse my palate.

This film is poorly conceived, badly acted, and inadequately written.

Jon Heder's performance is incredibly irritating, as he struggles to break free from his Napolean Dynamite persona—self-centered and clueless.

Additionally, Diane Keaton portrays the same type of mannish, overly obsessive mother seen in other films, caring excessively yet strangely detached from her children's lives (similar to her role in *Because I Said So*).

Although I generally appreciate Anna Faris, she comes across here as superficial and dim-witted.

Jeff Daniels' performance is mediocre—nothing memorable.

Honestly, it's best to avoid this movie if you want to preserve your inner well-being.

All the world's a stage, and its people are the actors within it—something along those lines. Who declared that theater ends at the orchestra pit, or even at the theater door? Why shouldn't the audience be considered active participants in the theatrical experience, including the story itself? 

This film was a bold experiment that proclaimed: “Hey! The story is you, and it demands more than just your attention—it calls for your active involvement.” Sometimes we bring the story to you; other times, you must seek out the story yourself.

Unfortunately, no one listened. But that doesn’t mean the message wasn’t worth sharing.

I had high hopes for this movie, especially since it was a Yashraj Film.  

Jimmy runs a call center, and one day he is approached by Pooja Singh to teach her boss, Lakhan Singh, English. The two fall in love and consider running away together, but Pooja confesses she can't go through with it because she owes a debt to Lakhan Singh, also known as Bhaiyyaji. Despite this, they decide to steal money from him, only for Jimmy to later discover that Bhaiyyaji is actually a notorious Don. Meanwhile, Bhaiyyaji hires Bachchan Pandey to find Jimmy and Pooja.  

The film features Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Anil Kapoor, and Akshaye Kumar, under the direction of debutant Viay Krishna Acharya, with production by Aditya Chopra and Yash Chopra.  

"Tashan" ranks among the worst movies I have ever seen. While the scenery is appealing and Kareena Kapoor (noted for her well-publicized weight loss) looks good, the story is extremely薄 and often nonsensical from scene to scene, which is why I found myself disappointed.

I can't understand the intense dislike for this episode. If you're looking for a poorly executed Smallville episode, you might want to check out Subterranean—it's quite rough. Tom Welling delivers a strong performance, which is impressive given how rarely I mention that, and Michael Rosenbaum is consistently excellent. The alternate universe concept feels surprisingly believable. In the episode, the Martian Manhunter, who previously appeared in "Static," returns and informs Clark that the doctor leading the asylum where they are held is actually a phantom from the Phantom Zone. He tells Clark that if he wants to return to his own universe, he must eliminate him. Overall, it's a well-crafted episode with solid acting and a good pacing.

This film goes far beyond the simple story of a middle-aged man rediscovering the joy of ballroom dancing (though it’s part of that too). It’s a heartfelt journey of one individual's reawakening to life, overcoming the pressures of work and finances to find happiness once again. An added delight is the compelling glimpse into Japan’s slowly evolving attitudes toward ballroom dancing, physical contact, and social norms. You’ll find moments that will make you laugh out loud, scenes that will inspire you to get up and dance the tango, and many others that will simply leave you feeling uplifted. 

It serves as an excellent introduction to modern Japanese cinema, especially for those who may think Japanese films are all “serious” or difficult to access.

Believe it or not, this film from 1912 runs a full 12 minutes, making it quite lengthy for its time—very few films back then exceeded that duration. However, what truly sets this quirky little film apart isn’t its length but its unique cast: all the actors, except for one frog, are bugs—yes, bugs! This simple domestic comedy could have easily resembled the works of Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy, or Max Linder, but instead, this Russian production employs bugs—or, I believe, models that look exactly like bugs. Given that Chaplin and Laurel and Hardy had yet to make their mark and Linder was busy elsewhere, perhaps that’s why bugs were used! Thanks to stop-motion animation, these bug characters moved, danced, and fought with astonishing realism—far more convincing than King Kong, which appeared just 21 years later.

The story begins with Mr. Beetle sneaking out for a good time. He visits a lively, bawdy club while his wife supposedly waits at home. Unfortunately for Mr. Beetle, he is caught on camera by a local film enthusiast. Unbeknownst to him, Mrs. Beetle is also engaging in her own bohemian escapade with a grasshopper.

Honestly, I can't believe what passes for entertainment these days. Themes like death (and mockery of death), violence, sexual innuendos, adults threatening children, crudeness, minors abusing alcohol, drug theft, dysfunctional families, babysitters from hell, stereotypes about African Americans, police, and overweight individuals, along with kids sneaking out at night—surely this sounds like a kids' movie? Not at all! Adding to that are dark and frightening elements: a deceased woman possessing and transforming a house, holding her loving husband captive for over 20 years, and terrorizing an entire neighborhood—what a lovely message for children. Parents, is this truly what you want your kids to watch? Is this the lesson you want them to learn about life? 

This film is too scary for young children, and I worry that teenagers might be living some of these scenarios in real life—so why expose them to it? As for adult viewers, it isn’t frightening or funny—just dull, contrived, and predictable. The characters are all wrong—clueless parents, ignorant police, foolish and irritating friends, and mean, manipulative figures.

Melissa Joan Hart truly shines! This show is incredible—there's nothing quite like it. Perhaps only Melissa's performance in Clarissa Explains It All comes close; she was fantastic in that role as well. Honestly, this series surpasses Buffy the Vampire Slayer by a mile. It's absolutely wonderful!

Many years after watching the original television series, I initially didn’t appreciate this film. However, as time passed and my memory of the series faded, I revisited it and found it absolutely hilarious. Based on Neil Simon’s stage play, it remains largely unchanged for the big screen, which is part of its charm. Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon deliver exceptional performances as Oscar and Felix, complemented by a fantastic supporting cast, especially John Fielder as Vinnie. Even now, certain scenes make me burst into laughter—Felix interrupting Oscar during a ball game to ask about dinner, Oscar cracking up and chasing Felix around the apartment, the giggling Pigeon Sisters brought low by Felix’s sob stories, and, of course, the legendary cafeteria scene (later echoed in Nora Ephron’s ‘When Harry Met Sally’). The film’s dialogue is razor-sharp too. When the boys suspect Felix has overdosed, Oscar quips, “They could be vitamins! He might be the healthiest one in the room!” Truly brilliant!

The Fluffer may incorporate some genuine elements from the porn industry, but that doesn't compensate for its poor direction, weak performances, and an uninspired script. It feels like a B-grade production from beginning to an overly prolonged conclusion. It would be embarrassing if the general public regarded this as a showcase of contemporary gay filmmaking. Hopefully, it will have a brief run on the gay film festival circuit and quietly fade away on home video. This film is set to premiere at the Queer Film Weekend in Brisbane on April 10, 2002, but its reception there will likely hinge on how much alcohol attendees have consumed at the pre-event cocktail party—they're going to need it.

It seems that the talented team behind Shonda Rhimes has perhaps outsourced this particular script overseas, possibly to the so-called MediocreLand. "PP" immediately brought to mind the many dull yet initially promising, but ultimately predictable, David E. Kelley series such as Picket Fences, Ally McBeal, and now Boston Legal. The absurd cases they encounter are so exaggerated that they hardly inspire sympathy or emotional engagement. That's actually a key element in successful medical dramas—presenting dramatic scenarios that feel relatable and evoke a sense of "This could happen to me." Unfortunately, this show misses that mark and also fails to deliver any humor.

While the cast delivers solid performances, the storylines are lifeless and fail to come to life. As a therapist myself, I can say Amy Brennan's character is portrayed as the most outrageously ineffective, unethical, and untrained therapist imaginable. Whoever writes her dialogue clearly flunked ethics and transference courses at Stanford. Someone should hand them a proper Code of Ethics—they could learn a thing or two, especially after that episode involving the nose-bleeding wife and the therapist’s inappropriate involvement. No real therapist would behave that badly.

As for the storyline involving women longing for men who have moved on—it's been done to death; we've all moved past “Sex and the City.” Addison’s youthful, aggressive pursuit of a man she’s interested in also feels recycled.

Diane and I enjoyed an exceptional film today in Fremantle, and we both agreed it surpassed all others in the pastiche genre. What made it stand out was our fascination with the brief, five- to ten-minute segments that composed the movie, each built around a central theme—love in its many manifestations.

The film is set across various Parisian arrondissements, giving each segment a distinct flavor. Having visited Paris a few times, I wasn’t entirely familiar with all the locations, but I’m confident that Europeans, especially French viewers, would recognize them easily. Regardless, the high quality of the production draws viewers into each story so convincingly that the specific cityscapes become secondary.

The pacing is swift, allowing the audience to immerse themselves in one narrative before moving seamlessly to the next. The stories are subtle, thought-provoking, and gentle—unlike the more explicit Hollywood fare—evoking the nuanced nature of life itself, free from the overwhelming media coverage that often drowns out such quiet truths.

Brian Yuzna is often dismissed as a director of cheap, gory horror films, but the reality is that his movies are quite underrated. While the Re-Animator sequels don't quite match the original's brilliance, they still stand as respectable entries in horror history. Return of the Living Dead 3 is arguably the best installment in the series, and Society approaches surrealist horror at its finest. Although this thriller isn't a masterpiece, it showcases Yuzna's sharp sense for horror, with a plot that keeps viewers on the edge of their seats. I find it surprising that a horror film centered on dentistry didn't emerge until 1996—perhaps because visiting the dentist taps into a primal fear, akin to fleeing from a tiger in modern times. Dentistry doesn't terrify me, but evidently, I am in the minority. The story revolves around Dr. Feinstone, a perfectionist dentist with a comfortable life, a successful practice, and a beautiful wife—everything most people desire. However, his world unravels when he discovers his wife's affair with the pool cleaner, and his life is soon to be forever changed.

I chose to rent this film on DVD without any prior knowledge, as part of a winter marathon of watching one movie each night. After enduring several terrible American action-adventure flicks (Ballistic, Daredevil, Cradle of Life), Zhu Warriors stood out as brilliantly inventive filmmaking. The plot is utterly nonsensical, but I appreciated the film’s genuine sincerity, warmth, and absence of irony, which felt refreshingly authentic. Visually, the film is stunning. While the special effects may not be as technically perfect as Hollywood’s highest standards, the directors focus more on vibrant color, composition, and dynamic movement than on realism, resulting in many breathtaking shots. 

In one scene, two superhuman characters stand atop jagged rock spires, with a massive moon rising behind them—an image beautifully balanced among the three elements. In another, a princess-warrior leaps through the sky behind her glowing sword, resembling a heat-seeking missile. The color palette shifts dramatically from shot to shot, used expressively to convey emotion rather than to depict realistic scenes.

The characters are as straightforward and archetypal as comic book figures—lacking complex depth but resonating on a more fundamental level through familiar archetypes. Physically, several of the actors are astonishingly...

I've been reviewing the AFI's list of the top 100 comedies, and honestly, this one ranks among the worst. Not just of the 90 films I've seen from the list, but of any movie I've ever watched. While drunken antics can be amusing at times, Dudley's antics just fall flat. Liza almost elevates the film, but ultimately, it's not enough—if you want to see her in something worth watching, check out Arrested Development. Really, expecting humor from Dudley laughing and drinking? I strongly recommend almost any other film from the AFI top 100 comedies for a better laugh. For a funnier take on drunkenness, watch The Thin Man. And for genuinely hilarious movies, any Marx Brothers classic will do the trick—especially if you're as intoxicated as Arthur.

I just watched this film at TIFF (Toronto International Film Festival), and fans of Hal Hartley will not be disappointed! If you're not familiar with this director's body of work, that's okay—this film stands strongly on its own. I loved it so much that I had to attend a second screening immediately; it was incredible and I need to see it again—and soon!

This film is incredibly funny, with sharp, intelligent dialogue, and Parker Posey's performance as Fay Grim is truly outstanding. Fay Grim is the latest feature that revisits the characters and universe introduced in Hartley's 2000 film Henry Fool. Visually, the film employs Hartley's characteristic use of the canted or Dutch angle, a stylistic choice seen in his earlier shorts included in the collection Possible Films: Short Works by Hal Hartley 1994-2004, as well as in The Girl from Monday (2005).

I watched this film most fittingly on September 11th. The story of Fay Grim unfolds against the backdrop of a transformed world following the events of September 11, 2001. Without revealing too much, I see this work as a boldly political and thought-provoking piece that reflects on our changing realities.

Many people dismissed Vanilla Sky as just another odd Tom Cruise film, like Magnolia or Eyes Wide Shut, but it truly stands on its own. While some labeled it weird, it’s more accurate to categorize it as different and occasionally confusing—yet not weird. Weird is Stanley Kubrick or Pauly Shore; different is The Truman Show; confusing is The Matrix or The Game. Unlike Kubrick’s films, Vanilla Sky offers a clear conclusion. Everything may not make perfect sense immediately—or even now—but it will eventually. The confusion stems from David Aames’s (Tom Cruise) own bewilderment. That’s the essence of the film. That’s where the so-called "weirdness" that initially deterred critics originates. Had they taken the time to truly "open their eyes," as the original 1997 Spanish version did, they would have understood this. And if that alone isn’t enough to persuade you, go see the film for its music. Cameron Crowe crafts an exceptional soundtrack that helps establish the movie’s unique atmosphere—an element many films overlook. With tracks like The Beach Boys’ “Good Vibrations” swelling during the film’s emotional climax, he creates an offbeat yet perfectly fitting mood. It’s a remarkable film in every sense.

The entire Biker Movie genre seems to be composed of some of the worst films ever created. This particular entry is packed with constant fights, copious amounts of blood, clashes between bikers and Native Americans, and a shanty town that gets systematically destroyed, one shack at a time. The acting is alarmingly bad. Whatever happened to Robert Walker, Jr.? He was once featured in major studio films, yet he simply disappeared from the scene. While this movie is genuinely terrible, it might be a fun watch if you haven't seen a Biker movie in a long while. By the end, you'll likely feel a bit guilty for having spent time on it!

"The Thief of Bagdad" captivates with the imposing figure of the malevolent magician Jaffar (Conrad Veidt). He schemes using deception and enchantments to seize the kingdom from its rightful ruler, the young King Ahmad, and to claim a stunning princess for himself. Ultimately, he falls prey—like many tyrants in stories and legends—to the power of love and the common folk he disregarded, represented here by the humble thief (Sabu). The forces of good versus evil, darkness against light, are vividly brought to life both visually and narratively. The screenplay is poetic, straightforward, and exquisitely crafted. The costumes of Jaffar and his followers flutter and rise like black-winged birds, striking swiftly under the cover of night to sow destruction and terror. The noble hero is adorned in white turbans and robes, while his princess is dressed in soft pinks and pale blues. The film features breathtaking scenes that match its predecessors in splendor, utilizing color to vividly depict a fantastical world previously thought impossible. With flying carpets and white horses, a giant genie superbly portrayed by Rex Ingram, and wicked sorcerers, it continues to enchant audiences with its spectacular visuals and imaginative storytelling.

The first aspect you encounter when studying fascism is ostracism: because this "philosophy" is a sham, it relies on scapegoats to evaluate its "thought." Ettore Scola's film, arguably his masterpiece, centers on the outcasts—the scapegoats of the regime.  
Regarding the historical events—Hitler and Mussolini's alliance—it offers little detail: a few military marches, some garlands, scattered voices. Our two protagonists are not summoned to the celebration of masculinity. "Genius is essentially masculine," declares Antonietta (played by a radiant Sophia Loren), embroidered on her cushion; Antonietta’s world is confined to her kitchen, her pride rooted in her children. At the film’s start, she is a victim of this hyper-macho environment but remains unaware. She believes she should be content. Gabriel, on the other hand, is politically conscious; he perceives the insidious cancer eroding his country. Yet, as a gay man, he feels alienated and faces imminent arrest.  
Setting aside all obstacles between them, they recognize their shared bond and make love. This act serves as a rebellion, especially for Antonietta, whose ethics should prohibit such intimacy. Her act of infidelity, in a land where politics and religion jointly oppress women, leads her into a form of political defiance.

As I settled in to watch the 14th season of The Bachelor, titled "On the Wings of Love," I anticipated an "interesting" experience. I had only seen bits and pieces of previous seasons—watching an episode or two before missing the next few. While I often find The Bachelor to be both captivating and fascinating, its overall quality and moral grounding are frequently questionable.

This season follows Jake, a 31-year-old commercial pilot from Dallas, Texas, on his quest to discover genuine love—something as authentic as one can hope for in a season-long reality dating show. He meets 25 gorgeous women from across the country. Their interactions are mostly superficial; after all, how well can you truly get to know someone through fleeting five-minute conversations? From the outset, Jake attempts to communicate his true intentions—at least to the viewers. He makes it clear that he isn’t simply seeking love or a fun fling, but is genuinely looking for a fiancée or wife. One can only assume that he has conveyed this earnest desire to the women competing for his affections as well.

Following his classic film noir tribute Chinatown, Roman Polanski revisited the themes that brought him fame in the 1960s with this unsettling psychological horror. Like Repulsion and Rosemary's Baby, it explores the paranoia and sense of confinement born from apartment living.  

Polanski excels at crafting claustrophobic settings, and this film stands as his most suffocating and enclosed work yet. The use of narrow side walls and distant vanishing points is more pronounced than before, and even during the rare exterior shots, the sky is scarcely visible. However, The Tenant is not only confined by space but also by its intense focus on the protagonist. Trelkovsky, portrayed by Polanski himself, appears in every scene—almost every shot frames him. When he's not on screen, the camera often adopts his perspective. Throughout, he is surrounded by reflections, constantly seeing his own image staring back at him in mirrors.  

Few films delve so deeply into a character’s internal world and isolation. Unlike some psychological thrillers like M or Peeping Tom, which manipulate our perceptions, this film immerses us in the protagonist’s inner turmoil.

This was my favorite film as a child, and having appeared in the stage production multiple times, it will always hold a special place in my heart as my favorite musical. I seriously doubt anyone could reimagine Oliver Twist on screen any better than this version.  

My all-time favorite villain has to be Oliver Reed as Bill Sikes. Not only did he terrify me when I watched it as a six-year-old, but now, as an adult woman, I can more deeply empathize with Nancy’s character—the barmaid and prostitute who helps Oliver find the life he deserves.  

Jack Wilde's portrayal of the Artful Dodger was outstanding, and I doubt anyone could surpass him as the clever street pickpocket and Fagin's close friend. The music is truly wonderful, especially Fagin's songs. I also appreciate that they didn't give Bill Sikes a musical number; his sinister nature just wouldn't have suited it.  

I think Carol Reed did an excellent job handling Nancy’s tragic ending, maintaining a G rating by subtly suggesting her assault while still conveying the violence Bill inflicts upon her.

This is the essence of the musical genre—humor, talent, romance, and excitement all seamlessly combined. Frank Sinatra's performance was outstanding; there's really nothing more to say. Although Marlon Brando wasn’t a singer, he captured hearts with his portrayal of Sky Masterson, and his inability to sing only added to the authenticity of his character. The women in the film were charming, but it was the male characters that truly stole the spotlight. 

A timeless classic, it resonates with audiences of all ages, evoking smiles and laughter alike. This is certainly a movie worth watching and savoring!

While I generally avoid dismissing others' personal preferences, I must say this movie was absolutely terrible and there’s no defending it. I don’t particularly admire Ani Difranco, but I acknowledge she’s a talented guitarist and songwriter. However, I cannot find any redeeming qualities in this film. Many claim it offers an accurate depiction of high school issues, but everything feels exaggerated and far-fetched. The attempt at "Naked Gun"-style comedy falls flat; the timing is awkward, with actors pausing excessively between lines as if waiting for laughter that never came. The script was scattered and unfocused, trying to incorporate numerous controversial topics without properly developing any of them—especially the subplot about the girl getting pregnant by a teacher. I didn’t laugh once; instead, I was simply annoyed by the failed attempt at humor and satire, to the point of rolling my eyes in disbelief.

I watched this film just once about 25 years ago, and to this day, I often tell people it’s possibly the best movie I’ve ever seen. Despite having no spoken dialogue and relying solely on visual and thought communication, I found the film captivating, so much so that I caught myself holding my breath to avoid making any noise. I highly recommend this film and wish it were available on DVD.

WINCHESTER 73 tells the story of a man, played by Jimmy Stewart, driven by an obsession to recover his cherished repeating rifle crafted by Winchester. The firearm changes ownership multiple times, and Stewart persistently pursues it. Directed by Anthony Mann in 1950, this black-and-white film leans more toward a crime story than a conventional Western, with many of the cowboys resembling modern-day gangsters rather than traditional cowboys. Shelley Winters portrays a morally ambiguous woman headed to a ranch with a man, Charles Drake, whom she might marry. She eventually falls for Stewart, but not before experiencing some tumultuous encounters. Winters stands out as the most layered character in a cast full of unconventional figures. Look out for a young Dan Dureyea playing a crazed killer and Tony Curtis in a minor role. Will Geer is notably miscast as Wyatt Earp.

I'll keep this brief. I believe this is an exceptional film. Some reviewers have criticized it as poorly written, poorly shot, with a terrible soundtrack, and even questioned its realism. While it may not be entirely believable throughout, the film conveys a powerful message of hope that some critics seem to have overlooked—that it’s not too late to rescue people from the horrors that many endure. Yes, gangland violence is a harsh reality, and though it’s undeniably dire, this movie delivers a vital social message that cynics might dislike but should still be acknowledged and praised. I’ve watched it at least eight times, and each viewing leaves me equally captivated, inspiring a belief that perhaps the world can still be improved and saved—at least until 2008. I give it 9 out of 10; in my opinion, it’s nearly perfect. JMV

Did the filmmakers even preview this before releasing it? The script jumps erratically from one scene to another without providing sufficient context. The opening doesn't clarify whether it's a prequel or not; it begins with Superman's early days on Earth then abruptly shifts to a timeline after the previous film—all without any indication to the audience. Very confusing! Superman himself is portrayed as weak and in need of Prozac. He's depicted as a potential home-wrecker, a stalker, and clearly depressed and confused. Such a character rarely makes for an compelling hero. The ending is utterly absurd—Superman ending up in a hospital made me want to see him get offed myself. I couldn't help but imagine a hilarious SNL skit where Superman appears on Maury Povich, and Maury announces, "The results are in—Superman, you ARE the father." In summary, while the acting by Superman and Kevin Spacey is decent, the script is terrible. Overall, the movie is practically unwatchable.

This is a charming little film with a delightfully quirky flair, complemented by some equally quirky performances. It tells the story of a young man chasing his dream of becoming a renowned Las Vegas illusionist, exploring both his personal aspirations and the hopes of others, all while navigating the often turbulent world of showbiz. I found the movie endearing, with a few genuinely magical moments that elevate the experience. Alan Arkin delivers a fantastic performance as the magician who never quite made it, and his relationship with Max—full of humor and tenderness—is especially memorable. While it might not appeal to everyone, if you enjoy movies that focus on the journey itself, I believe you'll find this one quite enjoyable.

Initially, my review of this film was so harsh that it wasn't published. I'll try to be more balanced this time. Honestly, no one watches a Chuck Norris movie expecting him to be a supporting role. The film did have a solid fight scene at the end, but overall, the rest fell flat. I can’t help but wonder if Chuck has slowed down and is now relying on past fame, producing subpar work hoping his reputation will carry it. Chuck is an incredible martial artist and, as demonstrated in Walker, Texas Ranger, a capable actor. The key is to blend these talents effectively on screen, but unfortunately, this movie missed the mark. It's quite disappointing for us Norris fans. Chuck, please keep yourself in the main role—you’ve got the star power for it. —Gary

This movie is not porn, nor was it intended to be. Unless my uncle runs for president of the world, it should never be classified as porn. 

Now that that's clear, I can confidently recommend this film, as its themes remain highly relevant. It's funny, boasts excellent acting, and prompts intriguing, even provocative, questions. 

I can't quite understand why this film was so unfairly treated; perhaps that's part of the reason I have no plans to visit the US. Lena truly embodies the spirit of the modern riot grrrl movement—she's known for her confusion, curiosity, and wit. While she can be angry at times, isn't that just human nature?
