I was quite disappointed with Love's Abiding Joy. I had been eagerly anticipating it for a long time and finally got the chance to watch it when it re-aired Thursday night on Hallmark. I love the first three "Love" movies, but this installment fell far short of my expectations. The entire film was filled with sadness and gloom, and it was plagued by numerous goofs. The editing was poor, with many scenes seemingly out of context. I also felt that the death of Baby Kathy happened too quickly, and Clark's appearance in the story felt out of place. It seemed as though none of the actors were genuinely invested; they all appeared to lack emotion. Additionally, there was no real interaction between Missie and Willie.

I believe the scriptwriters should have stayed more faithful to the original books. It seems like each subsequent movie drifts further from Janette Oke's original writings. For example, the film never mentioned the mine, the two boys, or Clark getting injured because of it. I also think Missie and Willie's reactions to Kathy's death could have been portrayed with more depth and authenticity.

This movie is incredibly entertaining—a perfect way to relax and enjoy yourself. It’s one of those films you can watch without needing to follow a complicated plot, as it becomes increasingly absurd and hilarious with each twist. The cast features well-known, talented actors like Sally Field, Teri Hatcher (in her prime), Kevin Kline, Elisabeth Shue, and Robert Downey Jr., all playfully channeling soap opera stars and producers. If you've ever wondered how some soap opera storylines come to life, you're bound to love this film. I've watched it several times, and each viewing only deepens my appreciation for its humor and the skill of the performances. Don’t expect an Oscar-winning masterpiece—this film is purely for fun, not an artsy exploration of human nature. Just sit back, relax, and enjoy the laughs.

The opening flourishes filled me with delight, their inventiveness shining through—from the reimagined Archers' logo and the introductory disclaimer to the camera gracefully sweeping across the cosmos. It’s amusing to recall that ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ was released in the same year. Not entirely coincidental, considering the 1940s were rich with films exploring heaven and earth; yet, the soft cotton-wool nebulas and the charming angels of that era now seem faded and quaint—better left unmentioned when contrasted with Alfred Junge’s visionary work.  

The film maintains its visual brilliance throughout, continually introducing more captivating ideas. Though I’m generally not fond of blending color with black and white, as one scheme often clashes unpleasantly with the other, Powell defies this tendency. He seamlessly dissolves color into monochrome and vice versa, as if switching palettes is just another straightforward technique. Both the color footage and the black-and-white segments stand independently on their own merits.  

Regarding the story itself... this may be Pressburger’s finest screenplay, or at least it would have been if the ending had offered a more coherent and satisfying conclusion.

Sorry everyone… I know this is supposed to be an "art" film, but honestly, they should have handed out guns at the screening so viewers could put themselves out of their misery. While the scene design and cinematography were impressive, the story was simply too painful to endure. The lack of a soundtrack was harsh and added to the brutality. The extended shots felt way too long—how much can you really watch two people sit and talk, especially when their dialogue revolves around complaining? It was a real struggle just to get through the film. The performances were strong, but how much dark, somber, uninspired material can one stomach? The only highlight was Maureen Stapleton in her red dress and her dancing scene. Otherwise, this felt like a ripoff of Bergman—and I’m not even a big fan of his either. Anyone claiming they enjoyed an hour and a half of this is probably just lying.

I have long admired Chavez's opposition to globalization, but it wasn't until I watched the documentary at the Amsterdam International Documentary Film Festival that I truly understood his accomplishments. The film reveals the plot orchestrated by Venezuela's elite, along with oil corporations and corrupt Western governments eager to reinstate a brutal dictatorship by overthrowing democratically elected President Chavez. This documentary is essential viewing for anyone who values freedom and justice, offering a powerful lesson to the world. I commend the Venezuelan people for taking action to protect their sovereignty and resist the influence of companies like Halliburton and the Bush administration.

If you're seeking an accurate and comprehensive biography of boxer James Corbett's life, this film may not be your best choice. Instead, it offers a Hollywood-inspired portrayal from the 1940s that dramatizes and amplifies his story for entertainment, making it more captivating than reality. Nonetheless, thanks to strong performances—especially by Errol Flynn—and a charming script, the film's creative liberties are easily forgiven.

In this depiction, Errol Flynn stars as James "Gentleman Jim" Corbett, a boxer from the Gay Nineties who became the world heavyweight champion in 1892. The narrative traces his journey from modest beginnings through his rise to victory over John L. Sullivan. While the film could have concentrated more on the boxing matches themselves, many are surprisingly brief (except for the climactic title bout), with greater focus placed on Corbett's daring personality and his romantic involvement with Alexis Smith’s character. Supporting performances are equally impressive, featuring familiar faces like Alan Hale, whose presence adds depth to the cast. The well-crafted script brings these characters vividly to life.

One of the film’s highlights is the depiction of Corbett’s athletic prowess, offering viewers an exciting glimpse into the physicality and skill of the sport.

"The Muppets Take Manhattan" stands out from all other Muppet films in several ways. Notably, it remains the only Muppet movie not owned by Disney. As of 2008, the rights still belonged to 20th Century Fox (then CBS Fox at the time of its release), despite Disney owning the overall Muppets franchise. Additionally, this film features a notably non-linear storyline with unpredictable events, setting it apart in narrative structure.

While it's tough to surpass the original 1979 "Muppet Movie," especially since that film boasts more memorable songs than "Manhattan," one area where "The Muppets Take Manhattan" excels is in its portrayal of surprisingly realistic scenarios. Unlike the first film, where the Muppets simply head to Hollywood, walk into an agent's office, and instantly secure a "Rich & Famous" deal, this movie shows the Muppets facing the true challenges of achieving success. They learn that much hard work is required in the entertainment industry, a valuable and often overlooked lesson—provided one is willing to suspend disbelief.

Last November, I had the pleasure of watching this film at the Reno Film Festival. I must say, it was incredibly enjoyable. Despite a few technical glitches, the overall experience was fantastic. I was particularly impressed with the writing and performances, especially from the actor playing the lead role. The movie is full of heart and clever wit. After the screening, I had the opportunity to chat with some of the filmmakers, and they were genuinely nice people. Overall, watching this film was a positive experience that I highly recommend. The story captivated me and felt fresh, and as a woman who has faced many similar challenges to the protagonist, I deeply related to his struggles. The film does a wonderful job of creating characters we can truly empathize with. The friends in the film are also very well developed and realistic—I know people like them. I only wish my friends and I could sound as cool and charismatic when we talk as these characters do. The whole movie exudes a cool vibe, and I truly wish there were more films like it.

For those seeking an understanding of the Soviet perspective on modern Russian history, this monumental film is a true treasure. The narrative begins around 1900, depicted in the yellowish sepia tones of vintage photographs, gradually transitioning to black and white as the story moves through the mid-20th century, and finally unfolding in full color as it approaches contemporary times, notably the 1960s.

The story centers on a boy from a distant Siberian village, whose life is shaped by the arrival and imprisonment of an anarchist during the czarist era. He later joins the Bolsheviks following the revolution, bringing Soviet communism to his homeland. His son, born to a local beauty, fights against the Germans in World War II. Upon returning home, the village experiences an oil industry boom, offering a glimpse of Soviet economic aspirations.

Although the film is lengthy and slow-paced, it is entirely coherent and expertly crafted. It is best enjoyed in three parts.

This film might resonate with staunch followers of organized Christian doctrine, but for anyone with an open mind—who values free will, rational thought, the separation of church and state, and quality science fiction—it falls flat as a joke. 

Some well-known actors appear either desperate for work or eager to showcase their personal beliefs to the rest of us skeptics. 

I found myself entertained by this movie in the same way I was amused by "Reefer Madness"—both rely on scare tactics to convey their messages. "Reefer Madness" aimed to teach drug prevention through fear, much like this film attempts to promote "Christian" principles by threatening eternal hellfire and misery for well-meaning individuals who don't buy into their particular interpretations. 

It had me laughing out loud while also making me realize with horror how many people genuinely believe society should revert to the simpler, more restrictive days of the 19th century.

Here's a hidden treasure for those of you who may have never seen or even heard of this film. In the 1980s, Dennis Quaid was at the height of his popularity, but by the early 1990s, he seemed to vanish from the spotlight. Then, in 1993, he re-emerged on the big screen with three movies, all of which unfortunately did not fare well at the box office. However, two of those films I enjoyed very much, and I want to focus on one of them in particular.

The movie is "Wilder Napalm," a wild and unconventional film about two brothers, Wallace (played by Quaid) and Wilder (Arliss Howard), who are…fire starters—yes, they possess pyrokinetic abilities. Wilder has chosen to stop using his powers for anything other than necessary actions, following a tragic event in his youth where he and Wallace accidentally blew up an abandoned house, resulting in the death of an unwitting occupant. Today, Wilder works as a firefighter and is married to the eccentric Vida (Debra Winger), who is under house arrest for arson—something you'll understand better once you watch the film. Wilder has also not spoken to Wallace for five years because Wallace set his hair on fire during his bachelor party.

Wallace, on the other hand, relishes his pyrokinetic abilities and continues to use them.

I can't claim that this film warrants the same level of criticism some reviewers have directed at it. Admittedly, it suffers from a sluggish pace, clumsy editing, and an overuse of cheesy special effects. It also lacks the vibrant energy typically needed in a comedy to keep viewers engaged without frequently glancing at their watches. 

However, it does feature some genuinely hilarious lines, a talented and sincere cast, and the classic underdog story at its core. Macy, Stiller, and Azaria shine as the main team, while Garofalo and Studi bring valuable conflict and variety to the group. Reubens and Mitchell, though each had a few moments to stand out, don't significantly impact the overall film. 

As mentioned before, the story follows the familiar "underdog rises to the occasion" trope—nothing surprising there, since the outcome is predictable. What truly elevates the film is the sharp dialogue and the chemistry among the characters. Beneath the surface, these characters are essentially children at heart, driven by a desire to do what's right. The most memorable scenes are those that imbue the film with genuine emotional depth.

Fishbourne's performance, which somehow comes across as strangely humorous, and Ed Harris's brief appearance are truly noteworthy. In contrast, Connery seems to struggle to find meaning in his role, often drifting into the mannerisms of an eighty-year-old man. Essentially, the screenplay lacks coherence; it feels as though a 60-minute feel-good ending was tacked on, followed by an abrupt twist that doesn't align with the established character development. The result is more accidental than crafted—more of a rough draft than a polished script—and might serve as a useful example in screenwriting classes. The more you analyze the details, the more pronounced these shortcomings become. Although capital punishment is introduced early on, it ultimately fades into the background without further exploration. The themes and setting had the potential to be compelling, but they are underdeveloped.

Harman and Isings' 'Old Mill Pond' stands as a true masterpiece in the realm of animation. The exceptional skill and artistry evident in this work exemplify the duo's talent. It is unfortunate that many viewers can only find offense in a piece that was originally intended as lighthearted entertainment, with no aim to demean or diminish black people. In fact, the cartoon celebrates the lively humor and musical spirit of the Black community. For years, I have been unable to watch this charming film, as the 'race commissars' in England have deemed it too offensive to be shown in multicultural Britain. If anyone knows where I might find a copy, I would be eager to revisit this masterpiece. I believe those who constantly interpret hidden messages or intentions in these cartoons—most of which are over sixty years old—should try to relax and recognize that society has changed significantly. However, this does not give anyone the right to censor works from the past simply because they now appear outdated or problematic.

Look, since it's the third installment, you already know it's going to be bad. And considering that "Maniac Cop" wasn't even strong enough to justify a sequel, you can be certain this one is even worse. But just how much worse? Horrible—bordering on truly atrocious.

In one scene, a reporter declares, "What happened here can ONLY be described as a black rainbow of death."

First, rainbows are never black, nor can they be. Second, rainbows are harmless—they cannot cause pain or death. Third, a skilled journalist covering such carnage would surely find a better way to describe the scene. The phrase "a black rainbow of death" is an overly dramatic and inaccurate choice.

This is what you have to look forward to.

I watched this film again and realized how closely it resembles the novel, aside from the brief mention of Cary's [Leslie Howard] childhood. Given the limitations of screen storytelling at the time—and there isn’t much in the novel either—the film effectively captures the character's obsession with Mildred [Bette Davis] and conveys it compellingly to the audience. I recommend this film to anyone who has ever fallen for someone and felt that the other person tried to exploit that vulnerability. I also read that Maugham was asked to record an audiobook version of the novel for sale, but when he attempted to record in the studio, he became emotional and couldn’t finish more than a few lines, leading to the project being abandoned. It’s clear that the novel is written from the heart, and the film is at least a good adaptation of a part of it.

Please note that I have rated this film with one star; if there had been an option for zero stars, I would have chosen that. When I inserted this DVD into my TV and settled on my couch, I anticipated witnessing some of the worst filmmaking at its most exaggerated. After checking its rating on IMDb and seeing it labeled as the worst-rated movie, I approached it with a critical eye for every mistake. Unfortunately, nothing could have prepared me for the garbage that spewed from my television screen.

The packaging portrays this movie as reasonably okay at best. Do not be fooled by that. This film should be banned from shelves worldwide.

The best way to describe it is like porn—minus any actual sex scenes. The acting (if you can even call it that), the so-called "plot" (with more holes than Swiss cheese), and the special effects are all utterly terrible.

Please don't make the mistake I did by renting this movie just to find it amusingly bad.

In the end, I'm not claiming I could make a better film than this, but…

I used this film during a lesson in my religion class. The scene opens with a golden fish happily swimming in its bowl in an apartment on the upper floor. Meanwhile, a young boy and his mother are away from home. The boy has been entrusted with money to buy milk. On his way back, he pauses at a carnival to play a game. Standing nearby is a man dressed in a black suit, who appears somewhat intimidating. During the game, the boy accidentally drops and breaks the bottle of milk. The man in black offers him money to replace it. This moment is interwoven with scenes from the boy’s home. A black cat climbs the fire escape and enters the apartment, discovering the fish bowl. It watches the energetic fish as it swims and suddenly flips out of the bowl. By this point, many students in my class, including myself, have become enamored with the fish. The cat catches the fish in its mouth, and everyone holds their breath. Then, the cat gently places the fish back into the bowl. The story develops along two parallel threads: one involving the suspicious man in black, and the other featuring the mysterious black cat. Both characters evoke suspicion but are actually innocent. This narrative served as an excellent starting point for discussion in my class.

When a film is released under at least five different titles, it generally indicates several issues, and almost always signifies significant flaws within the movie itself. Necromancy is fundamentally flawed and simply poorly made. I watched the version titled Rosemary's Disciples on video. While I acknowledge it may differ from other versions, I doubt that those differences or the additional few minutes would significantly improve the film. The story is arguably its biggest weakness: it begins with Laurie waking up while her husband takes her to a town where he has a new job at a toy factory run by occultists—yes, it gets that bad this early on. The town, called Lillith, features a man with a rifle on the bridge, ensuring only those chosen by the town’s "owner" are permitted entry. We soon learn that everyone in Lillith is a witch, all following the commands of Mr. Cato—leader of the local coven who longs to bring back his deceased son (hence the title Necromancy). The townspeople engage in various forms of witchcraft, adding to the film’s chaotic and unconvincing premise.

Prix de Beauté was produced during the transitional period from silent cinema to sound, a shift that occurred later in Europe than in Hollywood. Initially envisioned as a silent film, it was ultimately released in France with a dubbed soundtrack featuring a French actress delivering Louise Brooks' lines. In contrast, the film was distributed as a silent in Italy and other European countries. I had the privilege of viewing the Cineteca di Bologna's exquisite new restoration of an Italian silent print at the Tribeca Film Festival. Although I haven't yet seen the sound version, it’s reasonable to believe that the silent edition offers a more compelling experience, especially considering that reports indicate the dubbing is of poor quality—Louise Brooks is unmistakably speaking English, making lip-matching impossible. The film adheres entirely to the silent film style, minimizing intertitles and dialogue, relying instead on visual storytelling. It employs dynamic, inventive cinematography, beginning with a burst of energy—rapidly edited scenes capturing urban life and swimmers frolicking at a public beach. Throughout, there is a strong focus on visual richness: details in costumes, machinery, decor, and symbolic imagery such as a caged bird and a pile of...

This is an extremely poor film, with only a few moments or qualities worth mentioning. It begins with pregnant Linda Blair running down a hallway to escape what might be monsters or perhaps men with pitchforks—it's unclear. She jumps through a window, wakes up, and it's revealed she's heavily pregnant, though her pregnancy seems to fluctuate significantly throughout the movie.  

She is accompanied by a bothersome and possibly cognitively challenged young boy, whom I suspected was her son, as they make their way to an abandoned hotel on an island. Italian horror filmmakers seem to have a penchant for including the most irritating young boys in their movies. On the island, they encounter David Hasselhoff and his German-speaking, virginal girlfriend—it's a cliché that Germans are said to adore Hasselhoff. He is busy taking photographs, while she translates an obscure German book about witches, or so it seems.  

Also present are an older couple who have bought the island, a real estate agent, and a woman I initially thought was their daughter. It turns out she was an architect, and Linda Blair along with the boy are revealed to be the children of the older couple. It appears they all traveled to the island together, but it honestly seemed as if only Linda and the boy were there, making the group dynamics quite confusing.

I watched "Brother's Shadow" at the Tribeca Film Festival and found myself reflecting on it days later. Centered on a prodigal son, Scott Cohen, returning to his family's bespoke furniture business after serving time in prison, the film embodies all the hallmarks of a compelling drama—memorable characters, incisive dialogue, and a visually conscious director who understands the power of imagery.

Beyond these elements, it offers something increasingly scarce in today's multiplex environment: an unwavering artistic vision driven by mature insight. Director and screenwriter Todd S. Yellin's talent appears to be fully realized from the outset, yet there's a sense that, like his protagonist, he's earned his stripes through hard-won experience. He captures the genuine struggles of real people navigating a tough world and acknowledges our collective desire to witness, or vicariously live through, moments of success. Importantly, Yellin shows his respect for the audience, refraining from hollow optimism. Ultimately, Jake's victory isn't measured by commissions or family approval but by the unwavering dedication to "the work" he cannot forsake—even if he wanted to.

This theme resonates deeply in a film industry—and a world—that too often fixate on profits above all else.

What went wrong with the actors involved in that mess? Michael Dorn should probably stick to Star Trek merchandise. And John Diehl—does anyone remember his role in Miami Vice? I liked him there... But honestly, what can you expect when the lead is one of the lifeguards from Baywatch? Not much, and that's exactly what we got. None of the characters are even remotely likable, the special effects are comically bad—though not intentionally funny. The story is a terrible joke, lacking any sense of logic or coherence. It felt like the filmmakers were attempting some sort of "Attack of the Killer Tomatoes" parody, especially during that scene where all the key players discuss national security in what looks like a closet... If you happen to catch this on TV, just change the channel—your TV will thank you.

How did this even come into existence? I generally enjoy sci-fi, Bigfoot, and similar films, but I still expect them to be crafted with a bit more finesse than this. The special effects were disappointing, and the dialogue was even worse. I would recommend avoiding it at all costs. I only rented it because it was in the wrong case—I was actually looking for the Sasquatch film starring Lance Henriksen, which I still haven't seen. The core concept of the film is actually quite good, with plenty of potential to turn it into a solid little movie. I just can't understand how something like this ends up like this. If you talk to high school students interested in film, arts, or English, you'll likely find people who could come up with a better script.

I was utterly captivated by just how terrible this movie truly was. Was there any intended message or deeper meaning for the audience to grasp? What was the significance of the pumpkins? Was I meant to be impressed by the shots of the motel? Does it even matter that there are garbage bags on a rooftop across from a hotel? Why does the narrator attempt to mock the interviewees unsuccessfully—it's clear he edited out the more insightful parts to craft a mockery? The only highlight was the interview with the film professor, who predicted how poor the movie would be even before it was completed. 

I'm genuinely astonished. It seems the creator is either struggling to establish intellectual credibility or is desperately trying to impress the intellectual community.

This Kiyoshi Kurosawa ghost film is quite chaotic, with at least one jump scare that genuinely caught me off guard. Overall, however, the movie is largely foolish, featuring a detective on the trail of a suspected serial killer who unexpectedly may have committed one of the crimes. Soon, he is haunted by a stunning Asian ghost woman, without any explanation—leaving both him and the audience baffled. As more murders occur, he becomes increasingly perplexed, especially since the killers are easily identified, yet the ghost continues to torment him for no clear reason. The plot is utterly nonsensical, and the lady ghost is more amusing than frightening—particularly when she suddenly soars across the city like Wonder Woman. The ending makes little sense, and overall, the entire film is perplexing, leading me to recommend it not at all. If it hadn’t taken itself so seriously, I might have thought it was a dark comedy. Aside from "Bright Future," this is the worst film by Kiyoshi Kurosawa I’ve seen.

Evil Breed: The Legend of Samhain is a film that demonstrates minimal effort or thought. It is filled with rapid, slasher-style kills and grotesque acts of violence that border on disgusting. The acting receives a grade of D, as the performers exhibit limited talent, and their characters often behave in ways that seem utterly implausible for their age. The film's attempt to incorporate elements of adult content feels misplaced and adds little to the story, quickly overshadowed by brutal and gut-wrenching deaths. For instance, one unfortunate character is disemboweled through his anus, with the scene lasting approximately five minutes. It's painfully obvious that the victims make little effort to fight back. Overall, this movie may appeal to viewers who enjoy watching graphic deaths and scenes of torture.

A complete waste of time—poor acting, a weak plot, and lackluster directing. This is honestly the dullest movie I've ever seen! Some bad films can still be enjoyable (like Freddy vs. Jason), but this one falls into the category of truly HORRIBLE. Overall, it's best to skip it altogether.

This is undoubtedly the worst movie I have ever watched! I can honestly say I have never encountered a film more disappointing than this one! And I truly mean never. As a huge fan of "B" horror movies, I’ve seen my fair share of the worst the industry has to offer. I was drawn in by the title—"Vampires vs. Zombies"—a title that sparks the imagination. Who wouldn't be intrigued by images of the undead battling each other for "undeath"? I thought to myself, "This is a must-see!" Unfortunately, I wish I hadn't. The title is highly misleading; there are no vampires fighting zombies, and surprisingly, there’s no coherent plot at all. If you asked me what this movie is about, I honestly couldn't tell you. There’s no story, no structure—nothing that resembles a meaningful narrative. This film makes absolutely no sense. By the end of this disaster, I found myself feeling nothing but pity for the time I wasted watching it.

I had heard (and read) so many positive things about Weeds that I was eager to become engrossed in another acclaimed cable series—similar to Entourage, The Sopranos, or Mad Men. However, my enthusiasm gradually faded with each episode of Season One; I didn't even make it past the sixth episode.  
The writing felt uninspired, forced, and at times embarrassing in its portrayal of Black characters. The dialogue seemed contrived, as if the writers were desperately trying to appear clever and trendy. There were rare moments when I genuinely laughed out loud, but they were few and far between.  
The characters lacked sufficient development for me to care about them. They came across as selfish and unlikable. I particularly disliked the introduction of the brother-in-law, who seemed more suited for a show like To Catch a Predator. Additionally, the decision to send Quinn, the Hodes' daughter, to boarding school in Mexico felt unoriginal and clichéd, as if the writers were testing the audience’s patience.  
With each passing episode, my opinion of the characters worsened, and numerous technical flaws in the storyline further diminished my enjoyment.  
I also heard that Season Two didn't live up to the first, so...

A childless couple (Brooke Adams and Jeff Hayenga) visits a doctor (James Karen) in hopes of conceiving. Their efforts are successful, but Adams gradually senses that something is terribly wrong with the baby...  

The concept is intriguing and has potential, but it’s squandered by a poorly written script—while the premise is decent, it becomes painfully predictable as the story progresses. I anticipated every plot twist. The direction is lacking; the filmmaker seems unsure how to shoot even simple scenes. The production quality is subpar—shabby at best. The gore scenes are excessively disturbing (I nearly turned away when a pregnant woman started stabbing herself in the stomach), and the special effects are unimpressive. The film completely falls apart at the end, clearly revealing that the creators had no clear idea how to conclude the story.  

Despite these flaws, solid performances from Adams, Hayenga, and Karen help make the film somewhat watchable; their acting kept me engaged, at least. Nonetheless, that’s about as far as it goes. Released quietly in 1991, the movie remains largely obscure—and it’s easy to see why. I’d rate it a 4 out of 10.

Featuring a captivating performance by Will Smith and a story that pulls at your heartstrings more fiercely than a rock guitarist mid-solo, "Seven Pounds" surpasses the director's previous collaboration with the actor, "The Pursuit of Happiness," which I also greatly enjoyed. Remember Gabriele Muccino’s name, as some of his films may go unnoticed if the lead actor isn’t a major star.

Unfortunately, I anticipated Will Smith’s plan early on; I connected the dots when he reveals his own suicide in the opening scene and when Rosario Dawson’s character is introduced as suffering from a terminal heart condition.

Nevertheless, I believe the writer and director made the right choice with how they structured the opening and closing scenes—they serve as the film’s emotional core, creating a sense of urgency and tension as the audience slowly uncovers just how far a man is willing to go in his ultimate act of sacrifice. Watching Smith and Dawson’s characters develop a deep connection was heartbreaking, knowing what lay ahead for these two unfortunate souls.

One of my friends, with whom I watched the film...

When will the pain end? I never want to watch another adaptation of A Christmas Carol. Filmmakers keep rehashing the same story, each one scrambling to outdo the last, but all too often missing the mark. Unfortunately, it's not a story that resonates anymore—moralistic, outdated, and overly optimistic, as if life’s lessons are easily learned. The countless versions produced only demonstrate that we haven't quite grasped them yet.

You know you're really in trouble when John Cassavetes appears to be operating at half-speed rather than full-throttle in a film, and *The Incubus* turns out to be a terrible, worst-case example of a great actor merely going through the motions to make a paycheck. Frustratingly, the cheesy script and John Hough's overly ornate (almost baroque) production design hardly make it his fault. The plot revolves around a series of rape-murders in a small town, sprinkled with a hefty dose of supernatural nonsense. Unfortunately, the direction drains every scene of tension and interest, and Cassavetes often looks visibly annoyed. The titular Incubus, which only appears in the final scene, is a convincingly crafted creature, but by then, it's too little, too late.  
1/10

Before watching this film, I read a review claiming it could potentially be one of the greatest movies ever! Haha. The tension slowly builds scene by scene, largely due to the annoying characters. From the little girl babbling nonsense and trying to drown the boy, to the killer casually running around without any explanation (and who was that guy at the beach talking to the boy!?). Things just happen randomly and are left unanswered throughout the film. As I watched, it seemed like the story was heading in one direction, then suddenly veered off into another, and then another, with no clear purpose. 

The acting is solid, but the writing falls flat. Each character, in every scene, says or does things that are completely unbelievable and unrealistic, and the reactions from other characters or extras are just bizarre. No resolutions are offered for the issues introduced, leaving the story confusing and ultimately making it a big waste of time.

What an episode! Last week, Mellisa's constant cameos about Annie and Brandi's friendship nearly made me gag. But that was nothing compared to her meltdown after being fired. Watching her hobble around on her cast, spewing obscenities and screaming for someone to grab her purse was absolutely the funniest moment in reality TV history. She kept yelling off-camera for someone to get her clothes—"all of them"—as if anyone would want to wear her questionable outfits. Mellisa, you're around 40 years old and still throwing tantrums? Then Joan starts hurling insults at Annie and Brandi and suddenly quits the show! Both Rivers are spoiled brats, kept on only to boost ratings. Mellisa crying and refusing an exit interview just confirms what everyone already knew—you’re a spoiled baby. WAH WAH, I can't get my way! I loved how Annie told the cameras she could manipulate Mellisa into thinking her way—and then she did exactly that. Without a doubt, Mellisa is the smartest contestant and genuinely deserves to win the entire game.

This film was created by a group of white men who attended the same school. While there's nothing inherently wrong with that, the result feels like a project driven by a close-knit group of white men of similar age. Nearly 90 percent of the cast are white males around the same age, making it resemble a reunion of guys at a boys' camp turning the camera on themselves. The movie lacks a coherent plot, instead cycling through relentless scenes of bloodshed and violence. Although it has some humorous moments and comedic touches, they fail to break the monotony of its dull and repetitive nature.

The use of graphic cartoon sequences appears to be a way to compensate for scenes that were beyond the film's budget or technical capabilities, and these are poorly executed. Anything that can't be portrayed with real actors—like characters running on a beach covered in blood—is replaced with cheap animation, which diminishes the overall quality.

I decided to watch this film after seeing the trailer, which suggested a Tarantino-style experience. However, the trailer's impressive scenes are the peak of the film. The rest of the movie is filled with repetitive, uninspired comedy that, while occasionally effective, ultimately becomes tiresome and dull.

I watched this film because its outrageous plot piqued my curiosity, and it certainly did not disappoint. At times, it makes for quite uncomfortable viewing. Unlike other Meyer films, the sexual content is kept to a minimum, but some of the violence is unnecessarily excessive and offensive. The storyline is chaotic, and the acting and dialogue are truly dreadful.  

The movie presents a bizarre blend of sado-masochistic fantasy and stark brutality associated with slavery, ultimately failing on every front. It seems as though Meyer was attempting to compensate for the exploitation elements by embedding a higher moral message. Aware of our potential guilt over the provocative early scenes—such as Lady Susan in a whip-wielding, seductive outfit—he then attempts to shift the narrative toward a theme of good triumphing over evil. Yet, the conflicting tones cancel each other out, leaving little for the audience to latch onto.  

Due to its many flaws, the film is actually worth watching if you have an appreciation for the art of intentionally crafting a terrible movie.

Once upon a time, there was a charming land called France... where the people lived in happiness. Women were easy to charm, and men indulged in their favorite pastime: war—the only recreation available to kings and, by extension, to their subjects. This particular conflict was the Seven Years' War, and when it became apparent that the battlefield was strewn with more fallen soldiers than living ones, recruiters were dispatched to fill the ranks.  

Thus, Fanfan (Gérard Philipe), while caught in the act of tumbling a farmer’s daughter in a haystack, evaded marriage by enlisting in the Régiment d'Aquitaine... but only after believing a gypsy’s prophecy that he would gain fame and fortune in His Majesty’s service and marry the king’s daughter. Unfortunately, Adeline (Gina Lollobrigida) is not a gypsy but the daughter of the regiment’s recruiting sergeant.  

When Fanfan suddenly charges with his saber drawn to rescue a carriage under attack, he finds himself face-to-face with the Marquise de Pompadour and—inside the carriage—the king’s daughter. Convinced that his fortunes are destined to rise, Fanfan dreams of a high marriage, despite Adeline’s revealing low-cut blouses. In turn, Adeline begins to discover her own growing affection for Fanfan. And so our story unfolds in...

New York, I Love You is a compilation of eleven short films, each approximately ten minutes in length. While the segments are mostly independent, they are all united by the theme of love—whether it involves a romantic couple or simply two strangers engaging in a conversation. The film features an impressive ensemble cast, including Shia LaBeouf, Natalie Portman, Hayden Christensen, Orlando Bloom, Chris Cooper, Andy Garcia, Christina Ricci, Irrfan Khan, Robin Wright Penn, Julie Christie, Ethan Hawke, Bradley Cooper, Rachel Bilson, and Anton Yelchin. With such a talented lineup and a compelling concept, I anticipated a remarkable film; however, New York, I Love You ultimately feels disjointed. It amounts to little more than a collection of individual parts. While some segments are humorous, inventive, and engaging, others are quite insubstantial—such as the Orlando Bloom/Christina Ricci and Ethan Hawke/Maggie Q segments—which is disappointing. The film's tone is notably experimental and uneven, and its storytelling often resembles a project that might be assembled by film students. Despite these flaws, it does feature notable moments, including a touching segment about an elderly couple, played by Eli Wallach and Cloris Leachman, taking a walk.

This film is a shameless ripoff of a dozen better movies. In particular, Steven Martin's "LA Story" at least had the decency to be clearly fictional, even though it starred his then-girlfriend as his on-screen love interest.

Yes, naive boys and girls, "20 Dates" IS a mockumentary, though I am not entirely sure that was Myles Berkowitz's original intention. It seems he began the project with a semi-serious approach, only to quickly realize that it would come across as pathetic and unfunny unless he ramped up the absurdity of the situations. Consequently, the entire film feels awkward, cheap, and insincere.

As a sharp observer noted, the film features two of the "dates" suing Myles and obtaining restraining orders against him, yet these same women appear in the film—something impossible without their consent forms. It also appears that most of the women cast as "the dates" are professional actresses—though not widely famous, aside from Tina Career—they are too striking, polished, slim, and at ease on camera to be ordinary civilians.

Berkowitz makes a fundamental mistake by casting exclusively very pretty women, which undermines the authenticity of his mockumentary.

Probably inspired by the acclaim of her much better-received "Orlando," Potter here creates a vehicle for herself in the worst possible way: she writes, directs, stars, and even co-writes the music, including a mawkish love song. The film bears a strong resemblance to a high school or college project undertaken by a teenager who believes her own intimate loves and melodramatic obsessions are as captivating to others as they are to her. However, Potter's character is as unlikable as her romantic interest is unsympathetic, making the entire film an awkward display of narcissism disguised as a celebration of the tango. Perhaps the film might have been more successful had she not cast herself, as her acting remains unconvincing whether she's playing herself or someone else. Ultimately, it comes across as pretentious, over-ambitious, dull, and silly.

What truly embodies the French spirit in this film is the deliberate pace used to introduce the two main characters. This may demand some patience, particularly since neither fits the conventional Hollywood standard of attractiveness. Yet, once the heist begins, the narrative accelerates swiftly—perhaps sometimes a bit too much. Nevertheless, it becomes a genuine rollercoaster, and if you're willing to overlook some details, it all remains surprisingly credible. It's the kind of film that Hollywood likely would have mishandled.

Kate Beckinsale truly steals the spotlight—bravo! It's a shame that Knightly isn't as striking as Jeremy Northam. Mark Strong delivered an outstanding performance, and Bernard Hepton was impeccable as Emma's father. I especially loved the final scene—an addition to the novel but very well written—where the harvest is in, and Knightly shares a meal with both his workers and high society friends. Emma must now demonstrate her acceptance of this new life; she's a changed woman. The transition feels a bit swift, but I’m willing to accept it. Samantha Bond plays Emma's former governess and trusted confidante wonderfully, just as I had imagined her. Honestly, I believe that when the UK adapts Jane Austen’s works, they do it best. American adaptations often prioritize monetary gain over quality. So, definitely see this version!

Alright, I’ll admit, the casting in this film is quite unusual—partly due to the storyline, but I still found it a bit hard to believe Pierce Brosnan in the lead role (even though he did a pretty good job).

The story is based on a true account of an Englishman who moved to live with Canadian Indigenous communities in the early 20th century. He claimed to be of mixed Indigenous heritage. In reality, he became so influential and respected that people from far and wide came to hear his lectures and join his wilderness adventures—despite the fact that he was not of mixed blood, and all his expertise was borrowed from books or outright fabricated. The film focuses on this deception and what happened when the truth was finally revealed.

The acting and cinematography were excellent, and I quite enjoyed the movie—once I managed to suspend disbelief about Brosnan’s casting. It didn’t see broad distribution, probably because it’s quite cerebral—neither a Bond blockbuster nor a romantic story, but rather a curious and compelling film about an extraordinary man.

After Highlander 2 (which I still refuse to accept as real), I believed it was impossible for a sequel to make me cry because of how terrible it was. I was mistaken. I loved the original Wargames, but this version is riddled with inaccuracies about computers and departs significantly from the original film. The first Wargames at least featured some plausible hacking scenes. The writers of this movie clearly knew nothing about computers, aside from how to use a word processor. I highly doubt they even watched the original. The acting is unconvincing and lacks authenticity. Please, do yourselves a favor—avoid watching this film at all costs. I don't care if your TV is stuck on it and you can't turn it off; this movie will ruin your experience.

This film is a complete failure. The cast appears fully aware of its shortcomings. It begins poorly and only deteriorates further by the conclusion. The acting is painfully bad, and the script seems to have been cobbled together spontaneously. Although classified as a horror movie, it lacks any genuinely frightening moments. Overall, a terrible film deserving a 1 out of 10 rating.

Diagnosis Murder has been broadcast on most weekday afternoons on BBC1 since I used to watch it while recovering from illness at school over a decade ago. I know I probably shouldn't enjoy it, just as I shouldn't enjoy 'Murder, She Wrote,' but I'm completely hooked on both and even own the DVD box sets... Yes, I realize that's a bit sad!

Dick Van Dyke stars as Dr. Mark Sloan, a physician at Community General Hospital in Los Angeles who also serves as a police consultant for the LAPD. His son, Steve (played by Barry Van Dyke, Dick Van Dyke's real-life son), is a police officer who frequently seeks his father's assistance with numerous suspicious deaths.

Joining the cast is Dr. Amanda Bentley, the resident pathologist at Community General. In the first couple of seasons, Scott Baio appeared as Dr. Jack Stewart, but he left the series in 1995, aiming for bigger opportunities—which perhaps didn’t pan out, as his career since then has been relatively quiet, with his only notable film role being in Baby Geniuses 2: Superbabies... Oh dear! 

Eventually, Dr. Jack Stewart was replaced by the younger Dr. Jesse.

If you enjoy movies featuring school bullies, courageous kids, funny toddlers, and worm-eating adventures, then How to Eat Fried Worms is sure to capture your interest.  

The story follows Billy, a boy who, on his first day at a new school, discovers his classmates played a prank by slipping worms into his lunch. The school bully, Joe, along with his friends, begins to taunt Billy, calling him "worm boy."  

In response, Billy pretends he's no stranger to worms, claiming he eats them all the time. Although Joe and his friends doubt him, Billy convinces them and makes a bet: he will eat ten worms in one day, or else he’ll arrive at school with worms in his pants.  

Accepting the challenge, Billy sets out on a mission to earn his classmates' respect by eating worms prepared in various ways—cooked, fried, or even alive.  

While the idea might seem gross, the film carries meaningful messages. It highlights the importance of true friendship, accepting others for who they are, and understanding why some kids resort to bullying.

I believe I have said nearly everything I need to say. However, I feel compelled to clarify my perspective. I have rarely encountered such an amateurish production, and I mean that in every sense. The technical aspects—such as camera work, boom mic operation, and other technical details—are frankly laughable. Unfortunately, those shortcomings are just the beginning. 

Unlike some classic independent films that are redeemed by strong scripts, compelling characters, and engaging plots, this film suffers from a terrible screenplay, poor acting, and most regrettably, annoying characters. 

It's tragic that for every indie film like Haiku Tunnel that manages to secure distribution, countless others fade away unnoticed. I’m puzzled about how the Kornbluth brothers managed to get this family project distributed—perhaps through their connections at Sony—but I can't see any other explanation. Frankly, I’m baffled as to why it was picked up in the first place. 

The only aspect of the film that shows any hint of interest is its title. Unfortunately, even that turns out to be a disappointment. I hope this review helps prevent others who might be intrigued by the title from wasting their time on this movie.

I believe most viewers were rather let down by this sci-fi film. Firstly, it was directed by Tim Burton, which raised some expectations. Secondly, it was a remake of what is considered a classic. Personally, I found it dull, revolting, and absurd. If you've watched it, you'll understand what I mean. Nearly everyone on IMDb agrees it's terrible, and I couldn't agree more. If you haven't seen it, steer clear—it's a real snooze-fest. I’d give it a 1 out of 10.

Just Cause is one of those films that initially leaves you wondering why it was so heavily criticized upon release. It’s nothing extraordinary, but it’s competently made, with a standout supporting performance by Ed Harris. However, as the story progresses into its final act, things start to descend into absurdity—culminating in a bizarre scene where a killer with a flashlight strapped to his forehead threatens to cut open Sean Connery's wife (played by the typically stiff and unconvincing Kate Capshaw) and their young daughter (a very young Scarlett Johansson) inside an alligator skinner’s shack. 

Ultimately, it’s the kind of movie that’s probably best watched on a plane—and even then, only once.

"Dressed To Kill" stands as one of the greatest thrillers ever created. Its exploration of sex and violence makes it an adult-oriented masterpiece. Brian De Palma once again demonstrates why he is unmatched in his mastery of visual storytelling. He directs numerous scenes without dialogue, relying heavily on striking visuals and Pino Donnagio’s exceptional score to convey the narrative. Filmed in Panavision, the film demands to be viewed in widescreen, as De Palma skillfully uses the full width of the frame to enhance the story. When cropped on video, "Dressed To Kill" loses much of its impact. With compelling performances, expert direction, and arguably the finest film score ever composed, this film is an essential viewing experience.

I want to point out that this production is quite one-sided and lacks the neutrality necessary to be taken seriously. Additionally, there are no credits for the individuals interviewed, making it difficult to assess whether their perspectives are credible or valuable. The story is presented from a single viewpoint, which is risky because it can lead future generations to adopt flawed perspectives—contributing to the ongoing cycle of conflict. While this isn't the sole cause of wars, it certainly doesn't help. You may watch this documentary, but I recommend researching extensively online beforehand. The Balkans, like human history itself, are incredibly complex.

This film serves as a eye-opener for those who only glimpse the glamorous lives of celebrities. It reveals the struggles of well-intentioned individuals who are often unable to make a positive impact. The bomb blast scene is disturbingly realistic. 

What you learn and are told doesn't always reflect reality! 

Watching this might raise your blood pressure by about 10%. 

All the actors delivered their performances convincingly. 

Some scenes involving teenagers could have been avoided. 

The movie has a mature theme and is not suitable for viewing with family. 

The casting is excellent!

Steve McQueen undoubtedly has a dedicated fanbase and was truly one of the most captivating actors to grace the big screen. However, even his star power can't salvage this dud of a movie, which was apparently filmed on what looks like a consumer-grade brownie camera at real locations in St. Louis.

In the film, McQueen plays a novice with no criminal record who is brought into a bank heist planning by one of the other gang members. There are subtle hints suggesting a romantic relationship between young Steve and David Clarke. He is disliked by the rest of the heist crew, primarily due to his lack of a criminal background.

McQueen’s character also has a girlfriend, Molly McCarthy, who senses that something’s amiss—especially when he begins associating with rough characters like Crahan Denton, James Dukas, and Clarke. That would certainly raise my suspicions.

The film, "The Great St. Louis Bank Robbery," was directed by Charles Guggenheim and John Stix. Guggenheim was mainly known for documentaries, while Stix didn’t have much directing experience. One of these directors apparently thought the best way to portray Steve’s performance was to mimic a poor imitation of Marlon Brando.

A group of treasure hunters ventures into the West Indies in pursuit of a concealed fortune. The promise of gold heightens the tension as they draw nearer to the treasure's hiding place. While deep-sea divers aim to recover the gold, their greed and animosity ultimately lead to murder, according to the DVD sleeve's synopsis. The vessel they sail on is named "Manfish," not a monstrous creature. The skeleton that provides the rugged Captain John Bromfield (portrayed as Brannigan) with his half of the treasure map is particularly impressive. Veteran actor Victor Jory (credited as Professor) supplies the other half. First mate Lon Chaney Jr. (as Swede) pretends to be clueless, while the alluring Tessa Prendergast (as Alita) ineffectively guards the rum. Despite potential, the film is hampered by significant editing and continuity issues, which diminish its overall impact.  
***  
Manfish (1956) directed by W. Lee Wilder — featuring John Bromfield, Victor Jory, and Lon Chaney Jr.

This was the worst movie I have ever paid to see, and aside from "They Saved Hitler's Brain," it is the worst film I have ever experienced, period. When it was released, I was a big fan of SNL and SCTV, so I eagerly anticipated what I believed would be the funniest movie ever, given that it wasn't constrained by TV improv show restrictions.  

The writers clearly thought that adding gross humor, fart jokes, cheap sex gags, and a few risky moments would guarantee laughter. The game show skits were nothing more than absurd, unoriginal parodies of "Let's Make a Deal," filled with disgusting and silly antics. The sitcom parody featuring the single girl and her boyfriend was simply in poor high school humor. The stun gun commercial felt more suitable for Sesame Street. The LA subway skit was dull, relying on tasteless blood and gore. The French chef wandering around blindly, constantly muttering "there is no difference" in a French accent, was just painful to watch.  

The only genuinely funny moment was a Chevy Chase sketch that lasted about a minute—meaning it was only 60 seconds of genuine humor in an otherwise disappointing film.

I thoroughly enjoyed this movie. Tobey Maguire delivered an outstanding performance as Jake; he's truly one of the finest actors I've seen. I was also pleasantly surprised by the number of humorous lines sprinkled throughout the film. Maguire excelled in these moments as well, even though I hadn't seen him do comedy before. The movie draws you into the characters’ lives and keeps you guessing about their futures. I wasn't sure what to expect from Jewel’s performance, but she did quite well. The film features many exciting scenes and offers a truly enjoyable experience. I am now a devoted fan of Maguire. Be sure to watch *Cider House Rules*—it's one of the greatest films of all time.

I'm genuinely impressed that this project was brought to life. The director, writer, and actor must possess a remarkable charisma in person, as I can't imagine any other way it would have passed the scripting stage. 

While watching the film, I couldn't help but feel sympathetic for the actors. It was like being at a stand-up comedy show where the comedian is clearly struggling to get laughs, and you're just sitting there, not enjoying it but feeling genuinely sorry for him because he's trying so hard. 

I'm curious about the budget—my guess is it was quite low, given the poor quality of the film production. I might say the jokes didn't appeal to me, but honestly, for them to resonate with you, you'd have to be either the person who wrote them or perhaps someone with a different perspective altogether. 

Now, imagine that scenario in script form—someone managed to get such a project approved and greenlit. That’s truly impressive, isn’t it?

This film is an absolute nightmare—a tedious, predictable slog that drains the soul and dulls the mind. Watching it made me feel as though cutting my wrists with a rusty bread knife might be a preferable escape. The acting overacts in response to the sparse dialogue, and each scene drags on at least twice as long as necessary. The plot detail about careers crumbling or rising is so dull and insignificant that words fail to capture how uninspired it is. The soundtrack has potential, but after sitting through the movie, only three decent songs hardly justify the effort. During viewing, I found myself praying for narcolepsy or a quick end. I vow never to endure this again.

The U.S. State Department would prefer we not watch this film, owing to their disagreements with the Iranian government. However, it offers a revealing glimpse into Iran’s true level of civility, despite the film’s focus on a serious issue: women’s fight for basic rights, exemplified by their desire to attend a soccer match—an activity strictly reserved for men. The movie is unexpectedly hilarious and serves as a powerful testament to the existence of free speech and expression in Iran. I thoroughly enjoyed it. The story follows five girls attempting to breach police barriers at the ticket entrance to an Iran-Bahrain soccer game. The comedic chaos that ensues—from their bus ride to the stadium, to police intervention and their subsequent detention, culminating in an unforgettable ending—is simply too amusing to capture fully. This film is a must-watch—one of the finest foreign films I’ve seen in years.

I must admit that watching an Antonioni film from start to finish on the first try has always been a challenge for me. Even with this one, I found myself breaking it into three parts, watching it repeatedly. Ultimately, I realized that perhaps this fragmented approach was beneficial, as it allowed me to shift away from conventional plot expectations and simply appreciate each scene in its own right.  

The initial segment feels more fragmented, which isn't necessarily a flaw—it merely demands a greater effort to follow. However, once the film transitions to the desert sequences, all those efforts are richly rewarded. The breathtaking cinematography is just one element; what truly makes these moments unforgettable is how the landscape takes on an overwhelming presence—the silence, the vastness, the mixture of sadness and freedom. It merges with and contrasts against the two young protagonists, creating a powerful interplay. The desert feels both lifeless and less distant or alien than the urban scenes from the earlier part. The interplay between the airplane soaring overhead and the girl's car crafts a series of striking visuals. The love...
